It catalyzes the NADH‑dependent reduction of long‑chain trans‑2‑enoyl‑ACP fatty acids during fatty‑acid (and ultimately mycolic‑acid) biosynthesis. The article notes that EnvM is the target of the antibacterial compound triclosan, which binds to the enzyme and inhibits its activity. {PubMed:10869170}. The envM gene of Escherichia coli encodes the NADH‑dependent enoyl‑ACP reductase, a dissociable component of the bacterial type II fatty‑acid synthase (FAS) complex. This enzyme catalyzes the final reduction of the enoyl‑ACP intermediate in the fatty‑acid elongation cycle, making it essential for core fatty‑acid biosynthesis and a rate‑limiting step in the conversion of C16:1 (palmitoleic acid) to C18:1 (cis‑vaccenic acid). The bacterial enoyl‑ACP reductase is specifically inhibited by the antibiotic diazaborine in an NAD⁺‑dependent manner, whereas the plant counterpart is resistant. The envM transcript is monocistronic, and its product can be functionally replaced by the plant enoyl‑ACP reductase in hybrid bacterial‑plant FAS systems. {PubMed:8075395}. The envM gene encodes the enzyme enoyl‑acyl carrier protein reductase (also known as FabI), a key component of the bacterial fatty‑acid synthesis II (FAS II) pathway. FabI catalyzes the NADH‑dependent reduction of enoyl‑ACP to saturated acyl‑ACP, a rate‑limiting step required for membrane lipid biosynthesis. Because of its central role in fatty‑acid production, FabI is a primary target of the antimicrobial agent triclosan. The study shows that post‑translational lysine 2‑hydroxyisobutyrylation (K_hib) at residue K201 modulates FabI activity by decreasing its catalytic turnover (k_cat) and substrate affinity (K_m) without altering NADH binding, and that this modification increases bacterial resistance to triclosan. {PubMed:33485933}.
Curated_Functions: Binds promoter regions of glnA, rbcL, nifH and xisA and functions as a transcriptional regulator that can act as both activator and repressor, influencing nitrogen assimilation and heterocyst development. {PubMed:8391534}. Catalyzes the NAD(P)H-dependent reduction of trans‑2‑enoyl‑ACP to saturated acyl‑ACP, the terminal step of each fatty‑acid elongation cycle in the bacterial type II fatty‑acid synthase (FAS‑II) pathway. {PubMed:28161514, PubMed:18193820, PubMed:31670463, PubMed:17062631, PubMed:10398587, PubMed:10869170, PubMed:33485933, PubMed:8284673, PubMed:8075395}. Is essential for bacterial viability and membrane phospholipid biosynthesis; inhibition blocks cell growth. {PubMed:18193820, PubMed:17062631, PubMed:31670463, PubMed:10398587}. Serves as a primary target of antibacterial compounds such as triclosan, xanthorrhizol and diazaborine; binding of these inhibitors suppresses enzymatic activity. {PubMed:33130290, PubMed:10869170, PubMed:8075395, PubMed:33485933}. Overexpression increases resistance to triclosan, and elevated fabI transcript levels are observed in triclosan‑resistant Escherichia coli isolates. {PubMed:33008474}. Point mutations (e.g., Y156V, F203L/V) alter inhibitor binding and confer triclosan resistance. {PubMed:33130290}. Lysine 2‑hydroxyisobutyrylation at K201 decreases catalytic turnover and substrate affinity, thereby enhancing triclosan resistance. {PubMed:33485933}. Expression is down‑regulated under cadmium stress, indicating involvement in metal‑induced alteration of fatty‑acid metabolism. {PubMed:28161514}. Shares sequence similarity with mycobacterial InhA and participates in fatty‑acid (including mycolic‑acid) biosynthesis. {PubMed:8284673}. Can be functionally complemented by plant enoyl‑ACP reductase in hybrid bacterial‑plant fatty‑acid synthase systems. {PubMed:8075395}. Belongs to the short‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) family and contains a catalytic triad (Tyr, Lys, and a third residue) together with a substrate‑binding pocket (e.g., K163, K201, K205). {PubMed:18193820, PubMed:33485933}. Follows an ordered bi‑bi kinetic mechanism in which NAD(P)H binds before the enoyl‑ACP substrate. {PubMed:31670463}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Formate dehydrogenase allows E.coli to use formate as major electron donor during anaerobic respiration, when nitrate is used as electron acceptor. Subunit gamma is the cytochrome b556 component of the formate dehydrogenase-N, and also contains a menaquinone reduction site that receives electrons from the beta subunit (FdnH), through its hemes. Formate dehydrogenase-N is part of a system that generates proton motive force, together with the dissimilatory nitrate reductase (Nar). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11884747}.
Merged_Functions: Encodes the FdnI (γ) subunit of the membrane‑bound respiratory formate dehydrogenase N (FDH‑N) complex. Together with the FdnG (α) and FdnH (β) subunits, FdnI forms the (αβγ)₃ trimer‑of‑trimers that catalyze oxidation of formate and transfer electrons to nitrate during anaerobic respiration, contributing to the generation of a proton‑motive force. {PubMed:15342602}. The b1476 gene encodes the FdnG subunit of the respiratory formate dehydrogenase N (FDH‑N) complex in Escherichia coli. FDH‑N is a membrane‑bound, seleno‑molybdoenzyme that forms a trimer‑of‑trimers (αβγ)₃ architecture (FdnG, FdnH, and FdnI subunits). The enzyme catalyzes the oxidation of formate and transfers the resulting electrons to nitrate reductase‑A, thereby contributing to anaerobic respiration and generation of a proton‑motive force. FdnG carries an N‑terminal twin‑arginine (Tat) signal peptide that directs the assembled complex to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane via the Tat translocase. The article also describes a regulatory feature: the mRNA region encoding the first 17 codons of fdnG forms a stable stem‑loop structure that modulates translation efficiency, with mutations disrupting this hairpin leading to up‑ to 60‑fold increased protein synthesis. {PubMed:15342602}.
Curated_Functions: Forms part of the membrane‑bound respiratory formate dehydrogenase N (FDH‑N) (αβγ)₃ trimer‑of‑trimers complex. {PubMed:15342602}. Catalyzes oxidation of formate and transfers the resulting electrons to nitrate (nitrate reductase‑A), contributing to anaerobic respiration and generation of a proton‑motive force. {PubMed:15342602}. Contains an N‑terminal twin‑arginine (Tat) signal peptide that directs the assembled complex to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane via the Tat translocase. {PubMed:15342602}. Regulates translation efficiency through a stable stem‑loop structure in the mRNA region encoding the first 17 codons; disruption of the hairpin increases protein synthesis up to 60‑fold. {PubMed:15342602}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Allows to use formate as major electron donor during aerobic respiration. Subunit gamma is probably the cytochrome b556(FDO) component of the formate dehydrogenase.
Merged_Functions: Encodes the γ (gamma) subunit of formate dehydrogenase‑O (FDH‑O). Together with the α (fdoG) and β (fdoH) subunits, it forms the three‑subunit FDH‑O enzyme complex that catalyzes the oxidation of formate to carbon dioxide in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:8346018}.
Curated_Functions: Associates with the α (FdoG) and β (FdoH) subunits to form the three‑subunit formate dehydrogenase‑O (FDH‑O) complex. {PubMed:8346018}. Catalyzes the oxidation of formate to carbon dioxide as part of the FDH‑O complex. {PubMed:8346018}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: PPIases accelerate the folding of proteins (Probable). Substrate specificity investigated with 'Suc-Ala-Xaa-Pro-Phe-4-nitroanilide' where Xaa is the amino acid tested, was found to be Phe > Leu >> Ile > Lys = Ala > Trp > His >> Gln (PubMed:9188461). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:9188461, ECO:0000305}.
Catalytic activity: CATALYTIC ACTIVITY: Reaction=[protein]-peptidylproline (omega=180) = [protein]-peptidylproline (omega=0); Xref=Rhea:RHEA:16237, Rhea:RHEA-COMP:10747, Rhea:RHEA-COMP:10748, ChEBI:CHEBI:83833, ChEBI:CHEBI:83834; EC=5.2.1.8; Evidence={ECO:0000269|PubMed:9188461};
Merged_Functions: FkpB encodes a cytoplasmic FKBP‑type peptidyl‑prolyl cis/trans isomerase (PPIase) that catalyzes the isomerization of Xaa‑Pro peptide bonds, thereby accelerating the folding of a broad set of client proteins in Escherichia coli.  Pull‑down and immunoprecipitation experiments identified numerous physiological substrates that depend on FkpB’s PPIase activity, including the envelope‑stress sigma factor RpoE, its anti‑sigma factor RseA, ribosomal proteins S2 (RpsB) and S3 (RpsC), the LPS transport ATPase LptB, the transcription terminator Rho, the RNA chaperone ProQ, metabolic enzymes such as GapA and FabF, the cell‑shape determinant MreB, and the oxidative‑stress enzyme AhpC.  Isothermal titration calorimetry confirmed direct, micromolar‑affinity binding of FkpB to peptides derived from RpoE, RseA and S2, demonstrating that substrate interaction requires an intact active site.  Mutagenesis of residues predicted to lie in the catalytic pocket (e.g., N126A, P128A, H126A/N127A) reduced both PPIase activity and substrate co‑purification, confirming the catalytic role of these residues.  Overall, FkpB functions as a folding catalyst that ensures proper conformation and activity of essential regulatory, ribosomal, and metabolic proteins, contributing to protein homeostasis and cellular viability. {PubMed:32545723}. The fkpB gene encodes a wheat FKBP‑type peptidyl‑prolyl cis‑trans isomerase (PPIase), designated FKBP73. The protein contains three FKBP‑like domains, a tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) region and a calmodulin‑binding motif. Recombinant FKBP73 catalyzes the cis‑trans isomerization of proline residues in peptide substrates, a reaction that is efficiently inhibited by the immunosuppressive drugs FK506 and rapamycin, indicating that the first FKBP‑like domain provides the classical FKBP PPIase activity. Northern and western analyses show that the gene is expressed predominantly in young wheat tissues (immature and imbibed embryos, etiolated shoots and roots), suggesting a role in early development. The presence of TPR and calmodulin‑binding motifs implies potential interactions with heat‑shock proteins (e.g., HSP90) and calmodulin, supporting a broader function in protein folding, assembly or regulation of cellular processes. Overall, fkpB functions as a multifunctional FKBP‑type PPIase likely involved in protein folding and related essential biological activities in wheat. {PubMed:8980498}. The slpA gene encodes the S‑layer protein of Lactobacillus acidophilus, a surface‑layer protein that naturally forms a crystalline layer on the bacterial cell surface. In this study the native slpA promoter (P_SlpA) was used to drive expression of heterologous genes, and the full‑length SlpA protein was employed as a carrier/anchor to display the recombinant β‑1,4‑mannanase (ManB) on the cell surface of Lactobacillus casei. Thus, slpA functions as a structural S‑layer protein and as a tool for surface‑display or secretion of foreign proteins. {PubMed:26562012}. The slpA gene encodes the surface‑layer (S‑) protein of Lactobacillus acidophilus ATCC 4356. The gene contains a single large open reading frame of 1,332 nucleotides that translates into a 444‑amino‑acid precursor with an N‑terminal signal peptide; after cleavage of the first 24 residues the mature protein consists of 420 amino acids (≈44 kDa). The mature S‑protein self‑assembles into a regular, crystalline S‑layer that completely covers the bacterial cell wall. This S‑layer is thought to provide a protective sheath against environmental stresses, mask underlying cell‑wall properties such as charge and phage receptors, and may influence cell shape and adhesion to host epithelial cells. {PubMed:8407780}. The slpA gene encodes a chromosomal factor that is essential for the AlpA‑dependent suppression of Δlon phenotypes in Escherichia coli. Transcription of slpA is strongly up‑regulated (6‑ to 8‑fold) when the alpA⁺ gene is present on a multicopy plasmid, indicating that AlpA acts as a positive transcriptional regulator of slpA. Expression of slpA is required for the appearance of the Alp protease activity that can substitute for Lon in degrading Lon substrates such as SulA and RcsA, thereby restoring normal capsule production and UV resistance in lon mutants. Although slpA is necessary for this proteolytic activity, the article states that neither SlpA nor AlpA is a structural component of the protease itself; instead, they function in a regulatory cascade (part of a cryptic P4‑like prophage) that indirectly enables the protease activity. {PubMed:7511582}. The slpA gene encodes a 413‑amino‑acid protein that is a site‑specific integrase belonging to the P4‑like integrase family. It is transcribed positively by the AlpA protein and is required for the excision of the cryptic P4‑like prophage CP4‑57 from the Escherichia coli chromosome. Excision of this prophage, which depends on SlpA activity (and integration host factor), removes DNA that overlaps the 3′ end of the ssrA‑encoded 10Sa stable RNA, thereby inactivating this RNA. Inactivation of 10Sa RNA lifts its inhibition of the Alp protease, allowing the protease to degrade Lon substrates and suppress lon mutant phenotypes. Thus, SlpA functions as the integrase/excisionase that mediates prophage removal, a key step in the regulatory cascade leading to Alp protease expression. {PubMed:7511583}. The slpA gene encodes the protein product of ORF149, a SlyD‑like protein that belongs to the FK506‑binding protein (FKBP) family of peptidyl‑prolyl cis/trans‑isomerases (PPIases).  SlpA exhibits catalytic activity that accelerates the cis‑trans isomerization of Xaa‑Pro peptide bonds in polypeptides, as demonstrated by its ability to increase the rate of trypsin‑coupled PPIase assays (e.g., kcat/Km ≈ 7,400 M⁻¹ s⁻¹ for the substrate Suc‑Ala‑Phe‑Pro‑Arg‑4NA).  Unlike the full‑length SlyD protein, SlpA lacks the C‑terminal histidine‑rich region and therefore its PPIase activity is not regulated by Ni²⁺ ions or inhibited by typical FKBP inhibitors (FK506, CsA).  The protein is expressed in Escherichia coli and likely contributes to protein folding processes through its PPIase activity. {PubMed:9188461}. SlpA encodes the most abundant surface‑layer protein (SLP) of *Clostridium difficile*.  It functions as a major colonization factor by mediating adherence of the bacterium to human gastrointestinal and intestinal epithelial cells.  In addition to supporting bacterial survival and growth, SlpA interacts with the host immune system; it is recognized by Toll‑like receptor 4 (TLR4), leading to TLR4 activation and cytokine production that are important for mounting an immune response against the pathogen.  Recombinant vaccines targeting SlpA have been shown to reduce gut colonization in animal models, underscoring its role in bacterial attachment and persistence. {PubMed:34244557}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the cis‑trans isomerization of Xaa‑Pro peptide bonds, accelerating folding of a broad set of client proteins and maintaining protein homeostasis. {PubMed:32545723}. Binds directly to physiological substrates such as RpoE, RseA and ribosomal protein S2 via its active site, facilitating their proper conformation. {PubMed:32545723}. Exhibits classical FKBP PPIase activity in its N‑terminal domain, which is efficiently inhibited by the immunosuppressive drugs FK506 and rapamycin. {PubMed:8980498}. Is expressed predominantly in young wheat tissues (immature embryos, etiolated shoots and roots), suggesting a role in early developmental processes. {PubMed:8980498}. Interacts with heat‑shock proteins (e.g., HSP90) and calmodulin through its TPR and calmodulin‑binding motifs, contributing to protein folding, assembly or regulation of cellular activities. {PubMed:8980498}. Forms a regular, crystalline S‑layer that completely covers the Lactobacillus acidophilus cell wall, providing a protective sheath against environmental stresses and masking cell‑wall properties. {PubMed:8407780}. Serves as a carrier/anchor for surface display of heterologous proteins, enabling recombinant β‑1,4‑mannanase presentation on the cell surface of Lactobacillus casei. {PubMed:26562012}. May influence cell shape and adhesion to host epithelial cells through its S‑layer architecture. {PubMed:8407780}. Is required for AlpA‑dependent suppression of Δlon phenotypes by enabling the Alp protease activity that degrades Lon substrates, thereby restoring capsule production and UV resistance. {PubMed:7511582}. Acts as a site‑specific integrase/excisionase that mediates excision of the cryptic P4‑like prophage CP4‑57, leading to inactivation of 10Sa RNA and activation of the Alp protease cascade. {PubMed:7511583}. Accelerates the cis‑trans isomerization of Xaa‑Pro peptide bonds with high catalytic efficiency, contributing to protein folding; its activity is not regulated by Ni²⁺ ions and is resistant to typical FKBP inhibitors. {PubMed:9188461}. Functions as the major colonization factor of Clostridium difficile by mediating adherence to human gastrointestinal and intestinal epithelial cells. {PubMed:34244557}. Activates Toll‑like receptor 4 (TLR4) upon host recognition, triggering cytokine production and modulating the immune response. {PubMed:34244557}. Serves as an effective vaccine antigen; recombinant vaccines targeting this protein reduce gut colonization in animal models. {PubMed:34244557}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Sigma factors are initiation factors that promote the attachment of RNA polymerase to specific initiation sites and are then released. This sigma factor controls the expression of flagella-related genes. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00962, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2644646, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3536871, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7590326, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8866483}.
Merged_Functions: FlaD encodes a secondary flagellin protein that is incorporated into the flagellar filament of Agrobacterium tumefaciens at low abundance. Deletion of flaD alone does not impair flagellar assembly or swimming motility, indicating it is not essential by itself. However, FlaD can function together with the major flagellin FlaA (and other secondary flagellins) to form functional, helical filaments that support normal motility. Mutations in flaD were also identified in suppressor strains, suggesting it can contribute to filament structure and motility under certain genetic contexts. {PubMed:30201783}. Encodes the 37 kDa minor sigma factor (σ⁽³⁷⁾) of Bacillus subtilis RNA polymerase. This sigma factor associates with the core enzyme to confer promoter specificity for a distinct regulon, including the extracellular subtilisin protease gene (aprA) and the cryptic spoVG and ctc genes. Although σ⁽³⁷⁾ is present during logarithmic growth and can direct transcription of these genes, a null mutation in the gene does not affect cell growth, sporulation efficiency, or spore heat resistance, indicating that the factor controls functions that are not essential for vegetative growth or sporulation under the conditions tested. {PubMed:3027048}. FliA encodes the flagellar sigma factor σ28, which directs RNA polymerase to transcribe the class 3 flagellar regulon (genes encoding the filament, chemotaxis components and other late‑stage flagellar proteins). Its activity is initially blocked by the anti‑sigma factor FlgM; when the hook‑basal body is assembled, FlgM is secreted via the type III secretion system, freeing FliA to activate class 3 transcription. FliA is also a substrate for regulated proteolysis, primarily by the Lon protease (with minor contributions from Clp and HslUV). FlgM protects FliA from degradation, and Lon‑mediated turnover helps restore a 1∶1 FliA : FlgM stoichiometry and contributes to timely shut‑off of class 3 expression. {PubMed:17537210}. The fliA gene encodes an alternative sigma factor of the σ^28 class (also called FliA) that directs RNA polymerase to transcribe flagellar genes, most notably the flagellin gene flaA. In Legionella pneumophila, FliA binds the core RNA polymerase and initiates transcription from the flaA‑specific promoter, thereby controlling the temperature‑dependent expression of flagellin. It is part of a hierarchical regulatory cascade governing flagellum assembly and chemotaxis, acting at the final (class III) level to activate structural flagellar proteins and motility genes such as motA. When introduced into an Escherichia coli fliA mutant, the L. pneumophila fliA gene restores flagellation and motility, demonstrating that its σ^28 protein can functionally interact with the E. coli RNA polymerase core enzyme. {PubMed:8981975}. FliA is an RNA polymerase sigma factor that acts as a master transcriptional activator of flagellar genes in Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli. It directly boosts the expression of flagellar components such as the major flagellin (fliC) and the motor protein (motA), thereby enabling bacterial swimming motility. The study showed that acetate exposure increases fliA transcript levels, leading to up‑regulation of flagellar genes and enhanced motility. Deletion of fliA abolishes this acetate‑induced motility and reduces flagellar gene expression, indicating that the acetate‑mediated activation of motility is dependent on FliA. {PubMed:30076004}. The fliA gene encodes the alternative sigma factor σ^F (also called σ^28), a member of the σ^28 family of sigma factors. σ^F functions as a transcriptional regulator in the flagellar motility hierarchy of Escherichia coli. It is a class II gene product that directs RNA polymerase core enzyme to σ^F‑dependent promoters, thereby initiating transcription of the class III genes that encode the filament protein, hook‑associated proteins, motor proteins, and chemotaxis proteins. Expression of fliA is controlled by two overlapping promoters: a σ^F‑dependent promoter (P_F) and a σ^70‑dependent promoter (P_A). σ^F activity is modulated by the anti‑sigma factor FlgM, which binds σ^F when basal‑body assembly is incomplete and releases it once the basal body is assembled, allowing class III transcription to proceed. Overexpression and purification of σ^F demonstrated its ability to form an active holoenzyme (Eσ^F) that can transcribe σ^F‑dependent promoters in vitro. {PubMed:8550423}. FliA encodes the σ28 (sigma‑28) factor, the downstream sigma factor in the flagellar transcriptional hierarchy of Escherichia coli. It associates with RNA polymerase to drive transcription of class 3 flagellar genes. In the Crohn disease‑associated AIEC strain LF82, FliA also acts as a central regulatory node that links flagellar biogenesis to the synthesis of type 1 pili. Deletion of fliA abolishes motility, dramatically reduces type 1 pili expression, and consequently impairs bacterial adhesion to and invasion of intestinal epithelial cells. Expression of fliA in trans restores flagellar gene expression, type 1 pili production, and the associated adhesive and invasive phenotypes. FliA exerts these effects partly by activating transcription of the c‑di‑GMP phosphodiesterase gene yhjH (an EAL‑domain protein) and the c‑di‑GMP receptor gene ycgR. By increasing YhjH activity, FliA lowers intracellular c‑di‑GMP levels, which promotes phase‑ON orientation of the fimS invertible element and up‑regulation of type 1 pili, thereby enhancing adhesion and invasion. Thus, FliA functions both as a classic flagellar sigma factor and as a key regulator of virulence‑related surface structures through a c‑di‑GMP‑dependent pathway. {PubMed:17827157}. The fliA gene encodes the 28‑kDa sigma factor σ^F (also called σ^28 or σ^28), which confers promoter specificity to the core RNA polymerase for transcription of flagellar and chemotaxis genes in Escherichia coli.  σ^F directs RNA polymerase to class III flagellar promoters (e.g., fliC, fliD, flgK) and to chemotaxis gene promoters such as tar (aspartate sensor) and tsr (serine sensor).  The protein carries σ activity in vitro, binds the –10 and –35 regions of σ^F‑dependent promoters as part of the holoenzyme, and is essential for expression of the flagellar formation cascade and chemotactic response.  The gene was later renamed rpoF, reflecting its role as a specialized σ subunit distinct from the major σ^70 factor. {PubMed:9209042}. Encodes a flagellum‑specific sigma factor that directs transcription of the flagellin (fliC) operon and other late flagellar operons, thereby regulating expression of genes required for filament formation and late stages of flagellar assembly. {PubMed:1527488}. In the article, fliA is identified as the gene encoding the alternative sigma factor RpoF (also called sigma‑F). RpoF/FliA is a class‑2 flagellar sigma factor that directs RNA polymerase to transcribe flagellar genes, including the flagellin gene fliC, and thus is essential for the synthesis and assembly of flagella and for bacterial motility. Its cellular level rises during exponential growth, peaks in late exponential phase, and declines as cells enter stationary phase, coinciding with a reduction in flagellum number. The decrease in RpoF/FliA activity in stationary phase is linked to the increased expression of the stationary‑phase sigma factor RpoS, indicating a regulatory switch from flagellar gene expression to stationary‑phase gene programs. {PubMed:12562804}. The fliA gene encodes an alternative σ28 (RpoF) sigma factor that directs RNA polymerase to transcribe the flagellin gene and other flagellar genes in *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. It is essential for flagellin synthesis: disruption of fliA eliminates flagellin production and renders the bacterium non‑motile, while complementation restores flagellin expression and motility. fliA acts at the transcriptional level, as a fliA‑lacZ promoter fusion shows a >40‑fold reduction in flagellin promoter activity in an fliA mutant. The protein contains the conserved regions 2, 3, and 4 characteristic of σ28 factors, which mediate core RNA polymerase binding and promoter −10/−35 recognition. Expression of fliA is independent of the σ54 factor RpoN. Overall, fliA functions as a transcriptional regulator required for flagellin gene expression and flagellar motility. {PubMed:1560774}. Encodes the 37 kDa minor sigma factor (σ^37) of Bacillus subtilis RNA polymerase (gene rpoF). σ^37 associates with the core enzyme to direct promoter recognition for a specific regulon that includes genes such as aprA (subtilisin protease) and the cryptic spoVG and ctc genes. Although present during logarithmic growth, σ^37 is not essential for vegetative growth or sporulation under laboratory conditions; a null rpoF mutation shows no detectable phenotype in rich medium, suggesting it controls a non‑essential regulon. The gene product is a 264‑amino‑acid protein (~30 kDa) homologous to other bacterial sigma factors and contains conserved core‑binding and DNA‑binding domains. {PubMed:3027048}. The article states that rpoF is one of the genes belonging to the σ^28 (alternative sigma factor) family. Members of this family, including rpoF, are required for the expression of motility and chemotaxis genes, implying that rpoF encodes an alternative sigma factor that directs RNA polymerase to transcribe flagellar and chemotaxis gene promoters, thereby contributing to bacterial motility. {PubMed:8981975}. The rpoF gene encodes the RNA polymerase σ^F (σ^28) subunit, a minor σ factor that associates with the core RNA polymerase to form the Eσ^F holoenzyme. This holoenzyme specifically recognizes and initiates transcription from promoters of flagellar and chemotaxis genes (e.g., fliC, fliD, flgK, tar, tsr, tcp), which are not transcribed by the major σ^70‑containing holoenzyme. σ^F binds the core enzyme with approximately twice the affinity of σ^70, conferring strict promoter selectivity through recognition of conserved –10 and –35 elements and a characteristic spacer length. σ^F‑dependent transcription is modulated by salt type and concentration, temperature, and interaction with the anti‑σ factor FlgM, allowing regulation of flagellar formation in response to environmental conditions. {PubMed:9209042}. RpoF is a sigma factor (also known as FliA) that directs RNA polymerase to transcribe the flagellum‑chemotaxis regulon. It is required for the expression of flagellar genes, including the flagellin gene fliC, and thus for the assembly of functional flagella. The level of RpoF decreases in stationary phase, correlating with reduced flagellum numbers, while its absence (rpoF disruption) results in cells lacking flagella. {PubMed:12562804}. The rpoF (also called fliA) gene encodes an alternative σ^28 sigma factor that is essential for the transcription of the flagellin gene in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This sigma factor directs RNA polymerase to a σ^28‑type promoter upstream of the flagellin operon, thereby enabling flagellin synthesis and flagellar motility. Disruption of rpoF abolishes flagellin production, eliminates flagellar motility, and reduces flagellin promoter activity >40‑fold, demonstrating that rpoF functions as the key transcriptional activator of flagellin expression. Its expression is independent of the σ^54 factor RpoN. {PubMed:1560774}. The rpoF gene encodes the 37,000‑dalton minor sigma factor (sigma‑37) of Bacillus subtilis RNA polymerase. Sigma‑37 associates with the core enzyme to confer promoter specificity, directing transcription of a small regulon that includes the extracellular subtilisin protease gene (aprA) and the cryptic spoVG and ctc genes, which are expressed primarily in stationary phase. Although sigma‑37 is also detectable during logarithmic growth, disruption of rpoF does not affect cell growth or sporulation under laboratory conditions, indicating that sigma‑37 controls a non‑essential, vegetative or stationary‑phase transcriptional program rather than the core sporulation pathway. {PubMed:3027048}.
Curated_Functions: Incorporates into the flagellar filament as a minor flagellin that cooperates with major flagellins to form functional helical filaments supporting bacterial motility. {PubMed:30201783}. Associates with RNA polymerase to direct transcription of a specific regulon (e.g., aprA, spoVG, ctc), controlling extracellular protease and cryptic genes without affecting vegetative growth or sporulation. {PubMed:3027048}. Specifies promoter recognition for flagellar and chemotaxis genes, driving expression of filament, motor, hook‑associated and chemotaxis proteins required for flagellum assembly and chemotactic behavior. {PubMed:1527488, PubMed:1560774, PubMed:8981975, PubMed:9209042, PubMed:12562804}. Is inhibited by the anti‑sigma factor FlgM, which sequesters FliA until hook‑basal body assembly triggers FlgM secretion and also shields FliA from Lon‑mediated proteolysis, allowing timely activation and subsequent turnover of class 3 transcription. {PubMed:17537210}. Mediates acetate‑responsive up‑regulation of flagellar genes, enabling enhanced swimming motility upon acetate exposure. {PubMed:30076004}. Activates transcription of the c‑di‑GMP phosphodiesterase yhjH and the c‑di‑GMP receptor ycgR, lowering intracellular c‑di‑GMP levels, which promotes phase‑ON orientation of fimS, up‑regulates type 1 pili expression and enhances adhesion and invasion of host cells. {PubMed:17827157}. Its cellular level peaks during exponential growth and declines in stationary phase, coordinating a switch from flagellar gene expression to stationary‑phase programs. {PubMed:12562804}. Functions independently of the σ54 factor RpoN to activate flagellin gene transcription. {PubMed:1560774}. Controls temperature‑dependent expression of the flaA flagellin gene in Legionella pneumophila, contributing to temperature‑regulated motility. {PubMed:8981975}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex TcyJLN involved in L-cystine import (PubMed:20351115, PubMed:25139244, PubMed:25837721, PubMed:26350134). This high affinity cystine transporter is involved in resistance to oxidative stress by forming a L-cysteine/L-cystine shuttle system with the EamA transporter, which exports L-cysteine as reducing equivalents to the periplasm to prevent the cells from oxidative stress. Exported L-cysteine can reduce the periplasmic hydrogen peroxide to water, and then generated L-cystine is imported back into the cytoplasm via the TcyJLN complex (PubMed:20351115, PubMed:25837721). Functions at low cystine concentrations (PubMed:26350134). The system can also transport L-cysteine, diaminopimelic acid (DAP), djenkolate, lanthionine, D-cystine, homocystine, and it mediates accumulation of the toxic compounds L-selenaproline (SCA) and L-selenocystine (SeCys) (PubMed:25139244, PubMed:26350134). FliY is a periplasmic protein belonging to the bacterial extracellular solute‑binding protein family 3. The fliY gene encodes a flagellar switch protein that is homologous to the FliN/FliY family found in other bacteria. In Treponema pallidum, the FliY protein is predicted to localize to the cytoplasmic face of the MS ring and to be a component of the flagellar switch complex. It is thought to control the direction of periplasmic flagellar rotation by interacting with phosphorylated CheY, thereby linking chemotactic signals to motor activity. Thus, fliY likely plays a key role in the regulation of flagellar rotation and may participate in the chemotactic signaling pathway governing spirochete motility. {PubMed:8529894}. FliY is a flagellar rotor protein that belongs to the CheC phosphatase family and resides in the flagellar switch (C‑ring) complex. It serves as the primary CheY‑P phosphatase in organisms that lack CheZ, catalyzing the dephosphorylation of the response regulator CheY‑P to terminate the chemotactic signal. The protein contains two pseudosymmetric catalytic centers (Glu35/Asn38 and Glu132/Asn135), with the second site being the more active contributor to phosphatase activity. Both sites can bind CheY‑P, and mutation of either reduces activity; mutation of both abolishes it. Structurally, the middle domain of FliY resembles the rotor protein FliM, while its C‑terminal domain is homologous to FliN and mediates dimerization. Unlike FliM, FliY does not interact with the stator‑coupling protein FliG, indicating a distinct role within the rotor architecture. {PubMed:23532838}. FliY encodes a large protein that replaces the FliN subunit in the Bacillus subtilis flagellar switch complex.  It contains an N‑terminal region homologous to FliM, a middle (FliY_M) domain homologous to the FliM middle domain and to the CheC phosphatase, and a C‑terminal domain (FliY_C) that is structurally similar to FliN.  The FliY_M domain self‑assembles into an additional ring of subunits within the switch, interacting with adjacent FliY_M domains but not directly with FliG.  The FliY_C domain forms both homodimers and heterodimers with the C‑terminal domain of FliM, contributing to the lower part of the C‑ring.  Functionally, the middle domain possesses phosphatase activity that specifically dephosphorylates CheY‑P, thereby providing a counter‑regulatory mechanism that limits CheY‑P signaling and influences the CW/CCW bias of flagellar rotation (CheY‑P promotes CCW rotation in B. subtilis, opposite to its effect in Gram‑negative bacteria).  Together, FliY’s structural role in assembling the switch complex and its enzymatic dephosphorylation of CheY‑P are essential for proper flagellar assembly, chemotactic response, and motility. {PubMed:30455280}.

FsrC encodes a membrane‑bound sensor histidine kinase that is the AgrC‑like component of the E. faecalis fsr (Enterococcus faecalis regulator) locus.  It forms part of a three‑gene, agr‑like operon (fsrA‑fsrB‑fsrC) that is autoregulated.  FsrC, together with FsrA (response regulator) and FsrB, positively controls transcription of the downstream gelatinase gene (gelE) and the adjacent serine protease gene (sprE); disruption of fsrC abolishes gelE and sprE mRNA, eliminates gelatinase and serine protease activities, and markedly reduces virulence in a mouse peritonitis model.  Complementation of an fsrC mutant with the intact fsr operon restores gelE/sprE expression and virulence, confirming its role as a key regulatory sensor in this quorum‑sensing‑like system. {PubMed:10768947}. FsrC is a component of the Enterococcus faecalis fsr quorum‑sensing locus.  Based on sequence similarity to the Staphylococcus aureus AgrC protein, FsrC is predicted to be a membrane‑bound histidine kinase sensor that, together with the response regulator FsrA, forms a classic two‑component regulatory system.  This system positively regulates transcription of the downstream gelE‑sprE operon, which encodes the extracellular proteases gelatinase (GelE) and serine protease (SprE).  Disruption of fsrC (as in the TX5242 insertion mutant) leads to loss of gelatinase and serine protease activity and results in markedly reduced virulence in both Caenorhabditis elegans killing assays and mouse peritonitis models, indicating that FsrC is essential for full pathogenic potential of E. faecalis. {PubMed:12228293}. Encodes the UbiF oxygenase that introduces a hydroxyl group at carbon‑5 of the benzoquinone intermediate (2‑octaprenyl‑3‑methyl‑6‑methoxy‑1,4‑benzoquinol), converting it to 2‑octaprenyl‑3‑methyl‑5‑hydroxy‑6‑methoxy‑1,4‑benzoquinol. This reaction is a crucial hydroxylation step in the biosynthesis of ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:10802164}. The fre gene encodes NAD(P)H:flavin oxidoreductase (flavin reductase), an enzyme that reduces soluble flavins (riboflavin, FMN, and FAD) using NAD(P)H as electron donor. In Escherichia coli it participates in a multienzyme system that reduces the Fe(III) center of ribonucleotide reductase to Fe(II); this reduction is the first step that allows dioxygen to regenerate the Fe(III) center and to convert a specific tyrosine residue (Tyr‑122) of the inactive ribonucleotide reductase into a stable tyrosyl radical required for enzymatic activity. The enzyme therefore supports iron metabolism and the activation of ribonucleotide reductase. Similar flavin reductases in other organisms provide reduced flavins for processes such as bacterial luciferase reactions and may generally facilitate the release of Fe(II) from storage forms of Fe(III). {PubMed:2050627}. The fre gene encodes an NAD(P)H‑dependent flavin reductase (also referred to as a riboflavin reductase) in Escherichia coli.  Fre catalyzes the reduction of flavin mononucleotide (FMN) or riboflavin to the reduced form FMNH₂, using electrons from NADH or NADPH with only a slight preference for riboflavin.  This reduced flavin serves as the essential substrate for bacterial luciferase, enabling the bioluminescent reaction that converts FMNH₂, O₂, and an aldehyde into oxidized FMN, a carboxylic acid, and light.  Deletion of fre reduces bioluminescence by >99 % without affecting luciferase expression, demonstrating that Fre is the primary source of reduced flavin for luciferase in recombinant E. coli.  Purified Fre supports luciferase activity in vitro at levels comparable to the native Vibrio harveyi reductase (Frp).  Fre functions as a monomeric enzyme, lacks strict nicotinamide nucleotide specificity, exhibits broad substrate specificity, and does not form a stable protein‑protein complex with luciferase, implying that reduced flavin is delivered to luciferase by free diffusion. {PubMed:19139094}. The fre gene encodes a NAD(P)H‑flavin oxidoreductase (flavin reductase) that catalyzes the reduction of flavins—preferentially riboflavin, but also FMN—using NADPH (or NADH) as electron donor. In both Escherichia coli and luminous bacteria (e.g., Photorhabdus luminescens, Vibrio fischeri, V. harveyi, V. orientalis), Fre provides reduced flavin mononucleotide (FMNH₂), which serves as the essential electron donor for the bacterial luciferase reaction that produces bioluminescence. In V. fischeri the Fre‑like enzyme represents a minor flavin reductase (<10 % of total activity) but still contributes to FMNH₂ supply for light emission. {PubMed:8206831}. The fre gene encodes an NAD(P)H‑flavin reductase that catalyzes the reduction of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) to its reduced form (FADH₂) using NADH or NADPH as electron donors. In Cupriavidus nantongensis X1ᵀ, Fre supplies the reduced flavin required by the 2,4,6‑trichlorophenol monooxygenase (TcpA) to carry out stepwise dechlorination of 3,5,6‑trichloro‑2‑pyridinol (TCP). Recombinant Fre was shown to convert yellow FAD to colorless FADH₂ in vitro, and its addition enabled TcpA to degrade TCP, whereas TcpA alone could not. The fre gene is part of the TCP degradation gene cluster, is up‑regulated in the presence of TCP, and works together with TcpA to achieve complete removal of chlorine atoms from TCP during biodegradation. {PubMed:30721044}. The fre gene encodes a 26.2 kDa monomeric NAD(P)H:flavin oxidoreductase (Fre) in *Escherichia coli*. Fre catalyzes the reduction of free flavins (riboflavin, FMN, and, to a lesser extent, FAD) by using NADPH or NADH as electron donors. The enzyme operates by an ordered sequential Bi‑Bi mechanism: NAD(P)H binds first to the active site, followed by the flavin substrate; electron transfer occurs, after which the reduced flavin is released first and NADP⁺ (or NAD⁺) is released second. Fre does not contain a bound flavin prosthetic group; substrate recognition relies mainly on the isoalloxazine ring of the flavin, with methyl groups at C‑7, C‑8 and the N‑3 position contributing to binding affinity. Functionally, Fre supplies reduced flavin for cellular processes such as the reactivation of ribonucleotide reductase, thereby protecting *E. coli* from radical scavengers like hydroxyurea. Inhibition of Fre (e.g., by lumichrome) enhances hydroxyurea‑mediated growth inhibition, highlighting its role in DNA synthesis and oxidative stress response. Overexpression of fre under an IPTG‑inducible tac promoter yields a 100–150‑fold increase in enzyme activity, facilitating purification and kinetic studies. {PubMed:8530465}. The product of b3844 is the Escherichia coli flavodiiron protein known as flavorubredoxin (FlRd, encoded by norV). The fadI gene encodes an NAD(P)H‑flavin mononucleotide (FMN) reductase, an enzyme that binds free flavins (riboflavin and FMN) and catalyzes their reduction to the reduced flavin forms. The article reports that gsp is a gene encoding a component of the type II secretion system in Escherichia coli. This secretion system is one of the most prevalent virulence determinants identified in both granulomatous colitis (GC) and healthy control (HC) isolates (present in ~72% of GC strains). Type II secretion systems are used by Gram‑negative bacteria to transport a variety of virulence factors—including toxins—into the host environment, and they contribute to processes such as epithelial cell adhesion, invasion, intracellular survival, and bacterial growth. {PubMed:32854367}. The gsp operon (gspC‑O) encodes components of the main terminal branch of the general secretory pathway (GSP) in Escherichia coli K‑12. Two of its genes have been shown to be functional: 
• gspO (formerly hopD) encodes a prepilin peptidase that cleaves type IV prepilin‑like substrates, including the pullulanase secretion system protein prePulG and the Neisseria gonorrhoeae prePilE. When expressed from a plasmid, GspO can complement a pulO mutation and restore processing of these substrates. 
• gspG (formerly hopG) encodes a protein homologous to PulG, a structural component of the pullulanase secretion apparatus. GspG can substitute for PulG, restoring pullulanase secretion in a pulG mutant, and it is also processed by GspO. 
Together, GspO and GspG constitute functional elements of a cryptic GSP‑MTB in E. coli K‑12 that are normally expressed at very low levels under laboratory conditions, rendering the pathway non‑functional unless the genes are artificially over‑expressed. {PubMed:8655552}. The gsp gene encodes a bifunctional enzyme, glutathione‑spermidine synthetase/amidase (GspSA), composed of an N‑terminal amidase domain (GspA) and a C‑terminal synthetase domain. The synthetase activity catalyzes the ATP‑dependent formation of an amide bond between the γ‑carboxylate of glutathione (GSH) and the N¹ of spermidine, producing glutathione‑spermidine (Gsp). The amidase activity hydrolyzes Gsp back into GSH and spermidine, thereby recycling Gsp and enabling reduction of Gsp‑S‑S‑Gsp and Gsp‑S‑protein mixed disulfides that accumulate during oxidative stress. This amidase function is essential for redox sensing, protein S‑thiolation, and protection against oxidative damage in Escherichia coli, and it prevents a futile ATP‑consuming cycle by regulating the opposing synthetic and hydrolytic reactions. {PubMed:21226054}. The gss gene encodes glutamine synthetase (GS), an enzyme that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent conversion of ammonia (NH₃) and glutamate into glutamine. This reaction is a central step in nitrogen metabolism of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. GS activity is essential for bacterial survival, as disruption of the glnA1 (GS) gene is lethal. The enzyme also contributes to the synthesis of the mycobacterial cell wall, which contains high concentrations of glutamine‑derived peptidoglycans and poly(Glu/Gln) proteins. Additionally, GS may help regulate intracellular NH₃ levels, a factor that could influence phagosome‑lysosome fusion in infected macrophages. GS activity is modulated by reversible adenylylation of a specific tyrosine residue (Tyr‑406); adenylylation decreases the activity of the Mg²⁺‑bound form of the enzyme. Because of its essential role and drug‑sensitive nature, GS is considered a potential therapeutic target for tuberculosis. {PubMed:15037612}. The gss gene encodes glutathione synthetase, the enzyme that catalyzes the final step of glutathione (GSH) biosynthesis in the γ‑glutamyl cycle. It joins γ‑glutamylcysteine and glycine to form GSH, thereby maintaining cellular GSH levels. Loss of GSS activity results in markedly reduced GSH, leading to feedback over‑production of γ‑glutamylcysteine, its conversion to 5‑oxoproline, and the clinical manifestations of 5‑oxoprolinuria (metabolic acidosis, haemolytic anaemia, CNS damage). {PubMed:8896573}.

Disruption of hdhA reduces HDH activity and impairs growth on AEH, demonstrating that hdhA is essential for hydrazone utilization. In addition to HDH activity, HdhA exhibits conventional aldehyde dehydrogenase activity, oxidizing acetaldehyde to acetate, and thus contributes to ethanol assimilation. Overall, hdhA provides the bacterium with the metabolic capacity to catabolize hydrazones and related aldehydes. {PubMed:22267508}. The enzyme uses NAD⁺/NADH as a cofactor, with Lys163 binding the nicotinamide ribose of NAD⁺ and lowering the pKₐ of the catalytic Tyr159, while Ser146 stabilizes the substrate, reaction intermediate, and product through hydrogen bonding. This reaction is a key step in microbial bile‑acid metabolism, contributing to the 7α‑dehydroxylation pathway that generates secondary bile acids such as deoxycholic and lithocholic acids. Structurally, the protein adopts a Rossmann‑fold NAD(H)‑binding domain and a catalytic domain containing a conserved Tyr‑Ser‑Lys triad (Tyr159, Ser146, Lys163) that mediates substrate binding and catalysis. The enzyme functions as a tetramer (dimer of dimers) and exhibits induced‑fit movements of a substrate‑binding loop upon ligand binding. {PubMed:8672472}. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Molecular chaperone that interacts specifically with outer membrane proteins, thus maintaining the solubility of early folding intermediates during passage through the periplasm. Required for the efficient release of OmpA from the inner membrane, the maintenance of its solubility in the periplasm, and, in association with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), for the efficient folding and insertion of OmpA into the outer membrane. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10455120, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11278858, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12509434, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8730870, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9914480}.
Merged_Functions: The ompH gene encodes the protein Skp (also called OmpH in Salmonella), which is synthesized as a precursor with an N‑terminal signal peptide, exported across the inner membrane by the SecA/SecY pathway in an ATP‑ and H⁺‑gradient dependent manner, and processed to a mature 15 kDa periplasmic protein. In the periplasm, Skp/OmpH functions as a soluble factor that can stimulate the translocation of other outer‑membrane proteins (e.g., LamB) and is proposed to assist late steps of protein translocation across the plasma membrane and/or sorting of proteins to the outer membrane. Its strong cationic nature also allows binding to lipopolysaccharide, but this interaction is considered non‑specific and results from electrostatic attraction. {PubMed:1838129}. In the article, ompH (also referred to as Skp or HlpA) is described as a periplasmic protein of Escherichia coli that functions as a molecular chaperone. Overexpression of ompH increases the amount of correctly folded recombinant proteins in the periplasm, leading to higher functional yields of single‑chain Fv antibody fragments both when secreted to the periplasm and when displayed on filamentous phage (as g3p fusions). This results in more active antibody molecules being incorporated into phage particles and a several‑fold increase in soluble periplasmic protein recovery. The protein is suggested to assist folding of aggregation‑prone substrates, possibly by preventing harmful interactions with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or other outer‑membrane components, and may also participate in the transport of outer‑membrane proteins. ompH is regulated by the Cpx stress response system and is co‑expressed with genes involved in lipid A/LPS biosynthesis, supporting a role in outer‑membrane biogenesis and periplasmic protein quality control. {PubMed:9555730}. The ompH gene encodes the major outer membrane protein OmpH of Pasteurella multocida, which functions as a porin. OmpH forms trimeric channels in the bacterial outer membrane that allow the diffusion of small hydrophilic solutes (pore‑forming activity demonstrated by planar lipid bilayer assays with an average single‑channel conductance of 0.62 nS). As a surface‑exposed protein, OmpH is highly immunogenic, exposing epitopes that elicit protective antibodies. Immunization with purified native OmpH confers 100 % homologous protection in chickens against P. multocida challenge, indicating its role as a protective antigen and a potential vaccine candidate. The gene is conserved across all examined P. multocida serotypes. {PubMed:9401047}. OmpH (also known as Skp) is a highly basic, periplasmic protein that binds anionic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and contributes to the integrity of the outer membrane in Escherichia coli.  Mutations in ompH/skp cause temperature‑sensitive growth, increased sensitivity to detergents, and a strong induction of the σ⁽ᴱ⁾ regulon, indicating a defect in extracytoplasmic protein folding.  The protein is proposed to act as a folding catalyst or chaperone for outer‑membrane proteins (OMPs), possibly by facilitating the exchange of LPS on nascent OMP monomers and promoting their insertion and oligomerization in the outer membrane.  Overproduction of ompH does not suppress the membrane‑defect phenotypes of htrM (rfaD) mutants, suggesting that OmpH functions downstream or sequentially to other periplasmic folding factors such as SurA. {PubMed:8878048}. The ompH gene encodes outer membrane protein H (OmpH), a major outer membrane protein of Pasteurella multocida. OmpH is implicated in bacterial resistance mechanisms and serves as a prominent antigenic target; it is widely used in recombinant vaccine studies to elicit humoral and cellular immune responses against various P. multocida serotypes. {PubMed:23195557}. OmpH encodes an outer membrane protein (OMP) of Salmonella Typhi.  According to the article, OMPs form a sophisticated macromolecular assembly that mediates interaction with host tissues, facilitating bacterial adhesion to and invasion of host cells.  They also serve as channels for the exchange of nutrients across the outer membrane of Gram‑negative bacteria.  As a porin, OmpH (like other OMPs such as OmpC, OmpF, OmpS) is highly immunogenic and possesses adjuvant properties, making it a candidate target for protein‑based vaccine development. {PubMed:31629569}. The ompH gene encodes the major outer membrane protein (OmpH) of Pasteurella multocida, which functions as a porin. OmpH forms a trimeric β‑barrel composed of sixteen antiparallel transmembrane β‑strands linked by eight external loops and eight periplasmic turns, creating pores in the bacterial outer membrane. As a typical Gram‑negative porin, it exhibits a high density of charged residues, lacks long hydrophobic α‑helices, and displays surface‑exposed loops that contain serotype‑specific epitopes. The native, correctly folded OmpH is a strong immunogen capable of inducing protective immunity in chickens against homologous P. multocida challenge, whereas recombinant or denatured forms lacking native conformation do not confer protection. {PubMed:10067687}. Skp (Seventeen Kilodalton Protein) is an ATP‑independent periplasmic holdase chaperone that functions in the biogenesis of outer‑membrane proteins (OMPs) in Gram‑negative bacteria. It assembles as a homo‑trimer with a β‑barrel trimerization domain and three α‑helical “tentacle” arms that create a central cavity resembling a jelly‑fish. This cavity can expand via a hinge at the conserved phenylalanine‑30, allowing the trimer to accommodate client proteins ranging from ~150 to >700 residues. Skp binds unfolded OMPs (e.g., OmpA, OmpF, LamB, OmpX, tOmpA) with high affinity (low‑nanomolar K_D) through a combination of hydrophobic contacts and electrostatic interactions, encapsulating the client in a dynamic, largely disordered state. The interaction is multivalent, with many weak, short‑lived contacts that together give the complex a long global lifetime (hours). By shielding OMPs from the aqueous periplasm, Skp prevents aggregation and misfolding, acting as a protective chaperone. Release of the client is thought to occur in an ATP‑independent manner, possibly via transient contacts with the β‑barrel assembly machinery (BAM) that allow stepwise insertion of β‑hairpins into the outer membrane. Skp exists primarily as a trimeric species, though a monomer‑trimer equilibrium is observed at physiological concentrations. Functionally, Skp serves as a secondary or backup pathway for OMP transport; its depletion causes only mild phenotypes compared with the primary chaperone SurA, but it can outcompete SurA for client binding and even exhibit a mild disaggregase activity. The beneficial effect is dose‑dependent: higher levels of Skp (achieved by mutating its natural GTG start codon to ATG and placing it under a strong T7 gene‑10 translational initiation region) correlate with greater solubility and phage‑display yields.  In dicistronic expression vectors Skp is produced in excess of that required, indicating that while Skp is not limiting, its expression must be balanced to avoid growth inhibition. {PubMed:10092493}. Overall, Skp functions as a key periplasmic escort for a subset of OMPs, providing redundancy and specificity within the periplasmic chaperone network. {PubMed:23772069}. The protein adopts an inward‑open conformation with a large, hydrophilic central cavity and a hydrophobic groove formed by TM13‑TM14 that likely accommodates the isoprenoid tail of lipid II. It functions as the lipid II flippase, translocating the peptidoglycan precursor lipid II (C55‑MurNAc‑pentapeptide‑GlcNAc) from the cytoplasmic leaflet of the inner membrane to the periplasmic leaflet where it can be incorporated into the growing peptidoglycan layer. MurJ activity is required for normal peptidoglycan synthesis; depletion or inhibition of MurJ causes accumulation of lipid II, irregular cell shape and eventual lysis. In vivo, MurJ localizes both diffusely in the lateral membrane and specifically at midcell during division, where its recruitment depends on the presence of a mature divisome, active FtsW/PBP3 complex, and ongoing lipid II synthesis. However, MurJ’s catalytic activity is not required for its midcell localization, as non‑functional mutants and MTSES‑treated cysteine variants still localize to the septum. Thus, MurJ provides the essential lipid II flipping step that couples substrate availability to septal peptidoglycan synthesis during cell division. {PubMed:30112777}. Mutations at residues A29 and D269 reduce lipid II binding, and chemical modification of A29 (e.g., by MTSES) abolishes binding, indicating these regions are important for substrate interaction. MurJ also interacts with endogenous cardiolipins, which can competitively inhibit lipid II binding, suggesting a regulatory role for membrane lipids. Antibiotic studies show that vancomycin can form a ternary complex with MurJ‑lipid II (indicating the pentapeptide remains accessible), whereas ramoplanin disrupts the MurJ‑lipid II interaction. MurJ is an essential inner‑membrane protein that functions as the lipid II flippase in Escherichia coli. This transport requires the membrane potential (Δψ) component of the proton motive force; loss of Δψ prevents the inward‑open conformation and traps MurJ in the outward‑open state, leading to accumulation of lipid II in the inner leaflet. By flipping lipid II, MurJ enables its subsequent polymerization into peptidoglycan in the periplasm, making it a critical component of cell‑wall biogenesis and a potential target for novel antibiotics. {PubMed:30482840}. The nagA gene encodes N‑acetyl‑glucosamine‑6‑phosphate deacetylase (NagA), an enzyme that catalyzes the deacetylation of N‑acetyl‑glucosamine‑6‑phosphate (Nag‑6‑P) to glucosamine‑6‑phosphate during the catabolism of the amino sugar N‑acetylglucosamine. nagA is part of the nag regulon, positioned between the repressor gene nagR and the deaminase gene nagB, and its expression is highly inducible by external N‑acetylglucosamine, showing a 50‑ to 100‑fold increase in activity upon induction. The enzyme activity is essential for the conversion of imported Nag‑6‑P (via the EII^Nag transport system) into a form that can enter further metabolic pathways. {PubMed:2693951}. nagA encodes the enzyme N‑acetyl‑glucosamine‑6‑phosphate deacetylase, which catalyzes the removal of the acetyl group from N‑acetyl‑glucosamine‑6‑phosphate (GlcNAc‑6‑P) to produce glucosamine‑6‑phosphate. Genetic complementation and enzyme assays in the study confirmed that disruption of nagA abolishes GlcNAc‑6‑P deacetylase activity, while expression of the nagA ORF restores high deacetylase activity, establishing nagA as the gene responsible for this enzymatic step in the nagBACD operon. {PubMed:2668691}. The nagA gene (cg3158, referred to as nagA₂ in the article) encodes a β‑N‑acetylglucosaminidase belonging to glycoside hydrolase family 3. In Corynebacterium glutamicum the native enzyme shows very low activity and is only weakly secreted; however, when overexpressed—especially with heterologous Tat or Sec signal peptides—it is secreted efficiently and displays measurable activity (Kₘ ≈ 0.27 mM for 4‑nitrophenyl N,N′‑diacetyl‑β‑D‑chitobioside). Thus, JW0663 (nagC) likely functions as a transcriptional repressor that modulates expression of the nagBACD operon in response to N‑acetylglucosamine availability. {PubMed:2668691}.

Merged_Functions: The frdR gene encodes a trans‑acting regulatory protein that controls nitrate‑dependent expression of multiple anaerobic respiratory and fermentative operons in Escherichia coli. Loss of frdR leads to derepression of frdABCD, failure to induce nitrate reductase, and altered regulation of TMAO reductase and alcohol dehydrogenase, demonstrating that FrdR functions as a global regulator linking nitrate availability to anaerobic growth pathways. {PubMed:3276662}. The narL gene encodes a regulatory protein that, in the presence of nitrate under anaerobic conditions, activates transcription of the narC operon encoding nitrate reductase. The same NarL protein is required for nitrate‑mediated repression of the frd operon (fumarate reductase) and the tor operon (trimethylamine N‑oxide reductase). NarL‑dependent repression occurs independently of the pleiotropic activator FNR and is not subject to strong O₂ repression. NarL does not participate in nitrate repression of ethanol dehydrogenase. Thus NarL functions as both an activator of nitrate reductase expression and a repressor of alternative anaerobic electron‑acceptor operons, coordinating the hierarchical use of terminal electron acceptors in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:3035558}. NarL is a two‑component response regulator that functions as both a transcriptional activator and repressor in Escherichia coli.  In the presence of nitrate, the sensor kinases NarX or NarQ autophosphorylate and transfer phosphate to NarL, generating NarL‑phosphate.  High levels of NarL‑phosphate activate expression of the nitrate reductase operon (narGHIJ) and the formate dehydrogenase‑N operon (fdnGHI), and simultaneously repress expression of alternate anaerobic respiratory operons such as fumarate reductase (frdABCD) and the atypical aeg‑46.5 and aeg‑93 (nrf) operons.  NarL also mediates repression of frdA by nitrate.  In the presence of nitrite, NarQ can still phosphorylate NarL efficiently, whereas NarX acts mainly as a NarL‑phosphate phosphatase, resulting in intermediate NarL‑phosphate levels that partially activate narG and fdnG while only weakly repressing or activating other targets.  Thus, NarL integrates signals from the dual sensors NarX and NarQ and the metabolites nitrate and nitrite to control hierarchical expression of multiple anaerobic respiratory genes. {PubMed:8501030}. NarL is the response regulator of the NarX‑NarL two‑component system that senses high concentrations of nitrate and modulates transcription accordingly. When phosphorylated in response to nitrate, NarL directly activates the expression of about 51 operons and represses about 41 operons, influencing genes involved in nitrate reduction, anaerobic metabolism, and reactive nitrogen compound management. NarL can bind to the canonical NarP 7‑2‑7 inverted repeat sites as well as other promoter motifs, allowing it to regulate a broad set of genes, including some (e.g., frdABCD, aspA, ansB) that are repressed solely by NarL. {PubMed:16417494}. The narL gene encodes the 24 kDa response‑regulator protein NARL, which is phosphorylated on Asp‑59 to become DNA‑binding competent. NARL mediates nitrate‑dependent regulation of anaerobic respiratory genes in Escherichia coli. It activates transcription of operons whose products are required for nitrate respiration—including fdnGHI (formate dehydrogenase‑N), narGHJI (nitrate reductase), narK (nitrate–nitrite antiporter), and nirB (nitrite reductase)—and represses operons encoding alternative anaerobic respiratory enzymes such as frdABCD (fumarate reductase) and dmsABC (DMSO/TMAO reductase). NARL also influences nitrate regulation of alcohol/acetaldehyde dehydrogenase and pyruvate‑formate lyase synthesis, but does not affect the formate‑hydrogen lyase complex. Loss‑of‑function (null) alleles of narL abolish both nitrate activation and repression of these target operons, demonstrating that NARL is essential for the nitrate‑responsive control of gene expression. {PubMed:8412692}. NarL is the response regulator of the Escherichia coli Nar two‑component system that controls transcription of genes required for nitrate respiration during anaerobiosis. The protein consists of an N‑terminal receiver domain (RD) that contains the phosphorylation site (Asp59) and a C‑terminal output domain (OD) that binds DNA. In the unphosphorylated state the RD occludes the DNA‑recognition helix of the OD, preventing promoter binding. Phosphorylation of the RD by the sensor kinases NarX/NarQ triggers a conformational change that releases the OD, allowing it to bind specific promoter sequences (often inverted 7‑2‑7 sites). This enables NarL to repress the fumarate reductase operon (frdA) and to activate the nitrate reductase operon (narG). The RD also dimerizes upon phosphorylation, which further increases the DNA‑binding affinity of the OD and can directly stimulate transcription at promoters where the OD alone is insufficient. Thus, NarL functions as a nitrate‑responsive molecular switch that integrates phosphorylation‑dependent RD dimerization with OD‑mediated DNA binding to regulate promoter‑specific transcriptional outcomes. {PubMed:26307095}. The article states that narL is a regulatory gene that positively controls the expression of the nitrate reductase structural genes (narGHI). It functions as a positive regulator of nitrate reductase transcription, contributing to the cellular response to nitrate. {PubMed:3276662}.

Merged_Functions: ZapB (Z‑associated protein B) is a cell‑division protein that forms part of the ter linkage connecting the chromosome terminus (ter) to the divisome. It interacts directly with ZapA, which recruits ZapB to the midcell division site, and with MatP, which binds the 23 matS sequences distributed across the ter domain. Through these interactions ZapB helps concentrate the ter region at the division plane, thereby coordinating chromosome segregation with cytokinesis. When ZapA is absent or unable to recruit ZapB (e.g., in cells expressing the non‑tetramerizing ZapA^183E mutant), ZapB relocalizes predominantly to one cell pole, leading to altered nucleoid positioning and asymmetric cell division. Overall, ZapB contributes to proper placement of the chromosome terminus during cell division and to the synchronization of chromosome segregation with septum formation. {PubMed:32365468}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Enhances distal genes transcription elongation in a specialized subset of operons that encode extracytoplasmic components. Also negatively controls expression and surface presentation of AG43 and possibly another AG43-independent factor that mediates cell-cell interactions and biofilm formation. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00951, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10660066, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11983161, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12007406, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1584020, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16452414, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8606157, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8951819, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9171395, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9426123}.
Merged_Functions: RfaH is described as a specialised transcription elongation protein that acts as a positive transcriptional regulator at the level of transcript elongation. It functions as an antiterminator, reducing transcriptional polarity and enabling full transcription of certain operons, notably the hlyCABD hemolysin operon and operons involved in synthesis of extracellular components such as polysaccharides and the F‑factor sex pilus. RfaH activity requires the short cis‑acting ops element located upstream of the affected operons. The protein is related to the essential transcription factor NusG, suggesting it modulates RNA polymerase pausing and termination in a subset of operons. Mutations in rfaH increase transcriptional polarity, indicating loss of its antitermination function. {PubMed:9604894}. RfaH is a bacterial transcription elongation factor that specifically enhances the expression of a subset of long operons encoding cell‑surface and extracellular components such as lipopolysaccharide core, exopolysaccharides, the F conjugation pilus and haemolysin toxin. It does not affect promoter initiation but acts post‑initiation to suppress transcription polarity, allowing efficient transcription of distal genes within these operons. RfaH is recruited to the transcription complex via the conserved 8‑bp ops element located downstream of the promoter; the ops element lowers the concentration of RfaH required for activity. Once bound, RfaH modifies the RNA polymerase complex (or associated factors such as Rho) to increase its processivity and resistance to termination signals, thereby promoting elongation through long transcriptional units. RfaH is a weak homologue of NusG and contains a KOW motif, suggesting possible interactions with RNA or the transcription machinery. {PubMed:9426123}. RfaH is a transcriptional antiterminator that enhances expression of several UPEC virulence determinants. It acts at the Rho‑independent terminator located between the hlyA and hlyB genes of the hlyCABD operon, preventing premature termination and allowing synthesis of the full‑length hlyCABD transcript required for secretion of the α‑hemolysin toxin. RfaH also promotes transcription of the cnf1 gene, which lies downstream of the hly promoter, by the same antitermination mechanism. Loss of rfaH markedly reduces UPEC virulence: it abolishes serum resistance, diminishes colonization of the bladder and kidney, alters lipopolysaccharide structure, decreases expression of the K‑15 capsule, the hemin receptor ChuA, and α‑hemolysin production, and greatly lowers CNF1 toxin levels. {PubMed:26443571}. RfaH is a transcriptional elongation factor required for wild‑type expression of the Escherichia coli hlyCABD hemolysin operon and several other long operons (e.g., rfaQ‑K, traY‑Z, rplK‑rpoC). It does not affect transcription initiation or mRNA stability, but enhances promoter‑distal transcript synthesis by acting post‑initiation. RfaH functions together with a conserved 39‑bp upstream element called JUMPStart; both are epistatic, indicating they belong to the same pathway. The protein likely interacts with RNA polymerase at a pause site within the JUMPStart region (around +162 nt downstream of the start site), facilitating a modification of the transcription complex that allows processive elongation (an antitermination‑like activity). Its role is analogous to that of NusG, suggesting it may bind RNAP and promote efficient elongation through otherwise pausing or termination‑prone regions. {PubMed:9171395}. The rfaH gene encodes a small (~18 kDa, 162‑amino‑acid) transcriptional activator that is required for high‑level transcription of several distinct operons in Escherichia coli. In addition, rfaH had previously been shown to be necessary for expression of genes involved in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core synthesis and for the F‑factor tra operon, linking it to both cell‑surface structure formation and bacterial fertility.  The protein shows no similarity to known transcription factors and lacks typical DNA‑binding motifs, suggesting a novel mechanism of action that the authors favor as primarily stimulating transcription initiation rather than antitermination.  Overall, RfaH functions as a central positive regulator of multiple virulence‑ and fitness‑related gene clusters in E. coli. {PubMed:1584020}. The rfaH gene encodes an ~18 kDa regulatory protein that acts as a transcription antiterminator/positive regulator. It is required for full expression of the F‑tra operon by preventing premature rho‑dependent transcription termination, thereby allowing synthesis of late tra genes and production of functional F pili. rfaH also positively regulates genes involved in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core synthesis; mutants lack normal levels of the galactosyl‑ and glucosyl‑transferases needed for LPS assembly and display heterogeneous LPS chemotypes (Ra‑Rc). Thus, rfaH is essential for both F‑factor functions and proper LPS core formation. {PubMed:3009418}. The hlyT gene encodes a small 162‑amino‑acid (≈18.3 kDa) protein that acts as a transcriptional activator. It is essential for high‑level transcription of the haemolysin (hly) operon, increasing hlyA mRNA levels 20–100‑fold and thereby enabling synthesis of intracellular pro‑haemolysin and its secretion as active toxin. In this crystal binding of RMF induces movement of the 30S head domain away from the rest of the ribosome, presumably so they would more easily form dimers (PubMed:22605777). Merged_Functions: The b0953 gene encodes the ribosome modulation factor (RMF), a small basic protein of 55 amino acids that associates with ribosomes during the transition from exponential to stationary phase. RMF is required for the formation of 100S ribosome dimers (dimers of 70S ribosomes) that accumulate in stationary-phase cells. Loss of b0953 abolishes ribosome dimer formation and leads to a rapid decline in cell viability during stationary phase, indicating that RMF plays a crucial role in maintaining cell survival when growth ceases. Expression of b0953 is tightly regulated: transcription is induced at the growth‑phase transition to stationary phase and is inversely correlated with growth rate, being higher under slow‑growth conditions. This regulation occurs at the transcriptional level and does not require the stationary‑phase sigma factor σ^S (katF). {PubMed:8440252}. Encodes the Ribosome Modulation Factor (RMF), a small basic 55‑amino‑acid protein that specifically associates with 100S ribosome dimers formed when Escherichia coli cells transition from exponential to stationary phase. RMF is essential for the formation of these ribosome dimers, and its presence promotes prolonged cell viability during stationary phase. Expression of rmf is tightly regulated: it is silent during rapid exponential growth, induced at the onset of stationary phase, and inversely correlated with growth rate. The gene’s transcription does not require the stationary‑phase sigma factor σ^S (katF). {PubMed:8440252}. Encodes the ribosome modulation factor (RMF), a protein that drives hibernation of the translation machinery in stationary‑phase Escherichia coli. RMF binds to active 70S ribosomes and induces their conversion into an immature 90S particle; together with the hibernation promoting factor (HPF) this intermediate is further converted into the mature, translationally inactive 100S ribosome dimer. The 100S dimer stores excess ribosomes in a silent form, conserving energy and supporting survival under nutrient limitation and various stresses. Deletion of rmf abolishes 100S formation and reduces viability in stationary phase, acidic conditions, and heat shock. rmf transcription is controlled by multiple stress‑responsive transcription factors and by the alarmone ppGpp, while its translation is enhanced by polyamines that accumulate during stationary phase. {PubMed:31867037}. Ribosome modulation factor (RMF) is a small basic protein (~55 aa) that is the essential trigger for ribosome hibernation in Gammaproteobacteria such as *Escherichia coli*. Upon entry into stationary phase or other stress conditions, RMF is synthesized and binds to the 30S subunit at a pocket formed by ribosomal proteins S2, S7, S9, S21 and 16S rRNA helices h28, h37 and h40. This binding sterically blocks the anti‑Shine‑Dalgarno sequence, preventing formation of the mRNA‑SD helix required for translation initiation. RMF first promotes the transient dimerization of two active 70S ribosomes into a 90S intermediate; the 90S particle is then converted into a stable, translationally inactive 100S dimer by the subsequent binding of hibernation promoting factor (HPF). Deletion of *rmf* abolishes 100S formation, and RMF disappears within minutes when stationary‑phase cells are transferred to fresh medium, indicating its rapid turnover is key to reactivating translation. Thus, RMF functions to inactivate ribosomes by forming 100S dimers, conserving resources during nutrient limitation, and facilitating rapid resumption of growth when conditions improve. {PubMed:30476446}. The rmf gene encodes the ribosome modulation factor (RMF), a small basic protein of 55 amino acids (≈6.5 kDa). RMF specifically associates with 70S ribosomes to promote their dimerization into 100S ribosome dimers that accumulate when Escherichia coli cells transition from exponential to stationary phase. Formation of these dimers is reversible; they dissociate back to 70S ribosomes when stationary‑phase cells are returned to fresh medium, suggesting a role in conserving ribosomes during non‑growth conditions. Disruption of rmf abolishes 100S ribosome formation and markedly reduces cell viability during stationary phase, indicating that RMF is essential for maintaining ribosome integrity and long‑term survival in stationary phase. The gene’s expression is tightly regulated: rmf transcription is silent during rapid exponential growth, induced at the onset of stationary phase, and inversely correlated with growth rate. Its transcription does not require the stationary‑phase σ factor KatF (σ^S). {PubMed:8440252}. Ribosome modulation factor (RMF) is a small, highly basic protein (pI ≈ 11.3, Mr ≈ 6.5 kDa) whose expression rises sharply as Escherichia coli cells transition from log to stationary phase. RMF binds to 70S ribosomes and promotes their dimerization into translationally inactive 100S ribosomes (ribosome dimers). It inactivates ribosomes by covering the peptidyl‑transferase centre and the entrance to the peptide‑exit tunnel. During stationary phase, RMF together with hibernation‑promoting factor (HPF) stabilizes the 100S ribosome, allowing cells to survive nutrient stress. When stationary‑phase cells are returned to rich medium, RMF is rapidly released, the 100S dimers dissociate back to 70S ribosomes within about one minute, and protein synthesis resumes. Deletion of the rmf gene abolishes 100S ribosome formation and shortens cell lifespan, highlighting its essential role in ribosome hibernation. {PubMed:19170772}. Ribosome Modulation Factor (RMF) is a stationary‑phase‑induced protein whose expression is positively regulated by the alarmone ppGpp. RMF binds specifically to the 50S ribosomal subunit and directs the dimerization of two 70S ribosomes to form an inactive 100S ribosome complex. This conversion renders ribosomes translationally silent, providing a novel negative control of protein synthesis during nutrient starvation and the stationary phase. The formation of 100S ribosomes by RMF contributes to cell survival under prolonged starvation; rmf deletion mutants fail to produce 100S ribosomes and exhibit markedly reduced viability in stationary phase. {PubMed:11532026}. The rmf gene encodes the ribosome modulation factor (RMF) protein, a stationary‑phase‑specific factor that dimerises 70S ribosomes into inactive 100S ribosome complexes, thereby suppressing translational activity. RMF expression rises sharply in the stationary phase and is positively regulated by the stringent response alarmone ppGpp. By inactivating ribosomes, RMF helps cells survive stress conditions and slows metabolic activity during nutrient limitation. Disruption of rmf prevents 100S ribosome formation, leading to higher translational capacity, increased L‑lysine production rates, and altered growth responses depending on phosphate availability. {PubMed:15831252}.
Curated_Functions: Promotes dimerization of active 70S ribosomes into translationally inactive 100S ribosome dimers (ribosome hibernation). {PubMed:8440252, PubMed:30476446, PubMed:19170772, PubMed:11532026, PubMed:15831252}. Binds to ribosomal subunits at the 30S pocket and sterically blocks the anti‑Shine‑Dalgarno sequence while covering the peptidyl‑transferase centre and peptide‑exit tunnel, thereby inhibiting translation initiation. {PubMed:30476446, PubMed:19170772}. Enhances long‑term cell survival during stationary phase and under nutrient limitation, acidic and heat‑shock stresses by conserving ribosomes and cellular energy. {PubMed:8440252, PubMed:31867037, PubMed:11532026, PubMed:19170772}.
