Merged_Functions: FtsN is an essential cell‑division protein in Escherichia coli. It is a membrane‑anchored protein with an N‑terminal hydrophobic segment that spans the cytoplasmic membrane and a larger C‑terminal domain located in the periplasm, unusually rich in glutamine residues. Inactivation of ftsN leads to filamentous cells and cell death, demonstrating its requirement for septum formation. When present on a multicopy plasmid, ftsN suppresses temperature‑sensitive mutations in ftsA, ftsI (PBP3) and, to a lesser extent, ftsQ, indicating functional interactions with these division proteins. This suggests that FtsN participates in a membrane‑associated complex that links the cytoplasmic division machinery (e.g., FtsZ/FtsA) to the periplasmic peptidoglycan synthesis apparatus during cytokinesis. Overproduction of FtsN has little impact on growth unless expressed at very high levels, which can inhibit division and cause cell lysis. {PubMed:8509333}. Escherichia coli FtsN is a bitopic inner‑membrane protein that is essential for triggering the active constriction phase of bacterial cytokinesis. It contains a short cytoplasmic N‑terminal domain (N⁽FtsN⁾), a transmembrane segment, and a large periplasmic region that includes three juxta‑membrane helices, a linker, and a C‑terminal SPOR domain. The essential activity is confined to a very small periplasmic peptide (E⁽FtsN⁾, ≤35 residues centred on helix H2; the critical residues are W83, Y85 and L89). E⁽FtsN⁾ allosterically induces a conformational switch in the periplasmic FtsBLQ subcomplex, relieving its repression of the PBP3‑FtsW septal peptidoglycan synthase complex and thereby stimulating septal PG synthesis. At the same time, the cytoplasmic N⁽FtsN⁾ domain binds directly to the IC domain of FtsA, promoting an “on” conformation of FtsA that reinforces the activated state of FtsBLQ and may also facilitate Z‑ring contraction. Through these dual interactions FtsN coordinates sPG synthesis, membrane invagination and Z‑ring dynamics, acting as a key trigger and maintainer of cell division. {PubMed:25496160}. FtsN is an essential cell‑division protein in Escherichia coli that spans the inner membrane with a small N‑terminal cytoplasmic segment, a single transmembrane helix, and a large C‑terminal periplasmic domain.  The periplasmic domain alone is sufficient for its activity and for targeting the protein to the division site.  FtsN is recruited to the septum later than the early division proteins FtsZ and FtsA; its localization requires the prior assembly of the Z ring and the presence of functional FtsA, as well as the activities of the later division proteins FtsI (PBP3) and FtsQ.  By becoming part of the septal division complex, FtsN is thought to contribute to septal‑specific peptidoglycan synthesis and to stabilize the protein complex required for invagination of the septum.  Depletion of FtsN results in filamentous cells that lack the normal septal indentations, indicating its role early in septation despite its late recruitment. {PubMed:9282742}. FtsN (b3933) encodes an essential, bitopic inner‑membrane protein that participates in bacterial cell division.  It possesses a short N‑terminal cytoplasmic segment, a single transmembrane helix, and a large C‑terminal periplasmic domain.  The periplasmic domain is sufficient for its activity and for targeting the protein to the division site.  FtsN localizes to the mid‑cell septum in a ring‑like pattern, but appears later in the division sequence than FtsZ, FtsA, and ZipA.  Its recruitment to the septum requires the prior localization of FtsZ and FtsA and also depends on functional FtsI (PBP3) and FtsQ, suggesting that it interacts—directly or indirectly—with these later‑acting division proteins.  Although FtsN is not required for the initial formation of the Z‑ring, it is required for subsequent stages of septation, likely contributing to septal peptidoglycan synthesis and invagination of the septum.  Overexpression of ftsN can suppress temperature‑sensitive mutations in ftsA, ftsL, and ftsQ, indicating a role in stabilizing the division complex. {PubMed:9282742}. Encodes the N‑terminal fragment (msg15‑1119) of the major surface glycoprotein (Msg) of Pneumocystis jirovecii. Msg is a 95‑kDa surface protein that mediates interaction of the fungus with the host lung, serves as a major target of B‑cell and T‑cell immune responses, and plays a central role in the immunopathogenesis of Pneumocystis pneumonia. The recombinant MsgA fragment was generated to study serologic antibody responses to this portion of the Msg protein. {PubMed:12195351}.

Binds directly to the cytoplasmic domain of FtsA, promoting an active conformation of FtsA and reinforcing activation of the FtsBLQ complex, which facilitates Z‑ring contraction. {PubMed:25496160}. The enzyme functions as a dimeric protein of ~35 kDa subunits (≈72 kDa native mass) and is not known to be regulated by the NadI repressor. {PubMed:8419294}. nadC is one of the three essential genes (nadA, nadB, nadC) required for the de novo biosynthesis of NAD in Escherichia coli. Loss of nadC function, like loss of nadA or nadB, results in NAD auxotrophy, indicating its role in the pathway that synthesizes NAD from aspartate. {PubMed:22174382}. The nadC locus encodes quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (decarboxylating), the enzyme that converts quinolinate into the next intermediate of NAD biosynthesis. nadC mutants lack significant quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase activity, excrete excess quinolinate, and are unable to synthesize NAD de novo, supporting its role as the structural gene for this enzymatic step. {PubMed:238844}. The nadC gene encodes quinolinic acid phosphoribosyltransferase (QAPRTase, EC 2.4.2.19). This enzyme catalyzes the transfer of a phosphoribosyl group from 5‑phosphoribosyl‑1‑pyrophosphate (PRPP) to quinolinic acid, producing nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NAMN). The formation of NAMN is a central step in the de novo biosynthetic pathway for NAD and NADP in Salmonella typhimurium. QAPRTase functions as a dimeric protein of ~72 kDa (native) composed of ~35 kDa subunits, displays Km values of ~32 µM for PRPP and ~20 µM for quinolinic acid, and is not known to be regulated by the NadI/NadR repressor. {PubMed:8419294}.

Merged_Functions: The rnt gene encodes RNase T, a 3'→5' exoribonuclease that specifically removes the terminal AMP residue from uncharged tRNA, thereby carrying out the majority (>90%) of tRNA end‑turnover in Escherichia coli. RNase T also contributes to the processing of tRNA 3' ends, as indicated by a modest reduction in aminoacylation efficiency of tRNA isolated from rnt‑deficient strains. Loss of RNase T slows bacterial growth, an effect that is amplified when other exoribonucleases are absent, and severely impairs the ability of cells to recover after prolonged starvation. Thus, rnt is essential for normal growth, efficient recovery from metabolic stress, and likely participates in additional, yet‑to‑be‑fully‑defined aspects of RNA metabolism. {PubMed:1704882}. The rnt gene encodes RNase T, a 3′→5′ exonuclease that belongs to the DEDD/DnaQ superfamily. RNase T preferentially degrades single‑stranded DNA (ssDNA) in a distributive manner, requiring Mg²⁺ or Mn²⁺ ions, and shows only very weak activity on double‑stranded DNA. It has a very high affinity for ssDNA (Kₘ ≈ 5 nM) and can processively chew long ssDNA molecules (up to ~30 kb) in vitro, producing mononucleotides. RNase T can generate blunt ends from 3′ ssDNA overhangs, such as those created by restriction endonucleases. Although originally identified as an RNA exonuclease involved in tRNA and 5S rRNA maturation, its DNA exonuclease activity is biologically significant: overexpression of rnt suppresses UV sensitivity in strains lacking the ssDNA exonucleases RecJ, ExoI, and ExoVII, and it can improve survival of cells deficient in nucleotide excision repair (uvrA or uvrC mutants). Thus, RNase T likely functions as a backup DNA exonuclease that participates in DNA repair and processing of DNA ends, contributing to genome stability and mutation avoidance. {PubMed:26442508}. In DNA metabolism, RNase T exhibits a Mg²⁺‑dependent 3′→5′ exonucleolytic activity on single‑stranded DNA, with a low Kₘ (~5 nM) indicating high affinity, and can degrade long ssDNA molecules (up to ~40 kb). This DNase activity likely underlies the ability of high‑copy rnt to suppress UV‑sensitivity in strains deficient in other ssDNA exonucleases, suggesting a role in DNA end‑trimming during recombination, repair, or mutation avoidance. {PubMed:9857048}. The article identifies b1652 as the lhr (long helicase‑related) gene.  It encodes a very large protein of 1,538 amino acids (~170 kDa) that contains all seven conserved motifs of helicase superfamily II, including the DEVH signature in motif II, indicating that it is a member of the helicase family.  Sequence analysis predicts that Lhr functions as a nucleic‑acid‑dependent ATPase/helicase, although the authors were unable to detect ATPase activity with the substrates tested.  Disruption of the gene shows that it is not essential for growth under a wide range of laboratory conditions and no obvious phenotypes (e.g., sensitivity to UV, H₂O₂, phage infection, or anaerobic growth) were observed.  Thus, the gene’s precise physiological role remains unknown, but it is presumed to act as a helicase involved in DNA or RNA metabolism, possibly under specific conditions not reproduced in the study. {PubMed:7559321}.

Merged_Functions: The lhr gene encodes a member of a novel clade of Superfamily‑2 (SF2) helicases found in bacteria such as Escherichia coli and Mycobacterium smegmatis. The N‑terminal ~850‑aa Core domain contains the conserved SF2 helicase motifs and functions as an ATP‑dependent motor: it hydrolyzes ATP, translocates unidirectionally 3′→5′ along single‑stranded DNA, and unwinds duplex nucleic acids. Lhr preferentially unwinds RNA:DNA hybrids over DNA:DNA duplexes, but does not act on RNA:RNA hybrids. The C‑terminal domain (CTD), composed of five tandem winged‑helix modules and a β‑barrel, assembles into a homo‑tetramer that drives oligomerization of the full‑length protein; this oligomeric CTD may enhance duplex‑unwinding activity, although direct nucleic‑acid binding by the CTD was not detected. In mycobacteria, lhr expression is up‑regulated by the PafBC DNA‑damage response pathway after exposure to the inter‑strand crosslinking agent mitomycin C, suggesting a role in repair of DNA inter‑strand crosslinks, possibly through a combination of helicase activity (Core) and an AlkZ‑like DNA‑recognition module (CTD). {PubMed:33744958}. The locus of heat resistance (LHR) is a genomic island that encodes a suite of proteins (sHSP20, ClpKGI, sHSP, YdfX1, YdfX2, HdeD, KefB, Trx, PsiE, DegP, and a hypothetical protein). Expression of these LHR‑encoded proteins gives Escherichia coli extreme heat resistance, markedly reduces protein aggregation (inclusion body formation) after heat or high‑pressure stress by preventing misfolded protein accumulation or by disaggregating existing aggregates, and thereby confers cross‑protection against hydrostatic pressure. The LHR also contributes to resistance against oxidative stress, envelope stress, and osmotic stress, providing multifaceted protection against diverse environmental challenges. {PubMed:32117137}. The locus of heat resistance (LHR) is a 14‑kb genomic island that encodes multiple putative heat‑shock proteins, proteases, and transport proteins. Presence of the LHR confers a marked increase in thermal tolerance to Enterobacteriaceae, reducing the loss of viable cells during exposure to 60 °C for several minutes. LHR‑positive strains of Escherichia coli, Salmonella enterica and Enterobacter cloacae survive heat treatments that reduce LHR‑negative strains by >7 log units, and they retain greater viability during cooking of ground beef to 71 °C. The LHR also enhances heat resistance under elevated NaCl concentrations, suggesting a role for its encoded transporters in compatible‑solutes accumulation and for its proteases in managing protein damage during heat stress. Overall, the LHR functions as a genetic determinant that markedly increases heat resistance in diverse Enterobacteriaceae. {PubMed:28213040}. The locus of heat resistance (LHR) is a genomic island that encodes multiple proteins (including small heat‑shock proteins, the disaggregase ClpK, periplasmic chaperones YfdX1/YfdX2, and the Na⁺/H⁺ antiporter KefB).  According to the article, the LHR confers resistance to several severe stresses: extreme heat, chlorine, and oxidative stress by reducing protein aggregation, protein oxidation, and membrane‑lipid oxidation.  While the LHR does not influence the activity of the Cpx envelope‑stress two‑component system nor improve growth at mildly alkaline pH (6.9–9.2), it enhances survival of Escherichia coli under lethal alkaline conditions (pH ≈ 11) **only when chlorine is present**.  Expression of the LHR is up‑regulated at alkaline pH (pH 8.0) in the absence of the CpxR regulator, indicating that CpxR negatively regulates LHR transcription under normal conditions.  Thus, the primary function of the LHR is to protect E. coli from lethal challenges involving heat, chlorine, oxidative stress, and extreme alkaline pH combined with chlorine. {PubMed:33800639}.

Merged_Functions: The leuB gene encodes 3‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase, an enzyme that catalyzes a key step in the biosynthetic pathway of the amino acid leucine. This enzyme is essential for leucine production in the host organism, and its activity can be measured as isopropylmalate dehydrogenase activity in cell extracts. {PubMed:9354372}. The leuB gene encodes the enzyme β‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase, a key catalytic component of the leucine biosynthetic pathway. In Escherichia coli, the LeuB protein catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of β‑isopropylmalate to produce α‑keto‑isocaproate, a precursor for leucine synthesis. The article demonstrates that when the leuB coding region is placed under the control of yeast HIS3 promoter elements, it can complement a leu2 mutation in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, indicating that the β‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase activity supplied by leuB restores leucine prototrophy in the yeast host. {PubMed:3916734}. The leuB gene encodes β‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (β‑IPM), an enzyme that participates in the leucine biosynthetic pathway. It catalyzes a step in the conversion of intermediates toward the synthesis of the amino acid leucine, and loss of its activity results in leucine auxotrophy. {PubMed:3326787}. The leuB gene encodes the enzyme 3‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase, an NAD‑dependent dehydrogenase that participates in the leucine biosynthetic pathway of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The protein is 360 amino acids long (≈39 kDa) and belongs to the isocitrate/3‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase family. Its activity is essential for the synthesis of leucine, as disruption of leuB by insertional mutagenesis results in leucine auxotrophy, while the gene does not affect downstream asd expression. Unlike many bacteria where leuB is clustered with other leu genes, in P. aeruginosa leuB is physically separated from the other enzymes of the isopropylmalate pathway. {PubMed:9108278}. The leuB gene encodes a NAD‑dependent β‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (also called 3‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase). This enzyme catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of β‑isopropylmalate to produce α‑ketoisocaproate, a key step in the leucine biosynthetic pathway. Enzyme assays demonstrated that the cloned leuB product restores β‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase activity in E. coli leuB mutants and converts β‑isopropylmalate to α‑ketoisocaproate, confirming its role in leucine biosynthesis. {PubMed:8336106}. The leuB gene encodes the enzyme β‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.85), a key catalytic component of the leucine biosynthetic pathway. It is part of the leu operon, whose expression is controlled both by transcriptional attenuation specific for leucine and by the stringent response regulator ppGpp. Mutations in leuB (e.g., a C‑to‑T transition at nucleotide 857 causing a Ser‑286→Leu substitution) render cells leucine auxotrophic, and reversion of this lesion restores the wild‑type enzyme activity. {PubMed:9084168}. The leuB gene encodes the enzyme 3‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (EC 1.1.1.85), which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of 3‑isopropylmalate in the leucine biosynthetic pathway. {PubMed:8598270}. Encodes a Lactobacillus bulgaricus serine transfer RNA (tRNA^Ser) with the anticodon CGA. The tRNA gene includes promoter and terminator elements recognized by E. coli RNA polymerase, an unusually long extra arm (22 nucleotides), and lacks the 3′-terminal CCA that is added post‑transcriptionally. When expressed in Escherichia coli, the tRNA is produced at high copy number and is misacylated at a low frequency, allowing it to insert an amino acid other than serine at UCG codons. This missense suppression specifically restores activity of the mutant leuB6 allele (β‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase) and thereby confers leucine prototrophy. The complementation effect is dependent on gene dosage, with multicopy plasmid expression yielding restoration of growth, whereas single‑copy prophage integration does not. {PubMed:3326787}. Encodes the enzyme 3‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase, the NAD‑dependent dehydrogenase that catalyzes the third step of the leucine biosynthetic pathway in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The protein is 360 amino acids long (≈39 kDa) and belongs to the isocitrate/3‑isopropylmalate dehydrogenase family. Disruption of this gene results in leucine auxotrophy, confirming its role in leucine synthesis. {PubMed:9108278}.

Merged_Functions: HypF is an accessory protein required for the maturation of [NiFe] hydrogenases. In the presence of ATP, HypF converts carbamoyl phosphate into the activated intermediate AMP‑OCONH₂. This carbamoyl‑AMP is then transferred to the C‑terminal cysteine (Cys336) of the partner protein HypE, forming a thiocarbamate adduct on HypE. The HypF–HypE complex thus initiates the biosynthetic pathway that generates the cyanide ligands incorporated into the large subunit of the hydrogenase. Consequently, HypF functions as a key enzyme in the ATP‑dependent activation of carbamoyl phosphate and the delivery of the carbamoyl group to HypE during [NiFe] hydrogenase maturation. {PubMed:18065529}. hypF encodes an 81‑kDa protein that is essential for the maturation of all three [NiFe] hydrogenases in Escherichia coli. Deletion of hypF abolishes hydrogenase activity because the large subunits of hydrogenases 1, 2 and 3 are synthesized only as inactive precursor forms. The defect is due to a failure to incorporate nickel into the large subunit; ^63Ni labeling shows that the mutant cannot insert nickel into HycE (hydrogenase 3) and, by inference, into the other hydrogenases as well. Thus, HypF functions in the nickel‑insertion step of hydrogenase biosynthesis, a key step required for proteolytic processing and activation of the enzymes. The protein contains two zinc‑finger‑like motifs (CxxCx₁₈CxxC) that may participate in metal binding or protein‑protein interactions during this maturation process. {PubMed:8661925}. HypF is an accessory protein required for the synthesis and maturation of the four membrane‑bound reversible [Ni‑Fe] hydrogenases in Escherichia coli. It participates in the assembly of the large subunits of these hydrogenases, enabling their proper formation and activity. {PubMed:30161297}. The hypF gene encodes a prokaryotic hydrogenase maturation factor. Its N‑terminal domain (HypF‑N) is a 91‑residue protein that can form amyloid‑like aggregates in vitro. In the context of this study, HypF‑N serves as a model system for investigating the structure, formation, and toxicity of protein oligomers, particularly their ability to permeabilise mitochondrial membranes, form ion‑conducting pores, and induce mitochondrial dysfunction. The article does not describe additional cellular roles beyond its identification as a hydrogenase maturation factor. {PubMed:33082392}. HypF is an essential accessory protein required for the synthesis and maturation of hydrogenase (Hyd) enzymes. It participates in the assembly of ligands on the large subunits of Hyd enzymes and its activity is coupled to ATP hydrolysis. The article notes that loss of hypF (hypF mutant) leads to reduced growth rates under certain pH conditions and alters ATPase activity, reflecting its role in proper hydrogenase function. {PubMed:26049001}. HypF is one of the six NiFe‑hydrogenase maturase proteins (hypABCDEF). In the NiFe‑hydrogenase maturation pathway, HypF forms a stoichiometric complex with HypE (K_D ≈ 400 nM) and together they catalyze the synthesis of cyanide from carbamoyl phosphate. The cyanide produced is then transferred to an iron‐containing intermediate, likely bound to the HypCD scaffold, contributing the cyanide ligands that become part of the NiFe‑hydrogenase active site. {PubMed:24878200}. hydA corresponds to the hypF gene located in the hydA locus together with hydN. The HydA (HypF) protein is essential for the maturation of all three Escherichia coli [NiFe] hydrogenases (hydrogenases 1, 2 and 3). It is required for the incorporation of nickel into the large subunits of these enzymes, a step that precedes the proteolytic processing that yields active hydrogenases. Deletion of hypF (hydA) abolishes hydrogenase activity and leaves the large subunits in an inactive precursor form lacking nickel. HydA is expressed as part of an operon with hydN and is a member of the formate regulon; its transcription is activated under fermentative, formate‑producing conditions by the σ⁵⁴‑dependent promoter and the FhlA transcriptional activator. {PubMed:8661925}. HydA encodes the catalytic subunit of a [FeFe]-hydrogenase. It houses the H‑cluster active site, which consists of a [4Fe‑4S] cubane linked to a 2Fe subcluster bearing CO, CN⁻, and a bridging dithiolate ligand. HydA catalyzes the reversible reduction of protons to molecular hydrogen (H₂) during microbial metabolism. The enzyme requires prior assembly of the [4Fe‑4S] cubane by cellular Fe‑S cluster machinery and subsequent insertion of the 2Fe subcluster, a process mediated by the maturase proteins HydE, HydF, and HydG. {PubMed:24878200}. The article indicates that hydA is associated with the expression of hydrogenase activity in Escherichia coli. Maxicell analysis identified its gene product as an ~80 kDa polypeptide, but the authors suggest it is unlikely to be a structural subunit of the hydrogenase enzyme complex. Instead, they propose that hydA may function as a regulatory protein influencing hydrogenase activity, as evidenced by altered hydrogenase activity when hydA from E. coli or C. freundii is cloned and expressed. {PubMed:2157623}. hydA is not a structural subunit of hydrogenase but an essential gene required for the synthesis of all hydrogenase isoenzymes in Escherichia coli. Mutations in hydA abolish the production of any hydrogenase activity, indicating that its product is necessary for the assembly or expression of the hydrogenase enzymes. Although the precise biochemical role is unknown, the article suggests that the HydA protein (like HydB) influences other gene(s) that ultimately enable the formation of functional hydrogenases. {PubMed:2200847}. The hydA gene encodes a clostridial [Fe]-hydrogenase (HydA), a metal‑containing enzyme that catalyzes the release of molecular hydrogen (H₂) from reduced ferredoxin during anaerobic fermentation. Its activity channels excess reducing equivalents into H₂ production, thereby influencing the metabolic flux: overexpression of hydA in Clostridium paraputrificum increases hydrogen gas yield (by ~1.7‑fold), enhances acetate formation, and suppresses lactate formation by promoting NAD⁺ regeneration through over‑oxidation of NADH. {PubMed:15899410}. HydA encodes the small‑subunit protein of the Helicobacter pylori hydrogenase. It is a membrane‑bound component of the hydrogenase enzyme complex and contains a twin‑arginine (RR) signal peptide that targets it for export by the Tat (twin‑arginine translocation) system to the periplasm. The article identifies HydA as one of the few H. pylori proteins predicted to be Tat substrates and demonstrates experimentally that a HydA‑signal peptide can direct EGFP export to the periplasm, although export efficiency is limited. {PubMed:29735759}.

ThiH is a radical S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) enzyme containing a [4Fe‑4S]^+ cluster. It reductively cleaves SAM to generate methionine and a 5′‑deoxyadenosyl radical, which abstracts a hydrogen atom from the phenolic O‑H of L‑tyrosine. The resulting phenoxy radical undergoes Cα‑Cβ bond cleavage, producing p‑cresol and the reactive intermediate dehydroglycine. Dehydroglycine is subsequently transferred to ThiG for incorporation into the thiazole moiety of thiamine. The enzyme displays burst‑phase kinetics, is inhibited by accumulation of 5′‑deoxyadenosine (DOA) and methionine, and can perform multiple turnovers when product inhibition is relieved (e.g., by MTAN). {PubMed:19923213}. ThiH encodes an enzyme that is required for the biosynthesis of the thiazole moiety of thiamin, functioning as a component of the thiamin biosynthetic operon in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:10082377}. Mutants lacking thiH are thiazole‑auxotrophic (Thz⁻) and cannot grow with the thiazole precursor 1‑deoxy‑D‑threo‑2‑pentulose, indicating that ThiH functions downstream of this precursor in the thiazole biosynthetic branch of the thiamine‑pyrophosphate pathway. Although hyi transcripts were detected in some transgenic lines, no hyi protein was observed, indicating that functional enzyme was not produced in the plants. {PubMed:22104170}. The b0508 gene (also called gip and newly designated hyi) encodes a 58 kDa homodimeric hydroxypyruvate isomerase. This enzyme catalyzes the reversible isomerization of hydroxypyruvate to tartronate semialdehyde without requiring any cofactor. It shows optimal activity at pH 6.8–7.2, has an apparent Kₘ of 12.5 mM for hydroxypyruvate, and is specific for this substrate (no activity toward fructose, xylose, or amino‑acid racemization). In the glyoxylate utilization pathway of *E. coli*, the enzyme likely functions physiologically to convert tartronate semialdehyde—produced by glyoxylate carboligase—into hydroxypyruvate, which can serve as a precursor for serine biosynthesis. {PubMed:10561547}. The gip gene (also designated hyi, orf b0508) encodes a hydroxypyruvate isomerase enzyme. This enzyme catalyzes the reversible isomerization between hydroxypyruvate and tartronate semialdehyde without requiring any cofactor. It functions as a homodimer of 58 kDa (each subunit ~29 kDa) and shows optimal activity at pH 6.8–7.2. In the glyoxylate utilization pathway of Escherichia coli, the enzyme converts tartronate semialdehyde—produced by glyoxylate carboligase—from glyoxylate into hydroxypyruvate, which can serve as a precursor for serine biosynthesis. Thus, gip/hyi provides the enzymatic step that links tartronate semialdehyde to hydroxypyruvate in glyoxylate catabolism. {PubMed:10561547}. The gip gene encodes a glucose indicator protein (GIP) that consists of a mutated glucose‑binding protein (GBPₘ) flanked by fluorescent proteins (ECFP at the N‑terminus and either EYFP or a pH‑insensitive YFPᵢ at the C‑terminus). Upon binding glucose, GBPₘ undergoes a conformational change that alters the distance between the fluorescent tags, resulting in a measurable change in Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) efficiency. This FRET signal provides a continuous, real‑time readout of intracellular glucose concentrations. The pH‑insensitive version (C₀Yᵢ) retains its glucose‑responsive FRET signal across acidic pH ranges (pH 5.2–7.3), making it suitable for intracellular glucose monitoring under varying pH conditions. {PubMed:19194917}. Human glucose‑dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) is a 42‑amino‑acid peptide hormone secreted by duodenal K‑cells that normally stimulates insulin release, promotes β‑cell proliferation, and participates in bone metabolism and body‑weight regulation. In the context of this article, GIP functions as an antimicrobial adjuvant: it binds to bacterial membranes, induces rapid membrane depolarisation, and thereby disrupts the proton‑motive force that powers RND‑type AcrAB‑TolC efflux pumps in multidrug‑resistant Gram‑negative bacteria (Escherichia coli TG1 and Erwinia amylovora 1189). This inhibition of efflux pump activity leads to intracellular accumulation of ethidium bromide and markedly lowers the minimum inhibitory concentrations of a range of antibiotics and bile salts (4‑ to 20‑fold reductions). GIP itself shows no direct bactericidal activity or membrane permeabilisation, but its ability to attenuate efflux pumps and potentiate other antimicrobials defines its role as a novel antibiotic‑adjuvant peptide. {PubMed:33938181}.

Merged_Functions: The chlA1 allele encodes a protein that is essential for the biosynthesis of molybdopterin (MPT), the organic component of the molybdenum cofactor.  Strains carrying the chlA1 mutation are completely deficient in MPT, indicating that the normal chlA product functions in an early step of the MPT pathway.  Although chlA1 cells lack MPT, extracts from chlA1 can complement other chl mutants and the Neurospora nit‑1 mutant in vitro; this complementation is mediated by a chlA1‑encoded factor that acts on a low‑molecular‑weight compound (likely an MPT precursor) to generate MPT.  Thus, chlA (chlA1) is a key gene in MPT biosynthesis rather than in Mo insertion into the cofactor. {PubMed:2947896}. The chlA1 gene encodes a soluble protein (referred to as Protein PA) of approximately 72 kDa that is essential for the activation of nitrate reductase (and indirectly formate dehydrogenase) in Escherichia coli. Protein PA functions as a non‑catalytic activation factor that, together with the association factor FA supplied by the chlA mutant, enables the conversion of inactive nitrate reductase apoprotein into its active, molybdenum‑containing form during the complementation process. The protein appears to be involved in the insertion or maturation of the molybdenum cofactor into the nitrate reductase enzyme, although its precise biochemical role remains undefined. It is not a structural subunit of nitrate reductase, but is required for the proper assembly/activation of the enzyme, and a fraction of Protein PA becomes associated with newly formed membranous nitrate‑reductase particles after activation. {PubMed:6315066}. The chlA locus encodes the protein PA, a ~72 kDa polypeptide that binds the molybdenum cofactor and is essential for the in‑vitro activation of the apoprotein form of respiratory nitrate reductase in Escherichia coli.  chlA mutants lack functional molybdenum cofactor and therefore contain inactive nitrate reductase that cannot be reconstituted unless protein PA (or a source of molybdenum cofactor) is supplied.  Thus, chlA (chlA1) functions as a molybdenum‑cofactor‑binding/activating factor required for the maturation and activity of molybdoenzymes such as nitrate reductase. {PubMed:2956990}. The chlA1 gene encodes the MPT converting factor, a ~45 kDa protein that functions as an enzyme in the biosynthetic pathway of molybdopterin (MPT). This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of low‑molecular‑weight MPT precursors (provided by nit‑1 extracts) into authentic MPT, which can then bind to carrier proteins and reconstitute apo‑nitrate reductase activity. Mutants lacking chlA1 are deficient in MPT production, indicating that chlA1 is essential for MPT synthesis but is not involved in folate or riboflavin biosynthesis. {PubMed:3539912}. chlA1 is the allele of the moaA gene. The MoaA protein is required for the early steps of molybdenum cofactor (molybdopterin, MPT) biosynthesis in Escherichia coli, specifically for the production of the MPT precursor. Mutations in chlA1 (moaA) abolish the formation of the MPT precursor, leading to a defect in molybdopterin biosynthesis. {PubMed:8361352}. Encodes the MoaB protein, a ~18.7 kDa polypeptide that is one of the five components of the moa operon required for molybdenum cofactor (molybdopterin) biosynthesis in Escherichia coli K‑12. MoaB, together with MoaA and MoaC, participates in the early steps that generate the molybdopterin precursor. Sequence analysis shows similarity to thymidylate synthase and N‑(5′‑phosphoribosyl)anthranilate isomerase, suggesting a role related to pterin or purine metabolism in the formation of the molybdopterin backbone. {PubMed:8361352}. The moaA gene encodes a 354‑amino‑acid (~40 kDa) protein that participates in an early step of molybdopterin (MPT) cofactor biosynthesis. The protein is homologous to the E. coli MoaA and can complement E. coli moaA mutants, restoring activity of MPT‑dependent enzymes such as nitrate reductase and formate dehydrogenase. It contains conserved cysteine‑rich motifs (CxxxCxYC near the N‑terminus and FCxxC…C near the C‑terminus); mutation of the three N‑terminal cysteines eliminates biological activity, indicating these residues are essential, likely for metal ion coordination required for MPT synthesis. {PubMed:8588735}. MoaA encodes a radical S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) enzyme that catalyzes the first step of molybdopterin cofactor biosynthesis.  It contains two [4Fe‑4S] clusters: an N‑terminal cluster that reductively cleaves SAM to generate a 5′‑deoxyadenosyl radical, and a C‑terminal cluster that binds GTP.  The enzyme abstracts a hydrogen atom from the 3′ carbon of GTP, initiates a radical‐mediated cyclization, and drives an unprecedented insertion of the purine C8 carbon between the C2′ and C3′ carbons of the ribose.  This transformation converts GTP into pyranopterin triphosphate (PTP), an oxygen‑sensitive intermediate that is subsequently processed (by phosphatase oxidation and further enzymes such as MoaC) to cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (cPMP), the core scaffold of the molybdopterin cofactor. {PubMed:25896388}. moaA is a component of the moaABCDE operon, which encodes enzymes involved in molybdate utilization within the cell. The operon carries out the first steps of molybdenum assimilation, providing the enzymatic activities required for processing intracellular molybdate. {PubMed:9044285}. MoaA is a radical S‑adenosyl‑methionine (SAM) dependent enzyme that catalyzes the first step of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis in Escherichia coli. It converts 5′‑guanosine triphosphate (5′‑GTP) into cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (cPMP), acting as a GTP 3′,8‑cyclase. Each MoaA monomer binds two oxygen‑sensitive [4Fe‑4S] clusters, which are required for reductive cleavage of SAM and generation of the protein‑bound radical that drives the cyclization reaction. The activity of MoaA depends on the presence of functional Fe‑S clusters and therefore on cellular iron availability and the L‑cysteine desulfurase IscS, which supplies sulfur for Fe‑S cluster assembly. MoaA is encoded in the moaABCDE operon, whose transcription is regulated by FNR, ModE, CsrA and a Moco riboswitch. {PubMed:31235512}. The moaA gene encodes a protein that is essential for molybdenum cofactor (molybdopterin, MPT) biosynthesis. Genetic evidence shows that strains lacking moaA do not accumulate the MPT precursor, indicating that MoaA (along with MoaC) is required for the production of the molybdopterin precursor. Moreover, MoaA is one of the two proteins that constitute the MPT‑converting factor (the other being the product of moaD/E). The MoaA protein shares sequence similarity with NifB, FixZ, and a region of formate dehydrogenase‑H, supporting its role in early steps of MPT precursor formation and possibly in binding or processing of the cofactor precursor. {PubMed:8361352}. chlA encodes a protein required for the biosynthesis of molybdopterin (MPT), the organic pterin component of the molybdenum cofactor that is essential for all Mo‑dependent enzymes in Escherichia coli. Mutations in chlA (including the chlA1 allele) abolish cellular MPT production, leading to loss of nitrate reductase, formate dehydrogenase and other Mo enzymes. The chlA protein also participates in an in‑vitro complementation system, providing a factor that can convert a low‑molecular‑weight precursor present in nit‑1 extracts into MPT. {PubMed:2947896}. The chlA gene encodes a factor required for the biosynthesis or provision of a molybdenum cofactor that is essential for the activation of nitrate reductase (and also formate dehydrogenase). In chlA mutants the nitrate reductase subunits are synthesized but remain inactive; precursor polypeptides α' (≈105 kDa) and β' (≈48 kDa) accumulate and fail to be converted into the mature α (≈150 kDa) and β (≈60 kDa) subunits. Thus, chlA is necessary for the conversion of these precursor subunits into functional enzyme components, enabling proper assembly and membrane insertion of active nitrate reductase. {PubMed:6991254}. The chlA gene encodes a soluble protein (referred to as Protein PA) of ~72 kDa that is essential for the activation of nitrate reductase (and also formate dehydrogenase) during the complementation process. Protein PA is not a structural subunit of these enzymes; instead it participates in the post‑translational activation step, most likely by facilitating the insertion of molybdenum into the molybdenum cofactor of the apoproteins, thereby converting the cofactor to its active form. Loss of chlA function results in mutants that contain inactive nitrate reductase and formate dehydrogenase, and the defect can be rescued by adding purified Protein PA, indicating that the chlA product is required for molybdenum incorporation and subsequent enzyme activation. {PubMed:6315066}. chlA is one of the genes required for the synthesis of the molybdenum cofactor. In the study, mutations in chlA (as well as chlB, chlD, and chlE) eliminated the nitrate‑induced expression of the fdhE gene, indicating its role in molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis that is necessary for proper regulation of formate dehydrogenase‑PMS activity. {PubMed:2170340}. The chlA locus encodes the protein PA, a ~72 kDa polypeptide that is required for the in‑vitro activation of the apoprotein form of respiratory nitrate reductase. Protein PA functions by directly interacting with the molybdenum cofactor (MoCo); this interaction stabilises the labile cofactor and creates a competent holo‑enzyme complex that can catalyse nitrate reduction. In chlA mutants the MoCo is severely depleted (≈4 % of wild‑type levels) and protein PA is inactive, leading to loss of activity of all molybdoenzymes. Thus, chlA’s primary role is to provide a MoCo‑binding/activating factor (protein PA) that enables incorporation of the molybdenum cofactor into nitrate reductase and likely other molybdoenzymes. {PubMed:2956990}. The chlA gene is required for molybdopterin (MPT) biosynthesis in Escherichia coli. Mutations in chlA (e.g., chlA1) abolish production of MPT, the organic component of the molybdenum cofactor, leading to loss of nitrate reductase activity. The product of chlA is associated with the “MPT converting factor,” a ~45 kDa protein that catalyzes the conversion of low‑molecular‑weight MPT precursors into true MPT in vitro. Thus, chlA encodes an essential enzyme in the pathway that generates MPT from its precursors, a step distinct from MPT carrier proteins and unrelated to folate or riboflavin biosynthesis. {PubMed:3539912}. chlA (formerly known as moaA) encodes one of the proteins of the moa operon that is essential for molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis in Escherichia coli.  The MoaA protein participates in the early steps of molybdopterin (MPT) synthesis, generating the MPT precursor.  Together with MoaB and MoaC, it forms the ‘MPT‑converting factor’ that produces the pterin backbone of the cofactor.  Mutations in chlA/moaA abolish the formation of the MPT precursor, leading to loss of all molybdoenzyme activities.  Thus, chlA functions as a key enzyme in the biosynthetic pathway that creates the molybdopterin component of the molybdenum cofactor. {PubMed:8361352}. The bisA locus encodes a component required for the reduction of biotin sulphoxide to biotin in Escherichia coli. Mutants lacking bisA are unable to reduce biotin sulphoxide and display markedly low dimethyl sulphoxide (DMSO) reductase activity under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, indicating that bisA also contributes to the enzymatic system that reduces DMSO to dimethyl sulphide. Additionally, the bisA mutant is deficient in nitrate reductase, suggesting that bisA may provide a general reductase component shared among several reductive pathways. {PubMed:347031}.
Curated_Functions: Participates in the early steps of molybdopterin (MPT) biosynthesis, the organic component of the molybdenum cofactor. {PubMed:2947896, PubMed:3539912, PubMed:8361352, PubMed:25896388, PubMed:8588735, PubMed:31235512, PubMed:9044285, PubMed:2170340}. Catalyzes the radical S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine‑dependent conversion of GTP to pyranopterin triphosphate and subsequently to cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate, the first committed step of molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis. {PubMed:25896388, PubMed:8588735, PubMed:31235512}. Loss of function leads to loss of activity of nitrate reductase, formate dehydrogenase and other molybdenum‑dependent enzymes. {PubMed:2947896, PubMed:6991254, PubMed:2170340}. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in sulfur transfer in the conversion of molybdopterin precursor Z to molybdopterin. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17223713}.
Merged_Functions: The product of JW0767 (YnjE) is a three‑domain rhodanese‑like protein that participates in the second step of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis in Escherichia coli. YnjE forms a transient complex with the L‑cysteine desulfurase IscS, the adenylating enzyme MoeB, and the small subunit MoaD of MPT synthase. IscS transfers a persulfide to YnjE, and YnjE then facilitates the transfer of sulfur from IscS to the MoeB‑adenylated MoaD, promoting formation of the C‑terminal thiocarboxylate on MoaD. This action accelerates the conversion of cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (cPMP) to molybdopterin (MPT) without directly enhancing the desulfurase activity of IscS. YnjE therefore acts as a mediator that makes the sulfur‑transfer step of Moco biosynthesis more specific. The protein is found in both the cytoplasm (where it functions in Moco biosynthesis) and the periplasm, although only the cytoplasmic pool is required for its described role. {PubMed:21856748}. MoaD encodes a highly conserved small ubiquitin‑like protein that functions as a sulfur carrier in prokaryotic sulfur‑transfer systems.  In the experiments reported, MoaD was used as a fusion tag for heterologous proteins expressed in *E. coli*.  Fusion of MoaD to target proteins increased their overall expression levels, promoted aggregation of the fusion products by slowing the refolding of the partner protein, and—unlike the related ThiS tag—provided complete protection of an unstable target (murine ribonuclease inhibitor) from intracellular proteolytic degradation. {PubMed:24444081}. MoaD encodes the small subunit of Escherichia coli molybdopterin (MPT) synthase, a heterotetrameric enzyme composed of two MoaD and two MoaE proteins. The C‑terminal glycine of MoaD is modified to a thiocarboxylate (MoA‑SH), which carries the sulfur atoms that are transferred to the desulfo precursor Z during the final step of molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis, forming the cis‑dithiolene moiety of molybdopterin. MoaD must be adenylated by MoeB before thiocarboxylate formation, and a separate sulfur‑transferase supplies the cysteine‑derived sulfur to generate the thiocarboxylate. The thiocarboxylated MoaD inserts its C‑terminus into a pocket of MoaE to create the active site where sulfur transfer and phosphate cleavage occur, and two molecules of MoaD‑SH are required per molecule of precursor Z to produce one MPT. Thus, MoaD functions as the sulfur donor component of MPT synthase essential for converting precursor Z to molybdopterin. {PubMed:12571226}. MoaD encodes the small (≈8.8 kDa) subunit of the heterotetrameric molybdopterin (MPT) synthase complex (two MoaE and two MoaD subunits).  The C‑terminal carboxylate of MoaD is adenylated by the ATP‑dependent enzyme MoeB, forming a MoaD‑adenylate intermediate.  This activated MoaD is then sulfured to generate a C‑terminal thiocarboxylate, which serves as the direct sulfur donor for the synthesis of the dithiolene group of molybdopterin, a key component of the molybdenum cofactor.  After thiocarboxylation, MoaD re‑associates with MoaE to form the active MPT synthase that converts precursor Z into molybdopterin. {PubMed:11463785}. MoaD encodes a small subunit of the Escherichia coli molybdopterin (MPT) synthase complex. In the heterotetrameric MPT synthase, each MoaD protein binds to one MoaE subunit, forming two identical MoaE/MoaD interfaces. The C‑terminal tail of MoaD inserts into a pocket on MoaE, creating an active site at each interface. The carboxy‑terminus of MoaD can be thiocarboxylated (forming MoaD‑SH), and this thiocarboxylate group serves as the source of the two sulfur atoms that are incorporated into the dithiolene moiety of molybdopterin during its biosynthesis. Although the thiocarboxylate is essential for catalytic activity, both the unmodified MoaD and the thiocarboxylated MoaD‑SH can bind MoaE; the thiocarboxylated form binds with higher affinity, reflecting its role in the active MPT synthase complex. After sulfur transfer, the thiocarboxylate must be regenerated (by MoeB‑mediated adenylation followed by conversion to a thiocarboxylate) before MoaD can participate in another round of MPT synthesis. {PubMed:15709772}. MoaD encodes the small subunit of molybdopterin (MPT) synthase in Escherichia coli. It is structurally similar to ubiquitin and, after activation by the MoeB protein and ATP, carries a C‑terminal thiocarboxylate group that serves as the direct sulfur donor for the synthesis of the dithiolene moiety of the molybdenum cofactor (Moco). In the Moco biosynthetic pathway, MoaD is first adenylated by MoeB, then converted to its thiocarboxylated form through a persulfide transfer from the L‑cysteine desulfurase IscS, a process that can be facilitated by the rhodanese‑like protein YnjE. Once thiocarboxylated, MoaD dissociates from MoeB, associates with the large subunit MoaE to form the active MPT synthase heterotetramer, which catalyzes the insertion of two sulfur atoms into cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (cPMP) to produce molybdopterin (MPT). {PubMed:21856748}. MoaD encodes a small (~8.8 kDa) protein that, together with MoaE, constitutes the MPT‑converting factor required for the final step of molybdenum‑cofactor biosynthesis. Genetic evidence shows that mutants lacking MoaD accumulate the molybdopterin precursor, indicating that MoaD is essential for converting this precursor into mature molybdopterin. {PubMed:8361352}. Encodes the MoaB protein, a ~18.7 kDa polypeptide that is part of the moa operon required for molybdenum cofactor (molybdopterin) biosynthesis. MoaB shows sequence similarity to thymidylate synthase and N‑(5′‑phosphoribosyl)anthranilate isomerase, indicating it participates in the early steps that produce the molybdopterin precursor. {PubMed:8361352}. The chlM gene encodes the magnesium‑protoporphyrin IX methyltransferase (Mg‑protoporphyrin IX methyltransferase), a single‑subunit enzyme of ~25–27 kDa that catalyzes the SAM‑dependent methylation of Mg‑protoporphyrin IX to form Mg‑protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester. This reaction follows the Mg‑chelatase step in (bacterio)chlorophyll biosynthesis, converting the Mg‑inserted porphyrin into the methyl‑esterified intermediate required for downstream chlorophyll synthesis. The article demonstrates that recombinant chlM expressed in *E. coli* produces soluble protein that, in vitro, converts Mg‑protoporphyrin IX to its monomethyl ester, as confirmed by fluorescence spectroscopy and HPLC analysis. Co‑expression of chlM with the Mg‑chelatase subunits (chlH, chlI, chlD) enables a coupled conversion of protoporphyrin IX directly to Mg‑protoporphyrin IX monomethyl ester without detectable accumulation of the intermediate Mg‑protoporphyrin IX. {PubMed:10437802}. chlM encodes a factor required for the biosynthesis of molybdopterin (MPT), the organic pterin component of the molybdenum cofactor. Mutations in chlM produce an Mpt⁻ phenotype: cells lack detectable MPT, exhibit severely reduced activities of molybdenum enzymes (nitrate reductase and formate dehydrogenase), are chlorate‑resistant, and cannot grow anaerobically on nitrate‑containing media. Thus, chlM functions as one of the essential genes (along with chlA, chlE, and chlN) that synthesize MPT in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:2947896}. The article describes chlM as a mutant allele that lacks the activity of the molybdopterin (MPT) ‘converting factor’ and consequently accumulates an MPT precursor. This indicates that the wild‑type chlM gene (corresponding to moaA) is required for the conversion of the MPT precursor into mature molybdopterin, a key step in the biosynthesis of the molybdenum cofactor. Thus, chlM functions as part of the MPT‑converting factor, enabling the formation of functional molybdopterin needed for active molybdoenzymes. {PubMed:8361352}.
Curated_Functions: Mediates transfer of sulfur from IscS to MoeB‑adenylated MoaD, accelerating conversion of cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate to molybdopterin in molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis. {PubMed:21856748}. Is localized in both the cytoplasm and periplasm, although only the cytoplasmic pool is required for its role in molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis. {PubMed:21856748}. Acts as the sulfur donor component of molybdopterin synthase, being adenylated by MoeB, thiocarboxylated, and inserting its C‑terminal thiocarboxylate into MoaE to create the active site that transfers two sulfur atoms to precursor Z for molybdopterin formation. {PubMed:12571226, PubMed:11463785, PubMed:15709772, PubMed:21856748}. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Converts molybdopterin precursor Z to molybdopterin. This requires the incorporation of two sulfur atoms into precursor Z to generate a dithiolene group. The sulfur is provided by MoaD.

Merged_Functions: MoaE encodes the larger (~16.9 kDa) subunit of Escherichia coli molybdopterin (MPT) synthase, a heterotetrameric enzyme (α₂β₂) composed of two MoaE and two MoaD proteins.  In this complex MoaE forms a central dimer that creates two active sites at the MoaE‑MoaD interfaces, where the C‑terminal thiocarboxylate of MoaD is positioned for sulfur transfer.  MoaE catalyzes the final step of molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis by converting the pterin precursor Z into molybdopterin.  This reaction involves (i) addition of two sulfur atoms from two molecules of thiocarboxylated MoaD to the C‑1′ and C‑2′ positions of precursor Z, (ii) cleavage of the cyclic phosphate of precursor Z to generate a linear phosphomonoester, and (iii) formation of the characteristic cis‑dithiolene moiety that chelates molybdenum or tungsten.  MoaE functions catalytically; sub‑stoichiometric amounts of MoaE are sufficient for multiple turnover cycles.  Critical active‑site residues identified in the study include Lys‑119 (essential for activity and likely orientates the first thiocarboxylate), Arg‑39 (important for binding/positioning the phosphate of precursor Z), and Lys‑126 (required for the second sulfur transfer or structural rearrangement).  Mutations in these residues markedly reduce or abolish MPT synthase activity.  The protein is conserved across organisms, with the human ortholog MOCS2B performing an equivalent role in molybdopterin biosynthesis. {PubMed:12571226}. MoaE encodes one of the two subunits that form the central dimeric core of the Escherichia coli molybdopterin (MPT) synthase complex.  The MoaE homodimer (each subunit ~16.8 kDa) provides the structural scaffold that binds two MoaD subunits, creating two identical MoaE/MoaD interfaces where the C‑termini of MoaD are buried.  This heterotetrameric enzyme catalyzes the addition of two sulfur atoms to the precursor Z molecule, converting it into molybdopterin, a key component of the molybdenum cofactor required for all molybdenum‑ or tungsten‑containing enzymes.  Thus, MoaE functions as the catalytic platform and binding partner for MoaD (and its thiocarboxylated form MoaD‑SH) in the biosynthesis of the molybdenum cofactor. {PubMed:15709772}. MoaE encodes the large subunit of molybdopterin (MPT) synthase, an essential enzyme in the biosynthesis of the molybdenum cofactor (Moco).  In Escherichia coli, MoaE dimerizes to form a homodimer that associates with two copies of the small subunit MoaD, creating a heterotetrameric MPT synthase complex.  The MoaE subunits provide the active‑site cavity that binds the C‑terminal thiocarboxylate of MoaD and positions the substrate precursor Z for sulfur insertion.  Conserved residues in MoaE (e.g., Lys‑119, Lys‑126, Arg‑39, His‑103′, Arg‑104′, Trp‑125, Trp‑136) line the binding pocket, interact with the phosphate group of precursor Z or product MPT, and are implicated directly in catalysis (Lys‑119 and Lys‑126 are proposed catalytic residues).  By facilitating the transfer of sulfur from the MoaD thiocarboxylate to precursor Z, MoaE enables formation of the dithiolene moiety of molybdopterin, a key step that precedes insertion of molybdenum into the cofactor. {PubMed:12571227}. MoaE is the large subunit of the bacterial molybdopterin (MPT) synthase complex. Together with the small subunit MoaD, it assembles into a heterotetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of precursor Z to molybdopterin (MPT). In this reaction, the C‑terminal thiocarboxylate group of MoaD donates sulfur to precursor Z, forming the dithiolene moiety of MPT. The article describes MoaE as structurally similar to the human MOCS2B protein, forming the active site of the synthase and influencing substrate (precursor Z) binding and overall turnover rate of the enzyme. {PubMed:12732628}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the conversion of precursor Z to molybdopterin, the final step of molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis, by transferring two sulfur atoms from the thiocarboxylated small subunit MoaD, cleaving the cyclic phosphate and forming the cis‑dithiolene moiety that chelates molybdenum or tungsten. {PubMed:12571226, PubMed:15709772, PubMed:12571227, PubMed:12732628}. Forms a homodimer that assembles with two MoaD subunits into a heterotetrameric MPT synthase complex, providing the structural scaffold and catalytic platform that binds MoaD and positions precursor Z for sulfur insertion. {PubMed:12571226, PubMed:15709772, PubMed:12571227, PubMed:12732628}. Requires conserved active‑site residues (Lys‑119, Arg‑39, Lys‑126, His‑103′, Arg‑104′, Trp‑125, Trp‑136) for catalysis and phosphate binding; mutation of these residues markedly reduces or abolishes activity. {PubMed:12571226, PubMed:12571227, PubMed:12732628}. Is conserved across organisms; the human ortholog MOCS2B performs an equivalent role in molybdopterin biosynthesis. {PubMed:12571226}.

Merged_Functions: Encodes the ATP‑binding cassette (ABC) ATPase subunit (proposed to be renamed MetN) of the MetD D‑methionine transport system. Abc provides the energy‑coupling activity for the ABC transporter that imports D‑methionine (and also L‑methionine) into Escherichia coli. It functions together with YaeE (MetI), the membrane‑spanning permease, and YaeC (MetQ), the periplasmic substrate‑binding protein, to form a complete ABC transporter. The protein contains the conserved Walker A, ABC signature, and Walker B motifs characteristic of ABC ATPases. Deletion of abc abolishes or severely reduces growth on low concentrations of D‑methionine, confirming its role in D‑methionine uptake. Expression of abc is up‑regulated when methionine is scarce and is repressed by the MetJ regulator. {PubMed:12218041}. Encodes the proteobacterial chondroitin ABC lyase (ChSase), a secreted enzyme that catalyzes β‑elimination of the 1,4‑hexosaminidic bonds in chondroitin sulfate, chondroitin‑4‑sulfate (chondroitin A), dermatan sulfate (chondroitin B), chondroitin‑6‑sulfate (chondroitin C) and hyaluronate. Merged_Functions: The mfd gene encodes the transcription‑repair coupling factor (TRCF), also called Mfd protein. Mfd binds to RNA polymerase (RNAP) that is stalled at a DNA lesion on the template strand, removes the blocked RNAP, and then recruits the nucleotide excision repair (NER) proteins UvrA (and subsequently UvrB) to the damage site. This coupling accelerates repair of transcription‑blocking lesions, especially those poorly recognized by global NER such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers. Mfd contains an N‑terminal UvrA‑interaction module (domains D1A‑D2‑D1B), a central RNAP‑interacting domain (RID, residues 379‑571), and C‑terminal helicase‑motif domains (D5‑D6) that bind ATP and DNA and provide a latent translocase activity. Upon binding stalled RNAP, Mfd undergoes conformational opening, binds ATP, engages upstream DNA, and uses ATP hydrolysis to translocate DNA, collapse the transcription bubble, and dissociate RNA and RNAP from the template. The RNAP‑Mfd complex then presents a high‑affinity binding site for UvrA, allowing a 2UvrA‑1UvrB complex to be delivered to the lesion, after which normal NER incisions occur. Mfd also influences mutation frequency decline, UV sensitivity, and various cellular processes that involve removal of stalled RNAP. {PubMed:27864884}. Encodes the transcription‑repair coupling factor (TRCF), also called Mfd translocase. Mfd binds both RNA polymerase (RNAP) and the NER factor UvrA. When RNAP stalls at a DNA lesion, Mfd recognizes the stalled complex, uses its translocase activity to displace the RNAP, and recruits the UvrA₂UvrB₁ complex to the damage site. This coupling accelerates nucleotide excision repair of lesions on the transcribed strand, increasing the repair rate of the transcribed strand by roughly five‑fold. The article demonstrates that loss of mfd abolishes transcription‑coupled repair genome‑wide and in the lacZ operon, establishing Mfd as necessary and sufficient for transcription‑coupled repair in *E. coli*. {PubMed:28986449}. Mfd is a highly conserved bacterial DNA‑dependent translocase that acts on RNA polymerase (RNAP) stalled during transcription.  It recognizes RNAP arrested at bulky DNA lesions or other obstacles, binds to DNA upstream of the polymerase (requiring ~25 bp of free DNA), and uses its ATPase/translocase activity to push the enzyme forward or to displace it entirely from the template.  This displacement exposes the DNA lesion to the nucleotide‑excision‑repair machinery, and Mfd recruits the NER factor UvrA, thereby coupling transcription to DNA repair in the transcription‑coupled repair (TCR) pathway.  Beyond DNA repair, Mfd can move extensively back‑tracked RNAP forward, rescue arrested transcription complexes, or trigger transcription termination when the obstacle cannot be cleared.  In vitro reconstitution experiments show that Mfd can alleviate replication stalling by removing a head‑on RNAP, allowing the replisome to progress.  In vivo, Mfd reduces double‑strand breaks at co‑directional replication‑transcription conflicts involving back‑tracked RNAP, but it does not appear to resolve head‑on conflicts, likely because high RNAP density or R‑loops impede its access.  Moreover, Mfd promotes mutagenesis at head‑on genes, probably through error‑prone repair associated with its TCR activity.  Overall, Mfd functions as an RNAP‑associated factor that remodels stalled transcription complexes, links transcription to DNA repair, and modulates the outcomes of replication‑transcription conflicts. {PubMed:31311770}. Mfd is a DNA‑dependent ATPase that functions primarily in transcription‑coupled DNA repair. It recognizes RNA polymerase (RNAP) that has stalled on DNA, binds the upstream surface of RNAP, and, using its ATP‑driven DNA translocase activity, pushes the enzyme forward along the DNA. This forward translocation can rescue back‑tracked complexes by restoring the RNA 3′ end to the active site, or, when elongation cannot resume, it collapses the elongation complex and releases the nascent transcript, thereby removing RNAP from the DNA. In addition to displacing RNAP, Mfd recruits the nucleotide‑excision repair machinery by binding the UvrA protein. The protein contains seven domains that mediate RNAP β‑subunit binding, UvrA interaction, and DNA translocation, and it requires about 25 bp of upstream DNA for activity. {PubMed:30978344}. Encodes the transcription‑repair coupling factor (TRCF) in *Escherichia coli*. Mfd binds to RNA polymerase that has stalled at a DNA lesion on the transcribed strand, releases the stalled polymerase and the nascent RNA (Rho‑factor‑like activity), and recruits the nucleotide‑excision repair machinery (UvrA‑UvrB‑UvrC) to the damage site. This targeting directs the excision nuclease to lesions encountered during transcription, ensuring preferential (strand‑specific) repair of the template strand and contributing to the “mutation‑frequency decline” phenomenon that lowers UV‑induced mutation rates in the transcribed strand. Mutants lacking mfd show slower removal of UV photoproducts, moderate UV sensitivity, and an increased overall mutation rate. {PubMed:8393197}.

Merged_Functions: The b1019 gene encodes a polyphosphate kinase‑like protein that was originally annotated as a PPK2 but, based on sequence similarity to the other R. eutropha PPK (A2437), is now considered a type‑1 polyphosphate kinase (designated PPK1b_Reu).  In vivo fluorescence tagging showed that the B1019 protein forms distinct foci at one cell pole rather than co‑localising with polyphosphate granules, and deletion of b1019 alone does not impair polyP granule formation.  Thus, B1019 is a PPK‑type enzyme that localises to the cell pole and is not essential for the synthesis of polyP granules, suggesting a yet‑undefined role in phosphate metabolism distinct from the primary polyP‑synthesising enzymes (PPK1a_Reu and PPK2c_Reu). {PubMed:26407880}. EfeB/YcdB is a Tat‑dependent hemoprotein that binds heme in a large hydrophobic pocket and functions as a deferrochelatase, extracting iron from heme without cleaving the tetrapyrrole ring and producing protoporphyrin IX (PPIX).  It also displays modest guaiacol (and catechol) peroxidase activity at acidic pH, characteristic of the dye‑decolorizing peroxidase (DyP) family, but with unique catalytic features (e.g., Asp235 can be mutated without loss of guaiacol activity).  The protein is up‑regulated under iron‑deficient and low‑pH conditions and contributes to bacterial iron acquisition, making it a potential target for antimicrobial drugs.  Structurally, it contains an N‑terminal and C‑terminal domain linked by a flexible “switch loop” that forms a tunnel for an unidentified cofactor/substrate.  Binding of PPIX to EfeB markedly enhances fluorescence (excitation ~407.5 nm, emission ~622.5 nm), suggesting its use as a red‑fluorescent marker. {PubMed:21324904}. YcdB (also called EfeB) is a periplasmic, b‑type haem‑containing protein that is exported via the twin‑arginine (Tat) pathway. Structural studies place it in the haem peroxidase superfamily, and it exhibits low‑pH‑enhanced peroxidase activity. Within the ycdNOB (efeUOB) operon, YcdB works together with the membrane permease YcdN (EfeU) and the periplasmic cupredoxin‑like protein YcdO (EfeO) to form a tripartite ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) transporter that functions best under acidic, aerobic conditions. Although its exact catalytic role is not fully resolved, YcdB is thought to act as a ferroxidase—analogous to the multicopper oxidase Fet3p in yeast—facilitating the uptake of Fe²⁺ by oxidizing or otherwise processing iron during transport. All three components (EfeU, EfeO, and EfeB) are required for full EfeUOB activity. {PubMed:17627767}. EfeB (also called YcdB) is a bacterial enzyme that belongs to the dye‑decolorizing peroxidase (DyP) family but displays unique activities. It acts as a deferrochelatase, extracting iron from heme without cleaving the tetrapyrrole ring and releasing protoporphyrin IX (PPIX). This activity contributes to iron acquisition in Escherichia coli, especially under iron‑limiting or low‑pH conditions, and is linked to pathogenicity. In addition to deferrochelation, EfeB exhibits modest peroxidase activity, oxidizing substrates such as guaiacol and catechol in the presence of H₂O₂, with activity dependent on key residues (e.g., Asp235, His329, Arg347). The protein forms homodimers, contains a heme‑binding pocket in its C‑terminal domain, and possesses a flexible “switch loop” that creates a tunnel for an unidentified cofactor/substrate. The EfeB‑PPIX complex shows enhanced red fluorescence, making the protein useful as a fluorescent marker. {PubMed:21324904}. EfeB encodes a periplasmic member of the dye‑decolorizing peroxidase (DyP) family that binds heme and protoporphyrin IX.  It catalyzes a novel "deferrochelation" reaction in which iron is removed from heme while the tetrapyrrole ring remains intact, converting heme to protoporphyrin IX (PPIX).  This activity provides the bacterium with iron from exogenous heme sources, making EfeB the sole protein capable of retrieving iron from heme in the periplasm of Escherichia coli.  EfeB is exported by the twin‑arginine translocation (Tat) system, can functionally complement the cytoplasmic paralog YfeX, and works together with inner‑membrane iron transport systems (e.g., DppABCDF or the EfeUOB operon) to deliver the liberated iron to the cytoplasm.  Thus, its physiological role is to enable heme‑derived iron acquisition without degrading the porphyrin ring. {PubMed:19564607}. The efeb gene encodes the bacterial dye‑decolorizing peroxidase BaDyP, a heme‑containing peroxidase that catalyzes oxidative degradation of lignin model compounds and synthetic dyes. BaDyP cleaves the β‑O‑4 ether bond and the Cα‑Cβ bond of the phenolic lignin dimer guaiacylglycerol‑β‑guaiacyl ether (GGE), oxidizes the Cα position, and converts GGE into guaiacol, vanillyl alcohol, and vanillin without requiring external mediators. In addition, BaDyP decolorizes azo (congo red, eriochrome black T) and triphenylmethane (bromine cresol green, crystal violet) dyes in the presence of H₂O₂, achieving up to ~80 % decolorization after 72 h at pH 4.5 and 30 °C. Thus, efeb functions as the genetic determinant for a peroxidase with lignin‑degrading and dye‑decolorizing activities. {PubMed:31134460}. EfeB is a periplasmic, haem‑containing, peroxidase‑like protein that forms part of the three‑component EfeUOB ferrous‑iron transporter in Escherichia coli. Together with the inner‑membrane permease EfeU and the periplasmic cupredoxin‑like protein EfeO, EfeB is required for high‑affinity Fe²⁺ uptake, especially under acidic, aerobic, iron‑limited conditions. Deletion of efeB abolishes the growth advantage conferred by the EfeUOB system, indicating that EfeB is essential for its iron‑transport activity, likely acting as a ferroxidase or redox catalyst that facilitates iron translocation across the periplasm. {PubMed:17627767}. The JW1004 strain carries a disruption of the *efeB* gene (efeB::Km). According to the article, *efeB* encodes EfeB, a member of the dye‑decolorizing peroxidase (Dyp‑peroxidase) family that is exported to the periplasm via the twin‑arginine translocation (Tat) system. EfeB binds heme and protoporphyrin IX (PPIX) with nanomolar affinity and catalyzes a novel “deferrochelation” reaction: it extracts the ferrous iron from heme while leaving the tetrapyrrole ring intact, converting heme into PPIX (and meso‑heme into meso‑PPIX). This activity provides E. coli with a means to acquire iron from exogenous heme without degrading the porphyrin ring, making EfeB (together with its paralog YfeX) the sole proteins able to retrieve iron from heme in the studied strains. Deletion of *efeB* (as in JW1004) reduces the ability of the bacterium to grow using heme as an iron source, confirming its essential role in heme‑iron acquisition. {PubMed:19564607}.

CaiT is a highly hydrophobic, 504‑amino‑acid inner‑membrane protein of Escherichia coli that belongs to the betaine/carnitine/choline transporter (BCCT) family. Functional studies with intact cells, purified protein, and proteoliposomes demonstrate that CaiT operates as an antiporter (exchanger) rather than an ion‑coupled symporter. The transport does not require an electrochemical H⁺ or Na⁺ gradient and is not stimulated by increased medium osmolality, distinguishing it from other BCCT members. Substrate binding induces conformational changes detectable by tryptophan fluorescence; the affinity measured by fluorescence (K₀.₅ ≈ 2 mM for L‑carnitine) reflects the requirement for a trimethylammonium group and a carboxylate at a specific distance. Encodes the enzyme crotonobetainyl‑/γ‑butyrobetainyl‑CoA:carnitine CoA‑transferase (CaiB), a homodimeric class III CoA‑transferase that catalyzes the first step of the Escherichia coli carnitine degradation pathway. CaiB transfers the CoA moiety from crotonobetainyl‑CoA (or γ‑butyrobetainyl‑CoA) to free L‑carnitine, producing crotonobetaine and carnitinyl‑CoA, which are subsequently converted to γ‑butyrobetaine. The enzyme is part of the caiTABCDE operon, expressed under anaerobic, carnitine‑induced conditions, and belongs to the PF02515 family. Catalysis involves a key Asp169 residue that forms a transient anhydride intermediate, and CoA binding induces a ~15° rotation of the small domain relative to the large domain. {PubMed:15823031}. CaiB encodes a 45 kDa crotonobetainyl‑CoA:carnitine CoA‑transferase that catalyzes the reversible transfer of the CoA moiety between β‑inyl‑CoA derivatives (crotonobetainyl‑CoA, γ‑butyrobetainyl‑CoA, and L‑carnitinyl‑CoA) and the corresponding free betaines (crotonobetaine, γ‑butyrobetaine, and L‑carnitine). In the hydration pathway of crotonobetaine to L‑carnitine, CaiB works together with the hydratase CaiD: CaiD first hydrates crotonobetainyl‑CoA to L‑carnitinyl‑CoA, and CaiB then transfers CoA from L‑carnitinyl‑CoA to L‑carnitine (or from crotonobetainyl‑CoA/γ‑butyrobetainyl‑CoA to the free betaines), completing the conversion of crotonobetaine to L‑carnitine. The enzyme shows high specificity for CoA derivatives of trimethylammonium compounds and functions optimally when present at a 4:1 (CaiB:CaiD) ratio with crotonobetainyl‑CoA as cosubstrate (5:1 with γ‑butyrobetainyl‑CoA). Sequence analysis places CaiB in a new CoA‑transferase/CoA‑hydrolase family, sharing N‑terminal similarity with enzymes such as FldA, BaiF, Frc, and BbsE. {PubMed:11551212}. caiB encodes the enzyme carnitine dehydratase, which catalyzes the anaerobic dehydration of L‑(−)‑carnitine to crotonobetaine. This reaction is the first step in the E. coli carnitine catabolic pathway, providing an external electron acceptor for anaerobic growth. The activity of the CaiB protein determines the level of carnitine dehydratase activity in the cell and is regulated indirectly by the transcriptional activator CaiF and other global regulators (CRP, FNR, H‑NS, NarL, etc.). {PubMed:8631699}. CaiB is a type III acyl‑CoA transferase that catalyzes the formation of glutaryl‑CoA from glutarate by transferring CoA from succinyl‑CoA to glutarate. In Agrobacterium tumefaciens this reaction supplies the glutaryl‑CoA primer required by the BioZ enzyme for condensation with malonyl‑ACP, ultimately producing pimeloyl‑ACP for biotin (vitamin H) synthesis. Deletion of caiB causes biotin auxotrophy, confirming its essential role in providing the glutaryl‑CoA substrate for the biotin‑pimelate biosynthetic pathway. {PubMed:33154364}. The caiB gene encodes the L(-)-carnitine dehydratase enzyme (component I of the crotonobetaine reductase complex). The protein is a homodimer (~86 kDa native, 42.6 kDa per subunit) with an isoelectric point of 4.3. It catalyzes the dehydration of L(-)-carnitine, producing crotonobetaine, and requires a low‑molecular‑mass cofactor for activity. In the crotonobetaine reductase system, CaiB (component I) works together with the FAD‑containing component II (CaiA) to reduce crotonobetaine to γ‑butyrobetaine. {PubMed:10209289}. The b0038 gene (named caiB in the article) encodes the enzyme L‑(−)-carnitine dehydratase (CDHT). CDHT catalyzes the dehydration of L‑(−)-carnitine to crotonobetaine, the first step in the anaerobic carnitine degradation pathway of Escherichia coli. The enzyme is inducible under anaerobic growth conditions when L‑(−)-carnitine or crotonobetaine is present. It functions as part of a putative cai operon that includes at least one upstream gene, and its activity requires an as‑yet unidentified low‑molecular‑weight cofactor that is produced only under anaerobic, carnitine‑inducing conditions. {PubMed:8188598}. The product of b0038 (named caiF in the article) is a small (~15 kDa) protein that acts as a transcriptional activator of the carnitine‑degradation pathway in Escherichia coli. CaiF is expressed as a monocistronic mRNA under anaerobic conditions, independent of carnitine presence, and its promoter contains CRP, FNR, RpoN (σ⁵⁴) and NarL binding sites. Overproduction of CaiF markedly increases transcription of the divergent caiTABCDE and fixABCX operons, leading to a 8‑ to 17‑fold rise in carnitine dehydratase activity. Consequently, CaiF is required for the induction of these operons by L‑(−)‑carnitine (or crotonobetaine) during anaerobic growth. The gene is negatively regulated by H‑NS and σ^S (RpoS), and its activity can be repressed by glucose, oxygen, nitrate, or the pathway end‑product γ‑butyrobetaine. Mutation or loss of caiF (b0038) results in a regulatory defect where the cai and fix operons are not induced, which can be complemented in trans by multicopy caiF. Thus, b0038 encodes a key regulatory protein that positively controls expression of the enzymes required for carnitine metabolism under anaerobic conditions. {PubMed:8631699}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Protein and nucleotide deglycase that catalyzes the deglycation of the Maillard adducts formed between amino groups of proteins or nucleotides and reactive carbonyl groups of glyoxals (PubMed:26102038, PubMed:26774339, PubMed:28596309). Thus, functions as a protein deglycase that repairs methylglyoxal- and glyoxal-glycated proteins, and releases repaired proteins and lactate or glycolate, respectively. Deglycates cysteine, arginine and lysine residues in proteins, and thus reactivates these proteins by reversing glycation by glyoxals. Is able to repair glycated serum albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and fructose biphosphate aldolase. Acts on early glycation intermediates (hemithioacetals and aminocarbinols), preventing the formation of Schiff bases and advanced glycation endproducts (AGE) that cause irreversible damage (PubMed:26102038, PubMed:26774339). Also functions as a nucleotide deglycase able to repair glycated guanine in the free nucleotide pool (GTP, GDP, GMP, dGTP) and in DNA and RNA. Is thus involved in a major nucleotide repair system named guanine glycation repair (GG repair), dedicated to reversing methylglyoxal and glyoxal damage via nucleotide sanitization and direct nucleic acid repair (PubMed:28596309). Has been reported to display chaperone, peptidase and glutathione-independent glyoxalase activities (PubMed:12235139, PubMed:12565879, PubMed:14731284, PubMed:15550391, PubMed:21696459, PubMed:7848303). However, these apparently disparate activities are all recruited to execute its protein deglycase primary function (PubMed:26102038, PubMed:26774339). Plays an important role in protecting cells from carbonyl stress, severe heat shock and starvation, as well as in acid resistance of stationary-phase cells (PubMed:12235139, PubMed:16796689, PubMed:17158627). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12235139, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12565879, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14731284, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15550391, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16796689, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17158627, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21696459, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26102038, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26774339, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28596309, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7848303}.
