Merged_Functions: The ogt gene encodes the constitutive O⁶‑alkylguanine‑DNA alkyltransferase (AGT) enzyme in Escherichia coli. This enzyme repairs DNA lesions at the O⁶ position of guanine, such as O⁶‑chloroethylguanine formed after treatment with chloroethylating anticancer drugs (e.g., ACNU and BCNU), by transferring the alkyl group from the damaged base to a cysteine residue in the protein, thereby restoring the normal guanine and preventing GC→AT transition mutations. Loss of ogt (together with ada) eliminates AGT activity and leads to increased mutagenesis from O⁶‑chloroethylguanine, demonstrating its role in lesion repair. {PubMed:30988834}. Ogt encodes an O6‑alkylguanine DNA alkyltransferase (MGMT) that directly repairs O6‑alkyl‑2′‑deoxyguanosine (O6‑alkyl‑dG) lesions in Escherichia coli.  It removes the alkyl group from the O6 position of guanine by transferring it to a cysteine residue in the protein, thereby restoring the normal base and inactivating the enzyme.  Ogt is constitutively expressed at a basal level that is about ten‑fold higher than the inducible Ada protein, and it is more efficient than Ada at repairing O6‑alkyl‑dG lesions bearing larger alkyl groups.  Deletion of ogt leads to markedly increased G→A mutation frequencies for these lesions, indicating its key role in preventing mutagenesis caused by O6‑alkyl‑dG adducts. {PubMed:30068548}. The ogt gene encodes a constitutive DNA‑repair alkyltransferase (ATase) that removes alkyl groups from O⁶‑alkylguanine (including O⁶‑methylguanine and bulkier O⁶‑ethyl/​butylguanine) and O⁴‑alkylthymine residues in DNA. Unlike the Ada protein, ogt is expressed at a low basal level (~30 molecules per cell) and is not inducible by adaptive response. It acts as a suicide enzyme, transferring the alkyl group to itself. The enzyme is especially efficient at repairing larger ethylation products, thereby preventing mutagenesis caused by low levels of such agents; it also provides additional resistance to mutation by low doses of methylating agents, particularly in an ada‑deficient background. Its activity is crucial for in vivo removal of O⁶‑alkylguanine lesions when nucleotide excision repair is absent. {PubMed:1600955}. Ogt encodes an O6‑alkylguanine‑DNA alkyltransferase that contributes to the direct repair of certain O4‑alkyldT DNA lesions in Escherichia coli.  In the study, Ogt was shown to efficiently remove the alkyl group from O4‑methyl‑dT (O4‑MedT) and, to a lesser extent, from O4‑ethyl‑dT (O4‑EtdT) and O4‑n‑propyl‑dT (O4‑nPrdT).  This repair activity reduces the mutagenic T→C transition caused by these lesions.  By contrast, Ogt does not repair other O4‑alkyldT lesions (e.g., those with larger or branched alkyl groups), and the related protein Ada was found not to be involved in repairing any of the O4‑alkyldT lesions examined. {PubMed:26400162}. The article states that ogt encodes O6‑methylguanine‑DNA methyltransferase, a DNA repair protein. It is located downstream of the abg genes and may be part of the same operon, although its specific role in the p‑aminobenzoyl‑glutamate pathway was not experimentally characterized in this study. {PubMed:17307853}. The ogt gene encodes an O⁶‑alkylguanine DNA alkyltransferase, a DNA repair enzyme that removes alkyl groups from chemically damaged guanine residues (O⁶‑alkylguanine) in DNA. This activity protects the cell from genotoxic effects caused by reactive nitrogen species and other alkylating agents, providing a prophylactic defense against DNA damage associated with nitrate metabolism. {PubMed:19245365}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the transfer of alkyl groups from O⁶‑alkylguanine lesions in DNA to its own cysteine residue, restoring the normal base and preventing GC→AT (G→A) transition mutations. {PubMed:30988834, PubMed:30068548, PubMed:1600955}. Removes alkyl groups from O⁴‑alkylthymine lesions (O⁴‑methyl‑dT, O⁴‑ethyl‑dT and O⁴‑n‑propyl‑dT) in DNA, thereby reducing T→C transition mutations. {PubMed:1600955, PubMed:26400162}. Provides resistance to mutagenesis caused by alkylating agents, especially larger ethylation products and low doses of methylating agents, and is essential for lesion removal when nucleotide excision repair is absent. {PubMed:30988834, PubMed:30068548, PubMed:1600955}. Is expressed constitutively at a low basal level (~30 molecules per cell), about ten‑fold higher than the inducible Ada protein, and is not up‑regulated by the adaptive response. {PubMed:30068548, PubMed:1600955}. Protects cells from genotoxic damage induced by reactive nitrogen species and nitrate‑metabolism‑related alkylating agents. {PubMed:19245365}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex OppABCDF involved in the uptake of oligopeptides and of the ABC transporter complex MppA-OppBCDF involved in the uptake of the cell wall murein tripeptide L-alanyl-gamma-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelate (PubMed:9495761). Probably responsible for the translocation of the substrate across the membrane (Probable). Plays an important nutritional role and is involved in the recycling of cell wall peptides (PubMed:9495761). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:9495761, ECO:0000305}.
Merged_Functions: Encodes OppB, the trans‑membrane subunit of the Escherichia coli OppABCDF oligopeptide ABC transporter. OppB partners with OppC (and the ATP‑binding subunits OppD/F) to form the membrane‑embedded channel that enables import of extracellular oligopeptides (typically 5–35 amino acids) into the cytoplasm. As part of this multi‑subunit transporter, OppB contributes to nutrient acquisition, cell‑to‑cell communication, and resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides by mediating peptide translocation across the inner membrane. {PubMed:31704256}. OppB encodes a trans‑membrane protein that is one of the two integral membrane subunits of the E. coli OppABCDF ABC‑type oligopeptide transporter. Together with the partner subunit OppC, OppB forms the membrane channel through which oligopeptides are imported from the periplasm into the cytoplasm, a process driven by the ATP‑hydrolyzing subunits OppD and OppF. The article highlights OppB as a low‑abundance, membrane‑bound component whose expression is tightly regulated at the transcriptional level, and notes that it is detectable only by specific immunoblotting or when expressed from its native promoter fused to a reporter. {PubMed:31704256}. oppB is one of the genes of the trp‑linked opp operon that encodes the Escherichia coli oligopeptide permease, a multicomponent, binding‑protein‑dependent transport system responsible for the uptake of extracellular peptides (used as carbon and nitrogen sources). Transcription of oppB, like that of oppA and oppD, is induced by the presence of L‑leucine or L‑alanine in the growth medium and by anaerobic conditions, leading to increased synthesis of the permease complex and enhanced peptide transport. {PubMed:3080404}. OppB encodes one of the two highly hydrophobic integral membrane proteins (OppB and OppC) that constitute the membrane‑spanning core of the Salmonella typhimurium oligopeptide permease (Opp) ABC transporter. Together with OppC, OppB forms the channel through which oligopeptides are translocated across the cytoplasmic membrane. The protein spans the membrane six times, with both its N‑ and C‑termini located on the cytoplasmic side, and contains periplasmic loops that likely interact with the periplasmic peptide‑binding protein OppA. OppB works in concert with the cytoplasmic ATP‑binding subunits OppD and OppF, which provide the energy for transport by ATP hydrolysis, thereby enabling uptake of peptides up to six residues in length and recycling of cell‑wall peptides. {PubMed:1738314}. oppB encodes one of the membrane permease components (OppB) of the ABC‑type oligopeptide transporter operon in Xenorhabdus nematophila. Together with OppC, OppD, and OppF, OppB forms the channel that translocates short peptides (2–6 amino acids) from the periplasm into the cytoplasm after they have been bound by the periplasmic peptide‑binding proteins OppA1 or OppA2. Disruption of oppB abolishes transcription of downstream permease genes, eliminates uptake of leucine‑containing tripeptides, and leads to slower growth in peptide‑rich laboratory medium and in insect hemolymph, although it does not prevent colonization of nematode or insect hosts. {PubMed:15345451}. OppB is one of the two integral membrane subunits of the Escherichia coli oligopeptide permease (Opp) system. Together with OppC, it forms the transmembrane pore through which oligopeptides are transported across the inner membrane. In vivo interaction studies showed that OppB directly interacts with OppC and also contacts the ATP‑binding components OppD and OppF, placing it at the center of the protein‑protein interaction network of the Opp complex. Thus, OppB functions as a core membrane component essential for assembling the functional peptide uptake channel. {PubMed:26782429}. The article states that oppB is a component of the opp operon, which encodes an ATP‑dependent oligopeptide transporter belonging to the ABC (ATP‑binding cassette) superfamily. OppB is described as an integral membrane component of this ABC transporter. In the CTAB‑resistant mutant OW66, a mutation (oppB66) involving insertion of an IS186 element was identified, and the authors suggest that the OppB66 variant may cooperate with other mutations (e.g., rpoN66) to contribute to the overall resistance to the antimicrobial surfactant cetyltrimethylammonium bromide. {PubMed:20480162}. OppB is an integral membrane protein that forms part of the oligopeptide permease (Opp) system. Together with the partner membrane protein OppC, it creates the transmembrane channel through which peptide substrates are transported into the cell. The substrate‑binding proteins (OppA variants) deliver peptides to this channel, and the transport process is powered by the ATP‑binding proteins OppD and OppF. Thus, OppB functions as a core component of the peptide import machinery, enabling uptake of external peptides for nutritional use. {PubMed:11341969}.
Curated_Functions: Forms the membrane channel with OppC that imports extracellular oligopeptides (typically 5–35 amino acids) into the cytoplasm. {PubMed:31704256, PubMed:1738314, PubMed:11341969, PubMed:26782429}. Mediates translocation of short peptides (2–6 residues) across the inner membrane, enabling nutrient acquisition and recycling of cell‑wall peptides. {PubMed:1738314, PubMed:15345451}. Contributes to resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides. {PubMed:31704256}. Confers resistance to the antimicrobial surfactant cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB). {PubMed:20480162}. Is transcriptionally up‑regulated by L‑leucine, L‑alanine and anaerobic conditions, enhancing peptide transport. {PubMed:3080404}. Directly interacts with OppC and contacts the ATP‑binding subunits OppD and OppF, essential for assembly of the functional peptide‑uptake complex. {PubMed:26782429}. Possesses six transmembrane helices with periplasmic loops that likely engage the periplasmic peptide‑binding protein OppA. {PubMed:1738314}. Loss of oppB abolishes transcription of downstream permease genes, eliminates uptake of leucine‑containing tripeptides and impairs growth in peptide‑rich media and insect hemolymph. {PubMed:15345451}.

Probably responsible for the translocation of the substrate across the membrane (Probable). Plays an important nutritional role and is involved in the recycling of cell wall peptides (PubMed:9495761). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:9495761, ECO:0000305}.
Merged_Functions: OppC encodes the transmembrane component of the Escherichia coli oligopeptide permease (Opp) system. It partners with OppB to form the inner‑membrane pore that mediates uptake of oligopeptides. Deletion of oppC eliminates peptide uptake, indicating that OppC is essential for oligopeptide import but not required for cell viability. In vivo GFP‑fragment reassembly assays demonstrate that OppC directly interacts with OppB and also with the ATP‑binding subunits OppD and OppF, placing it at the core of the Opp protein‑protein interaction network. {PubMed:26782429}. OppC encodes one of the two highly hydrophobic integral membrane components of the Salmonella typhimurium oligopeptide permease (Opp) ABC transporter. Together with OppB, OppC forms the transmembrane channel that mediates the passage of oligopeptides (up to six amino‑acid residues) from the periplasm into the cytoplasm. The protein spans the cytoplasmic membrane six times, with both its N‑ and C‑termini located on the cytoplasmic side, and contains periplasmic loops that likely interact with the periplasmic peptide‑binding protein OppA. Energy for transport is provided by the ATP‑binding subunits OppD and OppF, which associate with the cytoplasmic loops of OppC. {PubMed:1738314}. The article identifies oppC as one of the two integral membrane subunits of the Escherichia coli OppABCDF oligopeptide transporter. Together with OppB, OppC forms the transmembrane channel component of this ABC‑type transporter that mediates the uptake of extracellular oligopeptides into the cell. The study notes that OppC is expressed at lower levels than the periplasmic binding protein OppA and the other membrane subunit OppB, reflecting its role as a membrane‑embedded part of the peptide import system. {PubMed:31704256}. The article predicts that oppC encodes a membrane protein homologous to the C‑terminal region of the Salmonella typhimurium oligopeptide permease component OppC, suggesting it functions as part of an oligopeptide transport system. However, no transcript was detected under the tested conditions, leaving its actual expression and activity uncertain. {PubMed:8905234}. OppC encodes an integral membrane protein that is a core component of the oligopeptide permease (Opp) ABC transporter. In the Opp system, OppC partners with the second membrane protein OppB to form the transmembrane channel that allows peptide substrates, which are first captured by the periplasmic binding protein OppA, to be translocated across the cytoplasmic membrane. Peptide transport through this channel is powered by the ATP‑binding proteins OppD and OppF. {PubMed:11341969}. oppC encodes one of the membrane permease subunits of the ABC-type oligopeptide transporter (Opp) in Xenorhabdus nematophila. Together with OppB, OppD, and OppF, it forms the permease complex that translocates short peptides (2–6 amino acids) from the periplasm into the cytoplasm after they have been bound by the periplasmic peptide‑binding proteins OppA1 or OppA2. The operon containing oppC was shown to be functional in peptide‑feeding assays, indicating that OppC contributes to oligopeptide uptake used as a nutrient source, although this transport activity is not essential for the bacterium’s mutualistic or pathogenic interactions with its nematode and insect hosts. {PubMed:15345451}.
Curated_Functions: Forms a transmembrane channel together with OppB that mediates uptake of periplasmic oligopeptides (2–6 amino acids) into the cytoplasm. {PubMed:26782429, PubMed:1738314, PubMed:11341969, PubMed:15345451, PubMed:31704256}. Interacts directly with the membrane subunit OppB and the ATP‑binding subunits OppD and OppF, placing OppC at the core of the Opp protein‑protein interaction network. {PubMed:26782429}. Provides periplasmic loops that likely bind the peptide‑binding protein OppA. {PubMed:1738314}. Couples peptide transport to ATP hydrolysis by associating with the cytoplasmic loops of the ATP‑binding proteins OppD and OppF, which supply the energy for translocation. {PubMed:1738314, PubMed:11341969}. Contributes to oligopeptide acquisition as a nutrient source, although its loss does not affect cell viability or the bacterium’s mutualistic and pathogenic interactions. {PubMed:26782429, PubMed:15345451}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: This protein is a positive regulator for the phosphate regulon. Transcription of this operon is positively regulated by PhoB and PhoR when phosphate is limited.
Merged_Functions: phoB encodes a positive regulatory protein that is essential for transcription of the alkaline phosphatase gene (phoA) and other genes of the phosphate (pho) regulon in Escherichia coli. The PhoB protein activates expression of these genes when cells experience phosphate limitation. Its own expression is also induced by phosphate starvation and is constitutively high in mutants lacking the negative regulators phoR, phoS, phoT, or phoU, while it is very low in a phoR‑phoM double mutant. Thus, PhoB functions as a transcriptional activator whose synthesis is positively controlled by the PhoR and PhoM proteins and negatively influenced, directly or indirectly, by PhoR, PhoS, PhoT, and PhoU. {PubMed:6310121}. PhoB is the response regulator of the PhoR/PhoB two‑component system that controls the phosphate regulon (pho) in Escherichia coli. According to the article, PhoB acts as the transcriptional activator for phosphate‑starvation‑inducible genes, including psiE. It becomes active when phosphorylated by the histidine kinase PhoR, which senses extracellular phosphate levels. Activated (phospho‑PhoB) binds to conserved 7‑bp direct repeat sequences called pho boxes located immediately upstream of pho regulon promoters. Binding of PhoB to these sites facilitates interaction with the σ⁷⁰ subunit of RNA polymerase, thereby stimulating transcription initiation. Thus, PhoB directly mediates positive regulation of genes required for phosphate acquisition and metabolism under low‑phosphate conditions. {PubMed:10986267}. PhoB is a member of the OmpR/PhoB family of response regulators. Its N‑terminal receiver (REC) domain accepts a phosphoryl group, and phosphorylation promotes dimerization of this domain. The C‑terminal winged helix‑turn‑helix (wHTH) effector domain then binds specifically to the “pho box” DNA sequence in target promoters. The DNA‑binding domain can recognize DNA on its own and is capable of acting as a constitutive transcriptional activator even when the regulatory domain is removed, indicating that PhoB functions as a transcription factor that regulates expression of downstream genes upon activation. {PubMed:26382712}. PhoB is the response regulator component of the PhoR/PhoB two‑component system in *Escherichia coli*.  It detects changes in extracellular inorganic phosphate (Pi) concentration and, together with its cognate histidine kinase PhoR, controls the transcriptional response required for phosphate acquisition and homeostasis, which is essential for bacterial growth.  As a member of the OmpR/PhoB family, PhoB contains an N‑terminal receiver domain that can be phosphorylated on a conserved aspartate, triggering conformational changes that promote dimerization and activation of its C‑terminal effector domain to bind DNA and regulate downstream genes.  The article emphasizes that even in the unphosphorylated (apo) state, PhoB’s receiver domain can exist in monomer–dimer equilibrium and adopt multiple transient dimer interfaces, suggesting that these pre‑existing conformations may facilitate the phosphorylation‑dependent activation process. {PubMed:29722984}. PhoB is the positive, acid‑inducible regulator of the phosphate (Pho) regulon in Escherichia coli. It activates transcription of genes involved in phosphate acquisition when external phosphate is limiting. In addition, PhoB limits the production of fermentation acids; consequently, loss of phoB leads to increased acid production, which can improve growth under high‑pH conditions. The article notes that phoB expression is induced at low pH, and that an IS1 knockout of phoB (or a phoB::kanR deletion) enhances fitness at alkaline pH by promoting greater fermentation‑acid output. {PubMed:29802191}. The b0399 gene (also called psiE or yjbA) encodes a phosphate‑starvation‑inducible protein that is part of the Escherichia coli phosphate regulon. Its expression is directly activated by the PhoB response regulator under low‑phosphate conditions and is negatively regulated by the cAMP‑CRP complex under conditions of high cAMP (e.g., low glucose). The gene is transcribed from a single promoter with one transcription start site, and its product is predicted to be a hydrophobic membrane protein, although its precise biochemical role remains unknown. {PubMed:10986267}. The JW0389 gene (psiE, also known as yjbA) encodes a phosphate‑starvation‑inducible protein that is part of the Escherichia coli phosphate regulon. Its expression is directly activated by the PhoB response regulator under low‑phosphate conditions and is negatively regulated by the cAMP‑CRP complex under conditions of high cAMP (e.g., low glucose). The gene is transcribed from a single promoter with one transcription start site. Based on its predicted hydrophobic character, the PsiE protein is likely a membrane protein, although its precise biochemical role remains undefined. {PubMed:10986267}.
Curated_Functions: Acts as the response regulator of the PhoR/PhoB two‑component system, detecting extracellular inorganic phosphate and activating transcription of phoA and other phosphate‑starvation‑inducible genes. {PubMed:6310121, PubMed:10986267}. Binds conserved 7‑bp pho‑box DNA sequences upstream of target promoters, facilitating σ⁷⁰ RNA polymerase recruitment and transcription initiation. {PubMed:10986267}. Is phosphorylated by the histidine kinase PhoR, which induces dimerization of its receiver domain and activation of the C‑terminal winged‑helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding effector domain. {PubMed:26382712, PubMed:29722984, PubMed:10986267}. The isolated C‑terminal DNA‑binding domain can activate transcription independently of the receiver domain. {PubMed:26382712}. Its own expression is up‑regulated during phosphate starvation and positively controlled by PhoR and PhoM, while negative regulators PhoR, PhoS, PhoT and PhoU diminish its synthesis. {PubMed:6310121}. Restricts fermentation‑acid production, thereby influencing pH tolerance; loss of phoB increases acid output and enhances fitness at alkaline pH. {PubMed:29802191}. Directly activates transcription of psiE (yjbA), a predicted membrane protein of unknown function, under low‑phosphate conditions; psiE expression is repressed by the cAMP‑CRP complex when cAMP is high. {PubMed:10986267}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Required for the activity of the bacterial periplasmic transport system of putrescine and spermidine.
Merged_Functions:
The b1125 gene encodes PotA, a membrane‑associated nucleotide‑binding protein that forms part of the spermidine‑preferential uptake system in Escherichia coli. PotA provides the energy for spermidine transport by hydrolyzing ATP (Mg²⁺‑dependent ATPase activity, specific activity ≈400 nmol min⁻¹ mg⁻¹, Kₘ for ATP ≈385 µM). ATP binding involves the N‑terminal region (cysteine 26 is photo‑affinity labeled), while the catalytic center for ATP hydrolysis includes cysteine 54 within the first consensus nucleotide‑binding motif and residues between the two consensus motifs (e.g., valine 135). PotA’s ATPase activity is inhibited by spermidine, suggesting feedback regulation. Association of PotA with the inner membrane is enhanced through interactions with the channel‑forming proteins PotB and PotC. Loss of PotA function (e.g., C54T or V135M mutations) abolishes ATPase activity and spermidine uptake, confirming its essential role in the active transport of spermidine. {PubMed:7592703}. PotB encodes a membrane‑integral transmembrane protein that forms part of the ABC‑type polyamine uptake systems in Escherichia coli. In the spermidine‑preferential uptake system (encoded by clone pPT104), PotB together with PotC creates a channel through which spermidine is translocated across the inner membrane. In the putrescine‑specific uptake system (encoded by clone pPT79), the homologous PotB protein (along with PotC) forms the channel for putrescine transport. PotB is highly hydrophobic, contains six predicted membrane‑spanning segments, and interacts with the ATP‑binding subunit PotA to facilitate energy‑coupled import of polyamines. {PubMed:8721347}. PotB encodes one of the two transmembrane proteins of the spermidine‑preferential ABC transporter PotABCD in Escherichia coli. It forms part of the membrane channel that works together with PotC, the periplasmic substrate‑binding protein PotD, and the ATP‑binding subunit PotA. Specific functions identified in the article include: 
- **Membrane insertion:** The N‑terminal Trp⁸ residue is essential for proper insertion of both PotB and its partner PotC into the cytoplasmic membrane; mutation of Trp⁸ prevents membrane localization of the complex. 
- **Interaction with PotD:** Periplasmic loop residues Tyr⁴³, Trp¹⁰⁰ and Leu¹¹⁰ (and also Tyr²⁶¹) mediate binding of PotD to the PotB/C complex, facilitating transfer of spermidine from PotD to the transmembrane channel. 
- **Interaction with PotA (ATPase):** The cytoplasmic EAA motif (including Glu¹⁷²) and adjacent residues such as Trp¹⁰⁰ are important for coupling to the ATP‑hydrolyzing subunit PotA, allowing ATP‑driven conformational changes. 
- **Spermidine recognition:** Leu¹¹⁰ and Tyr²⁶¹ contribute to the recognition of spermidine on the periplasmic side (Leu¹¹⁰) and cytoplasmic side (Tyr²⁶¹) of the transporter, influencing Km values for substrate uptake. 
- **Coupling to ATPase activity:** Trp¹⁰⁰ and Tyr²⁶¹ affect the ATPase activity of PotA, linking substrate translocation to ATP hydrolysis. 
Overall, PotB functions as a critical membrane component that anchors the transporter, interacts with both the substrate‑binding protein and the ATPase, and participates directly in spermidine binding and transport. {PubMed:20937813}. PotB is one of the two transmembrane (channel‑forming) proteins that constitute the spermidine‑preferential ABC uptake system PotABCD in Escherichia coli. Together with PotC it forms the membrane‑spanning channel through which spermidine is transported, and it interacts directly with the ATP‑binding subunit PotA, as shown by disulfide cross‑linking experiments. Its role is structural/transport‑facilitating rather than catalytic. {PubMed:11976340}. PotB encodes a transmembrane, channel‑forming protein that is a component of the spermidine‑preferential uptake system in Escherichia coli. Together with PotC, it forms the membrane channel through which spermidine (and possibly spermine) is transported. The presence of PotB (and PotC) markedly enhances the association of the nucleotide‑binding protein PotA with the inner membrane, indicating that PotB interacts with PotA to stabilize the transport complex. {PubMed:7592703}. PotB is a chimeric flagellar stator B subunit engineered by fusing the N‑terminal (including the transmembrane and plug regions) of Vibrio pomB to the C‑terminal periplasmic region of Escherichia coli motB. In the study, PotB partners with the A‑subunit PomA (or MotA) to form a functional stator complex that conducts ions (Na⁺ in Vibrio, H⁺ in E. coli) across the membrane, generates torque, and drives rotation of the flagellar motor. The chimeric stator restores swimming motility to ΔpomAB or ΔmotAB mutant strains of V. alginolyticus and E. coli, even in the absence of the Vibrio T‑ring, although the mutants exhibit weak rotational switching. Suppressor mutations in either PomA or the PotB linker/plug region can improve switching, indicating PotB’s role in stator‑rotor interaction and motor directionality. {PubMed:25630862}. PotB is the B‑subunit of the chimeric PomA₄PotB₂ stator complex that powers the bacterial flagellar motor using sodium‑motive force.  It contributes a single transmembrane (TM) helix that together with the four TM helices of PomA forms the ion‑conducting channel through which Na⁺ ions flow to generate torque.  The C‑terminal portion of PotB contains a periplasmic peptidoglycan‑binding (PG‑binding) domain that anchors the stator to the cell wall, enabling the stator to engage the rotor.  Mutations in either the TM region (e.g., F22Y, L28Q) or the PG‑binding region (e.g., Y163F, M164V) alter phenamil resistance and sodium‑dependent rotation, demonstrating PotB’s role in ion translocation, torque generation, and stator‑PG interaction. {PubMed:30927553}.
Curated_Functions: Hydrolyzes ATP in a Mg²⁺-dependent manner to power spermidine import; activity is inhibited by spermidine. {PubMed:7592703}. Interacts with the membrane proteins PotB and PotC to associate with the inner membrane. {PubMed:7592703}. Forms a membrane channel with PotC for spermidine (and putrescine) uptake across the inner membrane. {PubMed:8721347, PubMed:11976340, PubMed:7592703, PubMed:20937813}. Binds the periplasmic substrate‑binding protein PotD to receive spermidine for translocation. {PubMed:20937813}. Interacts with the ATP‑binding subunit PotA to couple ATP hydrolysis with substrate translocation. {PubMed:20937813, PubMed:11976340}. Participates in spermidine recognition on both periplasmic and cytoplasmic sides of the transporter. {PubMed:20937813}. Requires an N‑terminal Trp⁸ residue for correct insertion into the cytoplasmic membrane. {PubMed:20937813}. Forms part of a PomA₄PotB₂ stator complex that conducts Na⁺ (or H⁺) ions across the membrane to generate torque for flagellar rotation. {PubMed:25630862, PubMed:30927553}. Anchors the stator to the cell wall via a C‑terminal peptidoglycan‑binding domain. {PubMed:30927553}. Contributes a single transmembrane helix that together with PomA helices creates the ion‑conducting channel of the stator. {PubMed:30927553}. Modulates motor directionality and switching through stator‑rotor interactions; suppressor mutations in PomA or PotB improve switching. {PubMed:25630862}. Alters ion selectivity and motor performance; mutations in the transmembrane or peptidoglycan‑binding region affect phenamil resistance and sodium‑dependent rotation. {PubMed:30927553}.

Merged_Functions: PotC is one of the two transmembrane components of the spermidine‑preferential ABC transporter PotABCD in Escherichia coli. It works together with PotB to form the membrane channel that transports spermidine from the periplasmic substrate‑binding protein PotD into the cytoplasm. Specific residues in PotC (Trp46, Asp108, Glu169, Ser196, Asp198, Asp199) are critical for: (1) interaction with PotD (Trp46, Asp108, Ser196, Asp198), (2) recognition of spermidine on the periplasmic side (Asp198, Asp199) and the cytoplasmic side (Asp108), and (3) coupling spermidine translocation to the ATPase activity of the membrane‑associated ATPase subunit PotA (Asp108, Glu169, Asp198). Mutations at these positions markedly reduce spermidine uptake, alter Km and Vmax, and diminish ATPase activity, demonstrating that PotC is essential for proper insertion of the transporter into the membrane (dependent on PotB Trp8) and for the coordinated passage of spermidine coupled to ATP hydrolysis. {PubMed:20937813}. PotC is a transmembrane protein that forms part of the spermidine‑preferential uptake system in Escherichia coli.  It is described as a channel‑forming component that, together with PotB, creates a pathway for spermidine transport across the inner membrane.  The presence of PotC (along with PotB) enhances the association of the nucleotide‑binding protein PotA with the membrane, suggesting a role in stabilizing the transport complex. The atl gene encodes an Alkyltransferase‑Like (ATL) protein that binds specifically and reversibly to O⁶‑alkylguanine lesions in DNA. ATL proteins do not transfer the alkyl group, nor act as glycosylases or endonucleases; instead they block the action of the human alkyltransferase MGMT by occupying the lesion. In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, loss of atl (atl1) abolishes this binding activity and makes cells hypersensitive to a range of SN1 and SN2 alkylating agents, indicating that ATL functions as a damage‑recognition sensor that protects the organism, likely by signaling the lesion to other repair pathways such as nucleotide excision repair. Thus, ATL proteins serve as non‑catalytic O⁶‑alkylguanine binding proteins that contribute to cellular resistance against alkylating DNA damage. {PubMed:17500045}. In the study, atl⁺ was always cotransduced with rtl⁺ and mapped near metG, behaving as an alternative to the galactitol utilization region (gat⁺). {PubMed:6339679}. The atl gene encodes the major autolysin (Atl), a bifunctional cell‑surface peptidoglycan hydrolase composed of an N‑terminal amidase (AM) domain and a C‑terminal glucosaminidase (GM) domain separated by three repeat regions. The ybaZ gene encodes the Escherichia coli alkyltransferase‑like protein (ATL). This interaction is thought to “mop up” a portion of cellular σ^70, modulating the balance between σ^70 and alternative sigma factors (such as σ^38) during stationary phase and allowing a more subtle regulation of gene expression under non‑growing conditions. {PubMed:14687566}.

Modulates sigma factor competition, biasing transcription toward the alternative sigma factor σ38 (RpoS) especially during stationary phase. {PubMed:19763331, PubMed:29686109, PubMed:31867037}. Interacts with HPr and SpoT, linking transcriptional regulation to carbon metabolism and (p)ppGpp signaling. {PubMed:31867037}. Affects cellular 6S RNA levels, providing feedback on sigma factor competition. {PubMed:29686109}. Reduces expression of σ38‑dependent genes when rsd is deleted, indicating a role in stress‑response transcription. {PubMed:29686109}.

Requires TrkE (sapD) for transport activity, 20% more uptake is seen with both SapD and SapF (PubMed:11700350). Transport in the absence of SapD and SapF is dependent on a high membrane potential and a high cytoplasmic ATP concentration, suggesting this protein may be able to interact with other ATP-binding proteins (PubMed:11700350). TrkH forms the transmembrane component of the Trk system, the major constitutive K⁺ uptake system in Escherichia coli. Either TrkH or its homolog TrkG is sufficient for high‑level Trk activity; loss of both genes abolishes K⁺ transport. When TrkH is the sole transmembrane subunit, the system shows a somewhat lower affinity for K⁺ (higher Kₘ) and an extremely low Vₘₐₓ for Rb⁺ (≈1 % of the K⁺ Vₘₐₓ). TrkH forms the K⁺‑translocating pore that, together with the cytoplasmic NAD⁺/NADH‑binding protein TrkA, mediates low‑affinity K⁺ uptake. Kinetic analysis of a ΔtrkI strain (which relies solely on TrkH) showed a half‑saturation constant (Kₘ) of 3.36 mM and a Vₘₐₓ of 137 nmol K⁺ min⁻¹ mg⁻¹ protein. Unlike the TrkI transporter, TrkH displays sigmoidal (cooperative) kinetics best described by V = aS²/(b+S²) with a Hill coefficient of ~2.1, indicating possible cooperative substrate binding. Deletion of trkH (ΔtrkH) does not markedly affect growth under most conditions because TrkI can compensate, but in strains lacking TrkI, the presence of TrkH allows limited K⁺ accumulation and growth at higher external K⁺ concentrations. Overall, TrkH functions as a low‑affinity, slower K⁺ transporter that contributes to K⁺ homeostasis, especially when the higher‑affinity TrkI system is absent. {PubMed:15659681}. TrkH is a bacterial ion channel belonging to the superfamily of K⁺ transporters (SKTs). It assembles as a homodimer in the membrane and partners with the cytosolic regulatory protein TrkA to form the TrkH‑TrkA complex. In this complex, TrkH mediates ion conduction, showing a slight preference for K⁺ over Na⁺, and participates in K⁺ uptake, pH regulation, and osmoregulation. Nucleotide binding to TrkA (ADP or ATP) controls TrkH gating: ADP‑bound TrkA forms a tetrameric ring that constrains TrkH in a closed conformation via two interfaces (HN1 and HN2), whereas ATP‑bound TrkA splits into two dimers, releasing the HN1 constraint and allowing TrkH to adopt an open (partially dilated) conformation. Opening of TrkH expands the pore‑lining helices and moves an intramembrane loop, increasing the ion permeation pathway radius. Functional studies show that loss of TrkA or disruption of the TrkA‑induced constraints leads to increased open probability of TrkH and depolarization of the bacterial membrane, indicating that TrkH activity can modulate membrane potential by allowing ion influx (primarily Na⁺) down electrochemical gradients. {PubMed:31992706}. In Vibrio alginolyticus, TrkH functions together with TrkA to mediate constitutive K⁺ uptake, displaying kinetic parameters (Kₘ ≈ 250 µM, Vₘₐₓ ≈ 220 nmol min⁻¹ (mg dry wt)⁻¹) that are independent of the growth K⁺ concentration. Overall, trkH provides a K⁺‑specific transport capability essential for cellular K⁺ homeostasis under low‑K⁺ conditions. {PubMed:9720051}. trkH encodes the primary potassium (K⁺) transporter of the low‑affinity, high‑rate Trk system in Escherichia coli. It mediates K⁺ uptake that is normally up‑regulated during osmotic stress, thereby influencing intracellular K⁺ homeostasis, pH balance, and the activity of many metabolic enzymes. In the evolved strains studied, a point mutation (L80Q) increases the rate of K⁺ transport, which alters glycogen accumulation, reduces the production of acetic acid, and sustains tricarboxylic‑acid‑cycle activity during phosphate starvation. Thus, TrkH functions as a key regulator of K⁺ influx that indirectly modulates central carbon metabolism and stress‑response phenotypes. {PubMed:26895825}. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Modulates the polysaccharide chain length of enterobacterial common antigen (ECA). Required for the assembly of the phosphoglyceride-linked form of ECA (ECA(PG)) and the water-soluble cyclic form of ECA (ECA(CYC)). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10515954, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16199561}.
Merged_Functions: Encodes the polysaccharide copolymerase WzzE, a member of the PCP‑1 family that is anchored in the inner membrane and acts as a chain‑length regulator for the enterobacterial common antigen (ECA). WzzE determines the number of repeat units incorporated into the growing ECA polymer, thereby imposing a unimodal length distribution on the surface polysaccharide. The protein functions as an octameric homo‑oligomer; formation of this higher‑order complex is essential for its role in glycan chain‑length control. {PubMed:25307743}. The wzzE gene encodes the Wzz_E protein, which functions as the O‑antigen chain‑length regulator for the enterobacterial common antigen (ECA) biosynthetic pathway. Wzz_E works together with the ECA‑specific translocase (Wzx_E) and polymerase (Wzy_E) in the Wzy‑dependent assembly of ECA polysaccharides, influencing the length of the polymerized ECA chains. Genetic experiments in the article show that expression of Wzz_E (along with Wzy_E) reduces the ability of Wzx_E to complement O16 LPS synthesis, indicating that Wzz_E participates in a specific protein complex that coordinates translocation (by Wzx_E) and polymerization (by Wzy_E) of ECA subunits, thereby regulating the final polysaccharide chain length. {PubMed:16816184}. The wzzE gene encodes a polysaccharide chain‑length regulator that modulates the length distribution of the phosphoglyceride‑linked form of enterobacterial common antigen (ECA_PG). Null mutations in wzzE do not prevent ECA_PG synthesis but produce a random, non‑modal population of polymer lengths, indicating its role in establishing the typical modal chain length (approximately 5–7 repeat units). In addition, wzzE is essential for the synthesis of the cyclic, water‑soluble form of ECA (ECA_CYC); strains lacking wzzE fail to produce detectable ECA_CYC, and this defect can be rescued by expressing wild‑type wzzE from a plasmid. The data suggest that WzzE may act together with the polymerase WzyE (and possibly the flippase WzxE) in a membrane‑bound complex that coordinates polymerization and cyclization of ECA trisaccharide repeat units, thereby enabling the formation of the four‑repeat‑unit cyclic ECA molecule. {PubMed:16199561}. WzzE is a membrane polysaccharide copolymerase (PCP) that serves as a chain‑length determinant for the O‑specific polysaccharide (O‑antigen) in Escherichia coli O157. According to the article, the presence of WzzE directs the synthesis of short O‑antigen chains, typically 5–7 repeat units in length. By controlling the length of the O‑antigen, WzzE influences the overall lipopolysaccharide (LPS) structure and contributes to the bacterium’s sensitivity to serum complement. {PubMed:23865758}. The article describes that the wzz gene product is an inner‑membrane protein that modulates the polymerization of polysaccharide chains by interacting with the O‑antigen polymerase (Wzy). In Escherichia coli O8 and O9 strains that carry type IB capsules, the wzz gene (referred to as wzzE in this request) does not affect the chain length of the conventional O‑antigen, but rather determines the modal length of the capsule‑related form of lipopolysaccharide (designated K_LPS). Expression of wzzE shifts the distribution of K_LPS chain lengths to new modal values (e.g., from 16–24 repeat units to 5–9 or 10–16 units) and increases the overall amount of K_LPS. Thus, wzzE functions as a chain‑length determinant for K‑type capsular polysaccharide attached to lipid A‑core in these strains. {PubMed:8606163}. The wzz gene encodes a Polysaccharide Copolymerase (PCP‑1) protein (e.g., WzzB or WzzE) that acts as a chain‑length regulator for surface polysaccharides such as the lipopolysaccharide O‑antigen and the enterobacterial common antigen (ECA). By forming homo‑oligomeric complexes—predominantly octamers—the Wzz protein determines the number of repeat units incorporated into the growing polysaccharide chain, thereby imposing a defined length distribution on the final polymer. Its periplasmic domain interacts with the nascent glycan, and the oligomeric state is essential for proper chain‑length control. {PubMed:25307743}. Wzz encodes an O‑antigen chain‑length regulator protein that functions in the Wzy‑dependent pathway of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) assembly. In Escherichia coli, distinct Wzz proteins (e.g., Wzz_E for enterobacterial common antigen and Wzz_O16 for the O16 O‑antigen) determine the modal length of the periplasmic polysaccharide chain by interacting with the corresponding polymerase (Wzy) and the flippase (Wzx). Genetic experiments in the article show that co‑expression of the appropriate Wzz protein with its cognate Wzy markedly reduces the ability of heterologous Wzx proteins to complement O‑antigen synthesis, indicating that Wzz participates in a multiprotein complex that sequesters its specific Wzx and directs translocated subunits to the correct polymerization machinery. Thus, Wzz acts as a regulator of polysaccharide chain length and as a component of a membrane complex that coordinates translocation (by Wzx) and polymerization (by Wzy) of O‑antigen and ECA glycans. {PubMed:16816184}. The wzzE gene encodes a polysaccharide chain‑length regulator that controls the length distribution of the phosphoglyceride‑linked enterobacterial common antigen (ECA_PG) polymers. In wild‑type cells it produces a modal population of ECA chains (≈1–14 repeat units, with a modal value of 5–7). Null mutations in wzzE do not block ECA_PG synthesis but eliminate this modal regulation, resulting in a random, non‑modal distribution of chain lengths and a marked reduction in overall ECA_PG levels. Importantly, the article demonstrates that wzzE is also required for the synthesis of the water‑soluble cyclic form of ECA (ECA_CYC); strains lacking wzzE fail to produce ECA_CYC, and this defect is rescued by expression of a wild‑type wzzE allele. The data suggest that WzzE functions together with the polymerase WzyE (and the flippase WzxE) in a membrane‑associated complex that coordinates polymerization and cyclization of the ECA trisaccharide repeat units, enabling formation of the four‑repeat‑unit cyclic ECA molecule. {PubMed:16199561}. The wzz gene encodes a membrane polysaccharide copolymerase (PCP) protein that regulates the modal distribution of O‑antigen (Oag) chain length in the lipopolysaccharide of Escherichia coli O157. Acting together with the O‑antigen polymerase Wzy and the flippase Wzx, Wzz determines whether the O‑antigen repeats are short (<15 repeat units), intermediate (15–20 units) or long (>20 units). Different wzz alleles confer distinct preferred chain‑length phenotypes (short, intermediate, or long) as demonstrated by the construction of wzz deletion mutants and complementation with wzz genes from strains producing each chain‑length type. Modulation of O‑antigen length by wzz directly influences bacterial susceptibility to human serum complement: strains bearing short O‑antigen chains (controlled by a short‑type wzz) are markedly more serum‑sensitive, whereas strains with intermediate or long O‑antigen chains exhibit greater resistance to complement‑mediated killing. {PubMed:23865758}. Encodes the chain‑length determinant protein Wzz, which terminates polymerization and regulates the modal distribution of the O‑polysaccharide (O‑antigen) chain length during lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis in Gram‑negative bacteria. Wzz assembles into an elongated tetramer, with oligomerization mediated by a predicted coiled‑coil region in its periplasmic domain. The protein directly binds O‑antigen substrates, inducing a substrate‑induced conformational change that likely signals termination of polysaccharide elongation. These findings support a role for Wzz as a molecular chaperone that interacts with the O‑antigen polymerase Wzy, the ligase WaaL, and nascent polysaccharide chains to control O‑antigen chain length. {PubMed:17900153}. The wzz gene encodes a membrane protein that acts as a chain‑length determinant for lipopolysaccharide (LPS) polymers. In Escherichia coli O8 and O9 strains carrying type IB capsules, Wzz does not affect the modal length of the O‑antigen polymer, but it specifically regulates the modal distribution of the capsule‑related LPS form (K_LPS). By interacting with the O‑antigen polymerase (Wzy) in the periplasm, Wzz sets preferred chain‑length ranges (e.g., 5–9, 10–16, or 16–24 repeat units) for K_LPS, thereby modulating both the length and the overall amount of capsular polysaccharide attached to lipid A‑core. {PubMed:8606163}. The wzz gene encodes a membrane-associated protein that acts as a chain‑length regulator for the group IB K antigen that is linked to lipid A (Kₗₚₛ).  Its product determines the modal distribution of Kₗₚₛ polymer lengths, producing a tight cluster of bands of defined size on SDS‑PAGE.  Disruption of wzz abolishes this modality, resulting in a broad, inverse‑proportional distribution of chain lengths, while multicopy wzz restores modality but can shift synthesis toward the lipid‑A‑linked form and reduce the amount of the LPS‑independent capsular K antigen.  The protein is highly similar to other Wzz proteins (e.g., from E. coli O75) and functions in the Wzy‑dependent polysaccharide assembly pathway, likely by influencing the interaction between the polymerase Wzy and the ligase WaaL to control when polymerization stops. {PubMed:9383197}. The wzz gene encodes a membrane‑anchored protein that regulates the length of the B‑band O‑antigen polysaccharide in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.  It functions as the “chain‑length determinant” (Cld) for Wzy‑dependent O‑antigen polymerization, ensuring that the polymerase Wzy produces O‑antigen chains of preferred lengths, which appear as a bimodal or multimodal distribution on LPS gels.  Disruption of wzz results in loss of this modality and an increase in both shorter and longer O‑antigen chains, indicating that Wzz normally limits excessive polymerization and promotes a defined range of chain sizes.  Complementation of wzz mutants restores the modal pattern, and the P. aeruginosa wzz can also complement an Escherichia coli wzz mutant, demonstrating functional interchangeability.  Co‑expression of P. aeruginosa and E. coli Wzz proteins yields two distinct populations of chain lengths, further supporting its role in determining chain‑length distribution.  The article discusses two mechanistic models: Wzz may act as a molecular timer that allows polymerization to proceed for a set period or until a specific length is reached, or it may function as a molecular chaperone that alters the stoichiometry of Wzy and the O‑antigen ligase WaaL, thereby balancing polymerization and ligation events. {PubMed:9045803}.

Acts in concert with UbiD to perform the decarboxylation of 4-hydroxy-3-octaprenyl-benzoate, a step in the biosynthesis of coenzyme Q (PubMed:16923914, PubMed:17889824). {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01984, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16923914, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17889824}.

Merged_Functions: UbiX is an essential component of the coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) biosynthetic pathway in Escherichia coli. The protein is required for the decarboxylation of the pathway intermediate 4‑hydroxy‑3‑octaprenyl‑benzoate (HP₈B) to produce 2‑octaprenylphenol, a reaction that also involves the partner enzyme UbiD and is critical during logarithmic growth. Loss of ubiX results in severe depletion of Q₈, accumulation of HP₈B, and a marked reduction in the activity of the downstream O‑methyltransferase UbiG. Complementation with either the native E. coli ubiX gene or the Saccharomyces cerevisiae PAD1 gene restores Q₈ synthesis, reduces HP₈B accumulation, and rescues UbiG activity, indicating that PAD1 is an ortholog of UbiX. Thus, UbiX functions as a partner protein that enables the UbiD‑catalyzed decarboxylation step in Q biosynthesis and indirectly supports subsequent methylation steps. {PubMed:17889824}. ubiX encodes a protein required for the biosynthesis of ubiquinone (coenzyme Q), an isoprenoid quinone that functions as an electron carrier in the aerobic respiratory chain. In the study, deletion of ubiX (along with other ubi genes) conferred increased resistance to D‑cycloserine, indicating that a functional ubiquinone synthesis pathway is important for D‑cycloserine sensitivity. {PubMed:23316042}. UbiX is a protein implicated in the coenzyme Q (ubiquinone) biosynthetic pathway of Escherichia coli. It is thought to participate in the decarboxylation step that converts 3‑octaprenyl‑4‑hydroxybenzoate to the next intermediate in the pathway. Genetic evidence presented in the article shows that overexpression of the wild‑type ubiX gene from E. coli K‑12 can rescue the Q‑deficient, thiol‑hypersensitive phenotype of the IS16 mutant, which carries a defective ubiG (O‑methyltransferase) allele. This rescue suggests that UbiX can interact directly with UbiG, possibly stabilizing the catalytic activity of the mutant UbiG (L132Q) or facilitating substrate channeling between the two enzymes. Thus, UbiX functions both as a decarboxylase in Q biosynthesis and as a partner that supports UbiG‑mediated O‑methylation steps. {PubMed:16923914}. UbiX is a flavin prenyltransferase that catalyzes the biosynthesis of the novel cofactor prenylated FMN (prFMN). In vitro, UbiX uses reduced flavin mononucleotide (FMNH₂) and dimethylallyl‑monophosphate (DMAP) as substrates, positioning DMAP above the FMN isoalloxazine ring to first form an N5‑C1′ dimethylallyl adduct followed by a C6‑C3′ bond, thereby creating a fourth non‑aromatic ring on the flavin. The reaction does not require metal ions and strictly depends on DMAP (rather than the common DMAPP). Conserved active‑site residues, including Glu140, bind the DMAP phosphate and likely act as a proton donor to facilitate leaving‑group departure. The resulting prFMN (still in the reduced FMNH₂ redox state) rapidly oxidizes to a radical form upon exposure to oxygen and can be further oxidized to various prFMN species that serve as cofactors for the partner enzyme UbiD, a prFMN‑dependent (de)carboxylase. Thus, UbiX provides the essential prenylated flavin cofactor that underpins the catalytic activity of the ubiquitous microbial UbiDX system. {PubMed:30326424}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: In eubacteria ppGpp (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate) is a mediator of the stringent response which coordinates a variety of cellular activities in response to changes in nutritional abundance. This enzyme catalyzes the formation of pppGpp which is then hydrolyzed to form ppGpp. The second messengers ppGpp and c-di-GMP together control biofilm formation in response to translational stress; ppGpp represses biofilm formation while c-di-GMP induces it. ppGpp activates transcription of CsrA-antagonistic small RNAs CsrB and CsrC, which down-regulate CsrA's action on translation during the stringent response (PubMed:21488981). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:14622409, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19460094, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21488981, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26051177}.

Merged_Functions: The relA gene encodes the enzyme ATP:GTP pyrophosphate transferase, commonly called stringent factor, which catalyzes the synthesis of the alarmone nucleotides ppGpp (guanosine 3'-diphosphate, 5'-diphosphate) and pppGpp. Its primary role is to generate high levels of ppGpp during “emergency” conditions such as amino‑acid starvation, when deacylated tRNA accumulates in the ribosome. This surge of ppGpp mediates the negative regulation of ribosomal RNA and protein synthesis and influences the expression of various biosynthetic enzymes. The gene is not essential for cell viability; cells lacking functional relA can still produce basal levels of ppGpp (70‑100 % of normal) via an alternative pathway and grow normally, indicating that relA’s sole indispensable function is the high‑level, stress‑induced synthesis of ppGpp. {PubMed:365354}. Encodes the guanosine pentaphosphate/tetraphosphate synthetase that synthesizes the alarmone ppGpp. In Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli, RelA‑produced ppGpp positively regulates transcription of the perABC operon, which in turn activates expression of the bfp operon (bundle‑forming pilus) and the LEE‑encoded intimin adhesin. Thus RelA is required for maximal production of the BFP pilus and intimin and for optimal adherence of EPEC to epithelial cells. Deletion of relA eliminates ppGpp accumulation, reduces perABC transcription, lowers BFP and intimin levels, and markedly impairs bacterial adherence; complementation with a wild‑type relA allele restores these phenotypes. {PubMed:24643076}.

Mediates the stringent response by generating high levels of ppGpp during amino‑acid starvation or other emergency conditions, which negatively regulates ribosomal RNA and protein synthesis and modulates expression of various biosynthetic enzymes. {PubMed:365354}. Merged_Functions: MltE is a lytic transglycosylase that initiates the first step of peptidoglycan recycling in Escherichia coli. Unlike other lytic transglycosylases that act exolytically, MltE functions as an endoenzyme, capable of cleaving internal bonds without requiring a free chain end. {PubMed:21206052}. MltE is a periplasmic, outer‑membrane‑anchored lytic transglycosylase of *Escherichia coli* that cleaves the β‑1,4‑glycosidic bond between N‑acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) and N‑acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) residues in peptidoglycan (PG). The reaction is intramolecular, generating non‑reducing 1,6‑anhydro‑MurNAc‑containing muropeptides. Unlike most E. coli LTs, MltE displays endo‑specific activity, producing longer 1,6‑anhydromuropeptides that contain multiple disaccharide units rather than the single disaccharide products of exo‑LTs. Structural studies show that MltE possesses an extended, fully accessible PG‑binding groove comprising at least six saccharide subsites (‑4 to +2) with additional peripheral subsites (+3, +4). The catalytic acid/base residue is Glu64, which together with surrounding residues (e.g., Ser73, Gln188) facilitates substrate distortion and anchimeric assistance by the MurNAc N‑acetyl group. Efficient cleavage requires a glycan strand of at least four disaccharide units, occupying subsites ‑4 to +2, and the enzyme preferentially binds MurNAc at subsite +2, explaining its inability to act on terminal 1,6‑anhydro‑MurNAc residues. Overall, MltE functions in bacterial cell‑wall turnover, remodeling, and maintenance by endo‑cleavage of peptidoglycan strands. {PubMed:23075328}. MltE encodes a membrane‑bound lytic transglycosylase (LT) that catalyzes the non‑hydrolytic cleavage of the glycan strands of the bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall.  The enzyme performs an intramolecular transacetalization reaction that breaks the MurNAc‑GlcNAc glycosidic bond, generating a pair of products: one terminating in 1,6‑anhydro‑MurNAc (anhNAM) and the other ending in N‑acetylglucosamine.  This activity provides endolytic cleavage of peptidoglycan, facilitating cell‑wall expansion, remodeling, and the passage of secretion systems, flagella, pili, and fimbriae.  In pathogenic *E. coli* strains, MltE is recruited by the periplasmic domain of the T6SS protein TssM to excavate peptidoglycan during late stages of type‑6 secretion system assembly.  It is the smallest of the eight LTs encoded by *E. coli* and serves as the primary endolytic LT in this organism, playing a central role in cell‑wall turnover. {PubMed:30256085}. MltE encodes a membrane‑bound lytic transglycosylase (LT) that catalyzes the non‑hydrolytic cleavage of the β‑1→4 glycosidic bond linking N‑acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) and N‑acetyl‑D‑glucosamine (GlcNAc) in the peptidoglycan polymer. The reaction proceeds via an intramolecular transacetalization that generates a 1,6‑anhydroMurNAc terminus on one daughter strand and a free GlcNAc terminus on the other, without forming an oxazolinium intermediate. The catalytic glutamic acid residue (E64) functions as a general acid/base, facilitating proton transfer and activation of the C6‑OH for intramolecular attack, while substrate‑assisted dipole stabilization of an oxocarbenium‑like transition state drives the reaction. MltE is the primary endolytic LT in *Escherichia coli*, responsible for middle‑strand cleavage of peptidoglycan, and plays a critical role in peptidoglycan biosynthesis, remodeling, recycling, and especially in the late stages of type VI secretion system (T6SS) assembly, where it provides the cell‑wall‑penetrating activity required for T6SS deployment. {PubMed:29515200}. EmtA is a SAM‑dependent rRNA methyltransferase encoded on a plasmid‑borne transposable element. It acts endo‑specifically, generating longer 1,6‑anhydromuropeptide fragments rather than the short disaccharide products typical of exolytic LTs. The catalytic residue Glu64 functions as a general acid/base, and the enzyme utilizes a substrate‑assisted mechanism involving anchimeric assistance by the MurNAc N‑acetyl group. Merged_Functions: The b1951 locus encodes the small 85‑nt RNA DsrA. DsrA functions as an antisilencer that counteracts transcriptional silencing of the rcsA promoter by the histone‑like protein H‑NS. By doing so, DsrA markedly increases rcsA transcription, leading to higher levels of the RcsA positive regulator and consequently enhanced capsular polysaccharide synthesis. DsrA’s activity requires its own transcription and proper termination; mutations that block dsrA transcription or disrupt its terminator eliminate the antisilencing effect. The presence of RcsA (and thus CA production) confers protection against osmotic stress (high NaCl) and especially oxidative stress (H₂O₂) under low‑temperature conditions. Deletion of rcsA does not alter the ability of the strain to form biofilms on various abiotic surfaces, but it increases bacterial attachment to mammalian (caco‑2) cells, indicating that RcsA negatively regulates adhesion to biotic surfaces. Relief of H‑NS silencing (for example by the small RNA DsrA) increases rcsA transcription, leading to higher RcsA levels and consequently increased capsule production. {PubMed:7534408}. rcsA encodes an auxiliary regulator of the Rcs phosphorelay system in Escherichia coli. Up‑regulation of rcsA correlates with increased expression of CA biosynthetic genes, and deletion of rcsA abolishes CA production in LPS‑mutant strains, indicating that RcsA is essential for the Rcs‑mediated activation of CA synthesis. {PubMed:32590169}.

Merged_Functions: BcsQ (formerly YhjQ) is an essential component of the Escherichia coli cellulose biosynthesis machinery. Deletion of bcsQ abolishes cellulose production, while complementation restores it, indicating that BcsQ is required for the synthesis of the extracellular cellulose matrix that underlies biofilm formation. BcsQ is a MinD‑like ATPase that localizes specifically to the bacterial cell pole, as shown by GFP‑YcsQ fusion microscopy. This polar localization occurs independently of other cellulose‑synthesizing proteins (BcsA, BcsE, YedQ) and of the bcs operon products, suggesting that BcsQ itself directs spatial restriction of the cellulose synthase complex. Mutations in the N‑terminal putative ATP‑binding site eliminate BcsQ function without affecting its polar positioning, whereas truncations of the C‑terminal region reduce both polar localization and cellulose production. The polar accumulation of BcsQ correlates with the deposition of cellulose at the same pole, implying that BcsQ may act as a scaffold or adaptor that recruits or stabilizes the active cellulose biosynthesis apparatus at the cell pole, thereby initiating cell‑to‑cell adhesion and biofilm development. {PubMed:19400787}. BcsQ is an essential, SIMIBI‑superfamily NTPase that functions in the early assembly of the Escherichia coli cellulose secretion system. It forms a stable heterotetrameric complex (2 BcsR : 2 BcsQ) with the small protein BcsR, and the two proteins mutually assist each other’s folding and stability. The BcsRQ complex is recruited to the inner membrane through high‑affinity binding of BcsQ to the degenerate GGDEF* domain of the c‑di‑GMP‑sensing regulator BcsE; membrane targeting is further facilitated by the intra‑operon partner BcsF. By anchoring BcsRQ to the membrane, BcsQ contributes to the proper incorporation of the downstream synthase BcsA into the Bcs macrocomplex and thus is required for processive cellulose polymerization and secretion. {PubMed:32788377}. BcsQ is a non‑essential, ~26 kDa cytosolic protein that forms a 2:2 heterotetrameric complex with BcsR (BcsQ₂R₂). This complex binds to the PilZ domain of the catalytic subunit BcsA, thereby acting as a regulatory component that stimulates cellulose biosynthesis. BcsQ, together with BcsR, is recruited to the inner‑membrane cellulose synthase macrocomplex through interactions with BcsE (which itself contacts BcsF), positioning the complex at the cell poles where cellulose accumulates. The protein is homologous to the cell‑division ATPase MinD and requires BcsR for structural stability in solution. {PubMed:33712813}. The article demonstrates that yhjQ (renamed bcsQ) is an essential component of the Escherichia coli cellulose biosynthesis apparatus. Deletion of yhjQ abolishes cellulose production, while complementation restores it, indicating that BcsQ is required for the synthesis of cellulose. BcsQ is a MinD homologue that localizes specifically to the bacterial cell pole, and this polar localization correlates with the site of extracellular cellulose secretion. The N‑terminal putative ATP‑binding domain of BcsQ is necessary for its activity in cellulose biosynthesis but does not affect its polar positioning, whereas the C‑terminal region contributes to both polar localization and functional activity. BcsQ does not influence transcription of the bcs operon and its polar localization is independent of other cellulose‑biosynthesis proteins (BcsA, BcsE, YedQ) and of the MinCDE system. Overall, BcsQ appears to act as a spatial regulator that restricts the active cellulose synthase complex to the cell pole, thereby directing polar cellulose production and facilitating cell‑to‑cell adhesion in biofilms. {PubMed:19400787}.

In Escherichia coli RlpA is a SPOR‑domain‑containing protein that localizes to the septum and binds septal peptidoglycan.  This study shows that RlpA directly interacts with the periplasmic loops of the essential division protein FtsK (FtsK_N) and that loss of rlpA partially suppresses the filamentation and growth defect of a temperature‑sensitive ftsK mutant, indicating that RlpA participates in a checkpoint that restrains septation until the divisome is properly assembled.  The authors propose that RlpA may (i) link the outer membrane to the peptidoglycan and inner membrane during constriction, similar to the Tol‑Pal system, and (ii) help balance lateral cell‑wall growth versus septal synthesis, possibly acting as part of the elongation machinery.  Although no lytic transglycosylase activity has been detected for E. coli RlpA, its conserved SPOR domain and interaction with FtsK suggest a role in cell‑envelope remodeling and coordination of elongation‑to‑septation transitions during cell division. {PubMed:30154462}. JW0628 is the Keio collection strain in which the rlpA gene (encoding the RlpA protein) is disrupted by a kanamycin cassette. RlpA is a SPOR‑domain‑containing outer‑membrane lipoprotein that localizes to the septal ring during cell division and binds peptidoglycan in vitro. Although it is recruited to the division site, loss of RlpA (the JW0628 rlpA::kan mutant) does not produce detectable defects in cell length, chaining, or deoxycholate sensitivity under the growth conditions examined, indicating that RlpA is not essential for cytokinesis and may have a redundant or subtle role in cell‑wall metabolism. {PubMed:19880599}. The gene JW0628 encodes the outer‑membrane lipoprotein RlpA (Rare lipoprotein A).  RlpA is a septal peptidoglycan‑binding protein that resides in the periplasmic space attached to the outer membrane.  In Escherichia coli it directly interacts with the periplasmic loops of the essential divisome protein FtsK, as demonstrated by in‑vitro pull‑down assays and in‑vivo UV cross‑linking.  This interaction appears to be part of a checkpoint mechanism that restrains septation until the divisome is properly assembled; deletion of rlpA partially suppresses the growth defect and filamentation of a temperature‑sensitive ftsK mutant, indicating that loss of RlpA alleviates the block on cell division.  Although RlpA functions as a lytic transglycosylase in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, no enzymatic activity toward peptidoglycan has been detected in E. coli, and its primary role described here is regulatory—linking outer‑membrane remodeling to the cell‑division machinery. {PubMed:30154462}. RlpA is a SPOR‑domain containing outer‑membrane lipoprotein that localizes to the septal (division) ring in Escherichia coli.  Its C‑terminal SPOR domain binds peptidoglycan, indicating a role in interacting with the cell wall.  Based on its genomic context (adjacent to genes encoding PBP2, RodA, and PBP5) and the nature of other SPOR proteins, RlpA is hypothesized to participate in cell‑wall metabolism or to help link the outer membrane to the peptidoglycan layer during cytokinesis.  However, rlpA null mutants display no obvious division or morphology defects, so its precise physiological function remains unclear. {PubMed:19880599}. RlpA (rare lipoprotein A) is an outer‑membrane lipoprotein in Escherichia coli that contains a SPOR domain and binds septal peptidoglycan.  The study identified RlpA as a direct periplasmic interaction partner of the essential divisome protein FtsK (specifically the N‑terminal periplasmic loops of FtsK).  Deletion of rlpA partially suppresses the growth defect and filamentation of a temperature‑sensitive ftsK mutant, indicating that the RlpA–FtsK interaction contributes to a checkpoint that normally restrains septation until proper divisome assembly.  The authors propose that RlpA may (i) physically link the outer membrane to the peptidoglycan and inner membrane during constriction, similar to the Tol‑Pal system, and (ii) help balance lateral cell‑wall growth versus septal synthesis, possibly acting as part of the elongation machinery.  Although its enzymatic activity toward peptidoglycan has not been demonstrated in E. coli, RlpA appears to play a regulatory role in cell‑envelope remodeling and the transition from elongation to division. {PubMed:30154462}. RlpA encodes a lytic transglycosylase that localizes to the division septum during the late stages of cell division in Vibrio cholerae. It cleaves the glycosidic bond between N‑acetylglucosamine and N‑acetylmuramic acid residues in peptidoglycan, removing glycan strands that are cross‑linked beyond the reach of the amidase AmiB. This activity is required for proper daughter‑cell separation, especially under low‑salt growth conditions, and helps clear peptidoglycan debris that can impede outer‑membrane invagination. RlpA’s function is redundant with the LTG MltC under normal laboratory conditions, but it alone can support normal cell separation when MltC is absent. Outer‑membrane attachment via its lipobox is not essential for its septal activity. {PubMed:31286580}. RlpA (rare lipoprotein A) is a periplasmic lipoprotein of 345 amino acids that possesses an N‑terminal signal peptide (17 residues) directing export to the periplasm, where the signal peptide is cleaved and the resulting cysteine is lipid‑modified, anchoring the protein to the inner membrane. The gene resides in the mrdAB‑rlpA operon, a cluster of genes implicated in cell‑shape determination and peptidoglycan synthesis. Although its precise physiological role is not defined, the article notes that a truncated version (the first 102 residues retaining the signal peptide) can act as a multicopy suppressor of a prc (tsp) null mutation, likely by indirectly stimulating the σ^E‑dependent heat‑shock response and thereby increasing levels of the HtrA protease (DegP) or other stress proteins that compensate for loss of Prc activity. Thus, RlpA is described as a membrane‑anchored periplasmic lipoprotein potentially involved in cell wall biogenesis and stress‑response modulation. {PubMed:8576052}. RlpA is a SPOR‑domain containing periplasmic protein that binds peptidoglycan. In Escherichia coli it is not essential for cell division, but loss of rlpA increases sensitivity to the β‑lactam cefsulodin, indicating that RlpA contributes to the proper functionality of the class‑A penicillin‑binding protein PBP1B (and indirectly to PBP1A). Biochemical assays showed that RlpA does not directly stimulate the glycosyltransferase or transpeptidase activities of PBP1A or PBP1B. The article also notes that the homologous protein in Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a lytic transglycosylase acting on denuded glycan strands, but no enzymatic activity is reported for the E. coli RlpA. {PubMed:33144379}. RlpA is a lytic transglycosylase (LT) of *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* that is anchored to the inner leaflet of the outer membrane via an N‑terminal lipid. It contains a catalytic double‑ψ‑β‑barrel (DPBB) domain and a C‑terminal SPOR domain. The SPOR domain specifically binds to denuded peptidoglycan glycans (PG strands lacking peptide stems) that are generated at the septal ring by periplasmic amidases during cell division. This binding directs RlpA to the division septum, where its catalytic domain degrades the denuded PG, facilitating efficient separation of daughter cells and maintenance of rod shape in *P. aeruginosa*. The protein’s activity depends on the presence of exposed lactyl carboxylate groups of NAM residues; peptide stems sterically block SPOR‑mediated binding. Mutations in key basic residues of the SPOR domain reduce PG binding, confirming its role in septal localization and PG processing. {PubMed:31804467}.

Merged_Functions: LeuO (b0076) encodes a LysR‑like transcriptional regulator. It acts as a repressor of the small regulatory RNA DsrA; by limiting DsrA synthesis it reduces the low‑temperature stimulation of rpoS translation and consequently lowers σ^S (RpoS) protein levels. LeuO expression is normally very low and is repressed by the histone‑like protein H‑NS; loss of H‑NS derepresses leuO. Overproduction of LeuO (e.g., by the Tn10‑8 insertion that provides an outward IS10 promoter) leads to strong repression of dsrA and a marked decrease in rpoS translation, particularly at 25 °C. {PubMed:9302018}. LeuO is a LysR‑type transcription factor that acts as a master, pleiotropic regulator in Enterobacteriaceae.  It antagonizes the global nucleoid‑associated repressor H‑NS (and its paralogue StpA) by competing for DNA binding, thereby relieving H‑NS‑mediated repression of numerous loci.  LeuO directly activates transcription of the β‑glucoside (bgl) operon, outer‑membrane porins (ompS1, ompS2), the yjjQ‑bglU operon, the CRISPR‑associated cas operon, and other stress‑ and virulence‑related genes, while it represses the acid‑stress regulator CadC and the small RNA dsrA.  Its own expression is tightly controlled: it is repressed by H‑NS/StpA under standard conditions, strongly activated by the heterodimeric regulator RcsB‑BglJ (independently of Rcs phosphorylation), and subject to negative autoregulation—LeuO can modestly stimulate its own promoter but predominantly represses transcription from both H‑NS‑repressed promoters (P_leuO and P2_leuO).  LeuO also influences the divergent leu operon, contributing to a supercoiling‑dependent regulatory circuit that links branched‑chain amino‑acid starvation and stationary‑phase signals to leu operon expression.  Overall, LeuO integrates environmental cues to modulate stress responses, pathogenicity determinants, and metabolic gene expression. {PubMed:22295907}. LeuO is a conserved LysR‑type transcription regulator that acts as a global regulator in Enterobacteria. It controls a wide range of cellular processes, including pathogenicity (e.g., in Salmonella), biofilm formation (e.g., in Vibrio cholerae), the acid‑stress response, multidrug efflux, and activation of the CRISPR‑Cas immunity system. LeuO generally functions as an antagonist of the nucleoid‑associated protein H‑NS, counteracting H‑NS‑mediated silencing at many loci. Its own expression is tightly regulated: it is repressed by H‑NS and its paralogue StpA under standard laboratory conditions, can be modestly up‑regulated during amino‑acid starvation or stationary phase, is positively regulated by the heterodimeric transcription activator BglJ‑RcsB, and exhibits positive autoregulation that is overridden by its predominant role as an autorepressor. LeuO also participates in complex regulatory interplay with other regulators such as LrhA, LeuO itself, and H‑NS/StpA, influencing transcription from multiple leuO promoters (leuOp1, leuOp, leuOp3). {PubMed:28252809}. LeuO is a pleiotropic LysR‑type transcriptional regulator (LTTR) in Escherichia coli that can act both as an activator and a repressor of gene expression. It forms tetramers composed of N‑terminal winged‑helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding domains (DBDs) and C‑terminal effector‑binding domains (EBDs). LeuO regulates more than 100 loci, including genes for multidrug efflux systems, outer‑membrane porins, and the H‑NS‑repressed cas operon encoding the CRISPR‑Cascade complex. By antagonizing the nucleoid‑associated protein H‑NS, LeuO can relieve H‑NS‑mediated silencing of horizontally acquired, AT‑rich DNA, but it can also function as a “backup” repressor for certain H‑NS targets (e.g., Salmonella pathogenicity island 1). The leuO gene itself is repressed by H‑NS and its paralog StpA, and its activity is modulated by structural changes in the EBD, as shown by hyperactive mutants (e.g., LeuO‑S120D) that exhibit higher DNA‑binding affinity. Overall, LeuO serves as a global regulator that integrates signals (still unknown) to modulate transcription of diverse stress‑response, virulence, and metabolic pathways. {PubMed:31184713}. LeuO is described as a LysR‑type transcriptional regulator that acts as an activator of the iatB (latB) gene in Escherichia coli. Overexpression of LeuO caused a ~15‑fold increase in iatB transcript levels, indicating that LeuO positively regulates iatB expression. The article also notes that LeuO is involved in coordinating the bacterial stress response, is up‑regulated upon entry into stationary phase, and can activate several cryptic fimbrial loci, resulting in increased cell adhesion and biofilm formation. {PubMed:31462414}. LeuO is a LysR‑type transcriptional regulator in Escherichia coli that acts as a repressor of the small regulatory RNA DsrA. By down‑regulating DsrA, LeuO indirectly reduces translation of the general stress sigma factor RpoS (σ^S), an effect that is most pronounced at low growth temperatures. Overproduction of LeuO (e.g., via a Tn10 insertion that provides the IS10 p_out promoter) leads to decreased rpoS translational reporter activity and lower σ^S protein levels, whereas loss of LeuO does not affect rpoS. LeuO expression itself is normally very low and is strongly repressed by the nucleoid‑associated protein H‑NS; in an hns mutant, leuO is derepressed, leading to further repression of dsrA. Thus, LeuO functions as a component of an H‑NS → LeuO → DsrA → rpoS regulatory cascade that modulates rpoS translation in response to environmental cues, particularly low temperature. {PubMed:9302018}. LeuO is a LysR‑family transcriptional regulator that was first identified as the activator of the leucine biosynthetic operon leuABCD. Subsequent studies revealed that LeuO functions as a global regulator influencing a wide range of cellular processes, including bacterial virulence, quorum‑sensing, and motility. It therefore modulates expression of multiple genes beyond the leucine operon, contributing to the overall regulatory network of *E. coli*. {PubMed:31054315}.
