Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the binding-protein-dependent transport system for glutamine. Probably responsible for energy coupling to the transport system.
Merged_Functions: The glnQ gene encodes a cytoplasmic ATP‑binding cassette (ABC) protein that provides the energy for glutamine transport in Group B Streptococcus. Disruption of glnQ abolishes radiolabeled glutamine uptake and confers resistance to the toxic glutamine analog γ‑L‑glutamylhydrazide, confirming its role in glutamine import. In addition to its transport function, loss of glnQ leads to a >90 % reduction in binding to immobilized fibronectin, a >50 % decrease in adherence to and invasion of respiratory epithelial cells, and a marked attenuation of virulence in a neonatal rat model (increased LD₅₀ by 1–4 log units). The gene does not encode a surface adhesin (it lacks a signal sequence), and transcription of the known fibronectin‑binding adhesin scpB is unchanged in glnQ mutants. The authors propose that glnQ influences fibronectin adherence indirectly, likely by altering cytoplasmic glutamine levels and thereby affecting the post‑transcriptional regulation or activity of one or more fibronectin adhesins. {PubMed:12010975}. glnQ encodes a third essential component of the Escherichia coli glutamine permease (high‑affinity glutamine transport) system. Together with the periplasmic glutamine‑binding protein (glnH) and the membrane protein (glnP), the glnQ product is required for functional glutamine uptake. The gene was identified by complementation tests and its protein product was detected in an expression system, showing a size consistent with the predicted open reading frame and a moderate level of hydrophobic residues, suggesting a role in the membrane-associated permease complex. {PubMed:3027504}. The article identifies glnQ as encoding a subunit of a glutamine high‑affinity transport system (glutamine permease). It is one of the genes whose expression is repressed by the nucleoid‑associated protein Fis, and it functions in the uptake of glutamine across the cell membrane. {PubMed:7860604}. The glnQ gene encodes the membrane‑bound component (protein H2) of the glutamine transport system in Bacillus stearothermophilus. Together with the periplasmic glutamine‑binding protein encoded by glnH (protein HX), it forms an operon that mediates active uptake of L‑glutamine. Disruption of glnQ abolishes glutamine utilization as a sole nitrogen source, confers resistance to the toxic glutamine analog γ‑L‑glutamylhydrazide, and eliminates measurable glutamine transport, demonstrating that glnQ is essential for glutamine import. Its expression is temperature‑dependent, being strongly induced at 65 °C in nitrogen‑rich medium and repressed at 45 °C, indicating a role in thermoadaptation of nitrogen metabolism. {PubMed:1856180}.
Curated_Functions: Provides ATP‑binding cassette–type energy for high‑affinity glutamine transport. {PubMed:12010975}. Is required for glutamine import, enabling utilization of glutamine as a sole nitrogen source and conferring resistance to the toxic analog γ‑L‑glutamylhydrazide when absent. {PubMed:12010975, PubMed:3027504, PubMed:1856180}. Forms part of the membrane‑associated glutamine permease complex together with the periplasmic binding protein GlnH and the membrane protein GlnP (or H2), constituting an essential subunit of the high‑affinity glutamine transport system. {PubMed:3027504, PubMed:1856180}. Modulates fibronectin binding, epithelial cell adherence and invasion, and virulence, likely through indirect effects on cytoplasmic glutamine levels and downstream adhesin activity. {PubMed:12010975}. Is transcriptionally repressed by the nucleoid‑associated protein Fis. {PubMed:7860604}. Exhibits temperature‑dependent expression, being strongly induced at 65 °C in nitrogen‑rich medium, thereby contributing to thermoadaptation of nitrogen metabolism. {PubMed:1856180}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in translocation of long-chain fatty acids across the outer membrane. It is a receptor for the bacteriophage T2. FadL may form a specific channel.
Merged_Functions: The ttr locus encodes an outer‑membrane protein that is essential for the uptake and utilization of long‑chain fatty acids (approximately C12–C18, e.g., oleate C18:1) as a sole carbon source.  In addition, the Ttr protein serves as the receptor for bacteriophage T2, conferring sensitivity to the phage when present.  Mutations in ttr (or the identical fadL locus) abolish long‑chain fatty‑acid transport, prevent growth on oleate, and render cells resistant to T2; complementation with a fadL⁺ plasmid restores both fatty‑acid uptake and T2 susceptibility.  The protein is a ~43 kDa outer‑membrane component, is surface‑exposed (proteinase K‑sensitive), and appears to associate with the peptidoglycan layer. {PubMed:3286621}. The ttr locus encodes an outer‑membrane protein (≈52 kDa) that serves as the major receptor for bacteriophage T2.  In addition, the Ttr protein is required for the translocation of long‑chain fatty acids (e.g., oleate) across the outer membrane, enabling growth on these compounds as the sole carbon source.  Mutations in ttr (e.g., ttr::Tn10) abolish the 52‑kDa protein, confer resistance to phage T2, and produce an oleate‑negative (OA⁻) phenotype, indicating loss of fatty‑acid uptake.  The gene appears to be linked to fadL and may be part of an operon that includes the inner‑membrane fatty‑acid transporter FadL. {PubMed:3536849}. The article describes transthyretin (TTR) as a homotetrameric plasma protein that functions as a carrier for thyroid hormones (triiodothyronine and thyroxine) and for retinol, the latter via binding to retinol‑binding protein when it is loaded with retinol. TTR is primarily expressed in adult liver, the choroid plexus of the brain, and the retina, and its normal role is to transport these ligands in the bloodstream and cerebrospinal fluid. {PubMed:19250316}. Transthyretin (TTR) is a thyroid‑hormone‑binding protein that participates in the homeostatic ‘buffering’ system for circulating thyroid hormones.  It binds thyroxine (T4) with higher affinity than triiodothyronine (T3) in eutherian mammals, thereby regulating the free/bound ratio of these hormones in plasma and in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).  TTR is synthesized primarily in the liver of adult eutherians (and herbivorous marsupials) and, more intensely, in the choroid plexus epithelium of reptiles, birds and mammals.  Brain‑derived TTR is secreted unidirectionally into the ventricular CSF, where it either binds T4 directly or transports a pre‑formed TTR‑T4 complex into the CSF.  This CSF‑bound T4 serves as a reservoir that supplies the brain with substrate for local conversion of T4 to the biologically active T3 by type‑II deiodinases, supporting neurodevelopment and differentiation (maximal TTR expression precedes peak neuroblast replication).  By limiting rapid permeation of lipophilic thyroid hormones into cells, TTR helps maintain appropriate extracellular hormone pools and contributes to overall thyroid‑hormone distribution throughout the body.  The protein functions redundantly with other thyroid‑hormone‑binding proteins (albumin, TBG), such that loss of TTR alone produces minimal phenotypic change, underscoring its role within a network that safeguards thyroid‑hormone homeostasis. {PubMed:12379491}. The fadL locus encodes a protein required for the uptake of long‑chain fatty acids into Escherichia coli cells. Mutants lacking fadL cannot grow on fatty acids longer than C11 because they are unable to transport these substrates across the cytoplasmic membrane, even though downstream β‑oxidation enzymes (including acyl‑CoA synthetase) are functional. In fadR fadL double mutants, medium‑chain fatty acids can be utilized, indicating that FadL specifically facilitates transport of long‑chain (e.g., oleate, myristate, palmitate) fatty acids. Thus, FadL functions as a key component of the long‑chain fatty‑acid transport system, acting together with other loci such as fadD. {PubMed:356053}. Encodes the outer membrane protein FadL, which is essential for the uptake of exogenous long‑chain fatty acids in Escherichia coli. FadL binds long‑chain fatty acids with high affinity and enables their transport across the outer membrane, acting as a specific channel. The protein also functions as a receptor for bacteriophage T2 and displays a heat‑modifiable property typical of many gram‑negative outer membrane proteins. {PubMed:1987139}. Encodes an outer‑membrane protein that acts as a high‑affinity receptor for exogenous long‑chain fatty acids, binding these hydrophobic molecules and mediating their uptake into the cell. The FadL protein is central to the transport of long‑chain fatty acids and its expression is subject to osmotic regulation via the OmpR‑EnvZ two‑component system. {PubMed:8413182}. Encodes an outer‑membrane protein (~43 kDa) that is essential for the uptake of long‑chain fatty acids (C12–C18) in Escherichia coli. FadL binds these fatty acids at the cell surface, allows their passage through the outer membrane, and thus provides substrates for energy production and phospholipid biosynthesis. In addition, FadL acts as the receptor for bacteriophage T2; strains lacking FadL are resistant to T2 and cannot grow on oleate, while complementation with a fadL⁺ plasmid restores T2 sensitivity and growth on long‑chain fatty acids. The protein is surface‑exposed (proteinase K‑sensitive), associates with the peptidoglycan layer after SDS treatment, and functions as a specific, high‑affinity channel for long‑chain fatty acids. {PubMed:3286621}. The article states that fadL encodes an inner membrane protein that is required for the transport of long‑chain fatty acids (C12 or longer) into Escherichia coli cells.  Cells lacking fadL cannot grow on oleate as the sole carbon and energy source, indicating that FadL is essential for uptake of this long‑chain fatty acid.  The gene is located near the ttr locus, and the authors propose that fadL may be part of an operon whose other component (ttr) encodes an outer‑membrane protein that works together with FadL in long‑chain fatty‑acid transport and also serves as a receptor for bacteriophage T2. {PubMed:3536849}.
Curated_Functions: Mediates uptake of long‑chain fatty acids (C12–C18) across the outer membrane, enabling growth on these substrates as the sole carbon source. {PubMed:3286621, PubMed:3536849, PubMed:356053, PubMed:1987139, PubMed:8413182}. Binds long‑chain fatty acids with high affinity at the cell surface and facilitates their translocation through the outer membrane. {PubMed:3286621, PubMed:1987139, PubMed:8413182}. Acts as the high‑affinity receptor for bacteriophage T2, conferring susceptibility to infection. {PubMed:3286621, PubMed:3536849, PubMed:1987139}. Is surface‑exposed, proteinase K‑sensitive, and associates with the peptidoglycan layer after SDS treatment. {PubMed:3286621}. Displays a heat‑modifiable property characteristic of Gram‑negative outer‑membrane proteins. {PubMed:1987139}. Expression is up‑regulated under high‑osmolarity conditions via the OmpR‑EnvZ two‑component regulatory system. {PubMed:8413182}. Binds thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, serving as a carrier and buffer that regulates the free/bound hormone ratio. {PubMed:19250316, PubMed:12379491}. Transports retinol indirectly by forming a complex with retinol‑binding protein loaded with retinol. {PubMed:19250316}. Provides a cerebrospinal‑fluid reservoir of T4 that supplies the brain with substrate for local conversion to T3, supporting neurodevelopment and differentiation. {PubMed:12379491}. Is synthesized primarily in liver, choroid plexus, and retina and secreted into the bloodstream and ventricular cerebrospinal fluid. {PubMed:19250316, PubMed:12379491}. Functions redundantly with albumin and thyroxine‑binding globulin, such that loss of this protein alone yields minimal phenotypic effects. {PubMed:12379491}.

Merged_Functions: Encodes the structural gene for lipid A disaccharide synthase. The enzyme catalyzes the condensation of UDP‑2,3‑diacylglucosamine with 2,3‑diacylglucosamine‑1‑phosphate to produce a tetra‑acyl‑disaccharide‑1‑phosphate (the lipid A disaccharide precursor) and UDP, representing a key step in the biosynthetic pathway that generates lipid A, the membrane‑anchoring component of lipopolysaccharide in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:2824445}. LpxB encodes a membrane‑associated glycosyltransferase of the GT‑B family that catalyzes the third step of the Raetz pathway for lipid A (the membrane anchor of lipopolysaccharide) biosynthesis in Gram‑negative bacteria. Specifically, LpxB mediates an SN2‑type reaction in which the 6′‑hydroxyl group of lipid X attacks the anomeric carbon of UDP‑diacyl‑glucosamine (UDP‑DAG), releasing UDP and forming a β(1→6)‑tetraacyl‑disaccharide‑1‑phosphate (the lipid A disaccharide). This reaction creates the tetraacylated disaccharide that is subsequently further acylated to generate the mature lipid A anchor. LpxB is essential for Escherichia coli growth, is highly conserved among Gram‑negative bacteria, and functions as a C‑terminally swapped homodimer that uses a surface‑exposed hydrophobic/basic patch to associate with the membrane and extract its lipid substrates. {PubMed:29371662}. The lpxB gene encodes lipid A disaccharide synthase, an essential enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of the lipid A disaccharide core of the outer membrane lipopolysaccharide (LPS). This activity is crucial for cell growth and division, as mutations in lpxB render cells temperature‑sensitive for growth and division. {PubMed:3316192}. The lpxB gene encodes the enzyme lipid A disaccharide synthase, which catalyzes the key step in lipid A biosynthesis where UDP‑2,3‑diacyl‑GlcN is condensed with 2,3‑diacyl‑GlcN‑1‑P to form the lipid A disaccharide (β‑1→6 linked diacyl‑GlcN) and UDP. Mutations in lpxB abolish this activity, leading to accumulation of monosaccharide lipid A precursors and temperature‑sensitive growth, demonstrating that lpxB is the structural gene for lipid A disaccharide synthase. {PubMed:3531165}. The article states that lpxB encodes the enzyme lipid A disaccharide synthase, which catalyzes the fifth step of lipid A biosynthesis in Escherichia coli. This enzyme is responsible for forming the lipid A disaccharide backbone by linking two glucosamine‑containing lipid A precursors, thereby completing the core disaccharide structure that serves as the hydrophobic anchor of lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane. {PubMed:3277952}. The lpxB gene encodes a lipid A disaccharide synthase that catalyzes the key glycosyl‑transfer step in lipid A biosynthesis, joining UDP‑2,3‑diacyl‑glucosamine with 2,3‑diacyl‑glucosamine‑1‑phosphate to form the tetra‑acylated lipid IV_A precursor. Legionella pneumophila possesses two paralogues of this gene (lcsC/lpxB1 and lpxB2); both can partially complement an Escherichia coli conditional lpxB mutant, demonstrating that they retain lipid A disaccharide synthase activity. Overexpression of the lcsC/lpxB1 paralogue (referred to as lpxB1) makes L. pneumophila cytotoxic toward Acanthamoeba castellanii, whereas overexpression of lpxB2 does not, indicating functional divergence. LPS isolated from strains overexpressing either paralogue triggers tumour necrosis factor‑α production by macrophages with different potencies, reflecting that the enzymes influence the structure of lipid A and thus modulate host immune responses. {PubMed:17975091}. The pgsB gene encodes the membrane‑associated glycosyltransferase LpxB, an essential enzyme of the Raetz (lipid A synthesis) pathway in Gram‑negative bacteria. LpxB catalyzes the nucleophilic attack of the 6′‑hydroxyl group of lipid X on the anomeric carbon of UDP‑diacyl‑glucosamine (UDP‑DAG), producing a β(1→6)‑tetraacyl‑disaccharide 1‑phosphate (the lipid A disaccharide) and releasing UDP. This reaction forms the core membrane‑anchor moiety of lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The enzyme functions as a C‑terminally swapped homodimer with a GT‑B fold, requires specific catalytic residues (e.g., D98 as the catalytic base and R201 for stabilizing the UDP leaving group), and relies on a surface‑exposed hydrophobic/basic patch for membrane association and extraction of lipid substrates. {PubMed:29371662}. The pgsB gene (also designated lpxB) encodes the enzyme lipid A disaccharide synthase. This enzyme catalyzes the key step in lipid A biosynthesis that joins two monosaccharide lipid A precursors—UDP‑2,3‑diacyl‑GlcN and 2,3‑diacyl‑GlcN‑1‑P—to form the lipid A disaccharide (a β‑1→6 linked diacyl‑GlcN) and releases UDP. Mutations in pgsB (lpxB) lead to accumulation of the monosaccharide precursors and loss of lipid A disaccharide synthase activity, confirming that pgsB is the structural gene for this enzyme and is essential for proper lipid A assembly in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:3531165}. PgsB is one of the three subunits (PgsB, PgsC, PgsA) that form the membrane‑bound γ‑polyglutamic acid (γ‑PGA) synthetase complex. It belongs to the amide‑ligase superfamily and contains a conserved ATP‑binding motif (GIRGKS) at its N‑terminus. PgsB catalyzes the hydrolysis of ATP, supplying the energy required for the ATP‑dependent polymerization of L‑ and D‑glutamate into γ‑PGA. Thus, it provides the catalytic ATPase activity essential for γ‑PGA synthesis. {PubMed:23919316}. Encodes a crucial component of the poly‑γ‑glutamate synthetic (PGS) system in Bacillus subtilis IFO 3336. PgsB, together with PgsC and PgsA, is essential for the extracellular production of poly‑γ‑glutamate when expressed in Bacillus or heterologous Escherichia coli cells. The protein shows strong similarity to enzymes of the amide‑ligase superfamily, indicating it participates directly in the ribosome‑independent polymerization of L‑ and D‑glutamate residues via γ‑amide linkages to form the poly‑γ‑glutamate polymer. {PubMed:10486244}. The pgsB gene encodes one of the three core subunits (PgsB) of the poly‑γ‑glutamic acid synthase complex (PgsBCA) that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent polymerization of L‑glutamate and D‑glutamate into extracellular γ‑poly‑glutamic acid (γ‑PGA). PgsB, together with PgsC, forms the main part of the catalytic site of the membrane‑associated enzyme complex, enabling the assembly of glutamate monomers into the polymer. It is a rate‑limiting component of the γ‑PGA biosynthetic pathway, as demonstrated by two‑plasmid induction experiments where over‑expression of pgsB (and pgsC) significantly increased γ‑PGA production. {PubMed:31837088}. Encodes Lipid A disaccharide synthase, the enzyme that catalyzes the condensation of UDP‑2,3‑diacylglucosamine with 2,3‑diacylglucosamine‑1‑phosphate to form the tetraacyl‑disaccharide‑1‑phosphate intermediate of lipid A biosynthesis (UDP‑2,3‑diacylglucosamine + 2,3‑diacylglucosamine‑1‑phosphate → 2′,3′‑diacyl‑glucosamine(β1→6)‑2,3‑diacylglucosamine‑1‑phosphate + UDP). This reaction generates the first lipid A disaccharide precursor, a key step in the assembly of the lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:2824445}. The b0182 gene encodes LpxB, a membrane‑associated glycosyltransferase of the GT‑B family that catalyzes the third step of the Raetz pathway for lipid A (the membrane anchor of lipopolysaccharide, LPS) synthesis. LpxB mediates an inverting SN2 reaction in which the 6′‑hydroxyl of lipid X attacks the anomeric carbon of UDP‑diacyl‑glucosamine (UDP‑DAG), forming a β(1→6) tetra‑acyl‑disaccharide (the lipid A disaccharide) and releasing UDP. The enzyme functions as a C‑terminally swapped homodimer, with each subunit contributing to the other's Rossmann‑like domains, and contains a hydrophobic/basic surface patch that likely anchors it to the inner membrane to extract lipid substrates. LpxB is essential for growth of *Escherichia coli* and other Gram‑negative bacteria, making it a critical component of LPS biosynthesis and a potential target for novel antibiotics. {PubMed:29371662}. The b0182 gene encodes the 28‑kDa UDP‑N‑acetylglucosamine (UDP‑GlcNAc) acyltransferase, the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step of lipid A biosynthesis in Escherichia coli. It transfers a β‑hydroxymyristoyl group from R‑3‑hydroxymyristoyl acyl‑carrier protein to the 3‑position of the glucosamine ring of UDP‑GlcNAc, producing UDP‑3‑O‑(R‑3‑hydroxymyristoyl)‑N‑acetylglucosamine, the precursor for subsequent steps in the assembly of the lipid A component of lipopolysaccharide. {PubMed:3277952}.

Merged_Functions: The gene encodes RNase HII, an enzyme that specifically cleaves the RNA strand of RNA‑DNA hybrid molecules. In Streptococcus pneumoniae the encoded protein is a ~31.9 kDa polypeptide (290 aa) that represents the sole RNase H activity in this organism. RNase HII is thought to participate in DNA metabolism by removing RNA primers from Okazaki fragments, repairing ribonucleotides inadvertently incorporated into DNA, and possibly generating strand breaks that target the newly synthesized strand for mismatch repair. The enzyme requires divalent metal ions (Mg²⁺/Mn²⁺) for activity and contains three conserved sequence motifs characteristic of RNase HII proteins across bacteria and eukaryotes. {PubMed:9190796}. The rnhB gene encodes the RNase HII enzyme. RNase HII hydrolyzes the RNA strand of RNA‑DNA hybrid molecules, thereby removing RNA primers or ribonucleotides that become incorporated into DNA. In Streptococcus pneumoniae it is the sole RNase H activity (≈31.9 kDa protein) and can complement an E. coli strain lacking both RNase HI (rnhA) and RecC, demonstrating functional equivalence to the bacterial RNase HII. The enzyme is thought to participate in DNA replication (primer removal from Okazaki fragments), may generate single‑strand breaks at adventitious ribonucleotides to target mismatch repair, and appears to be universally present in living cells, with homologous genes identified in bacteria, yeast, roundworm, mouse and human. {PubMed:9190796}. Encodes the RNase HII enzyme (the Lmo1273/Imo1273 protein), a homolog of Bacillus subtilis rnhB. The enzyme specifically degrades the ribonucleotide moiety of RNA–DNA hybrid molecules, removing RNA primers from Okazaki fragments and excising misincorporated ribonucleotides during DNA replication or repair. Functional complementation of an Escherichia coli rnhA‑rnhB thermosensitive mutant demonstrates that Lmo1273 provides bona‑fide RNase H activity. In Listeria monocytogenes, rnhB is required for full virulence in vivo: deletion of the gene leads to strong attenuation in mouse infection, while over‑expression also reduces virulence, indicating that appropriate expression levels are critical. The protein exerts pleiotropic regulatory effects, altering the transcription of numerous genes—including amino‑acid/oligopeptide transporters and many sigma B‑dependent stress‑response genes—suggesting additional roles in DNA replication/repair and possibly in regulation of gene expression via antisense RNAs. {PubMed:19246760}.
Curated_Functions: Cleaves the RNA strand of RNA‑DNA hybrid molecules. {PubMed:9190796, PubMed:19246760}. Removes RNA primers from Okazaki fragments during DNA replication. {PubMed:9190796, PubMed:19246760}. Excises misincorporated ribonucleotides from DNA. {PubMed:9190796, PubMed:19246760}. Generates single‑strand breaks at ribonucleotides to initiate mismatch repair. {PubMed:9190796}. Requires Mg²⁺ or Mn²⁺ as a divalent metal cofactor for activity. {PubMed:9190796}. Acts as the sole RNase H activity in Streptococcus pneumoniae. {PubMed:9190796}. Complements RNase H deficiency in Escherichia coli, demonstrating functional equivalence to bacterial RNase HII. {PubMed:9190796, PubMed:19246760}. Is required for full virulence of Listeria monocytogenes; both deletion and overexpression impair infection. {PubMed:19246760}. Modulates transcription of numerous genes, including amino‑acid/oligopeptide transporters and sigma B‑dependent stress‑response genes, indicating pleiotropic regulatory effects and possible regulation via antisense RNAs. {PubMed:19246760}.

L‑fuculokinase activity is coordinately induced with the other L‑fucose enzymes (permease, isomerase, aldolase) and with D‑ribulokinase when cells are grown on L‑fucose or D‑arabinose. In addition to its primary substrate L‑fuculose, the enzyme can phosphorylate D‑ribulose with about 73 % of the efficiency observed for L‑fuculose, indicating a secondary activity toward D‑ribulose. Thus, fucK provides the kinase step that converts L‑fuculose into its phosphorylated form, enabling further metabolism of L‑fucose (and contributing to D‑arabinose utilization) in E. coli B. {PubMed:3056899}. The fucK gene encodes L‑fuculose kinase, an enzyme that phosphorylates L‑fuculose (the product of L‑fucose isomerization by FucI) to L‑fuculose‑1‑phosphate. This step is part of the native fucose catabolic pathway in Escherichia coli, which competes with the engineered salvage pathway that converts L‑fucose into GDP‑L‑fucose for 2′‑fucosyllactose production. {PubMed:31145478}. The article states that fucK encodes fucokinase, an enzyme involved in the native fucose catabolic (bypass) pathway in E. coli. Together with fucI (fucose isomerase) and FucA (L‑fuculose‑1‑phosphate aldolase), FucK phosphorylates L‑fucose to fucose‑1‑phosphate, directing fucose toward degradation rather than toward GDP‑fucose synthesis. Deletion of fucK (along with fucI) was shown to block this bypass metabolism, increase intracellular fucose availability for the salvage pathway, and thereby improve 2′‑fucosyllactose production. {PubMed:33499605}. The fucK gene encodes fuculose kinase, an enzyme that catalyzes the phosphorylation of L‑fuculose to L‑fuculose‑1‑phosphate as the second step in the inducible L‑fucose catabolic pathway of Escherichia coli. This pathway proceeds sequentially: L‑fucose is first isomerized by fucose isomerase (FucI) to L‑fuculose, then phosphorylated by the FucK‑encoded kinase, and finally cleaved by fuculose‑1‑phosphate aldolase (FucA). Deletion of the fucI‑fucK gene cluster blocks this catabolism, preventing the formation of downstream toxic intermediates such as L‑lactaldehyde and thereby improving cell growth and redirecting fucose flux toward 2‑fucosyllactose production. {PubMed:27217241}. The fucK gene encodes L‑fuculose kinase, the enzyme that phosphorylates L‑fuculose to produce L‑fuculose‑1‑phosphate. This phosphorylated sugar is the true inducer of the fucose regulon. fucK is a member of the clockwise‑oriented fucPIK operon and, like the upstream fucP and fucI genes, does not possess an independent promoter; its expression depends on transcription initiated at the fucP promoter. {PubMed:3325779}. The article states that fucK encodes the kinase component of the L‑fucose catabolic pathway. In the inducible fuc regulon, the fucK‑encoded enzyme catalyzes the phosphorylation of L‑fuculose to L‑fuculose‑1‑phosphate, a key step that follows the fucI‑encoded isomerase and precedes the fucA‑encoded aldolase. This kinase activity is part of the fucPIK operon and is essential for converting fucose into intermediates that can be further metabolized, enabling growth on L‑fucose as a carbon source. Enzyme assays in the study measured fucK activity by monitoring the formation of L‑[6‑³H]fuculose‑1‑phosphate. {PubMed:2834341}.

Loss of AmpD leads to accumulation of anhMurNAc‑tripeptide in the cytoplasm and triggers β‑lactamase induction, indicating a regulatory role in antibiotic resistance pathways. {PubMed:26443726}. ampD encodes a cytosolic N‑acetyl‑anhydromuramyl‑L‑alanine amidase that hydrolyzes 1,6‑anhydromuropeptide, a peptidoglycan‑derived signal molecule that triggers AmpC β‑lactamase expression. By cleaving this signal, AmpD limits the accumulation of 1,6‑anhydromuropeptide in the cytoplasm, thereby regulating the inducible expression of the chromosomal AmpC β‑lactamase. Inactivation of ampD results in cytoplasmic buildup of the signal, leading to moderate basal‑level and hyper‑inducible AmpC production and increased β‑lactam resistance. {PubMed:10681322}. Encodes a protein that functions as a negative regulator of ampC β‑lactamase expression. AmpD interacts with the AmpR regulator in the presence of β‑lactam inducers, decreasing activation of the ampC gene and thus lowering the amount of β‑lactamase produced. Higher levels of AmpD (e.g., from additional plasmid copies) reduce the rate and magnitude of β‑lactamase induction and lower MIC values, whereas loss‑of‑function mutations in ampD result in over‑production of β‑lactamase and high‑level resistance. {PubMed:3263688}. The ampD gene encodes a cytosolic protein that acts as a negative regulator of ampC β‑lactamase transcription, thereby controlling the inducible expression of AmpC β‑lactamase in gram‑negative bacteria. AmpD works together with AmpG to influence the activity of the transcriptional activator AmpR, and it is proposed to be involved in peptidoglycan metabolism, possibly by modulating carboxypeptidase activity and the availability of cell‑wall‑derived ligands that activate AmpR. {PubMed:8383940}. AmpD encodes an enzyme involved in peptidoglycan recycling that converts the AmpR allosteric activator 1‑6‑anhydromuropeptide into the blocker UDP‑N‑acetylmuramic acid‑pentapeptide. The blocker binds the transcriptional regulator AmpR and prevents activation of the ampC β‑lactamase gene, thereby repressing ampC expression. Consequently, functional AmpD keeps AmpC β‑lactamase production low; loss‑of‑function mutations in ampD eliminate this conversion, leading to constitutive AmpC expression and β‑lactam antibiotic resistance. {PubMed:19648247}. AmpD encodes a cytoplasmic amidase that participates in peptidoglycan recycling. After peptidoglycan turnover, the degradation product 1,6‑anhydro‑MurNAc‑tripeptide (and related anhMurNAc‑peptides) is imported into the cytoplasm via the AmpG permease. AmpD hydrolyzes the peptide bond in these anhMurNAc‑peptides, releasing the murein tripeptide, which is then ligated back to UDP‑MurNAc and re‑enters the peptidoglycan biosynthetic pathway. In an ampD‑deficient mutant, these anhMurNAc‑peptides accumulate, demonstrating AmpD’s role in clearing them during cell‑wall turnover. {PubMed:18390656}. AmpD encodes a cytoplasmic N‑acetylmuramyl‑L‑Ala amidase that cleaves the peptide bond linking the tripeptide (L‑Ala‑D‑Glu‑meso‑DAP) to 1,6‑anhydro‑N‑acetylmuramic acid (anhMurNAc‑tripeptide). By hydrolyzing this muropeptide, AmpD removes the tripeptide, preventing accumulation of the anhMurNAc‑tripeptide that serves as the inducer of β‑lactamase expression. Consequently, AmpD acts as a negative regulator of β‑lactamase production (loss of AmpD yields constitutive β‑lactamase) and is an essential component of the murein recycling pathway, enabling degradation of recycled cell‑wall fragments and maintaining low intracellular levels of the inducing ligand. {PubMed:9158731}.

Merged_Functions: GlpB encodes a 44‑kDa membrane‑associated protein that is essential for anaerobic growth on glycerol‑3‑phosphate. It is localized to the cytoplasmic (inner) membrane and contains one or more ferredoxin‑type iron‑sulfur clusters. GlpB receives electrons from the soluble GlpA‑GlpC catalytic dimer (the anaerobic glycerol‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase) and transfers them to the membrane‑bound menaquinone pool, which in turn delivers the electrons to the terminal electron acceptor fumarate (via fumarate reductase). Thus, GlpB functions as the membrane‑bound electron‑transfer intermediary linking GlpAC to fumarate reduction during anaerobic respiration. {PubMed:7576488}. The glpB gene encodes the membrane‑anchor subunit of the anaerobic sn‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase complex in Escherichia coli.  While the catalytic (62 kDa) and electron‑transfer (41 kDa) subunits are encoded by glpA and glpC, respectively, glpB provides the integral membrane component that anchors the enzyme to the cytoplasmic membrane.  Mutations in glpB abolish anaerobic growth on glycerol plus fumarate but do not eliminate enzymatic activity in vitro; instead, the active enzyme accumulates in the soluble (cytoplasmic) fraction, indicating that glpB is required for proper membrane association of the dehydrogenase.  The glpB gene is part of the glpA‑glpC‑glpB operon and is transcribed divergently from the adjacent glpTQ operon. {PubMed:3027032}. glpB encodes the 43 kDa subunit of the anaerobic sn‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase (GlpAB dimer) in Escherichia coli. This subunit contains a putative flavin mononucleotide (FMN)‑binding domain and harbors conserved residues (including a histidine and a cysteine) that form the catalytic centre responsible for oxidizing sn‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate. Together with the larger GlpA subunit, GlpB constitutes the catalytic core of the enzyme that initiates the anaerobic electron‑transport chain by transferring electrons from glycerol‑3‑phosphate to downstream acceptors. {PubMed:3286606}. In the typical anaerobic glycerol‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase (GlpABC) complex, GlpB is a flavoprotein that binds flavin mononucleotide (FMN). Together with GlpA (the catalytic subunit that oxidizes glycerol‑3‑phosphate) and GlpC, GlpB participates in forming an electron‑transfer pathway that shuttles electrons from the G3P oxidation reaction to the inner membrane, thereby linking glycerol metabolism to the respiratory chain. The article notes that GlpB is absent in Thermococcus kodakarensis, which instead uses a different set of proteins (MOX and NOX) in its operon. {PubMed:30583977}.
Curated_Functions: Required for anaerobic growth on glycerol‑3‑phosphate. {PubMed:7576488, PubMed:3027032}. Merged_Functions: MngR (formerly FarR) is a transcriptional repressor that controls the expression of the adjacent mngA‑mngB operon and its own gene. When KicA is present, it suppresses the killing function of KicB, allowing normal cell growth and protein synthesis. Moreover, when the kicA‑kicB operon is carried on a plasmid, KicA functions as the antitoxin component of a post‑segregational killing (toxin‑antitoxin) system, ensuring that plasmid‑free segregants are eliminated. {PubMed:7513784}. MukE is a protein required for proper chromosome partitioning in Escherichia coli. Null mutants lacking mukE are temperature‑sensitive for colony formation and produce a high frequency of anucleate cells, phenotypes identical to those of mukF and mukB mutants. The absence of MukE does not affect the initiation of chromosome replication nor the stable maintenance of the mini‑F plasmid, indicating that its role is specific to the segregation/positioning of chromosomal DNA during cell division. Overproduction of MukE does not cause anucleate cells, suggesting that precise cellular levels are important. Together with MukF and MukB, MukE functions as part of an operon (smtA‑mukF‑mukE‑mukB) that contributes to the chromosome partitioning machinery. {PubMed:8602138}. MukE encodes a 27 kDa protein that is an essential component of the MukFEB complex required for chromosome partitioning in Escherichia coli. Together with MukF and MukB, MukE forms a multimeric complex that associates with DNA and is necessary for accurate segregation of replicated chromosomes. MukE interacts directly with MukF (and indirectly with MukB via MukF), and multiple MukE molecules can bind to a MukF dimer, contributing to a heterotetrameric MukFE sub‑complex that then associates with a MukB homodimer. Loss of mukE results in temperature‑sensitive growth and a high frequency of anucleate cells, indicating its indispensable role in the chromosome segregation process. {PubMed:10545099}. MukE is a component of the MukF‑MukE‑MukB (MukFEB) complex in Escherichia coli. Together with MukF and MukB, MukE participates in the organization and segregation of the chromosome. The MukFEB complex forms discrete clusters (foci) that localize to the one‑quarter and three‑quarter positions of the cell, acting as “reorganization centres” for folded sister chromosomes after replication. Presence of MukE (and MukF) is required for MukB to assemble into these foci; loss of MukE results in a dispersed MukB distribution throughout the cell and phenotypes identical to muk null mutants, including temperature‑sensitive growth, anucleate cell production, and defects in chromosome structure and positioning. {PubMed:11401691}. MukE is an accessory protein of the Escherichia coli MukBFE complex that is essential for proper chromosome segregation and condensation.  In solution MukE exists in a reversible monomer‑dimer equilibrium (Kd ≈ 15–18 µM) and only the dimeric form interacts with the MukF dimer.  MukE dimers bind to a MukF dimer to generate two high‑affinity complexes, F₂E₂ (two MukE dimers bound to one MukF dimer) and F₂E₄ (two MukE dimers bound to one MukF dimer), both of which are observed in vivo.  By forming these complexes, MukE acts as a “latch” that stabilizes the otherwise unstable interaction between MukB and MukF, thereby contributing to the formation of higher‑order MukB‑MukF‑MukE structures that serve as a chromatin scaffold.  The presence of MukE (together with MukF) influences whether the MukBFE complex is locked (B₂F₂E₄, refractory to DNA binding) or remodeling‑competent (B₂F₂E₂), thus modulating DNA access and facilitating chromosome partitioning. {PubMed:17355972}. MukE encodes the regulatory subunit of the Escherichia coli condensin complex MukBEF. Together with MukB (the SMC ATPase) and MukF, MukE forms a multisubunit clamp that bridges distant DNA segments, thereby promoting global chromosome folding, condensation, and segregation. The presence of MukE is required for the focal subcellular localization of MukBEF clusters at mid‑cell or quarter‑cell positions, a localization that is essential for cell viability. The enzyme participates in the microbial utilization of acrylate, converting the toxic intermediate acrylyl‑CoA into the metabolically useful propionyl‑CoA, and thus contributes to pathways such as acrylate degradation, propionate biosynthesis, and related carbon‑flux processes. {PubMed:33860390}. The acuI gene encodes the enzyme acrylyl‑CoA reductase (EC 1.3.1.84), a homodimeric medium‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase that catalyzes the NAD(P)H‑dependent reduction of toxic acrylyl‑CoA to propionyl‑CoA. This reaction is a key step in microbial acrylate metabolism, allowing cells to detoxify acrylyl‑CoA and to utilize acrylate as a carbon source in pathways such as fermentation of β‑alanine, 3‑hydroxypropionate utilization, and autotrophic CO₂ fixation. The wild‑type AcuI preferentially uses NADPH over NADH, but its cofactor specificity can be altered by mutagenesis of residues in the Rossmann‑fold coenzyme‑binding pocket. {PubMed:33860390}.

Merged_Functions: The plsC gene encodes the Escherichia coli lysophosphatidic acid acyltransferase (LPAAT), an essential membrane‑bound enzyme that catalyzes the second acylation step of glycerol‑3‑phosphate‑derived lipid synthesis, converting lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) into phosphatidic acid (PA). Together with PlsB, it drives the conversion of intermediates toward phosphatidic acid, thereby increasing the cellular pool of glycerophospholipids and expanding membrane structures. Overexpression of plsC (often together with plsb) was shown in the article to enhance membrane synthesis, providing more membrane surface area for lycopene storage. {PubMed:29868307}. The plsC gene encodes the bacterial 1‑acyl‑sn‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate acyltransferase (also called lysophosphatidate acyltransferase, LPA‑AT). This enzyme catalyses the second acylation step of the Kennedy pathway, converting lysophosphatidic acid (1‑acyl‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate) to phosphatidic acid by adding an acyl group at the sn‑2 position. The activity restores normal phospholipid composition in Escherichia coli, allowing metabolism of accumulated lysophosphatidic acid into phosphatidylethanolamine and other phospholipids, and is essential for cell viability. {PubMed:7948871}. The plsC gene encodes the 1‑acyl‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate (1‑acyl‑G3P) acyltransferase, the enzyme that catalyzes the second acyl‑transfer step in bacterial phospholipid biosynthesis. This enzyme transfers a fatty acyl group to the sn‑2 position of 1‑acyl‑G3P, converting it into phosphatidic acid, a key intermediate in the synthesis of membrane phospholipids. The article references plsC as the gene responsible for this activity and uses a temperature‑sensitive plsC mutant to demonstrate its role. {PubMed:9393688}. ParF is the Salmonella typhimurium protein that is 94 % identical to the Escherichia coli PlsC enzyme. According to the article, ParF (like PlsC) possesses definitive 1‑acyl‑sn‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate acyltransferase activity, i.e., it functions as a lysophosphatidic acid acyltransferase (LPA‑AT). This enzyme catalyzes the acylation of 1‑acyl‑sn‑glycerol‑3‑phosphate (lysophosphatidic acid) to form phosphatidic acid, a key step in the Kennedy pathway of phospholipid and triacylglycerol biosynthesis. {PubMed:7948871}. ParF is a Walker‑type ATPase belonging to the ParA family that drives segregation of the low‑copy TP228 plasmid. In its ATP‑bound state it binds DNA non‑specifically and self‑assembles into higher‑order polymers that form a three‑dimensional meshwork permeating the nucleoid. This meshwork dynamically relocates (oscillates) between the opposite poles of the nucleoid, creating a territorial scaffold that captures ParG‑bound plasmid complexes. Stimulation of ParF’s ATP hydrolysis by the partner protein ParG (via an arginine‑finger‑like motif) triggers disassembly of local polymer segments, allowing coordinated movement of the plasmid cargo. Thus, ParF defines the spatial territory for plasmid trafficking, mediates plasmid positioning and segregation, and its proper polymerization, nucleoid association, and ATP‑hydrolysis cycle are essential for faithful plasmid inheritance. {PubMed:28034957}. ParF is a ParA‑type ATPase encoded by the TP228 multidrug‑resistance plasmid that mediates plasmid segregation during bacterial cytokinesis. It binds and hydrolyzes ATP; ATP binding triggers the protein to assemble into higher‑order oligomeric bundles that create a three‑dimensional meshwork (the “Venus flytrap”) that invades the nucleoid interior. This meshwork captures the ParG‑parH centromere complex attached to the plasmid and transports it to the nucleoid poles, where the plasmid is deposited after localized dissolution of the ParF network. ParF’s ATPase activity and polymerisation are modulated by ATP hydrolysis and by direct interaction with the partner centromere‑binding protein ParG, whose N‑terminal arginine‑finger‑like motifs stimulate ParF’s ATP hydrolysis and promote bundle formation. Self‑association of ParF forms dimers and dimer‑of‑dimers that underlie the higher‑order structures. Mutations that alter the nucleotide‑binding pocket (e.g., D111A) reduce ATP hydrolysis, impair interaction with ParG, prevent higher‑order assembly, and consequently block plasmid segregation. {PubMed:32613008}. ParF is a member of the ubiquitous ParA superfamily of Walker‑type ATPases that drives DNA segregation of plasmid TP228 in bacteria. In its ATP‑bound form it polymerizes into extensive multistranded filaments; ADP antagonises this filamentation. The intrinsic ATPase activity of ParF is weak, but is stimulated approximately 30‑fold by its partner protein ParG. Polymerization of ParF and its ATP hydrolysis are key steps in the formation and remodeling of the segrosome complex that mediates accurate plasmid partition to daughter cells. {PubMed:17261809}.

The rfaJ gene (formerly waaR) encodes a non‑processive α‑1,2 glucosyltransferase that participates in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis. Specifically, the WaaR/RfaJ enzyme transfers the third glucose residue from UDP‑glucose to the non‑reducing end of the second glucose in the R‑core region of LPS, thereby completing the addition of a single α‑linked glucose to the R‑core of the LPS molecule. {PubMed:10234827}. The article mentions waaR as the gene encoding the HexIII glycosyltransferase in Escherichia coli K‑12. WaaR is proposed to add the terminal glucose residue to the outer core oligosaccharide of lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The authors suggest that WaaR may mistakenly recognize the glucose added by WaaG (GlcI) as the substrate normally acted on by WaaO (GlcII) and therefore can inefficiently add a terminal glucose when the normal pathway is disrupted. {PubMed:24479701}. The waaR gene encodes a non‑processive α‑1,2 glucosyltransferase that participates in the biosynthesis of the R‑core region of Escherichia coli lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The enzyme catalyzes the transfer of the third glucose residue from UDP‑glucose to the non‑reducing end of the second glucose of the R‑core, forming an α‑1,2 glycosidic linkage. This activity is essential for proper LPS structure, as loss of waaR function results in LPS lacking the terminal glucose and altered electrophoretic mobility. The catalytic mechanism requires four strictly conserved aspartic acid residues (Asp‑129, Asp‑131 in region I and Asp‑215, Asp‑217 in region III), which are critical for formation of a β‑glycosyl‑enzyme intermediate and subsequent generation of the α‑glycosidic bond. {PubMed:10234827}. WaaR encodes an α1,2‑glycosyltransferase that catalyzes the addition of the third glucose residue (GlcIII) to the K‑12 lipopolysaccharide outer core. This modification completes the outer core structure by providing the GlcIII branch, which is required for subsequent attachment of the terminal heptose (HepIV) by WaaU. Loss of WaaR results in a truncated outer core lacking GlcIII and HepIV, leading to altered LPS architecture and reduced retention of group 2 capsular polysaccharides (e.g., K5 and K1) on the cell surface. {PubMed:16428421}. In Salmonella typhimurium, WaaJ is an outer‑core glycosyltransferase that adds the HexIII glucose residue to the outer‑core oligosaccharide. It catalyzes the transfer of a glucose from UDP‑glucose (preferred donor) to the Gal‑Glc‑Hep₂‑1‑deP‑KLA acceptor produced by WaaI, forming a Glc‑Gal‑[Gal]‑Glc‑Hep₂‑1‑deP‑KLA product and completing the outer‑core structure. {PubMed:24479701}. The article indicates that waaJ is one of the waa (rfa) genes required for the stepwise synthesis of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core oligosaccharide in Escherichia coli K‑12. The waaJ product contributes to the formation of the Glc(α‑1,2)Glc structure in the LPS core; loss of waaJ results in a truncated LPS that resembles the short LPS of E. coli B. Consequently, the presence of functional waaJ is necessary for the proper assembly of the LPS core that serves as a receptor for certain PilV proteins (e.g., PilVC) during R64‑mediated conjugation. {PubMed:10732685}.

Merged_Functions: The rfaK gene (also called waaK) encodes a UDP‑N‑acetylglucosamine:(glucosyl) lipopolysaccharide α1,2‑N‑acetylglucosaminyltransferase. This enzyme transfers an N‑acetyl‑glucosamine (GlcNAc) residue from UDP‑GlcNAc to the terminal glucose of the outer core oligosaccharide, creating an α1,2‑linked GlcNAc side‑branch. The presence of this terminal GlcNAc is essential for the proper recognition of the core oligosaccharide by the O‑polysaccharide ligase WaaL, thereby enabling ligation of O‑antigen polysaccharides to the lipid A‑core. Insertional inactivation of rfaK results in loss of the GlcNAc side‑branch, truncation of the core OS, and failure to ligate O‑PS, while complementation with a wild‑type rfaK restores both the GlcNAc addition and O‑PS ligation. {PubMed:9535865}. The article identifies the H. ducreyi losB gene, which is homologous to the Escherichia coli rfaK gene, as encoding a D‑glycero‑D‑mannose‑heptosyltransferase. This enzyme catalyzes the addition of a D‑glycero‑D‑mannose heptose (DD‑heptose) to the glucose residue of the lipooligosaccharide (LOS) core, forming the mature branched LOS structure. Loss of this activity truncates the LOS, eliminating the DD‑heptose branch and downstream sugars, leading to reduced bacterial adherence to and invasion of human keratinocytes. {PubMed:9260947}. The rfaK gene encodes a protein that functions as an N‑acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) transferase involved in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core biosynthesis. Mutants in rfaK lack most of the O antigen, are resistant to bacteriophage Felix O, and are sensitive to rough‑phenotype phages. Biochemically, these mutants have a normal core composition of glucose and galactose but fail to add the usual partial substitution of the non‑reducing terminal glucose residue with N‑acetylglucosamine. This suggests that RfaK catalyzes the addition of GlcNAc to the completed core, a modification that preferentially serves as the substrate for subsequent O‑antigen attachment, although O antigen can still be attached at reduced efficiency when this GlcNAc is absent. The protein shows limited sequence similarity to other sugar‑transferases, supporting its role as a specific GlcNAc transferase in LPS core completion. {PubMed:1624462}. The rfaK gene encodes a protein that participates in the modification of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core in Escherichia coli K‑12.  rfaK is required for the addition of a hexose (most likely N‑acetylglucosamine, GlcNAc) to an inner‑core heptose residue, thereby generating a specific core structure that serves as a substrate for subsequent attachment of O‑antigen.  In E. coli K‑12, loss of rfaK eliminates the two upper LPS bands seen on SDS‑tricine gels, abolishes the Rfp‑dependent galactosyl modification of the core, and prevents expression of Shigella dysenteriae 1 O‑antigen, indicating that rfaK activity is essential for both core heterogeneity and O‑antigen ligation.  The gene’s product also influences bacteriophage susceptibility: an rfaK mutant becomes sensitive to the rough‑specific phage Br2 and to the inner‑core‑specific phage C21, while introduction of a Salmonella typhimurium rfaK allele confers sensitivity to phage FO, reflecting its role in adding a terminal GlcNAc that defines phage receptors.  Overall, rfaK functions as a species‑specific hexose (GlcNAc) transferase that modifies the LPS inner core, thereby affecting core completion, O‑antigen attachment, and phage receptor formation. {PubMed:1385388}. The article indicates that RfaK belongs to a second family of Rfa proteins that are thought to be hexose transferases. These enzymes are implicated in the biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core, specifically in adding hexose residues to the inner core region of LPS. {PubMed:1732225}. The rfaK gene encodes an enzyme involved in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core biosynthesis. Specifically, RfaK catalyzes the attachment of N‑acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) to the glucose II residue of the LPS core oligosaccharide. {PubMed:7565117}. The waaK gene encodes a UDP‑N‑acetylglucosamine:(glucosyl) lipopolysaccharide α1,2‑N‑acetylglucosaminyltransferase. This enzyme transfers an N‑acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) residue from UDP‑GlcNAc to the terminal glucose of the outer core oligosaccharide, creating an α1,2‑linked GlcNAc side‑branch. The addition of this terminal GlcNAc is essential for the proper recognition of the core oligosaccharide by the O‑polysaccharide ligase WaaL, thereby enabling ligation of O‑polysaccharide to the lipid A‑core. Loss of waaK results in a truncated core lacking the GlcNAc side‑branch and abolishes O‑PS ligation. {PubMed:9535865}. The article describes waaK (formerly rfaK) as a gene whose mutants are resistant to bacteriophage Felix O, display rough‑phenotype phage sensitivity, and lack most O antigen. These mutants retain the normal core sugars (glucose and galactose) but lose the partial substitution of the non‑reducing terminal glucose residue by N‑acetylglucosamine. Consequently, waaK is inferred to encode an N‑acetylglucosamine transferase that adds N‑acetylglucosamine to the LPS core, a modification that normally facilitates efficient attachment of the O‑antigen polysaccharide. Although the transferase activity has not been definitively proven, the phenotype of waaK mutants (small amounts of O‑antigen‑containing LPS, altered phage susceptibility) supports its role in core completion and in preparing the LPS core as the preferred substrate for O‑antigen ligation. {PubMed:1624462}. Encodes a protein (RfaK) that belongs to a second family of Rfa/waa proteins thought to be hexose transferases. RfaK shares homology with RfaG and RfaB and is implicated in adding sugar residues distal to the inner core region of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) during core biosynthesis. {PubMed:1732225}. WaaK is a UDP‑N‑acetylglucosamine‑dependent glycosyltransferase in Salmonella typhimurium that transfers an N‑acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) residue to the outer core oligosaccharide of lipopolysaccharide. The article reports that overexpression of eptA—often accompanied by specific amino‑acid substitutions (e.g., T148A, K233T)—is observed in colistin‑resistant strains with chromosomal mutations (CL‑IR and CL‑chrR) and can also be elevated in mcr‑1‑positive strains, indicating that increased eptA activity contributes directly to the resistant phenotype. {PubMed:32477288}. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Regulatory DnaK co-chaperone. Merged_Functions: DjlA encodes a 30‑kDa type III membrane Hsp40 (J‑protein) whose N‑terminal transmembrane segment anchors it to the inner membrane while its J‑domain faces the cytoplasm. In vitro, DjlA can replace DnaJ in the DnaK‑dependent refolding of heat‑denatured luciferase, and in cell extracts it can partially substitute for DnaJ in DnaK‑mediated disaggregation of aggregated proteins. DjlA is a type III cytoplasmic‑membrane‑anchored DnaJ‑like protein that functions as a negative regulator of the Rcs phosphorelay signal‑transduction system in Escherichia coli. Overproduction of DjlA can paradoxically activate the Rcs system, an effect that requires its J‑domain and transmembrane segment, but this is considered an artificial, stress‑inducing condition. The negative regulatory role likely involves direct or indirect interaction of DjlA’s cytoplasmic region (and possibly its transmembrane helix) with the cytoplasmic domains of the Rcs sensor kinase RcsC and/or the phosphotransmitter YojN, modulating autophosphorylation or phosphotransfer steps. Additionally, DjlA can act as a DnaK co‑chaperone, although this activity is not directly linked to its Rcs regulatory function. {PubMed:16607041}. Overexpression of DjlA tightly regulates its level and triggers induction of the colanic‑acid (wca) capsule operon; this induction requires the RcsC/RcsB two‑component system and a direct DjlA‑DnaK interaction, as shown by allele‑specific suppression analysis. The djlA gene encodes DjlA, a membrane‑bound DnaK co‑chaperone (DnaL‑like protein A) that consists of an N‑terminal transmembrane domain (TMD), a central domain of unknown function, and a C‑terminal J domain that mediates interaction with the Hsp70 chaperone DnaK. Full‑length, membrane‑anchored DjlA is required to (i) suppress the cytotoxicity caused by overexpression of recombinant membrane proteins (MPs) and (ii) markedly increase the cellular accumulation of correctly folded, membrane‑integrated MPs in engineered E. coli strains SuptoxD. Among the E. coli J‑domain proteins, DjlA is unique in its ability to promote recombinant MP production. {PubMed:28501587}. The djlA gene encodes the membrane‑bound DnaK co‑chaperone DjlA.  Overexpression of DjlA suppresses the cytotoxicity caused by recombinant membrane‑protein (MP) overproduction, leading to markedly higher final biomass and dramatically increased yields of both prokaryotic and eukaryotic MPs.  The protective effect requires the full‑length, membrane‑anchored form of DjlA and operates through interaction with the molecular chaperone DnaK (rather than via activation of the Rcs response).  Consequently, DjlA acts as a potent suppressor of MP‑induced toxicity and a broad enhancer of recombinant MP accumulation in engineered E. coli strains (SuptoxD). {PubMed:27797488}. The article describes djlA as the gene encoding the membrane‑bound DnaK co‑chaperone DjlA. Co‑expression of djlA in engineered E. coli strains (SuptoxD) suppresses the cytotoxicity that normally accompanies overexpression of recombinant membrane proteins. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Required for the biogenesis of type 1 fimbriae. Binds and interact with FimH.
Merged_Functions: fimC encodes a structural component of type 1 fimbriae (type 1 pili). These fimbriae mediate bacterial adherence by binding to mannose‑containing receptors on host epithelial cells, facilitating the initial attachment step in diarrheagenic E. coli pathogenesis. In the study, fimC was detected in all DAEC and EAEC isolates, indicating its role as a conserved adhesin in these strains. {PubMed:30127859}. The fimC gene encodes a periplasmic, chaperone‑like protein of ~26 kDa that is essential for the biogenesis of Escherichia coli type 1 fimbriae. FimC is processed from a precursor with a 36‑amino‑acid signal peptide and resides in the periplasm, where it likely assists the transfer of fimbrial structural subunits (FimA, FimF, FimG, FimH, etc.) to the outer‑membrane platform protein FimD for polymerization.  By forming complexes with these subunits, FimC prevents premature polymerization and protects them from proteolysis, acting without an ATP‑binding domain.  Thus, FimC functions as a periplasmic chaperone required for proper assembly and surface exposure of type 1 fimbriae. {PubMed:1363735}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Integrase is necessary for integration of the phage into the host genome by site-specific recombination. In conjunction with excisionase, integrase is also necessary for excision of the prophage from the host genome. Part of the cryptic P4-like prophage CP4-57, it excises the prophage when overexpressed, which also requires integration host factor (encoded by ihfA and ihfB) (PubMed:7511583). Overexpression of AlpA leads to excision of the CP4-57 prophage, which inactivates ssrA (the gene upstream of the prophage) that encodes tmRNA which is required to rescue stalled ribosomes in a process known as trans-translation (PubMed:7511582). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:7511583}.

The gene contains a single large open reading frame of 1,332 nucleotides that translates into a 444‑amino‑acid precursor with an N‑terminal signal peptide; after cleavage of the first 24 residues the mature protein consists of 420 amino acids (≈44 kDa). The mature S‑protein self‑assembles into a regular, crystalline S‑layer that completely covers the bacterial cell wall. This S‑layer is thought to provide a protective sheath against environmental stresses, mask underlying cell‑wall properties such as charge and phage receptors, and may influence cell shape and adhesion to host epithelial cells. {PubMed:8407780}. Although slpA is necessary for this proteolytic activity, the article states that neither SlpA nor AlpA is a structural component of the protease itself; instead, they function in a regulatory cascade (part of a cryptic P4‑like prophage) that indirectly enables the protease activity. {PubMed:7511582}. The slpA gene encodes the protein product of ORF149, a SlyD‑like protein that belongs to the FK506‑binding protein (FKBP) family of peptidyl‑prolyl cis/trans‑isomerases (PPIases). The protein is expressed in Escherichia coli and likely contributes to protein folding processes through its PPIase activity. {PubMed:9188461}. SlpA encodes the most abundant surface‑layer protein (SLP) of *Clostridium difficile*.  It functions as a major colonization factor by mediating adherence of the bacterium to human gastrointestinal and intestinal epithelial cells.  In addition to supporting bacterial survival and growth, SlpA interacts with the host immune system; it is recognized by Toll‑like receptor 4 (TLR4), leading to TLR4 activation and cytokine production that are important for mounting an immune response against the pathogen.  Recombinant vaccines targeting SlpA have been shown to reduce gut colonization in animal models, underscoring its role in bacterial attachment and persistence. {PubMed:34244557}.

FUNCTION: Part of the tripartite efflux system MdtEF-TolC, which confers resistance to compounds such as rhodamine 6G, erythromycin, doxorubicin, ethidium bromide, TPP, SDS, deoxycholate, crystal violet and benzalkonium. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11566977}.

The pump is powered by the proton motive force, so its activity consumes cellular PMF.  Deletion of mdtE reduces this PMF‑driven efflux activity and was shown in the study to increase tolerance to benzoate, indicating that loss of the MdtEF‑TolC pump alleviates the energetic cost imposed by benzoate‑induced PMF depletion. {PubMed:31175192}. MdtE is a component of the MdtEF‑TolC tripartite efflux system in Escherichia coli O157:H7. Overexpression of mdtE markedly increased the export of medium‑chain fatty acids (MCFAs, C6–C10), raising extracellular MCFA concentration by ~83 % and decreasing intracellular MCFA levels by ~36 %, which led to a total MCFA titer increase of about 65 %. GadX encodes an AraC/XylS‑family transcriptional activator that positively regulates the Escherichia coli glutamic acid decarboxylase (Gad) system. The enzyme is part of the core c‑di‑GMP signaling module that balances DGC activity (e.g., DgcE) during entry into stationary phase. {PubMed:26303830}. In the article, yhjH encodes the phosphodiesterase PdeH, which is described as the master c-di‑GMP‑degrading enzyme in Escherichia coli. PdeH maintains a very low intracellular pool of c‑di‑GMP (≈80–100 nM in wild‑type cells) by hydrolyzing the second messenger. Disruption of yhjH does not affect flagellation or motility in wild‑type cells, suggesting its function is specifically important for motor activity under H‑NS‑deficient conditions. The protein contains a DUF2 domain, implying involvement in a signaling or regulatory process that supports proper flagellar motor operation. {PubMed:11031114}. YhjH encodes an EAL‑only protein that functions as a cyclic‑di‑GMP phosphodiesterase (PDE). It is one of the two most highly expressed GGDEF/EAL proteins during exponential and post‑exponential growth and is under class 3 flagellar control. By degrading c‑di‑GMP, YhjH maintains low intracellular c‑di‑GMP levels that are required for high motility in liquid medium. Consequently, loss of YhjH leads to reduced swimming motility. YhjH also antagonizes the c‑di‑GMP‑dependent activation of curli fimbriae: its deletion diminishes CsgD accumulation and curli gene (csgB) expression, indicating that YhjH normally limits curli production by keeping c‑di‑GMP low. YhjH encodes an EAL‑domain protein that functions as a cyclic dimeric GMP (c‑di‑GMP) phosphodiesterase, degrading c‑di‑GMP and thereby lowering its intracellular concentration. Its transcription is dependent on the flagellar sigma factor FliA. In the Crohn disease‑associated AIEC strain LF82, YhjH activity reduces c‑di‑GMP levels, which leads to increased phase‑ON orientation of the fimS invertible element, higher type 1 pili production, and consequently enhanced bacterial adhesion to and invasion of intestinal epithelial cells. The yhjH gene encodes a dicyclic GMP phosphodiesterase that is transcribed from a σ28‑dependent (class 3) flagellar promoter. It is part of the flagellar regulon and contributes to normal swimming motility; deletion of yhjH results in a measurable motility defect. {PubMed:16513753}. YhjH is an Escherichia coli cyclic‑di‑GMP phosphodiesterase. In the study it was overexpressed in Pseudomonas syringae to degrade intracellular c‑di‑GMP, resulting in c‑di‑GMP levels below the detection limit. Thus, YhjH functions as a c‑di‑GMP‑hydrolyzing enzyme that lowers cellular c‑di‑GMP concentrations and is used as a genetic tool to create a low‑c‑di‑GMP state for investigating c‑di‑GMP‑dependent phenotypes. {PubMed:30850427}. PdeH (YhjH) is a constitutively conserved phosphodiesterase that degrades the second messenger c-di‑GMP, thereby keeping intracellular c-di‑GMP concentrations low, especially in post‑exponential, flagellated cells. By lowering c-di‑GMP, PdeH prevents activation of the c-di‑GMP‑binding effector YcgR, which otherwise binds to the flagellar basal body and inhibits flagellar rotation. Consequently, loss of PdeH leads to elevated c-di‑GMP, YcgR‑mediated inhibition of flagellar rotation, and a non‑motile phenotype despite flagella production. PdeH thus plays a key role in regulating motility and the transition to stationary‑phase biofilm‑related behaviors. {PubMed:26303830}. PdeH is the major phosphodiesterase (PDE) in *Escherichia coli* that hydrolyzes cyclic‑di‑GMP (c‑di‑GMP), keeping the intracellular c‑di‑GMP pool at a very low level (≈80–100 nM in wild‑type cells). Deletion of pdeH raises cellular c‑di‑GMP ~10‑15‑fold, leading to increased extracellular matrix production while preserving local heterogeneity. Together with the diguanylate cyclase DgcE, which provides c‑di‑GMP input, PdeH antagonistically shapes the vertical gradient of c‑di‑GMP, establishing the long‑range asymmetry of matrix architecture in macrocolony biofilms. {PubMed:30954572}.

Merged_Functions: Encodes an endo‑1,4‑β‑glucanase (cellulase family D), designated bcsZ after renaming. This enzyme is part of the yhjO‑yhjN‑yhjM‑yhjL gene cluster that together constitute the bacterial cellulose synthesis (bcs) operon. The endo‑1,4‑β‑glucanase is thought to participate in cellulose biosynthesis by cleaving internal β‑1,4‑glucosidic linkages within the nascent cellulose polymer, thereby facilitating proper assembly or remodeling of the extracellular cellulose matrix. {PubMed:11260463}. The yhjM gene (identified in the article as bcsC) encodes a 368‑amino‑acid endo‑1,4‑β‑D‑glucanase (CMCase) that belongs to glycosyl‑hydrolase family 8. The enzyme is synthesized with a typical prokaryotic signal peptide, is secreted into the extracellular medium (≈60 % of total activity), and hydrolyzes soluble cellulose derivatives such as carboxymethylcellulose. It shows maximal activity at pH 7 and 40 °C, retains activity over a broad pH range (2–10) and temperatures between 20 °C and 60 °C, and displays little activity toward p‑nitrophenyl β‑D‑glucopyranoside or crystalline cellulose. The protein has an apparent molecular mass of ~40 kDa after signal‑peptide cleavage. {PubMed:10102357}. The gene yhjM (renamed ntdR) encodes a LacI‑family transcriptional regulator that acts as the positive regulator of the NTD (3,3'-neotrehalosadiamine) biosynthetic operon ntdABC. Disruption of ntdR abolishes ntdABC transcription, while IPTG‑induced expression of ntdR restores NTD production, indicating that NtdR is required for activation of the biosynthetic genes. NtdR also represses its own promoter, providing negative autoregulation. The regulator binds to an AT‑rich inverted repeat overlapping the –10 region of the ntdABC promoter, and its DNA‑binding activity is enhanced by direct interaction with the antibiotic product NTD, which functions as an autoinducer. Thus, NtdR mediates an autoinduction loop whereby NTD binds NtdR, promoting NtdR‑dependent transcription of the ntdABC operon. {PubMed:14612444}. BcsC is described as the outer‑membrane component of the bacterial cellulose synthase (Bcs) trans‑envelope complex. The article notes that BcsC is not essential for cellulose synthesis in vitro, suggesting that it may play a role in the translocation of β‑1,4‑glucan chains across the outer membrane during cellulose production. {PubMed:21454578}. bcsC (formerly yhjL) encodes an oxido‑reductase that is a component of the bcs (bacterial cellulose synthesis) operon. Together with bcsA, bcsB and bcsZ, it is required for the biosynthesis of cellulose in Salmonella typhimurium and Escherichia coli. Mutations in bcsC abolish cellulose production, indicating that the protein plays an essential role in the assembly or regulation of the cellulose synthase complex that polymerizes UDP‑glucose into extracellular cellulose. {PubMed:11260463}. The bcsC gene encodes a secreted endo‑1,4‑β‑D‑glucanase (CMCase) that belongs to glycosyl‑hydrolase family 8. The enzyme hydrolyzes soluble β‑1,4‑glucans such as carboxymethylcellulose, producing a yellow halo in Congo‑Red activity assays. It is exported to the extracellular medium (≈60 % of total activity), with additional periplasmic (≈26 %) and cytoplasmic (≈14 %) fractions. The mature protein is ~40 kDa after removal of a 21‑aa signal peptide. Optimal activity occurs at pH 7 and 40 °C, with activity over a broad pH range (2–10) and temperatures 20–60 °C. The enzyme shows little activity toward p‑nitrophenyl‑β‑D‑glucoside and virtually none on crystalline cellulose (Avicel). Thus, bcsC provides E. coli with extracellular endoglucanase activity for degrading soluble cellulose derivatives. {PubMed:10102357}. BcsC is the outer‑membrane porin component of the Gram‑negative bacterial cellulose secretion system. It forms a channel in the outer membrane that allows the nascent cellulose polymer, synthesized by the inner‑membrane BcsAB synthase complex, to be extruded to the cell surface. BcsC also contains peptidoglycan‑binding scaffolding motifs that help anchor the porin within the cell envelope, and it works together with the other Bcs subunits (BcsAB, BcsR, BcsQ, BcsE, BcsF, etc.) to complete the multi‑subunit nanomachine required for cellulose export and biofilm formation. {PubMed:32788377}. The bcsC gene encodes a 141 kDa protein that is essential for maximal cellulose production in Acetobacter xylinum. Mutants lacking bcsC produce markedly less cellulose in vivo even though they retain the metabolic precursors, cyclic diguanylic acid activator, and exhibit normal cellulose synthase activity in vitro. Complementation of bcsC‑deficient (group V) mutants restores the cellulose‑positive phenotype, indicating that bcsC is required for efficient cellulose biosynthesis. Although its precise biochemical role is not defined, the authors suggest that BcsC may participate in the transport and/or crystallization of the nascent cellulose polymer or act as a regulatory component of the membrane‑bound cellulose synthase complex. Sequence analysis shows an N‑terminal region resembling a signal peptide, supporting the idea that BcsC is a membrane protein associated with the cellulose synthase machinery. {PubMed:2146681}. The bcsZ gene encodes the secreted endo‑glucanase BcsZ, a member of the cellulose synthase operon bcsABZC. BcsZ is an endo‑1,4‑β‑glucanase (GH8 family) that hydrolyzes β‑1,4‑glycosidic bonds in soluble cellulose derivatives such as carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) and regenerated amorphous cellulose (RAC). Hydrolysis of CMC by BcsZ yields glucose, cellobiose, cellotriose and other cello‑oligosaccharides, providing the extracellular cellulolytic activity that enables E. coli ZH‑4 to grow on cellulose. The enzyme displays optimal activity at pH 6.0 and 50 °C, tolerates a broad pH range (4.5–9.0) and temperatures up to 65 °C, and its activity is enhanced by Mg²⁺ while inhibited by Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺ and Fe³⁺. Thus, bcsZ is responsible for the extracellular endoglucanase activity and overall cellulolytic capability of the cellulolytic E. coli ZH‑4 strain. {PubMed:31455320}. Encodes the sole cellulase found in the rumen‑derived E. coli isolates. BcsZ is a periplasmic endo‑β‑1,4‑glucanase that hydrolyzes cellulose, and is part of the bacterial cellulose synthesis (bcs) operon (bcsA, bcsB, bcsC, bcsZ). It is thought to be involved in the translocation of individual β‑1,4‑glucan chains across the periplasm and outer membrane. In rumen isolates BcsZ is secreted extracellularly, a process that is markedly enhanced by overexpression of the small heat‑shock chaperones IbpA and IbpB. {PubMed:32801187}. BcsZ encodes a periplasmic endo‑β‑1,4‑glucanase belonging to glycoside‑hydrolase family 8. The enzyme adopts an (α/α)6‑barrel fold with catalytic residues Glu55 and Asp243 and hydrolyzes β‑1,4‑glucan polymers. In vivo its activity is required for optimal synthesis and membrane translocation of bacterial cellulose, likely by processing nascent glucan chains during their passage through the periplasm and outer membrane, facilitating proper alignment or cleavage of the polymer before microfibril formation. In vitro BcsZ efficiently degrades carboxymethyl‑cellulose (CMC) embedded in agar plates, confirming its cellulolytic activity. Structural studies show BcsZ binds cellopentaose at the non‑reducing side of the catalytic cleft, representing a post‑hydrolysis state. {PubMed:21454578}. bcsZ (formerly yhjM) encodes an endo‑1,4‑β‑glucanase belonging to cellulase family D. It is part of the bcs operon (bcsA‑bcsB‑bcsZ‑bcsC) and is thought to participate in the biosynthesis or processing of bacterial cellulose, acting as a cellulase that may remodel the nascent glucan polymer during cellulose production. {PubMed:11260463}. Encodes a protein that carries out limited hydrolysis of the newly synthesized cellulose, serving as an enzymatic modifier of the exopolysaccharide during its secretion. {PubMed:32788377}.

Merged_Functions: BcsE is a multifunctional cytosolic regulator of the Escherichia coli cellulose secretion system. It contains three structural modules: (i) an N‑terminal RecA‑like domain (BcsE^NTD) that mediates homooligomerization, interacts with transcription antitermination components (S10/NusE and NusB), and is required for membrane targeting of the BcsERQ complex; (ii) a central degenerate receiver domain (REC*) that does not participate in phosphotransfer signaling; and (iii) a C‑terminal degenerate GGDEF domain (GGDEF*) that binds dimeric c‑di‑GMP via an I‑site motif (R415‑D418) and independently contacts the essential secretion proteins BcsR and BcsQ (binding BcsQ through a surface distinct from the c‑di‑GMP site). By simultaneously sequestering c‑di‑GMP and recruiting the BcsRQ heterotetramer, BcsE creates a membrane‑proximal pool of dimeric c‑di‑GMP that can activate the BcsA synthase PilZ domain, thereby promoting processive cellulose polymerization. Collectively, BcsE fine‑tunes multiple stages of cellulose secretion, from early macrocomplex assembly to maintenance of local c‑di‑GMP levels, resulting in enhanced cellulose production in vivo. {PubMed:32788377}. BcsE is a cytosolic regulatory subunit of the E. coli cellulose synthase macrocomplex. It binds cyclic di‑GMP via its C‑terminal domain, enhancing cellulose biosynthesis both in vivo and in vitro. The N‑terminal region interacts with the membrane‑integrated subunit BcsF, anchoring BcsE to the complex, while its C‑terminal cd‑GMP‑binding domain contacts the BcsQ‑R complex and the PilZ domain of BcsA. Through these protein‑protein interactions BcsE stimulates the activity of the BcsA‑B catalytic core and contributes to the production of phosphoethanolamine‑modified cellulose. {PubMed:33712813}. BcsE is a soluble cytoplasmic protein that binds the second messenger cyclic diguanylate monophosphate (c‑di‑GMP). It functions as an accessory, regulatory component of the BcsE‑BcsF‑BcsG transmembrane signaling pathway that controls the post‑synthetic phosphoethanolamine (pEtN) modification of cellulose. Through direct interaction with the membrane‑anchored peptide BcsF, BcsE transduces c‑di‑GMP signals to the periplasmic phosphoethanolamine transferase BcsG, enabling BcsG to attach pEtN groups to nascent cellulose emerging from the BcsA‑BcsB synthase complex. Loss of BcsE reduces or abolishes pEtN cellulose production and leads to defects in biofilm matrix architecture, indicating its essential role in coordinating cellulose modification with biofilm formation. {PubMed:29348238}.

Merged_Functions: YiaD is a novel outer‑membrane lipoprotein that acts as an accessory factor for the essential BamD protein of the β‑barrel assembly machine (Bam). FUNCTION: Increases biofilm dispersal. Acts by binding directly to the signaling molecule cyclic-di-GMP, which decreases the intracellular concentration of cyclic-di-GMP and leads to biofilm dispersal. Merged_Functions: The article describes bdcA as a gene that encodes a protein involved in biofilm dispersal. Biofilm formation is linked to increased antimicrobial resistance, so bdcA activity influences the ability of E. coli to disperse from biofilms, potentially affecting resistance phenotypes. The G135S nonsynonymous mutation identified in the study lies near the protein’s active‑site residues (Ser132 and Tyr146) and may alter a surface loop, thereby modulating enzymatic activity and biofilm‑dispersal function. Although bdcA is present in most isolates (85–90%), it is not essential for survival. {PubMed:34199768}. BdcA acts as an NADPH‑dependent oxidoreductase that regulates Escherichia coli biofilm dispersal. Expression of bdcA decreases extracellular polysaccharide production, cell length and cell aggregation, while increasing extracellular DNA release and motility—phenotypes associated with reduced intracellular c‑di‑GMP concentrations. Loss of bdcA reduces biofilm dispersal in both static and flow‑cell assays, whereas constitutive activation promotes dispersal of cells from mature biofilms, highlighting its role as a key regulator of biofilm disassembly and a potential therapeutic target. {PubMed:25244619}. The article reports that bdcA is highly up‑regulated (>20‑fold) during the biofilm phase of ocular E. coli, suggesting a role in biofilm physiology. It cites previous work indicating that deletion of bdcA reduces biofilm dispersal by decreasing bacterial motility, although it does not impair the initial formation of biofilm. Thus, bdcA appears to function as a regulator of biofilm dispersal, influencing motility rather than biofilm establishment. {PubMed:31293528}. Elevated intracellular c‑di‑GMP produced by BdcA suppresses bacterial motility by down‑regulating flagellin (FlaA) expression and reduces swimming in soft‑agar assays. At the same time, high c‑di‑GMP promotes formation of three‑dimensional biofilm structures on abiotic surfaces and on airway epithelial cells. BdcA (formerly YjgI) is a small (~237 aa) cytoplasmic protein that binds the second messenger 3',5'-cyclic diguanylic acid (c‑di‑GMP). By sequestering c‑di‑GMP, BdcA lowers the intracellular concentration of free c‑di‑GMP without degrading it (it is not a phosphodiesterase). Consequently, BdcA expression increases swimming motility and extracellular DNA production while decreasing exopolysaccharide synthesis, cell length, and cell aggregation. Deletion of bdcA leads to higher cellular c‑di‑GMP levels and a marked decrease in biofilm dispersal. BdcA activity is negatively regulated at the transcriptional level by the adjacent repressor BdcR (YjgJ). Engineered BdcA variants with higher c‑di‑GMP affinity (e.g., E50V, E50Q) further enhance biofilm dispersal. {PubMed:21059164}.
