Merged_Functions: The hrpA gene encodes a large (≈146 kDa) protein that contains conserved N‑terminal motifs characteristic of DEAH‑family RNA helicases, as well as a C‑terminal region weakly resembling the RNA‑binding S1 motif of ribosomal protein S1. Based on its sequence similarity to the yeast DEAH helicases PRP2, PRP16 and PRP22—proteins known to participate in mRNA splicing—the HrpA protein is inferred to function as an ATP‑dependent RNA helicase involved in RNA metabolism. In Escherichia coli, however, the gene is expressed at very low levels, its disruption does not affect growth or viability under the tested conditions, and no specific phenotype was observed, indicating that HrpA is not essential for normal cellular processes in this bacterium. {PubMed:7899078}. The hrpA gene encodes the HrpA protein, the structural subunit of the Hrp pilus in Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato. HrpA auto‑assembles into an extracellular filamentous pilus that can extend up to 5 µm, allowing the pilus to cross the plant cell wall. The Hrp pilus is an essential component of the bacterial type III secretion system (T3SS); it is required for the secretion of HrpA itself, other harpin proteins such as HrpZ, and additional effector proteins (e.g., Avr proteins). Mutants lacking functional HrpA or unable to assemble pili are non‑pathogenic, fail to secrete HrpA and HrpZ, and cannot accumulate effectors, demonstrating that HrpA is crucial for both pilus formation and the delivery of virulence factors into host plant cells. The pilus likely functions as a rapidly elongating “conveyor” that transports effectors from the bacterial surface across the plant cell wall into the plant cytoplasm. {PubMed:11277437}. The article describes hrpA as a member of the DExD/H-box protein family, which are ATP‑dependent enzymes that can act as DNA or RNA helicases. Purified HrpA exhibits robust ATPase activity, indicating that its primary biochemical function is to hydrolyze ATP, consistent with a role as an ATP‑driven helicase. {PubMed:16139517}. HrpA is the first gene of the hrpA operon (complementation group III) and encodes a protein that is homologous to the HrpA of Pseudomonas syringae.  The article indicates that HrpA (like its P. syringae counterpart) is likely a structural component of the type III secretion system, forming a pilus‑like surface structure that participates in the translocation and secretion of the harpin protein across the bacterial outer membrane. {PubMed:9045830}.
Curated_Functions: Acts as an ATP‑dependent RNA helicase involved in RNA metabolism. {PubMed:7899078, PubMed:16139517}. Hydrolyzes ATP, displaying robust ATPase activity. {PubMed:16139517}. Forms the structural subunit of the Hrp pilus, auto‑assembling into an extracellular filamentous pilus up to 5 µm that can cross the plant cell wall. {PubMed:11277437, PubMed:9045830}. Is essential for type III secretion system function, mediating secretion of HrpA, HrpZ and other effectors and enabling delivery of virulence factors into host plant cells; loss of HrpA abolishes pathogenicity. {PubMed:11277437, PubMed:9045830}. Is not required for growth or viability in Escherichia coli under tested conditions, as gene disruption yields no observable phenotype. {PubMed:7899078}.

By removing this subset of stalled, yet assembly‑competent substrates, YcaL prevents accumulation of non‑productive intermediates on the Bam machine, thereby contributing to proper OMP assembly and maintaining envelope integrity. Degrades stalled outer‑membrane protein assembly intermediates that have engaged the Bam complex, such as the LptD^Y721D mutant. {PubMed:28784813}. Prevents accumulation of non‑productive intermediates on the Bam machinery, thereby ensuring proper outer‑membrane protein assembly, maintaining envelope integrity and normal outer‑membrane permeability. {PubMed:28784813}.

Merged_Functions: The JW2955 strain carries a deletion of the pitB gene, which encodes one component of the PitAB phosphate transporter system in Escherichia coli. According to the article, PitB (together with PitA) mediates tellurite (TeO₃²⁻) uptake, particularly during the later stages of toxicant exposure. PitB has been reported in the literature as a putative Ca²⁺/PO₄³⁻ symporter in Escherichia coli. In this study the authors examined a ΔpitB knockout strain to assess its role in calcium handling. Their aequorin‑based measurements showed that loss of pitB did not affect either Ca²⁺ influx or Ca²⁺ efflux, and external phosphate addition had no impact on calcium transport in the mutant. Consequently, the authors concluded that, under the experimental conditions used, PitB does not contribute to Ca²⁺ transport in E. coli, despite its prior annotation as a Ca²⁺/phosphate symporter. {PubMed:19481094}. The pitB gene encodes the PitB component of the PitAB phosphate transport system in Escherichia coli. According to the article, PitB (together with PitA) participates in the uptake of tellurite, acting primarily at later stages of toxicant exposure. Its transcription is induced after the initial exposure period, suggesting a role in mediating tellurite entry into the cell once the early-phase ActP transporter activity declines. {PubMed:26211961}.

Deletion of pitB alters expression of other transporters (e.g., increases actP) and contributes to a multifactorial mechanism of tellurite entry. {PubMed:26211961}. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Pore-forming subunit of a potassium efflux system that confers protection against electrophiles. Catalyzes K(+)/H(+) antiport. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01412, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3301813, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9023177}.
Merged_Functions: The trkB gene encodes a component of an independent K⁺ export system in Escherichia coli, most likely a K⁺/H⁺ antiporter located in the inner membrane.  Mutations in trkB produce an abnormal, partially dominant increase in K⁺ efflux, indicating that the normal product functions to mediate controlled K⁺ efflux rather than K⁺ uptake.  Null (reverting) mutations in trkB do not affect K⁺ uptake or the rapid K⁺ loss induced by the inhibitors NEM or DNP, showing that TrkB is not required for those inhibitor‑triggered pathways.  Overall, TrkB participates in regulated K⁺ export, probably coupling K⁺ export to H⁺ import, and is not essential for cell viability. {PubMed:3888294}. The article describes trkB as a membrane receptor that can be activated by an agonist antibody. Activation of the TrkB receptor triggers downstream signaling pathways, which in the experimental system are reported by a fluorescence‑based reporter construct in mammalian cells. Thus, trkB functions as a cell‑surface signaling receptor whose activity can be modulated by specific antibodies. {PubMed:29915075}. The article states that the product of the trkB gene is a protein component essential for the formation and proper functioning of the gated potassium (K⁺) channel in Escherichia coli. Together with the product of trkC and the thiol molecule glutathione, TrkB contributes to the channel’s structure and its gating mechanism, which is crucial for potassium retention and regulation of K⁺ flux across the bacterial membrane. {PubMed:6325160}. The article indicates that trkB is a genetic locus required for growth on minimal medium lacking potassium (K⁺). Its presence (trkB⁺) enables cells to survive and proliferate under potassium‑limited conditions, implying that trkB functions in potassium transport or homeostasis. {PubMed:6378665}. In the article, TrkB is described as the receptor for brain‑derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Binding of BDNF to TrkB activates the PI3K‑Akt signaling cascade, which contributes to neuronal proliferation, survival and differentiation. Increased TrkB protein levels were observed after rolipram treatment, coinciding with elevated p‑CREB, p‑Akt and BDNF, suggesting that TrkB‑mediated signaling participates in the enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis and cognitive function recovery in prenatally infected offspring. {PubMed:30373424}. TrkB (tropomyosin receptor kinase B) is the high‑affinity receptor for mature brain‑derived neurotrophic factor (mBDNF). Binding of mBDNF to TrkB activates the receptor’s tyrosine‑kinase activity, causing phosphorylation of TrkB and triggering downstream signaling cascades such as the PLCγ1 pathway, the Ras/ERK pathway, and the PI3K/Akt pathway. These cascades promote neuronal cell survival and facilitate long‑term potentiation (LTP) and other forms of long‑lasting synaptic plasticity that are essential for hippocampus‑dependent memory consolidation. {PubMed:21411668}. The trkB gene encodes a cell‑surface receptor belonging to the tyrosine‑kinase family that functions as a high‑affinity receptor for neurotrophins, particularly brain‑derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).  The receptor’s extracellular region contains two distinct ligand‑binding domains: (1) an LRM‑3/cysteine‑cluster region (residues ~103–181) and (2) a second immunoglobulin‑like domain (residues ~342–394).  Both domains can bind BDNF independently, and specific residues within the second Ig‑like domain (e.g., Phe^347, Asp^354, Tyr^361) contribute to the interaction.  Binding of BDNF to trkB initiates downstream signaling pathways that mediate neuronal survival and differentiation.  The trk locus was originally identified as a transforming gene in human colon carcinoma, and trkB, together with TrkA and TrkC, constitutes a subfamily of neurotrophin receptors. {PubMed:9312147}. TrkB (tropomyosin receptor kinase B) is the high‑affinity receptor for brain‑derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). In the article it is described as a key mediator of BDNF‑dependent signaling pathways that regulate neuronal survival, growth, differentiation, synaptic plasticity, and protein‑synthesis‑dependent memory consolidation. Phosphorylated TrkB (pTrkB) levels are reduced by systemic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) exposure, which correlates with memory deficits, anxiety‑like and depression‑like behaviors, and increased neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress markers. The VGF‑derived peptide TLQP‑62 restores BDNF and pTrkB expression, thereby preventing LPS‑induced behavioral and biochemical abnormalities. Moreover, knock‑down of BDNF (and consequently reduced TrkB activation) abolishes the protective effects of TLQP‑62, indicating that TrkB activation is essential for the anti‑inflammatory, anti‑oxidative, and neuroprotective actions observed. Thus, within this study TrkB functions as a critical transducer of BDNF signals that support cognitive function and mood regulation and mediate the therapeutic effects of TLQP‑62 against inflammation‑induced neuropsychiatric dysfunction. {PubMed:28594546}. KefB encodes a potassium (K⁺) efflux system in Escherichia coli that is part of the cell’s defence against methylglyoxal (MG) and other electrophiles. Under normal conditions glutathione (GSH) represses KefB activity; however, when MG reacts with GSH, the resulting S‑lactoylglutathione (SLG)—the product of the glyoxalase I reaction—acts as a positive activator of KefB. Activation of KefB triggers rapid K⁺ efflux, leading to intracellular acidification, which protects cells from MG toxicity. The article shows that loss of glyoxalase I (gloA) abolishes SLG production and consequently diminishes MG‑induced KefB activation, while overexpression of glyoxalase I enhances KefB‑mediated K⁺ efflux. {PubMed:9489668}. The kefB gene encodes a component of the KefB potassium channel in Escherichia coli.  Activation of the KefB channel (together with the related KefC channel) by the metabolic intermediate S‑lactoylglutathione, which is generated during glutathione‑mediated detoxification of the toxic electrophile methylglyoxal, triggers rapid efflux of intracellular K⁺.  The loss of K⁺ is compensated by influx of H⁺, leading to a swift acidification of the cytoplasm.  This drop in intracellular pH protects the cell’s DNA from methylglyoxal‑induced damage and limits degradation of both plasmid and genomic DNA.  In mutants lacking KefB (and KefC), methylglyoxal causes greater DNA damage and loss of viability, which can be rescued by external weak acids that mimic the cytoplasmic acidification produced by KefB activation.  Thus, KefB functions as a potassium‑efflux channel whose activity mediates cytoplasmic acidification and provides protection against methylglyoxal‑induced DNA damage. {PubMed:10632882}. KefB encodes a potassium/hydrogen (K⁺/H⁺) exchanger that is present both on the chromosome of E. coli MG1655 and within the locus of heat resistance (LHR). In the study, KefB expression was markedly up‑regulated (≥30‑fold) in cells carrying the LHR compared with LHR‑negative cells, and it was found at higher abundance in inclusion‑body fractions. While the article does not detail its mechanistic role, its classification as a K⁺/H⁺ exchanger suggests involvement in ion homeostasis and contributes to the broader stress‑protective functions associated with the LHR. {PubMed:32117137}. Encodes a component of the KefB potassium‑efflux system in Escherichia coli.  Activation of KefB (along with KefC) by electrophilic compounds such as N‑ethylmaleimide (NEM) or glutathione‑electrophile adducts triggers rapid efflux of K⁺ from the cytoplasm, which leads to a swift drop in intracellular pH (pH_i).  This rapid cytoplasmic acidification is crucial for protecting cells against the toxic effects of high concentrations of electrophiles, enhancing survival and aiding recovery from sub‑lethal exposure.  KefB does not directly participate in the metabolic detoxification of NEM; its protective role is mediated through ion homeostasis and pH modulation rather than by accelerating NEM metabolism. {PubMed:9023177}. The kefB gene encodes a glutathione‑gated potassium (K⁺) efflux system in Escherichia coli. The KefB protein is a membrane channel that remains closed when bound by reduced glutathione (or the analogue ophthalmic acid) and becomes activated upon binding of glutathione‑electrophile adducts (e.g., N‑ethylmaleimide, methylglyoxal, chlorodinitrobenzene). Activation triggers rapid K⁺ efflux, accompanied by cytoplasmic acidification and sodium (Na⁺) influx. This regulated K⁺ loss lowers intracellular pH, which protects cells from electrophilic stress such as methylglyoxal exposure. Mutations (e.g., L75S) can cause constitutive, high‑level K⁺ efflux, demonstrating the gene’s role in controlling channel activity and cellular pH homeostasis. {PubMed:10092637}. KefB encodes a membrane K⁺ efflux protein (part of the KefB/KefC family) that forms a cation channel together with the ancillary protein YheR. In its basal state it is inhibited by reduced glutathione; it becomes strongly activated by glutathione adducts generated during detoxification of electrophiles, especially the S‑lactoyl‑glutathione produced from methylglyoxal. Activation triggers rapid K⁺ efflux, which lowers the intracellular pH (pHᵢ). This transient acidification is essential for protecting E. coli cells from the lethal effects of electrophiles such as methylglyoxal, linking potassium cycling to pH homeostasis and electrophile detoxification. {PubMed:10207911}. The b3350 gene encodes the KefB protein, a glutathione‑gated potassium (K⁺) efflux system in Escherichia coli. In its basal state the channel is kept closed by binding of reduced glutathione (or the analogue ophthalmic acid). When glutathione forms adducts with electrophilic compounds (e.g., N‑ethylmaleimide, methylglyoxal, chlorodinitrobenzene), these adducts bind to KefB and trigger rapid K⁺ efflux. The resulting loss of intracellular K⁺ is accompanied by cytoplasmic acidification and influx of Na⁺, which together help protect cells from electrophile‑induced damage. Mutations such as L75S cause the channel to become constitutively open, leading to spontaneous K⁺ loss, while other residues (e.g., A262, V428, the HELETAID motif) modulate the regulation of the closed state. Overall, KefB functions to regulate intracellular K⁺ homeostasis and cytoplasmic pH, contributing to cellular resistance against electrophilic stress. {PubMed:10092637}.

Enables growth on potassium‑limited minimal medium, indicating a role in potassium homeostasis. {PubMed:6378665}. Contributes to the structure and gating of a gated K⁺ channel together with TrkC and glutathione, essential for potassium retention and flux regulation. {PubMed:6325160}. Serves as a high‑affinity cell‑surface receptor for brain‑derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and other neurotrophins. {PubMed:9312147, PubMed:21411668, PubMed:29915075}. Functions as a critical transducer of BDNF signals that support cognitive function, mood regulation and confer anti‑inflammatory, anti‑oxidative neuroprotection. {PubMed:28594546}. Forms a glutathione‑gated K⁺/H⁺ exchange channel that is activated by glutathione‑electrophile adducts (e.g., S‑lactoylglutathione, NEM, methylglyoxal), leading to rapid K⁺ efflux, cytoplasmic acidification and Na⁺ influx. {PubMed:9489668, PubMed:9023177, PubMed:10092637, PubMed:10207911}. Requires the ancillary protein YheR for channel assembly/function. {PubMed:10207911}. Is up‑regulated in the locus of heat resistance, contributing to ion homeostasis and broader stress‑protective responses. {PubMed:32117137}. Mutations (e.g., L75S) cause constitutive channel opening, demonstrating its role in controlling cellular pH homeostasis. {PubMed:10092637}.

Merged_Functions: FkpA encodes a periplasmic peptidyl‑prolyl cis‑trans isomerase (FKBP‑type) that acts as a folding catalyst in the extracytoplasmic (periplasmic) compartment of Escherichia coli. The protein is synthesized with an N‑terminal signal peptide, processed to a mature ~30 kDa form that resides in the periplasm. FkpA accelerates the cis‑trans isomerization of Xaa‑Pro peptide bonds (kcat/Km ≈ 90 mM⁻¹·s⁻¹) and thereby facilitates the proper folding of exported proteins, including outer‑membrane proteins and periplasmic substrates such as mutant MalE31 and β‑lactamase hybrids. Overproduction of FkpA suppresses the constitutive activation of the σ⁽ᴱ⁾ regulon observed in strains lacking proper periplasmic folding catalysts (e.g., htrM/rfaD or dsb mutants), indicating its role in alleviating protein misfolding stress. Deletion of fkpA results in a modest increase in σ⁽ᴱ⁾‑dependent transcription and slight sensitivity to certain antibiotics and detergents, consistent with a general but non‑essential contribution to periplasmic protein quality control. {PubMed:8878048}. The fkpA gene encodes a 245‑residue periplasmic protein that acts as a bifunctional folding helper.  Its N‑terminal domain forms a dimeric V‑shaped scaffold that binds unfolded or partially folded polypeptides and prevents their aggregation, providing chaperone activity.  The C‑terminal domain belongs to the FKBP family and catalyzes the cis/trans isomerisation of peptidyl‑prolyl bonds (peptidyl‑prolyl isomerase, PPIase activity), a reaction that can be inhibited by the immunosuppressant FK506.  FkpA is expressed under the σE heat‑shock regulon and contributes to the maintenance of periplasmic protein homeostasis, reducing misfolding stress, suppressing the temperature‑sensitive phenotype of degP null strains, and assisting the proper folding of exported proteins such as the maltose‑binding protein mutant MalE31. {PubMed:14672666}. FkpA is a soluble periplasmic protein of Escherichia coli that belongs to the FK506‑binding protein family and possesses very high peptidyl‑prolyl cis/trans‑isomerase (PPIase) activity (kcat/Km ≈ 4 × 10⁶ M⁻¹ s⁻¹). In addition to its catalytic role, FkpA functions as an isomerase‑independent molecular chaperone. It binds transiently to early folding intermediates of client proteins, thereby preventing their off‑pathway aggregation and increasing the yield of soluble, correctly folded protein. FkpA can also reactivate partially unfolded or aggregated species present in equilibrium with the native state, further enhancing the amount of active protein. These chaperone activities are independent of its PPIase function and are not replicated by other periplasmic PPIases such as PpiA. FkpA expression is controlled by the σE regulon and is up‑regulated under extracytoplasmic stress, supporting a general role in periplasmic protein folding and quality control. {PubMed:10748201}. FkpA encodes a periplasmic protein belonging to the FKBP family that possesses peptidyl‑prolyl cis/trans‑isomerase (PPIase) activity. In Escherichia coli it functions as a folding‑assist factor for proteins exported to the periplasm, markedly improving the yield of correctly folded, functional antibody single‑chain variable fragments (scFv) and other disulfide‑containing proteins. Overexpression of FkpA can increase soluble periplasmic expression of scFv fragments up to ten‑fold, even for variants that lack cis‑prolines or whose rate‑limiting step is not proline isomerization, indicating a chaperone‑like activity that is largely independent of its catalytic PPIase function. FkpA expression is regulated by the extracytoplasmic stress sigma factor σ^E and is up‑regulated during envelope stress, suggesting a role as a general periplasmic folding catalyst. Deletion of fkpA is not lethal but leads to elevated σ^E activity, supporting its contribution to periplasmic protein homeostasis. {PubMed:10748200}. The fkpA gene encodes a 270‑amino‑acid FK506‑binding protein (FkpA) that belongs to the FKBP family and shares extensive similarity with the macrophage infectivity potentiator (Mip) proteins of Legionella and Chlamydia. Its C‑terminal domain matches the consensus FK506‑binding motif, suggesting it functions as a peptidyl‑prolyl cis‑trans isomerase (PPIase) that can accelerate protein folding, and it likely retains the ability to bind the immunosuppressive drug FK506. Although overexpression or deletion of fkpA does not affect normal laboratory growth of Escherichia coli, the protein may play a role in pathogenesis—potentially contributing to the ability of enteroinvasive Enterobacteriaceae to invade or survive within host cells, analogous to the virulence function of Mip proteins. Thus, FkpA is a non‑essential, FKBP‑type PPIase that may be involved in protein folding and bacterial virulence. {PubMed:7540828}. FkpA is a periplasmic protein‑folding factor composed of an N‑terminal domain that provides chaperone activity and a C‑terminal domain that functions as a peptidyl‑prolyl cis/trans‑isomerase (PPIase). In the context of periplasmic scFvD1.3 production, its chaperone activity prevents aggregation of misfolded scFv proteins, increases the soluble fraction of the antibody fragment, and markedly improves cell viability. The PPIase activity is not required for these beneficial effects; only the N‑terminal chaperone function is essential for rescuing cells from the metabolic stress caused by protein misfolding. {PubMed:20388215}.

Acts as an isomerase‑independent molecular chaperone that binds unfolded polypeptides, prevents aggregation and reactivates partially unfolded species, thereby increasing the yield of soluble, correctly folded proteins. {PubMed:8878048, PubMed:14672666, PubMed:10748201, PubMed:10748200, PubMed:20388215}. May participate in bacterial virulence by contributing to host cell invasion or survival, analogous to Mip proteins. {PubMed:7540828}.

Production of AI‑2 allows E. coli to monitor population density and coordinate the expression of numerous genes. In the study, deletion of luxS markedly reduced AI‑2 activity and led to a significant decrease in biofilm formation across four enterotoxigenic E. coli strains, indicating that luxS‑mediated AI‑2 signaling promotes biofilm development. The article also notes that luxS influences the expression of hundreds of genes, affecting virulence factor production, motility, cell division, and other physiological processes linked to bacterial pathogenicity. {PubMed:26549009}. LuxS encodes an autoinducer‑2 (AI‑2) synthase. In the study, the protein YgaG was identified as a homolog of LuxS and classified among proteins involved in quorum sensing, indicating that LuxS functions in the production of the AI‑2 signaling molecule that mediates cell‑to‑cell communication. {PubMed:17224607}.

Merged_Functions: GspD encodes the secretin protein that forms the large outer‑membrane pore of the bacterial type 2 secretion system (T2SS). The C‑terminal region of GspD assembles into a multimeric (≈12‑fold) channel that allows fully folded substrates, such as heat‑labile enterotoxin (LT) and cholera toxin (CT), to be exported across the outer membrane. Its N‑terminal periplasmic domain (peri‑GspD) consists of three subdomains (N0, N1, N2) that together create a compact globular lobe. The N0 subdomain is structurally related to TonB‑dependent receptor signaling domains and can bind an external β‑strand by β‑strand complementation, suggesting a role in transiently interacting with secreted proteins or other T2SS components. The N1 and N2 subdomains adopt KH‑like folds and provide additional interaction surfaces. Peri‑GspD interacts with several T2SS partner proteins, including the pseudopilin GspJ and the HR domain of the inner‑membrane protein GspC, and has been shown biochemically to bind secreted proteins. Thus, GspD functions both as the structural scaffold of the T2SS outer‑membrane channel and as a periplasmic docking platform that mediates substrate recognition and coordination with other T2SS components during secretion. {PubMed:19217396}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Putative thioesterase. Does not bind pectin, and has no pectinesterase activity. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15808744, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19452549}.
Merged_Functions: The article reports that YbhC is an outer‑membrane lipoprotein of E. coli classified in carbohydrate esterase family 8, but it does not exhibit detectable pectin methylesterase or palmitoyl‑CoA thioesterase activity. Structural analysis reveals a right‑handed parallel β‑helix fold with a blocked, hydrophobic active‑site cleft and a substitution of the catalytic Asp residue by Asn, explaining the loss of PME activity. Experimental assays failed to show hydrolysis of pectin, pNP esters, or CoA thioesters, and affinity gels showed no pectin binding. Consequently, YbhC’s enzymatic function remains unidentified. The authors speculate that, because of its periplasmic orientation and hydrophobic cleft, YbhC may bind or act on small hydrophobic molecules (e.g., lipids, lipopolysaccharides, quorum‑sensing N‑acyl homoserine lactones). Genomic and transcriptomic correlations with murein‑related proteins (MipA, DacA, MltD) suggest a possible involvement in murein turnover or cell‑division processes, but the precise biological role is still unknown. {PubMed:19452549}. The gene encodes the outer‑membrane lipoprotein YbhC, a member of carbohydrate esterase family 8 that adopts a right‑handed parallel β‑helix fold. Although initially annotated as a pectin methylesterase or a palmitoyl‑CoA thioesterase, the article reports that YbhC shows no detectable pectin‑methylesterase activity, no thioesterase activity toward palmitoyl‑CoA or short acyl‑CoAs, and does not bind pectin in affinity assays. The protein lacks the catalytic Asp residue typical of CE8 enzymes (it has Asn224 instead) and possesses a constricted, hydrophobic active‑site cleft, indicating loss of the ancestral esterase function. Consequently, the precise biochemical role of YbhC remains undefined. The authors note that YbhC is a periplasmic lipoprotein, is non‑essential for growth on rich medium, and is genomically associated with genes involved in murein biosynthesis and remodeling (e.g., MipA, DacA, MltD), suggesting a possible involvement in murein turnover or cell‑division processes rather than carbohydrate metabolism. {PubMed:19452549}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: May play a role in reduction of the SoxR iron-sulfur cluster. May work together with the RsxABCDGE complex. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12773378}.
Merged_Functions: RseC is an inner‑membrane protein encoded as the fourth gene of the rpoE operon. Genetic evidence shows that it acts as a positive modulator of σ⁽ᴱ⁾ (RpoE) activity, i.e., an anti‑anti‑σ factor. A null mutation in rseC reduces basal σ⁽ᴱ⁾ activity by about 30 %, whereas multicopy over‑production of RseC increases σ⁽ᴱ⁾ activity roughly two‑fold and can partially relieve the strong inhibitory effect of RseA on σ⁽ᴱ⁾. Yeast two‑hybrid assays indicate that RseC can interact with both RseA and RseB, suggesting that it fine‑tunes the σ⁽ᴱ⁾ regulatory cascade through protein‑protein contacts. {PubMed:9159522}. RseC is a membrane‑integral protein that forms part of the SoxR‑reducing system in Escherichia coli. Together with the RsxABCDGE complex, RseC participates in the NADPH‑dependent reduction of the transcription factor SoxR, keeping SoxR in its reduced (inactive) state under non‑stress conditions. Deletion of rseC leads to a markedly increased activation of the SoxR‑dependent NADPH biosensor, indicating that RseC normally acts to lower the level of oxidized (active) SoxR. The protein likely cooperates with RsxB (or other components of the Rsx complex) to transfer electrons to SoxR, possibly via an iron‑sulfur cluster in its N‑terminal region. {PubMed:30585443}. The article describes rseC as a gene that exerts a subtle, positive modulatory effect on the σ^E (RpoE) regulatory system. Deletion of rseC does not produce a noticeable σ^E‑dependent cell‑lysis phenotype, and the ΔrseC strain behaves similarly to wild‑type in terms of growth, optical density, and protein release up to 42 °C. When expressed from a plasmid, rseC slightly increases protein accumulation in the medium of wild‑type cells, indicating a minor positive role in promoting σ^E‑dependent lysis. At 45 °C, ΔrseC shows some protein release that appears to be σ^E‑independent, suggesting an additional, temperature‑dependent effect. Overall, rseC is portrayed as a non‑essential, modest enhancer of σ^E activity and cell‑lysis regulation within the rpoE‑rseABC operon. {PubMed:19549168}. In vitro, purified FliI exhibits basal ATPase activity (Vmax ≈ 0.12 nmol Pi min⁻¹ µg⁻¹, Km for MgATP ≈ 0.35 mM). Importantly, FliI specifically binds two axial export substrates—flagellin (FliC) and the hook protein (FlgE)—and this interaction reversibly stimulates its ATPase activity (Vmax increases to ≈0.35 nmol Pi min⁻¹ µg⁻¹, Km rises to ≈1.2 mM). The stimulation requires excess substrate and suggests that FliI functions analogously to SecA, coupling ATP hydrolysis to the translocation of flagellar proteins through the export channel during flagellum assembly. {PubMed:10350613}. FliI is the ATPase of the bacterial flagellar type III protein export apparatus. It forms a stable heterotrimeric complex with a dimer of the regulator protein FliH in the cytoplasm. The FliH–FliI complex binds to the C‑ring of the basal body through a specific interaction between FliH and the C‑ring protein FliN, thereby localizing the complex to the flagellar base. Once docked, the FliI ATPase facilitates the initial entry of export substrates into the export gate composed of six integral membrane proteins (FlhA, FlhB, FliO, FliP, FliQ, and FliR). ATP hydrolysis by FliI is used to promote release of the FliH–FliI complex from the gate and from bound substrate after substrate insertion, while the subsequent translocation steps are driven by the proton motive force. The catalytic activity of FliI is not required for its localization to the flagellar base. {PubMed:19889085}. Deletion of b1941 reduces β‑galactosidase activity, while overproduction causes prolonged lag phases on lactose or galactose, indicating that the enzyme modulates sugar metabolism and protects cells from metabolic congestion during carbon source transitions. {PubMed:26820469}. MukB binds DNA and ATP/GTP, and forms homodimers that adopt a rod‑and‑hinge architecture with globular domains at both ends. It is required for normal cell proliferation at elevated temperatures; cells lacking MukB can grow at low temperature (22 °C) but exhibit severe growth defects and reduced colony‑forming ability at higher temperatures (37–42 °C). Thus, MukB is essential for maintaining proper chromosome segregation and supporting growth under stress conditions. {PubMed:7513784}. MukF is essential for the positioning and segregation of daughter chromosomes during cell division; loss of MukF leads to temperature‑sensitive growth (inability to form colonies above ~30 °C) and production of anucleate cells. Overproduction of MukF also induces anucleate cell formation, indicating that precise cellular levels are critical. The protein contains a leucine‑zipper domain and an acidic C‑terminal region, both of which are necessary for its activity. MukF is not required for replication initiation control or for stable maintenance of the mini‑F plasmid, suggesting its role is specific to chromosomal, not plasmid, partitioning. {PubMed:8602138}. The kicB gene encodes a 440‑amino‑acid (≈50 kDa) protein that functions as a killing factor in Escherichia coli. Its activity is normally suppressed by the product of the upstream kicA gene; when KicA levels fall below a critical threshold, KicB becomes active and leads to rapid inhibition of protein synthesis and cell death. Although essential for the killing activity, KicB is not required for normal cell proliferation—kicB‑disrupted mutants grow like wild‑type cells. When both kicA and kicB are transferred to a plasmid, they constitute a post‑segregational killing system that eliminates plasmid‑free segregants, likely by targeting components of the translation machinery. {PubMed:7513784}. MukF is a protein required for proper chromosome partitioning in Escherichia coli. Null mutants lacking mukF produce anucleate cells and display temperature‑sensitive colony formation, indicating a defect in the segregation of daughter chromosomes. Overproduction of MukF also induces anucleate cells, showing that its cellular level must be tightly regulated. The MukF protein (440 aa, ~50 kDa) contains a leucine‑zipper motif (residues 160‑245) and a C‑terminal acidic domain; both regions are essential for its activity, as mutations disrupting either domain abolish complementation of the mutant phenotype. MukF functions together with MukE and MukB (encoded in the same operon) in a step of chromosome positioning/condensation prior to cell division, but it is not required for the maintenance or partitioning of the mini‑F plasmid. {PubMed:8602138}. It contains a central leucine‑zipper motif and a C‑terminal acidic region that confers Ca²⁺‑binding activity. Importantly, MukF is indispensable for the interaction between MukB and MukE; in its absence MukB cannot associate with MukE. The MukF‑mediated complex (MukB–MukF–MukE) is a large ~600 kDa assembly that likely coordinates DNA binding and ATPase activities of MukB during the segregation of replicated chromosomes. {PubMed:10545099}. MukF is a component of the MukF‑MukE‑MukB (MukFEB) complex in Escherichia coli. Together with MukE and MukB, MukF participates in the organization and proper partitioning of sister chromosomes. The protein is required for the formation of discrete MukB‑GFPUV4 foci, indicating that it helps recruit MukB (and the whole complex) into clustered structures that act as ‘reorganization centres’ for folded sister chromosomes during the cell cycle. Loss of MukF (as in mukF null mutants) disrupts MukB focus formation, leads to a dispersed distribution of MukB throughout the cell, and results in temperature‑sensitive growth, anucleate cell production, and defects in chromosome structure and positioning. {PubMed:11401691}. MukF is a kleisin-family protein that forms a stable dimer and serves as a bridge between the SMC‑like protein MukB and the accessory protein MukE. Together with MukB and MukE, MukF constitutes the essential MukBFE complex required for proper chromosome segregation and condensation in *Escherichia coli*. MukF’s winged‑helix domain mediates its interaction with MukB, while its dimeric form binds one or two MukE dimers, generating two high‑affinity complexes (F₂E₂ and F₂E₄). These MukFE complexes can associate with MukB to produce either a locked B₂F₂E₄ complex that restricts DNA access or a more open B₂F₂E₂ complex that facilitates DNA remodeling. Thus, MukF plays a critical structural and regulatory role in maintaining chromatin architecture during cell division. {PubMed:17355972}. MukF encodes the kleisin subunit of the Escherichia coli MukBEF SMC complex. It forms stable dimers through an N‑terminal winged‑helix domain and contains a four‑helix bundle (helices 8–9) that binds the ‘neck’ region of the MukB coiled‑coil adjacent to the ATPase head. Its C‑terminal domain contacts the cap of the MukB ATPase head. Both the N‑terminal (neck‑binding) and C‑terminal (head‑binding) domains independently and additively stimulate MukB ATPase activity, each contributing roughly half of the maximal activity. By linking the two MukB monomers, MukF creates a tripartite ring that can open and close to capture DNA, thereby facilitating chromosome segregation. MukF dimerisation is retained when it engages the MukB neck, allowing formation of “dimers of dimers” of MukBEF observed in vivo. Interaction of MukF with MukB is required for proper MukBEF function; disruption of either the N‑terminal or C‑terminal interface leads to ATP‑hydrolysis‑dependent release of MukBEF complexes from chromosomes and a loss of segregation fidelity. MukF also provides binding sites for the accessory kite protein MukE, which modulates the ATPase activity and can be antagonised by DNA. {PubMed:29323635}. MukF encodes a dimeric kleisin protein that is a core component of the Escherichia coli MukBEF structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complex. Each MukF dimer contains two C‑terminal domains that bind the caps of MukB ATPase heads and two N‑terminal 4‑helix bundles that engage the coiled‑coil “neck” region of partner MukB molecules. By simultaneously contacting both MukB heads, MukF links two MukB subunits into a tripartite proteinaceous ring. MukF also binds MukE dimers, and this interaction stabilizes the MukBEF assembly and promotes head engagement of MukB upon ATP (or AMPPNP) binding. The dimeric nature of MukF is critical for directing the formation of higher‑order “dimers of MukBEF dimers,” which are the functional units that cluster on the chromosome, organize DNA loops, and facilitate chromosome segregation. Experimental disruption of MukF dimerization (creating a monomeric MukF) abolishes MukBEF focus formation, prevents stable chromosome association, and yields a Muk‑ phenotype, demonstrating that MukF dimerization is essential for MukBEF function in vivo. {PubMed:31400115}.

Merged_Functions: GMK (poly(P)/ATP‑glucomannokinase) is a glucose kinase belonging to group B of the hexokinase (HK) family. It catalyzes the phosphorylation of glucose (and also mannose, with higher affinity for glucose) by transferring a phosphoryl group from inorganic polyphosphate (poly(P)) and/or ATP to the 6‑hydroxyl of the sugar. The enzyme functions as a monomer and contains two domains that form a cleft where glucose binds together with two inorganic phosphate molecules (Pi‑A and Pi‑B); these sites constitute a putative poly(P)‑binding pocket that can accommodate the terminal phosphates of poly(P), enabling phosphoryl transfer. GMK thus utilizes poly(P) as an energy source—potentially reflecting an ancestral energy‑carrier role—and also can use ATP. Its activity and structural features are discussed as a model for the evolutionary origin of other glucose kinases in the HK family. {PubMed:16233797}. The gmk gene encodes guanylate kinase, an enzyme that phosphorylates (deoxy)GMP to (deoxy)GDP, participating in guanosine metabolism within the spoT operon. {PubMed:9321663}. Guanylate kinase (GMK) is an essential nucleoside monophosphate kinase that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent phosphorylation of guanine‑monophosphate (GMP) and deoxy‑GMP (dGMP) to generate GDP and dGDP, providing crucial precursors for RNA and DNA synthesis. It also contributes to the recovery of cyclic GMP and helps regulate the cellular pool of guanine nucleotides required for signal‑transduction pathways. Moreover, GMK activates the chemotherapeutic agent 6‑thioguanine (6‑TG) by phosphorylating 6‑TG‑monophosphate (6‑TGMP) to 6‑TG‑diphosphate (6‑TGDP), a key step in the activation of several antiviral and antineoplastic prodrugs. {PubMed:19136674}. The product of b3648 is DamX, an Escherichia coli bitopic membrane protein that plays multiple roles in cell envelope physiology and division.  DamX contains a C‑terminal SPOR domain that adopts an RNP‑fold and binds peptidoglycan (PG), thereby targeting the protein to the septal ring during cytokinesis.  The SPOR domain is essential for DamX’s septal localization, for conferring full resistance to the bile salt deoxycholate, for improving the efficiency of cell division when expressed at native levels, and for the ability of DamX to inhibit cell division when overproduced.  Deletion or point mutations that disrupt the SPOR domain’s β‑sheet surface impair PG binding, septal localization, deoxycholate resistance, and the division‑related phenotypes, indicating that an intact SPOR domain is required for all examined DamX functions. {PubMed:23290046}. DedD (encoded by b3648) is a bitopic inner‑membrane protein of the Escherichia coli septal (divisome) ring. It contains a short cytoplasmic tail, a trans‑membrane helix, and a periplasmic region ending in a SPOR domain. DedD promotes cell constriction by stimulating septal peptidoglycan (sPG) synthesis, acting in parallel with the essential divisome protein FtsN. The N‑terminal 1‑54 residues (including the TM segment) are necessary and sufficient for its division activity; this region mediates a weak, SPOR‑independent recruitment to the septal ring, likely through interactions with the FtsBLQ subcomplex (especially FtsL). DedD becomes essential when FtsN activity is reduced and its loss is synthetically lethal with deletion of the PBP1B (ponB) synthase, indicating a role in full activation of the FtsW/PBP3 (FtsI) sPG synthase complex. Mutations in conserved TM residues (G11, P24) impair its function and interaction with FtsL. Overall, DedD functions as a positive regulator of sPG synthesis and provides feedback to the sPG‑loop that drives active cell division. {PubMed:30692172}.

Together with FolE, QueD, and QueC, QueE participates in the conversion of guanosine triphosphate (GTP) to the intermediate 7‑cyano‑7‑deazaguanine (preQ₀), a precursor for tRNA queuosine modification. {PubMed:28208705}. QueE encodes 7‑carboxy‑7‑deazaguanine synthase, an S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (AdoMet) radical enzyme that catalyzes the radical‑mediated ring contraction of 6‑carboxy‑5,6,7,8‑tetrahydropterin (CPH₄) to produce 7‑carboxy‑7‑deazaguanine (CDG). This reaction forms the characteristic pyrrolopyrimidine core of all 7‑deazaguanine natural products, including the modified tRNA nucleoside queuosine. QueE binds a [4Fe‑4S] cluster via a CX₃CXφC motif (or a variant thereof) and requires a catalytic Mg²⁺ ion. The enzyme utilizes reductive cleavage of AdoMet to generate a 5′‑deoxyadenosyl radical, which abstracts a hydrogen atom from the substrate to initiate the transformation. Activation of the [4Fe‑4S] cluster is achieved by electron transfer from the physiological reductant flavodoxin, and structural variations among QueE homologs appear to tailor the enzyme’s surface for specific flavodoxin interactions. {PubMed:30341796}. ygcF encodes the enzyme QueE, a 7‑carboxy‑7‑deazaguanine synthase (EC 4.3.99.3). In the queuosine (Q) biosynthetic pathway, QueE catalyzes the conversion of 6‑pyruvoyl‑5,6,7,8‑tetrahydropterin (CPH₄) into 7‑carboxy‑7‑deazaguanine (CDG), an early precursor that is subsequently transformed into 7‑cyano‑7‑deazaguanine (preQ₀) and later into the Q modification of tRNA. The article also notes that ygcF (queE) is transcriptionally up‑regulated by copper in Erwinia amylovora, linking it to the queuosine pathway. {PubMed:28208705}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the radical SAM‑dependent conversion of 6‑pyruvoyl‑5,6,7,8‑tetrahydropterin (CPH₄) to 7‑carboxy‑7‑deazaguanine (CDG) in the queuosine biosynthetic pathway. {PubMed:28208705, PubMed:30341796}. Participates with FolE, QueD and QueC in the conversion of GTP to the intermediate 7‑cyano‑7‑deazaguanine (preQ₀), a precursor of tRNA queuosine. {PubMed:28208705}. Binds a [4Fe‑4S] cluster via a CX₃CXφC motif (or variant) and requires a catalytic Mg²⁺ ion for activity. {PubMed:30341796}. Is activated by electron transfer from flavodoxin, which serves as the physiological reductant for the [4Fe‑4S] cluster. {PubMed:30341796}. Is transcriptionally up‑regulated by copper, linking its expression to metal stress response in Erwinia amylovora. {PubMed:28208705}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: An FAD assembly protein, which accelerates covalent attachment of the cofactor into other proteins (PubMed:22474332, PubMed:24374335, PubMed:26644464). Plays an essential role in the assembly of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH, respiratory complex II), an enzyme complex that is a component of both the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the electron transport chain, and which couples the oxidation of succinate to fumarate with the reduction of ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) to ubiquinol. Required for flavinylation (covalent attachment of FAD) of the flavoprotein subunit SdhA of SDH (PubMed:22474332, PubMed:24374335, PubMed:26644464). Required for flavinylation of the flavoprotein subunit FrdA of fumarate reductase (FRD) (PubMed:26644464). Binds 2 different sites on the flavoprotein target FrdA (and presumably also SdhA), possibly positioning FAD and protein to facilitate the covalent bond formation; covalent attachment of FAD is not required for SDH or FRD complex enzyme formation (PubMed:26644464). Overexpression of this protein and YgfX (formerly cptA) restores production of prodigiosin antibiotic (Pig) in Serratia strains with deletions of sdhE-ygfX (PubMed:22474332). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23657679, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24374335, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26644464, ECO:0000305|PubMed:22474332}.
Merged_Functions: In bacteria, SdhE is a highly conserved assembly factor required for the biogenesis of succinate:quinone oxidoreductase (SQR). It binds directly to the catalytic flavoprotein subunit SdhA, positioning itself between the FAD‑binding and capping domains. This interaction holds SdhA in an “open” conformation, creates a hydrogen bond between SdhE Gly16 and SdhA His45, and thereby facilitates efficient autocatalytic covalent attachment (flavinylation) of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) to the N³‑histidyl‑8α‑FAD linkage of SdhA. While promoting flavinylation, SdhE also displaces key active‑site residues of SdhA, rendering the complex catalytically inactive and preventing premature succinate oxidation and electron leakage. After flavinylation, SdhE remains bound until it is displaced by the iron‑sulfur subunit SdhB, allowing the capping domain to close and the mature, active SQR complex to form. {PubMed:29514959}. SdhE is a flavin‑adenine‑dinucleotide (FAD) assembly factor that catalyzes the covalent flavinylation and activation of the catalytic flavoprotein subunits of complex II enzymes. In bacteria it promotes the covalent attachment of FAD to the SDH flavoprotein SdhA, enabling full succinate dehydrogenase activity under aerobic conditions. The study shows that SdhE also interacts with the FRD flavoprotein subunit FrdA and is required for complete flavinylation and activation of fumarate reductase during anaerobic respiration. Deletion of sdhE reduces FAD incorporation into FrdA, lowers FRD activity, and impairs anaerobic growth, while expression of SdhE restores these phenotypes. The protein functions through a conserved RGxxE motif, interacts directly with its target flavoproteins, and is transcribed constitutively under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. {PubMed:24374335}. In *Escherichia coli* SdhE is a small (~90–140 aa) assembly factor for respiratory Complex II (succinate:quinone oxidoreductase / quinol:fumarate reductase). It binds to the flavoprotein subunit (FrdA/SdhA) at the same surface used by the Fe:S subunit, forming an extensive interface that includes a conserved RGxxE motif; the G16 carbonyl of SdhE hydrogen‑bonds to the N(1) atom of the histidine (H44) that becomes the covalent ligand of FAD. SdhE stabilizes an assembly intermediate in which the flavoprotein adopts a conformation that favors autocatalytic covalent flavinylation: it promotes rotation of the capping domain, destabilizes two active‑site loops (creating a tunnel to the flavin), and orients active‑site residues (e.g., H355 for proton abstraction, R390 for charge stabilization) to enable formation of the 8α‑N(3)‑histidyl linkage. At the same time, SdhE mis‑aligns the dicarboxylate substrate and displaces catalytic residues (e.g., T244), thereby inhibiting succinate/fumarate interconversion (IC₅₀ ≈ 1 µM). Consequently, SdhE functions as a transient regulatory/chaperone‑like subunit that shifts the conformational equilibrium of the Complex II flavoprotein toward a state that enhances covalent flavin attachment while suppressing its normal catalytic activity during assembly. {PubMed:29348404}. SdhE is a conserved bacterial FAD assembly factor required for the flavinylation and activation of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH). It interacts with the flavoprotein subunit SdhA and mediates the covalent attachment of FAD to SdhA, a step essential for SDH enzymatic activity. SdhE can flavinylate folded SdhA in the absence of the other SDH subunits (SdhB‑D), indicating that it acts before the full SDH complex assembles. A highly conserved RGxxE motif within SdhE is critical for its function; mutations in this motif abolish flavinylation and SDH activity without disrupting protein folding or SdhA binding. By accelerating the otherwise inefficient autocatalytic flavinylation of SdhA, SdhE ensures a high proportion of active SDH enzymes, whereas loss of SdhE results in markedly reduced SDH activity. {PubMed:24070374}. The product of ygfY (renamed SdhE) is a highly conserved assembly factor for bacterial succinate:quinone oxidoreductase (SQR). It binds directly to the catalytic flavoprotein subunit SdhA, positioning itself between the FAD‑binding and capping domains and keeping the capping domain in an “open” conformation. This structural arrangement facilitates efficient covalent attachment of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) to the conserved His45 residue of SdhA (flavinylation) while simultaneously displacing key active‑site residues, thereby preventing premature succinate oxidation. After flavinylation, SdhE remains bound to SdhA, stabilizing the holo‑protein in an inactive state until it can associate with the iron‑sulfur subunit SdhB, which displaces SdhE and allows the enzyme to become catalytically competent. Thus, ygfY/SdhE functions as a dual‑role assembly chaperone that promotes flavinylation of SdhA and safeguards against uncontrolled enzyme activity during complex II biogenesis. {PubMed:29514959}. YgfY (also known as SdhE) is a conserved bacterial FAD assembly factor required for the covalent attachment of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) to the flavoprotein subunit SdhA of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH). It interacts with folded SdhA and catalyzes its flavinylation, thereby activating SDH activity. YgfY functions independently of the other SDH subunits (SdhB–D) and is essential for efficient flavinylation; in its absence, SdhA can only acquire FAD via an inefficient autocatalytic mechanism, resulting in markedly reduced SDH activity. {PubMed:24070374}. In Acinetobacter baumannii, ygfY encodes the antitoxin component (CptB) of the conserved CptBA-like type IV toxin‑antitoxin system. The CptB protein counteracts the toxic activity of its cognate toxin CptA (ygfX) by competing for the same cellular targets—namely the cytoskeletal proteins MreB and FtsZ—that are required for cell‑wall synthesis and division. When expressed at sufficient levels, CptB restores normal growth and cell morphology after CptA‑induced inhibition, whereas low or delayed expression fails to neutralize the toxin. Thus, ygfY functions as a labile antitoxin that stabilizes MreB/FtsZ polymerization and protects the cell from CptA‑mediated growth arrest. {PubMed:34026293}. The ygfY gene encodes an 88‑amino‑acid protein of unknown biochemical function. Structural analysis shows it adopts a cyclin‑like five‑helix bundle, a fold commonly involved in protein‑protein interactions. Based on remote homology to a yeast protein required for sporulation and transcriptional induction of the meiotic transcription factor IME1, and on similarity to transcription factor IIB core domains, the authors propose that YgfY may be associated with complexes that regulate transcription, suggesting a possible role in transcriptional regulation. {PubMed:15593094}. cptB encodes the antitoxin component of a conserved CptBA-like type IV toxin‑antitoxin (TA) system in Acinetobacter baumannii. In this system the downstream gene cptA produces a toxic, membrane‑associated protein that inhibits cell division by interfering with the polymerization of the cytoskeletal proteins MreB and FtsZ, causing filamentous and lemon‑shaped cells. cptB counteracts this effect: when expressed from an IPTG‑inducible promoter, high levels of CptB (5–10 mM IPTG) restore normal growth and viability if present before or at the same time as CptA, indicating that CptB competes for the same cellular target and stabilizes the cytoskeletal filaments. However, post‑induction of CptB after CptA production cannot reverse the lethal phenotype, consistent with the competition‑based mechanism of type IV TA systems. Transcription of cptB (along with cptA) is down‑regulated in A. baumannii under oxidative stress and exposure to certain antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, meropenem), suggesting a role in stress response and possibly programmed cell death. {PubMed:34026293}. The article states that JW2865 (ygfY) encodes an 88‑amino‑acid protein of unknown biochemical function.  Structural analysis suggests the protein adopts a cyclin‑like five‑helix bundle typical of protein‑protein interaction domains.  The authors note a remote homology to a yeast protein required for sporulation and transcriptional induction of the meiotic factor IME1, and they speculate that YgfY (JW2865) may participate in transcription‑regulating complexes, possibly acting through protein‑protein interactions.  However, a definitive functional role is not experimentally established. {PubMed:15593094}. Encodes an 88‑amino‑acid protein of unknown biochemical function. Structural studies reveal a cyclin‑like five‑helix bundle that likely mediates protein‑protein interactions. The authors propose that YgfY (b2897) may be involved in transcriptional regulation, analogous to its yeast homolog YOL071W/EM15, which is required for transcriptional induction of the early meiotic transcription factor IME1. {PubMed:15593094}.
Curated_Functions: Binds directly to the catalytic flavoprotein subunit SdhA, positioning it between the FAD‑binding and capping domains in an open conformation that favors autocatalytic covalent flavinylation. {PubMed:29514959, PubMed:29348404}. Promotes covalent attachment of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) to the conserved His45 residue of SdhA, thereby activating succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) activity. {PubMed:29514959, PubMed:24374335, PubMed:24070374}. Interacts with the fumarate reductase flavoprotein subunit FrdA and is required for its complete flavinylation and activation during anaerobic respiration. {PubMed:24374335}. Remains bound to flavoprotein subunits after flavinylation, preventing premature substrate oxidation and electron leakage until displacement by the iron‑sulfur subunit SdhB, which allows complex II maturation. {PubMed:29514959, PubMed:29348404}. Acts as a transient regulatory/chaperone‑like assembly factor that suppresses catalytic activity of the flavoprotein during assembly, with an IC₅₀ of ~1 µM for succinate/fumarate turnover. {PubMed:29348404}. Requires a highly conserved RGxxE motif for binding and flavinylation activity; mutations in this motif abolish FAD attachment and SDH activity without affecting protein folding. {PubMed:29514959, PubMed:24374335, PubMed:29348404, PubMed:24070374}. Is constitutively transcribed under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, ensuring availability for complex II biogenesis. {PubMed:24374335}. Functions as the antitoxin component CptB of a type IV toxin‑antitoxin system, counteracting CptA toxicity by competing for the cytoskeletal targets MreB and FtsZ, thereby stabilizing their polymerization and protecting cells from growth arrest. {PubMed:34026293}. Restores normal growth and cell morphology when expressed prior to or simultaneously with CptA, but cannot reverse toxicity if induced after CptA production. {PubMed:34026293}. Expression of cptB is down‑regulated under oxidative stress and exposure to antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin and meropenem, indicating involvement in stress response. {PubMed:34026293}. Possesses a cyclin‑like five‑helix bundle fold suggestive of protein‑protein interaction domains and may participate in transcription‑regulating complexes, analogous to yeast proteins involved in meiotic transcription factor induction. {PubMed:15593094}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. A probable translation-dependent mRNA interferase. Overexpression causes cessation of cell growth and inhibits cell proliferation via inhibition of translation; this blockage is overcome by subsequent expression of antitoxin HigA. Overexpression causes cleavage of a number of mRNAs in a translation-dependent fashion, suggesting this is an mRNA interferase. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19943910}.
Merged_Functions: higB encodes the toxin component of the HigB‑HigA type II toxin‑antitoxin (TA) system in Escherichia coli K‑12. The HigB protein is a ribonuclease that is toxic to the cell when expressed alone, disrupting essential processes and inhibiting bacterial growth. Its toxicity is neutralized by direct binding to the cognate antitoxin HigA, forming a stable HigB‑HigA heterotetrameric complex with a dissociation constant of ~14 nM. While HigB itself does not bind operator DNA, its association with HigA enhances the DNA‑binding ability of the HigA homodimer, thereby contributing to transcriptional regulation of the TA operon. In summary, HigB functions as a potent growth‑inhibitory toxin whose activity is tightly controlled by the antitoxin HigA. {PubMed:31014676}. HigB is the toxin component of the type II HigBA toxin‑antitoxin (TA) system in Streptococcus pneumoniae. It functions as a ribonuclease that cleaves cellular mRNA, leading to degradation of transcripts and bacterial cell death. The protein adopts a β‑sheet core with several conserved catalytic residues (R68, R73, F90, K92) that constitute its active site. In the native HigBA complex, HigB’s toxicity is neutralized by binding to the antitoxin HigA, but release of free HigB—either by proteolytic degradation of HigA or by peptide‑mediated disruption of the HigB‑HigA interface—restores its RNase activity. Thus, HigB regulates bacterial growth and survival through mRNA cleavage and represents a target for novel antimicrobial strategies. {PubMed:32770723}. The higB gene encodes the toxin component of the HigBA type II toxin‑antitoxin system in Escherichia coli K‑12. HigB is a ribosome‑dependent mRNA interferase that belongs to the RelE family and adopts a microbial RNase T1 fold. It cleaves mRNAs at the ribosomal A‑site during translation, leading to global degradation of cellular mRNAs and cessation of cell growth. Unlike many RNases, HigB does not act on naked RNA in vitro; its activity requires incorporation into the ribosome. Thus, HigB functions as a growth‑inhibiting toxin whose toxicity is neutralized by the antitoxin HigA. {PubMed:27601326}. HigB is the toxin component of the V. cholerae higBA toxin‑antitoxin (TA) locus.  When overexpressed, HigB dramatically slows bacterial growth and reduces colony‑forming units by several orders of magnitude in both V. cholerae and Escherichia coli, indicating a potent growth‑inhibitory (toxic) activity.  Its toxicity can be counteracted by the cognate antitoxin HigA; simultaneous production of HigA fully restores viability, while delayed production of HigA partially rescues cells if the delay is short (≈30 min) but becomes increasingly ineffective with longer delays.  HigB does not act as a corepressor of its own operon; instead, HigA represses transcription of the higBA operon.  Transcripts of higB increase after exposure to translational inhibitors (chloramphenicol, kanamycin, spectinomycin), presumably because reduced synthesis of the unstable antitoxin HigA relieves repression.  Endogenous activation of HigB under these conditions does not cause detectable cell death, suggesting that short‑term toxin activity is bacteriostatic and longer‑term exposure may become irreversible.  Biochemical experiments show that HigB physically interacts with HigA in vivo, supporting the model that HigA neutralizes HigB by direct binding.  Overall, HigB functions as a toxin that inhibits bacterial growth/viability, with its activity tightly regulated by the antitoxin HigA. {PubMed:17085558}.
Curated_Functions: Acts as the toxin component of the HigBA type II toxin‑antitoxin system. {PubMed:31014676, PubMed:32770723, PubMed:27601326, PubMed:17085558}. Cleaves cellular mRNA, causing transcript degradation and bacterial cell death. {PubMed:31014676, PubMed:32770723, PubMed:27601326}. Functions as a ribosome‑dependent mRNA interferase that cleaves mRNAs at the ribosomal A‑site during translation; activity requires ribosome incorporation. {PubMed:27601326}. Is neutralized by direct binding to the cognate antitoxin HigA, forming a stable heterotetrameric complex (Kd ≈ 14 nM). {PubMed:31014676, PubMed:32770723, PubMed:27601326, PubMed:17085558}. Enhances the DNA‑binding ability of HigA, contributing to transcriptional regulation of the higBA operon. {PubMed:31014676}. Is up‑regulated under translational‑inhibitor stress, due to reduced synthesis of the unstable antitoxin HigA. {PubMed:17085558}. Exerts a short‑term bacteriostatic effect, whereas prolonged activity can become irreversible and lethal. {PubMed:17085558}. Overexpression dramatically slows bacterial growth and reduces colony‑forming units in V. cholerae and E. coli. {PubMed:17085558}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Upon overexpression inhibits growth.
Merged_Functions: YqjD is a stationary‑phase‑specific inner‑membrane protein in *Escherichia coli* that binds both 70S ribosomes and 100S ribosome dimers. Its N‑terminal domain interacts with the 30S ribosomal subunit, while its C‑terminal domain contains a transmembrane segment that anchors the protein in the inner membrane. By tethering ribosomes to the membrane, YqjD is proposed to mediate the localization of hibernating ribosomes during nutrient limitation or slow growth. Overproduction of YqjD leads to rapid growth arrest that depends on its ribosome‑binding ability, whereas deletion of yqjD does not affect basic growth parameters but reduces the formation of persister cells when exposed to the aminoglycoside netilmicin. Thus, YqjD functions as a ribosome‑associated factor that modulates ribosome positioning and contributes to stress‑related persistence in stationary phase. {PubMed:30476446}. The article describes yqjD as a stationary‑phase gene whose product participates in translational arrest during entry into stationary phase. Specifically, YqjD promotes the localization of inactive 100S ribosome dimers—formed by the action of RMF—to the cell membrane, thereby contributing to ribosome inactivation and a slowdown of protein synthesis. yqjD expression is part of the rpoS regulon; its transcription depends on the σ^S (RpoS) factor and is up‑regulated indirectly by polyamines through their stimulation of rpoS. The combined activity of YqjD (with RMF) leads to reduced metabolic activity, which the authors link to increased formation of persister cells tolerant to antibiotics. {PubMed:28431088}.
Curated_Functions: Binds 70S ribosomes and 100S ribosome dimers; its N‑terminal domain interacts with the 30S subunit and its C‑terminal transmembrane segment anchors the protein in the inner membrane. {PubMed:30476446}. Tethers ribosomes to the inner membrane, mediating localization of hibernating 100S ribosome dimers during nutrient limitation or entry into stationary phase, thereby contributing to ribosome inactivation and reduced protein synthesis. {PubMed:30476446, PubMed:28431088}. Induces rapid growth arrest when overproduced in a ribosome‑binding‑dependent manner. {PubMed:30476446}. Contributes to the formation of antibiotic‑tolerant persister cells in stationary phase; deletion reduces persister formation upon netilmicin exposure. {PubMed:30476446, PubMed:28431088}. Is transcriptionally regulated by the RpoS (σ^S) regulon and is up‑regulated indirectly by polyamines via stimulation of rpoS. {PubMed:28431088}. Works together with the ribosome‑modulating factor RMF to lower metabolic activity during stationary phase. {PubMed:28431088}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type V toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. Causes membrane damage when induced by MqsR, slowing cell growth and increasing the formation of dormant persister cells; involved with GhoS, its antitoxin, in reducing cell growth during antibacterial stress (PubMed:24373067). Overexpression causes cell lysis, forming ghost cells; both effects are neutralized by expression of GhoS. Overexpression in the presence of ampicillin increases persister cell formation (persister cells exhibit antibiotic tolerance without genetic change) (PubMed:22941047). Overexpression causes about 90-fold reduction in cellular ATP levels and dissipates the membrane potential (PubMed:24373067). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:22941047, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24373067}.
Merged_Functions: GhoT encodes the toxin component of the type V GhoT/GhoS toxin‑antitoxin system. When expressed, GhoT acts as a membrane‑damaging peptide that produces a “ghost‑cell” phenotype, disrupts the bacterial membrane and leads to a reduction in cellular ATP levels. Its toxicity is normally neutralized by the antitoxin GhoS, an enzyme that specifically cleaves the ghoT mRNA. The study also shows that full GhoT activity in E. coli depends on the chromosomal regulators IraM and MhpR, as loss of either regulator abolishes GhoT‑mediated growth inhibition. {PubMed:31429177}. GhoT encodes a small, highly hydrophobic peptide that acts as a toxin by inserting into and damaging bacterial inner membranes. This membrane disruption leads to loss of membrane integrity, reduction of cellular ATP levels, and a slowdown of metabolic activity. The toxin’s activity is particularly evident under stress conditions or in the presence of cell‑wall‑targeting antibiotics (e.g., carbenicillin, cefoxitin), where it contributes to growth inhibition and metabolic arrest. In the Escherichia coli GhoT/GhoS type V toxin–antitoxin system, GhoT’s translation is normally repressed by the antitoxin GhoS, which cleaves ghoT mRNA; however, when GhoS is depleted, GhoT is produced and exerts its membrane‑damaging toxic effect. {PubMed:31055774}. GhoT is the toxin component of the type V GhoT/GhoS toxin‑antitoxin system in Escherichia coli. It functions as a membrane‑targeting toxin that adopts an α‑helical conformation upon interaction with lipid bilayers. GhoT inserts into the inner membrane, where multimeric assemblies form transient transmembrane pores, increasing membrane permeability without causing macroscopic disruption. This pore formation leads to leakage of small molecules, a reduction in intracellular ATP levels, loss of proton motive force, and an overall decrease in cellular metabolism, enabling the cell to survive oxidative and bile stress. {PubMed:29470981}. GhoT is a small, hydrophobic inner‑membrane toxin that belongs to a type V toxin‑antitoxin (TA) system (GhoT/GhoS) in Escherichia coli. It damages the cell membrane, leading to rapid cell lysis and a dramatic loss of intracellular ATP (≈27‑fold reduction), indicating disruption of the proton‑motive force. The toxin’s activity is neutralized by its cognate antitoxin GhoS, which specifically cleaves ghoT mRNA rather than binding the protein directly. GhoT shares 63 % amino‑acid identity with the orphan toxin OrtT and contains a conserved Phe38 residue critical for toxicity; substitution of this residue (F38R) abolishes its toxic effect. In physiological contexts, GhoT reduces cellular metabolism and aids survival under membrane‑targeting antibiotic stress (e.g., carbenicillin and cefoxitin), contributing to a dormant, persister‑like state. {PubMed:25643179}. ghoT encodes the toxin component of the GhoT/GhoS toxin‑antitoxin (TA) system. In the study, ghoT was significantly up‑regulated in E. coli O157:H7 MC2 when incubated in bovine feces at low temperature (15 °C), indicating activation of this TA system under nutrient‑starvation and chemical‑stress conditions. The GhoT toxin induces bacterial growth arrest and dormancy, helping cells survive adverse environments, and it also influences early biofilm formation, thereby contributing to the persistence of the strain outside the bovine gut. {PubMed:29593666}. GhoT is the toxin component of the GhoT/GhoS type V toxin‑antitoxin system in Escherichia coli. It is a membrane‑targeting toxin that damages the cell membrane, leading to reduced ATP levels and growth inhibition. Production of GhoT causes characteristic “ghost‑cell” morphology, with condensed cytoplasmic material at the poles and a translucent nucleoid. Its mRNA is specifically cleaved and degraded by the antitoxin GhoS, which is an endoribonuclease that normally protects the cell by removing GhoT transcripts. {PubMed:24797297}. GhoT is the toxin component of a type 5 toxin‑antitoxin (TA) system in Escherichia coli. It acts as a membrane‑damaging toxin; overproduction of GhoT reduces cellular growth and dramatically increases antibiotic tolerance (persistence) to both ampicillin and ciprofloxacin. In the experiments reported, expression of GhoT raised tolerance ~71‑fold (ampicillin) and ~22‑fold (ciprofloxacin) in a ppGpp‑deficient strain, and even higher (~203‑fold and ~91‑fold, respectively) when ppGpp was present. Thus, GhoT contributes to persister cell formation by damaging the membrane and slowing growth. {PubMed:26837570}.
Curated_Functions: Damages the inner membrane by inserting and forming transient pores, increasing permeability and causing loss of membrane integrity. {PubMed:31429177, PubMed:31055774, PubMed:29470981, PubMed:25643179, PubMed:24797297, PubMed:26837570}. Reduces intracellular ATP levels and dissipates the proton motive force, leading to metabolic slowdown and growth inhibition. {PubMed:31429177, PubMed:31055774, PubMed:29470981, PubMed:25643179, PubMed:24797297, PubMed:26837570}. Induces a characteristic ghost‑cell morphology and rapid cell lysis. {PubMed:31429177, PubMed:25643179, PubMed:24797297}. Is neutralized by the antitoxin GhoS, which specifically cleaves ghoT mRNA. {PubMed:31429177, PubMed:31055774, PubMed:25643179, PubMed:24797297}. Is activated under oxidative, bile, cell‑wall‑targeting antibiotic stress, nutrient starvation, and low temperature, contributing to survival under these conditions. {PubMed:31429177, PubMed:31055774, PubMed:29470981, PubMed:25643179, PubMed:29593666, PubMed:26837570}. Promotes antibiotic tolerance and persister cell formation, markedly increasing tolerance to ampicillin and ciprofloxacin, especially in a ppGpp‑dependent context. {PubMed:25643179, PubMed:26837570}. HigA is the antitoxin component of the HigB‑HigA type II toxin‑antitoxin (TA) system in *Escherichia coli* K‑12. It neutralizes the ribonuclease toxin HigB by forming a very tight (Kd ≈ 14 nM) heterotetrameric TA complex, thereby preventing HigB‑mediated growth inhibition. HigA exists as a homodimer in solution; each monomer comprises an N‑terminal dimerization domain, a central linker domain, and a C‑terminal helix‑turn‑helix (HTH) DNA‑binding motif. As a transcriptional regulator, the HTH motif binds to a palindromic operator sequence upstream of the higBA operon, repressing its transcription. Binding of HigB induces large rigid‑body motions of the N‑ and C‑terminal domains around the linker, converting the elongated HigA dimer into a more compact form and shortening the distance between the two HTH motifs, which enhances operator DNA binding. Key residues involved in DNA interaction include M106, R109, R115, and K116. Thus, HigA functions both to inhibit toxin activity and to autoregulate expression of the higBA operon. {PubMed:31014676}. HigA is the antitoxin component of the chromosomal higBA type‑II toxin‑antitoxin module in Escherichia coli K‑12. It forms a tight complex with the toxin HigB, wrapping around each HigB molecule through a C‑shaped clamp composed of seven α‑helices. The N‑terminal helix (α1) mediates homodimerization of two HigA protomers, which is required for assembly of the hetero‑tetrameric (HigBA)₂ complex but not for formation of a heterodimeric HigBA complex. The C‑terminal domain of HigA adopts a helix‑turn‑helix (HTH) fold that specifically binds to two palindromic sequences (pal‑I and pal‑II) in the higBA promoter region, thereby auto‑repressing transcription of the higBA operon. Deletion of the HTH motif abolishes DNA binding, whereas removal of the α1 helix disrupts dimerization and tetramer formation but retains DNA‑binding ability in the heterodimer. Thus, HigA neutralizes HigB toxicity by sequestration and regulates its own operon through direct operator DNA interaction. {PubMed:27601326}. HigA is an 89‑amino‑acid antitoxin protein from Escherichia coli, serving as the antitoxin component of a toxin‑antitoxin system. In the article it is used as a model protein to study folding under crowded conditions. {PubMed:31763853}. The article describes HigA as a type II toxin‑antitoxin (TA) antitoxin protein. HigA antitoxins bind directly to their cognate toxin, neutralising its activity, and also act as transcriptional regulators by binding to operator DNA to repress expression of the TA operon. Three structural classes of HigA are noted, all forming obligate dimers and containing a helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding domain. The YdaS protein studied in the article is a distant homologue of HigA, representing a novel, monomeric class within the HigA superfamily. {PubMed:31625047}.
