Merged_Functions: Encodes the flagellin protein (designated Fla 30) that constitutes the filament of Salmonella flagella. In the experiments described, the fla gene was modified to create hybrid flagellins (Fla I, Fla II, Fla III, and Fla IV) by inserting short peptide sequences from the CFA/I fimbrial subunit into the central hypervariable region of the flagellin gene. These recombinant flagellins act as carriers that display heterologous linear epitopes on the bacterial surface, thereby eliciting specific antibody responses against the inserted CFA/I sequences. {PubMed:9353922}. The article describes the fla genes of Caulobacter crescentus as a set of flagellar genes required for flagellum biosynthesis. These genes encode products that form parts of the flagellum (e.g., hook, basal body, filament) and are transcriptionally regulated in a periodic manner that coincides with specific stages of the swarmer‑cell to stalked‑cell developmental cycle. Expression of fla genes follows a regulatory hierarchy in which activation of one level is necessary for transcription of the next, and their promoters often contain conserved -24 and -12 elements recognized by σ⁵⁴‑containing RNA polymerase. Thus, fla genes function to produce the structural components of the flagellum and to coordinate flagellar assembly with the cell‑cycle program. {PubMed:2644197}. The fla gene encodes the flagellin (Fla) protein, the structural subunit of the Legionella micdadei flagellar filament. Flagellin forms the filament that provides bacterial motility, enabling contact with host cells and potentially contributing to invasion and intracellular survival. The protein is highly conserved at its amino‑ and carboxy‑terminal regions, which are essential for export and polymerization of the filament, while the central region is non‑conserved and hypervariable, giving rise to antigenic diversity. Fla is immunogenic and cross‑reactive among Legionella species, making it a target for diagnostic antibodies. Expression of fla is regulated by a σ^28 (RpoF) promoter and is influenced by growth temperature, linking flagellum synthesis to environmental conditions and possibly to virulence. {PubMed:8562027}. The article describes fla as encoding the Salmonella flagellin protein (referred to as Fla 30 for the native flagellin and Fla II for a hybrid version). Flagellin is a major structural component of bacterial flagella and acts as a potent immunogen that can stimulate strong antibody responses. In this study, flagellin is used as a carrier protein to which a 15‑amino‑acid peptide derived from the CFA/I fimbriae is genetically inserted. The resulting chimeric flagellin (Fla II) retains its immunogenic properties, priming and boosting IgG antibody responses against both homologous (CFA/I) and heterologous (CS1, CS2, PCFO166) colonization factor antigens. Additionally, flagellin has regulatory functions, influencing cytokine synthesis in human phagocytic cells, making it valuable for vaccine development as a delivery platform for heterologous epitopes. {PubMed:11037135}. The fla genes (flaA and flaB) encode the two flagellin subunits that polymerize to form the filament of Helicobacter pylori’s unipolar, sheathed flagella. FlaA is the major flagellin component, while FlaB is expressed at lower levels; both are required for full motility. Mutations in either flaA or flaB abolish motility, and combined flaA‑flaB mutants are completely non‑motile. Full motility, mediated by the FlaA and FlaB flagellins, is essential for H. pylori to colonize the gastric mucosa and to establish persistent infection in animal models. Thus, the fla genes provide the structural building blocks of the flagellar filament that enable bacterial swimming and contribute directly to virulence. {PubMed:9023175}. The fla genes constitute a group of loci that are essential for the synthesis and regulation of the two major flagellar proteins in Escherichia coli K12: flagellin (the filament protein encoded by hag) and the hook subunit protein (encoded by flaK).  Mutations in most fla genes abolish detectable flagellin synthesis, indicating that normal fla function is required for expression of the hag gene and production of flagellin.  In contrast, hook subunit protein is produced in the majority of fla mutants, except for those lacking flaI, flaK, or flbB, showing that specific fla members (e.g., flaK, which encodes the hook protein itself, and regulatory genes such as flaI) are directly required for hook formation.  Overall, the fla loci act both as structural components of the flagellum (e.g., flaK) and as regulators that coordinate the expression and assembly of flagellar subunits, ensuring that flagellin synthesis occurs only when other flagellar components are present. {PubMed:6374380}. The flgB gene encodes a protein that is homologous to the Salmonella typhimurium FlgB protein and is a structural component of the flagellar hook‑basal body (HBB) complex in Bacillus subtilis.  FlgB, together with FlgC (and possibly FlgF), forms the proximal rod of the basal body, linking the membrane‑anchored M‑ring (FliF) to the distal rod (FlgG).  The protein participates in the assembly of the basal body by interacting with FlgC to build the proximal rod, thereby contributing to the overall architecture and stability of the flagellar motor apparatus. {PubMed:1905667}. In Salmonella, flgB encodes FlgB, the most proximal subunit of the flagellar basal‑body rod. FlgB is one of four rod proteins (FlgB, FlgC, FlgF, FlgG) that assemble sequentially after the MS‑ring protein FliF and the junction protein FliE. The study shows that FlgB interacts strongly with FliE, forming a junction zone between the annular MS ring and the helical rod. This interaction is essential for proper rod assembly and for efficient export of downstream substrates such as the hook‑capping protein FlgD. Suppressor mutations in flgB (G119E or G129D) can compensate for a defective FliE (V99G), indicating that FlgB stabilizes the FliE‑rod interface; these mutations alone have no phenotype but are dominant over wild‑type FlgB when mutant FliE is present. Thus, flgB’s primary function is to provide the proximal rod structure that links the MS‑ring/FliE complex to the rest of the axial flagellar apparatus, facilitating rod construction and subsequent flagellar assembly. {PubMed:10809679}. flgB encodes a component of the flagellar apparatus that is required for flagella synthesis and bacterial motility. In this study, flgB expression was significantly higher in biofilms formed by the ΔrpoS mutant (MBF) than in mature wild‑type biofilms (WBF), indicating that the RpoS sigma factor normally represses flgB during biofilm maturation. The up‑regulation of flgB (along with other flagellar genes) in the ΔrpoS strain is associated with continued flagellar production and motility, which the authors propose prevents the suppression of motility needed for the establishment of mature, stationary‑phase‑like biofilms. {PubMed:17979199}. The article describes FII as one of the three most frequent replicons (FIA, FIB, FII) belonging to the IncF plasmid group. IncF plasmids are typically multireplicon, often encoding FII together with FIA and/or FIB. Thus, FII functions as a replication-associated replicon element of IncF plasmids, which are commonly found in environmental Escherichia coli isolates and are linked to the carriage and transfer of antibiotic‑resistance genes. {PubMed:32528456}. Encodes an intracellular ~28 kDa carboxylesterase (YjfP) that hydrolyzes short‑chain acyl esters, including acetylated sugars. The enzyme is induced during the diauxic lag when E. coli grows on a glucose‑lactose mixture, and its expression peaks in the middle of the lag phase. YjfP deacetylates intracellular acetyl‑sugars, thereby regulating the pool of acetylated carbohydrates and facilitating their conversion back to metabolizable forms. Deletion of yjfP (ΔyjfP) reduces β‑galactosidase activity during diauxic shift, while overproduction of YjfP lengthens the lag phase on lactose or galactose, indicating its role in controlling sugar utilization and metabolic adaptation during diauxie. {PubMed:26820469}. The b1073 locus encodes YjfP, an intracellular ~28 kDa carboxylesterase belonging to the α/β‑hydrolase superfamily. YjfP hydrolyzes short‑chain acyl esters, showing highest activity toward p‑nitrophenyl acetate and α‑naphthyl butyrate, and is capable of de‑acetylating acetylated sugars (e.g., 1‑O‑methyl‑2,3,4,6‑tetra‑O‑acetyl‑α‑D‑galactoside). Its expression is strongly up‑regulated during the diauxic lag that occurs when E. coli shifts from glucose to lactose, and it declines once lactose utilization begins. By removing acetyl groups from intracellular acetyl‑sugars, YjfP regulates the pool of these metabolites, thereby influencing the induction of the lac operon and β‑galactosidase activity. Deletion of yjfP (ΔyjfP) reduces β‑galactosidase activity and alters the timing of the diauxic lag, whereas overproduction of YjfP impairs growth on lactose or galactose due to accumulation of toxic intermediates. Thus, YjfP functions as a regulatory carboxylesterase that controls intracellular acetyl‑sugar concentrations during carbon‑source transitions. {PubMed:26820469}. The flbA gene encodes a ~73 kDa membrane-associated protein that belongs to the FlbF/LcrD family. In Helicobacter pylori, FlbA is required for coordinated transcriptional regulation of flagellar structural genes. Disruption of flbA abolishes expression of the two flagellin genes (flaA and flaB) and markedly reduces expression of the hook protein gene (flgE) in a growth‑phase‑dependent manner, leading to an aflagellate, non‑motile phenotype. Thus, FlbA functions as a key regulator of flagellar biogenesis, acting upstream in the flagellar gene hierarchy to activate σ28‑ and σ54‑dependent flagellar promoters. {PubMed:9023175}. flbA is a component of the flbA operon that includes the structural gene flaK encoding the hook subunit protein. The operon is responsible for the transcription of flaK, and flbA’s expression is largely unaffected by most flagellar (fla) mutants; only the flbB and flaI genes are required for proper flbA operon expression. Mutations in flbA do not abolish hook subunit protein synthesis, indicating that flbA is not essential for production of the hook protein but participates in the regulatory framework governing its expression. {PubMed:6374380}.

Overexpression of nrdH (via promoter replacement with the constitutive Ptrc1 promoter) increases transcription of the cysM‑nrdH operon, enhancing thiosulfate utilization for cysteine biosynthesis while consuming minimal energy and reducing power. FUNCTION: This protein negatively controls the transcription initiation of genes such as deoCABD, udp, and cdd encoding catabolizing enzymes and nupC, nupG, and tsx encoding transporting and pore-forming proteins. Binds cytidine and adenosine as effectors.

The gene encodes the CytR protein, a transcriptional repressor that negatively regulates several nucleoside‑related genes in Escherichia coli. The b3934 gene encodes the enzyme cytidine deaminase (Cdd), which catalyzes the deamination of cytidine to uridine and thus participates in the uptake and catabolism of deoxyribonucleosides/nucleosides in Escherichia coli K12. The gene is required for growth on cytidine as the sole carbon source. Its expression is tightly regulated by a promoter (cddP) that is activated by the cAMP‑CRP complex and repressed by the CytR repressor; two tandem CRP binding sites located around –41 and –93 bp upstream of the transcription start site are essential for proper regulation. {PubMed:2575702}. The article identifies JW3905 as the nupG gene. nupG encodes a membrane protein that actively transports nucleosides across the inner membrane of Escherichia coli. It is a member of the CytR regulon and its expression is tightly controlled by two global regulators: the cAMP‑CRP activator complex and the CytR repressor. cAMP‑CRP activates nupG transcription (≈50‑fold activation) via two CRP‑binding sites (CRP2 at –92.5 and CRP1 at –42.5) and an additional downstream site (CRP_E). CytR binds to a distinct operator downstream of CRP2 and, together with cAMP‑CRP, forms nucleoprotein repression complexes that can reduce transcription (≈4‑fold repression). The gene therefore functions as a nucleoside uptake transporter whose expression is modulated by both activation and repression modules involving cAMP‑CRP and CytR. {PubMed:8596434}. CytR encodes a sequence‑specific DNA‑binding repressor that regulates transcription of genes involved in nucleoside uptake and metabolism (e.g., the nupG operon).  Repression by CytR requires cooperative binding with the global activator complex cAMP‑CRP; cAMP‑CRP increases CytR’s DNA‑binding affinity by more than 3000‑fold, allowing CytR to bind its operator and form nucleoprotein complexes that block RNA polymerase access.  In these promoters CytR functions as a co‑repressor while cAMP‑CRP also serves as an activator, so transcription initiation depends on cAMP‑CRP but is inhibited when CytR is bound.  Cytidine, the inducer of the CytR regulon, interferes with the protein‑protein interactions between CytR and cAMP‑CRP, reducing repression but not completely abolishing the intermediate CytR‑cAMP‑CRP complex.  Thus, CytR’s primary role is to repress transcription of target genes by forming cooperative nucleoprotein complexes with cAMP‑CRP, with its activity modulated by the inducer cytidine. {PubMed:8596434}. Encodes a DNA‑binding repressor protein that negatively regulates expression of several nucleoside‑related genes in Escherichia coli. The CytR‑encoded repressor represses the cdd (cytidine deaminase), udp (uridine phosphorylase), tsx (outer‑membrane nucleoside channel), and the nucleoside transport genes nupC and nupG. It also controls the deo operon, but its action is limited to the PO2 promoter‑operator site. Consequently, CytR functions as a transcriptional repressor governing nucleoside transport and catabolism. The protein has an estimated molecular weight of ~37 kDa. {PubMed:2998936}. CytR is the E. coli cytidine repressor protein that, together with the cAMP receptor protein (CRP), provides both positive and negative transcriptional control of the nine CytR‑regulated genes (mainly involved in nucleoside catabolism and recycling). Unlike typical LacR family repressors, CytR does not repress transcription when bound to its operator (CytO) alone; it requires cooperative binding with a CRP·cAMP dimer. In the common promoter architecture, two tandem CRP sites flank an intervening CytO, and CytR simultaneously contacts both flanking CRP dimers, forming a three‑protein DNA‑bound complex that interferes with CRP‑mediated activation (blocking class I AR1–αCTD and class II AR2–αNTD interactions). Binding of cytidine to CytR weakens these CRP‑CytR contacts, thereby restoring CRP activation. CytR is highly adaptable: its DNA‑binding domain is largely unfolded until it engages specific operator half‑sites, and the spacing between the inverted recognition motifs in CytO influences CytR conformation and cooperativity. Thus, CytR functions as an effector that modulates CRP activity, acting as a corepressor in the absence of ligand and allowing induction when cytidine is present. {PubMed:24138566}. The cytR gene encodes a repressor protein that binds to the cytPO promoter/operator region of the deo operon and inhibits transcription of the tetracistronic mRNA1 (which contains the four deo genes). This repression is observed only when the cAMP‑CRP activator complex is present, indicating that CytR acts in a double‑negative regulatory scheme together with the DeoR repressor. Cytidine and adenosine serve as effectors that bind to the CytR repressor; effector binding prevents CytR from attaching to the operator, thereby relieving repression and allowing synthesis of the deo enzymes. Thus, CytR functions as a negative transcriptional regulator whose activity is modulated by specific nucleoside effectors. {PubMed:204861}. CytR is a transcriptional repressor that controls a subset of promoters whose gene products are involved in the transport and catabolism of ribo‑ and deoxyribonucleosides. Its activity is induced by the presence of cytidine or adenosine. CytR binds DNA with low intrinsic affinity and exerts repression only when the global regulator cAMP‑CRP is present; the two proteins bind cooperatively to form a nucleoprotein repression complex (typically two cAMP‑CRP molecules flanking a CytR molecule) that blocks RNA polymerase access to the promoter. Thus, CytR functions as a co‑repressor, modulating expression of nucleoside‑related genes in response to nucleoside availability and cellular cAMP levels. {PubMed:7715459}. CytR functions as a transcriptional repressor in Escherichia coli. It binds to promoter regions (e.g., the cdd and deoP2 promoters) at DNA sites that overlap or are identical to the high‑affinity binding sites for the cAMP‑CRP activator complex. Effective CytR binding requires two or more properly spaced CRP‑like targets upstream of the transcription start site. Once bound, CytR antagonizes the activating effect of the cAMP‑CRP complex, thereby repressing transcription of the downstream genes (e.g., cdd encoding cytidine deaminase). The repression can be strong (approximately 40‑fold reduction in promoter activity) and depends on the presence of the CRP‑binding architecture. {PubMed:2575702}. CytR is a LacI‑family transcriptional regulator that controls the Escherichia coli CytR regulon, which encodes enzymes and transport proteins for nucleoside catabolism.  In the absence of its effector (cytidine), CytR binds to multiple operator sites (including the primary CytO site and additional degenerate sites) and interacts cooperatively with the cAMP receptor protein (CRP) to form a three‑protein repression complex (CRP‑CytR‑CRP) that blocks transcription.  CytR can also act as a co‑activator by recruiting CRP to its DNA‑binding sites when it binds cooperatively.  Binding of cytidine to CytR does not alter CytR’s intrinsic DNA affinity but disrupts CytR‑CRP cooperativity, thereby relieving repression (induction).  Thus CytR functions both as a repressor and a co‑activator, modulating CRP‑dependent transcription through cooperative and competitive interactions that are promoter‑specific. {PubMed:10347150}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Negative regulator for the gluconate utilization system GNT-I, the gntUKR operon.
Merged_Functions: GntR is a transcriptional repressor belonging to the GalR‑LacI family that negatively regulates the gluconate regulon in Escherichia coli. It binds specifically to two conserved operator sites in the promoter region of the gntT gene (one overlapping the -10 region and another downstream near +120). In the absence of inducer, GntR binding blocks transcription of gntT (and likely other gluconate‑inducible genes). Binding is abolished by the inducer gluconate (and, at higher concentrations, 6‑phosphogluconate), resulting in derepression of gntT. Deletion of gntR leads to constitutively high, catabolite‑repressed expression of gntT, confirming its role as the primary negative regulator. The protein contains an N‑terminal helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding motif and functions similarly to LacI/GalR repressors. {PubMed:9537375}. The article identifies gntR as encoding a DNA‑binding transcriptional repressor (GntR). It functions as a regulator of gluconate metabolism, and mutations in gntR observed during evolution are thought to alter gluconate uptake, thereby influencing the engineered methanol‑essential phenotype. {PubMed:29666370}. The gntR gene encodes a 331‑amino‑acid regulatory protein that functions as a transcriptional repressor.  GntR contains a helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding motif and binds to an operator site overlapping the promoter of the gntK‑gntU operon, thereby repressing transcription of the low‑affinity gluconate transporter (gntU) and the gluconate kinase (gntK).  In the presence of gluconate, the inducer binds to GntR, causing it to dissociate from the operator and allowing expression of gntK and gntU.  GntR also controls the induction of the Entner‑Doudoroff pathway genes edd and eda, acting analogously to LacI in the lac operon.  Its expression is essentially constitutive, though transcript levels are reduced in log‑phase cells grown on gluconate. {PubMed:8655507}. The gntR gene encodes a member of the GntR family of transcription regulators.  GntR proteins are two‑domain proteins that function as DNA‑binding transcription factors: the N‑terminal winged‑helix‑turn‑helix (wHTH) domain recognizes A/T‑rich palindromic or pseudo‑palindromic operator sequences, while the C‑terminal effector‑binding/oligomerization domain binds small‑molecule effectors (e.g., metabolites, metal ions).  Binding of an effector induces an allosteric conformational change that alters the relative orientation of the DNA‑binding domains, thereby modulating the protein’s affinity for its cognate DNA and switching target gene expression on or off.  In the original context, GntR was identified as the gluconate operon repressor in *Bacillus subtilis*, indicating its role in repressing genes involved in gluconate utilization.  More broadly, GntR family members regulate diverse metabolic pathways, antibiotic production, biofilm formation, and transport systems by acting as molecular switches that respond to environmental and nutritional signals. {PubMed:26172911}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Transcriptional activator for the tdcABCDE operon. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:8413189}.
Merged_Functions: The product of b3118 (TdcA) is a 35 kDa LysR‑type transcriptional activator that positively regulates the tdcABC operon in Escherichia coli. Thus, TdcA functions as a positive regulator of the tdc operon, facilitating transcription initiation through promoter binding and interaction with other transcription factors. {PubMed:7928991}. Sequence analysis shows that TdcA possesses an N‑terminal helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding motif and shares overall similarity with members of the LysR family of bacterial transcriptional activators; therefore it is classified as a LysR‑type regulator. Overall, TdcA acts as a LysR‑family transcriptional activator that positively regulates expression of the threonine dehydratase (tdcB) and threonine‑serine permease (tdcC) genes. {PubMed:8413189}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Regulatory protein involved in rpiB gene repression. Also involved in als operon repression. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:9401019}.
Merged_Functions: In the article AlsR is presented as an alternative name for the LacI‑family transcription factor RpiR. Its activity is modulated by sugar effectors, with D‑ribose acting as a more potent inducer than D‑allose, leading to derepression of the operon under appropriate growth conditions. {PubMed:29529243}. It activates transcription of the structural genes alsD (acetolactate decarboxylase) and alsS1 (acetolactate synthase), thereby promoting acetoin production. Deletion of alsR leads to a ~28 % reduction in acetoin yield and decreases alsD and alsS1 transcript levels by about 22–24 %, while the transcription of the second acetolactate synthase gene alsS2 remains unchanged. Thus, AlsR integrates regulatory control of acetoin biosynthesis by stimulating alsD and alsS1 expression. {PubMed:34066556}. Encodes a regulatory protein that negatively regulates expression of the rpiB gene (ribose phosphate isomerase B). RpiR functions as a transcriptional repressor, binding to an operator region upstream of rpiB and reducing rpiB transcription. Loss‑of‑function mutations in rpiR lead to constitutive rpiB expression, allowing ribose prototrophy in rpiA‑deficient strains. The protein contains a helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding motif and is expressed at low levels. {PubMed:8576032}. RpiR is a LacI‑family transcriptional regulator that controls the utilization of D‑ribose and D‑allose in Escherichia coli K‑12. It represses the rpiR‑alsBACE operon, which encodes the transporter and catabolic enzymes for D‑allose (and also contributes to D‑ribose uptake), as well as the divergent rpiB gene that encodes a secondary D‑ribose‑5‑phosphate isomerase. Genomic SELEX identified a single high‑affinity binding site for RpiR in the intergenic spacer between the rpiR‑alsBACE operon and rpiB, indicating that RpiR functions as a single‑target regulator. Expression of rpiR and rpiB is induced when cells grow on D‑allose (or D‑ribose) in the absence of glucose, suggesting that D‑allose (and more potently D‑ribose) act as effectors that relieve RpiR repression. {PubMed:29529243}. The article identifies rpiR as the gene encoding the transcriptional repressor AlsR. rpiR (renamed alsR) negatively regulates the als (formerly rpi) operon, which includes genes involved in d‑allose transport and metabolism (alsB, alsA, alsC, alsE, alsK) as well as the adjacent rpiB gene that encodes a secondary d‑ribose‑5‑phosphate isomerase. A mutation in rpiR relieves repression, leading to constitutive expression of the operon and rescuing ribose auxotrophy caused by a defect in rpiA. The Klebsiella pneumoniae gene ytfL encodes a membrane-associated protein that is essential for the bacterium‑induced disassembly of host microtubules. PaeA (formerly YtfL) is an inner‑membrane protein that functions as a selective exporter of the polyamines cadaverine and putrescine. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Required for mobilization of iron from the bacterioferritin (BFR) complex (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:Q9HY80}.

Bfd specifically associates with bacterioferritin, and its expression is repressed by the Fe²⁺‑Fur complex and induced during post‑exponential growth under iron‑starvation conditions. The article proposes that Bfd functions as a 2‑Fe ferredoxin that may mediate the release of iron from, or delivery of iron to, bacterioferritin (or other iron complexes such as ferri‑siderophores or iron‑sulphur clusters), thereby participating in intracellular iron metabolism. {PubMed:9889981}. The bfd gene encodes the bacterioferritin‑associated ferredoxin, a protein that participates in bacterial iron homeostasis. It is normally regulated by the ferric uptake regulator (Fur) and is expressed under iron‑restricted conditions to help manage intracellular iron pools. In this study, sub‑inhibitory concentrations of human hepcidin caused a 2‑ to 4‑fold increase in bfd expression (as measured by a lacZ reporter) under iron‑limited conditions, indicating that bfd is part of the bacterial response to altered iron availability and may contribute to the oxidative stress response triggered by hepcidin exposure. {PubMed:29659799}. The bfd gene encodes a small (≈64‑residue) ferredoxin‑like protein that binds a [2Fe‑2S] cluster. Bfd encodes a small NIFU‑like protein that binds a [2Fe‑2S] cluster and forms a specific complex with bacterioferritin (Bfr).  The protein is monomeric in solution and can exist in oxidized (+2) and reduced (+1) states, indicating redox activity.  The authors propose that Bfd functions as a general redox and/or regulatory component that participates in the iron‑storage or iron‑mobilization processes of Bfr, potentially facilitating electron transfer for iron oxidation or reduction during iron deposition into or release from the Bfr core. {PubMed:8639572}.

Structural studies reveal that CedA adopts a ββββα fold similar to known dsDNA‑binding domains, and biochemical assays (gel‑shift and NMR chemical‑shift perturbation) demonstrate that CedA binds double‑stranded DNA via its β‑sheet surface. Over‑expression of cedA restores cell division in dnaAcos cells at 30 °C, allowing growth despite excessive chromosomal DNA replication. CedA does not inhibit the over‑replication itself; instead it specifically promotes septum formation and cell division through a pathway that is independent of the SOS‑induced division inhibitor SfiA (SulA). In wild‑type cells, increased cedA dosage alters the timing of cell division, leading to larger cells at division without changing the initiation mass of chromosome replication. Thus, CedA functions as a positive regulator of cell division that links chromosome replication status to the division machinery. {PubMed:9427399}. CedA encodes a small (87‑aa) protein that acts as a cell‑division activator in Escherichia coli. Overexpression of CedA can stimulate division in dnaAcos mutant cells without preventing the accompanying over‑initiation of chromosome replication, suggesting that CedA functions in a regulatory pathway that relieves a division‑inhibition checkpoint linked to replication status. Structural analysis shows that CedA adopts a ββββα fold closely resembling known dsDNA‑binding domains (e.g., λ‑integrase DBD). Biochemical assays (gel‑shift, NMR chemical‑shift perturbations) demonstrate that CedA binds double‑stranded DNA primarily via its β‑sheet surface, which is positively charged and enriched in aromatic residues. The DNA‑binding activity is proposed to be central to CedA’s role in modulating cell‑division processes, although the exact DNA sequence specificity and downstream effectors remain to be defined. {PubMed:15865419}. CedA encodes a small (~12 kDa) protein that acts as a multicopy suppressor of the cold‑sensitive phenotype of the dnaAcos mutant. Over‑replication of the chromosome in dnaAcos cells at 30 °C blocks septum formation and causes filamentation, a block that is independent of the SOS‑induced division inhibitor SfiA. Increased dosage of cedA restores cell division in these cells without reducing the excessive chromosomal copy number, indicating that CedA does not inhibit DNA replication initiation. Instead, CedA modulates a division‑control pathway that couples chromosome replication status to septum formation, allowing cells with abnormally high DNA content to divide. In a wild‑type (dnaA⁺) background, multicopy cedA also alters the timing of cell division, increasing average cell size at division while leaving the initiation mass unchanged. Thus, CedA functions as a regulator that activates cell division when it is otherwise inhibited by chromosome over‑replication. {PubMed:9427399}. CedA encodes an ~10 kDa DNA‑binding protein that functions as a cell‑division activator in Escherichia coli. Over‑expression of CedA suppresses the filamentous morphology of dnaA^cos mutants by initiating septation and cytokinesis, thereby restoring regular cell morphology while chromosomal DNA over‑replication continues. Overexpression of cedA confers increased resistance to the gold nanoparticle antibiotic LAL-32, while disruption of cedA (e.g., via a transposon mutation) makes Escherichia coli more susceptible to LAL-32. Thus, CedA functions as a cell‑division regulator that modulates bacterial susceptibility to this nanoparticle‑based antibiotic. {PubMed:28636368}. The cedA gene encodes the cellodextrinase (CedA) protein, a periplasmic glycosyl‑hydrolase belonging to family 5 (family A) of the glycosyl‑hydrolases. CedA hydrolyzes short cellodextrins (cellotriose, cellotetraose, cellopentaose and cellohexaose) to release cellobiose, but it does not act on carboxymethylcellulose. The enzyme has a molecular mass of ~42 kDa, contains conserved catalytic motifs (including an E‑L‑L‑N‑E sequence and a key glutamic acid at position 284), and appears to consist solely of a catalytic domain without a separate cellulose‑binding domain. Expression of cedA is driven by a native Fibrobacter succinogenes promoter that functions in Escherichia coli, and the gene is constitutively expressed in F. succinogenes. {PubMed:8076254}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: May be involved in the biogenesis of curli organelles.

In addition, CsgE directly interacts with the major curli subunit CsgA and prevents its premature self‑assembly into amyloid fibers, thereby protecting the periplasm from toxic aggregation and promoting efficient extracellular curli fiber formation. {PubMed:21645131}. This complex creates a pre‑constriction chamber that entrains CsgA (and CsgB) for export, thereby acting as a chaperone that stabilizes unfolded CsgA, prevents premature amyloid fibrillation (inhibiting CsgA aggregation at a 1:1 ratio), and directs the substrate to the secretion pore. By regulating the delivery and polymerization of CsgA, CsgE controls functional amyloid formation, curli fiber assembly, and consequently cell adhesion, colonization, and biofilm (pellicle) formation. {PubMed:27298344}. CsgE assembles into a nonameric ring that caps the periplasmic vestibule of CsgG, thereby gating the channel and ensuring specificity for curli substrates while limiting passage of small molecules. Specific positively charged residues in the “head” region (e.g., R47) mediate essential charge‑charge interactions with CsgA, whereas negatively charged residues in the “stem” (e.g., E31, E85) modulate the strength of this interaction. Mutations in these regions affect CsgA aggregation, curli fiber formation, and CsgE oligomerization, which is temperature‑dependent and involves residues W48 and F79. Additionally, CsgE can bind CsgA_R1‑5 and inhibit premature amyloid fiber formation, preventing self‑assembly of CsgA in the periplasm. Overall, CsgE acts as a substrate‑binding chaperone that couples CsgA to CsgG, promotes efficient outward transport, and modulates amyloid assembly. {PubMed:31932609}.

The C‑terminal domain (residues 37–119) is flexible and projects to the extracellular side, where it specifically binds CsgB, acting as a bridge that links the CsgG channel to the curli fibrils and mediates curli‑cell surface association. Surface exposure of CsgF requires the CsgG channel, indicating that CsgF itself is secreted through CsgG. Once on the cell surface, CsgF interacts with the nucleator protein CsgB, promoting CsgB’s cell‑association, conferring protease resistance, and facilitating its conversion to an active nucleation‑competent form. This cooperative action directs CsgA polymerization at the cell surface, preventing release of subunits into the medium and ensuring proper formation of cell‑associated curli fibers that contribute to biofilm structure and stress resistance. {PubMed:19131513}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: This methylase recognizes the double-stranded sequence 5'-CCWGG-3', methylates C-2 on both strands. {ECO:0000303|PubMed:12654995, ECO:0000305|PubMed:2198248}.

Merged_Functions: The dcm gene encodes a DNA cytosine methyltransferase that methylates the internal cytosine of the pentanucleotide sequence CCWGG, producing 5‑methyl‑C. The article notes that CCWGG sites are hotspots for C→T transitions because deamination of 5‑meC creates T:G mismatches; a very short patch (Vsp) repair pathway can correct these mismatches, and early work implicated Dcm in this process, although later evidence points to the overlapping vsr gene as the essential factor. Additionally, the presence of Dcm sites within promoters (e.g., the lexA promoter) suggests a possible regulatory role, although no definitive effect on gene expression has been demonstrated. Overall, Dcm’s confirmed biological activity is site‑specific cytosine methylation that influences restriction sensitivity and may contribute indirectly to DNA repair and transcriptional regulation. {PubMed:8200522}. The dcm locus encodes a DNA cytosine methyltransferase that specifically methylates the 5‑position of the second cytosine in the sequence 5'‑CC(A/T)GG‑3'. This methylation protects EcoRII recognition sites from cleavage by the EcoRII endonuclease, as demonstrated by resistance of EcoRII sites in plasmid and λ DNA treated with extracts containing the dcm gene. The enzyme does not possess associated restriction activity. The cloned dcm gene can complement mutations in the EcoRII methylase (R⁺ M⁻ mutants), allowing cells to tolerate an active EcoRII endonuclease. Overproduction of the dcm‑encoded methylase from multicopy plasmids increases methyltransferase activity many‑fold compared with chromosomal expression. {PubMed:3011742}. The mec determinant is the genetic element that confers intrinsic resistance of Staphylococcus aureus to penicillinase‑resistant β‑lactam antibiotics (e.g., methicillin). It carries the mecA gene, which encodes the low‑affinity penicillin‑binding protein PBP2' (PBP2a), the essential component for methicillin resistance. In addition, the mec region contains a hypervariable segment with an unusual cluster of direct repeat units (dru) and the IS431mec insertion sequence, which contribute to length polymorphism and may facilitate recombination or mobilization of the resistance locus. {PubMed:1718947}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Capable of degrading both single-strand and double-strand DNA with 3' to 5' polarity. Has higher affinity for ssDNA ends than for dsDNA.
Merged_Functions: The b1844 locus (formerly yobC, renamed exoX) encodes a 25‑kDa protein called Exonuclease X (ExoX). It degrades both single‑stranded and double‑stranded DNA, showing a strong preference and higher affinity for ssDNA ends (Kₘ ≈ 1.7 nM) and a rapid catalytic rate (≈1,400 nucleotides min⁻¹ monomer⁻¹ for ssDNA). The enzyme acts distributively, binding, cleaving a few nucleotides, releasing, and rebinding. Overexpression of exoX confers DNase activity in cell extracts and can substitute for exonuclease I (ExoI) in vivo, improving UV survival of strains lacking RecJ, ExoI, and ExoVII. A null exoX mutation alone does not affect UV resistance, but when combined with deletions of RecJ, ExoI, and ExoVII it markedly increases UV sensitivity, indicating a redundant role in DNA repair, likely during recombinational processing of UV‑induced lesions. {PubMed:10514496}. JW1833 encodes Exonuclease X (ExoX), a 25‑kDa member of the DnaQ superfamily that functions as a Mg²⁺‑dependent 3′→5′ exonuclease. ExoX is a highly active, distributive nuclease capable of degrading both single‑stranded and double‑stranded DNA, with a strong preference and high affinity for ssDNA ends (Kₘ ≈ 1.7 nM). It rapidly removes nucleotides from 3′ termini (≈1,400 nucleotides min⁻¹ monomer⁻¹ for ssDNA) and can also act on duplex DNA, albeit with lower efficiency. In vivo, ExoX contributes to the repair of UV‑induced DNA damage; overexpression can compensate for loss of Exonuclease I (ExoI) in UV survival assays, while a null mutation alone has little effect but markedly increases UV sensitivity when combined with deletions of other ssDNA exonucleases (RecJ, ExoI, ExoVII). Thus, ExoX provides a redundant 3′→5′ exonucleolytic activity that supports DNA repair, particularly during recombinational processing of UV lesions. {PubMed:10514496}. Loss of ExoX, together with RecJ, ExoI, and ExoVII, abolishes normal MMR activity in vitro and yields a modest mutator phenotype, indicating its essential supportive role in MMR. {PubMed:11418610}. In the context of the study, mutants lacking exoX displayed survival and SOS‑induction responses to UVB radiation comparable to wild‑type cells, indicating that ExoX is not essential for repairing UVB‑induced photoproducts. However, previous work cited in the article suggests that ExoX is important for processing double‑strand breaks caused by γ‑radiation, highlighting its role in DSB repair rather than UV‑specific lesion removal. {PubMed:26967458}. Encodes the 3′‑5′ exonuclease ExoX, one of the major 3′‑5′ exonucleases in E. coli. In the study, deletion of exoX (alone or together with other exonuclease deletions) had no significant impact on transductional recombination or DNA‑repair efficiency in either the RecBFI or RecF pathways, indicating that ExoX activity is largely neutral for these recombination processes under the experimental conditions. {PubMed:31378505}. exoX encodes Exonuclease X, a 25‑kDa member of the DnaQ superfamily that functions as a Mg²⁺‑dependent 3'→5' exonuclease. It rapidly removes nucleotides from 3' termini (≈1,400 nt·min⁻¹·monomer⁻¹ on ssDNA) and can also act on dsDNA, albeit less efficiently.  In vivo, ExoX contributes to DNA repair: overexpression can substitute for exonuclease I (ExoI) in UV‑induced damage repair, and loss of exoX markedly increases UV sensitivity when combined with deletions of other ssDNA exonucleases (RecJ, ExoI, ExoVII).  Thus, ExoX provides a redundant 3'‑5' exonucleolytic activity that supports recombinational repair and UV damage tolerance in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:10514496}. ExoX is a 3′‑5′ double‑stranded DNA exonuclease that participates in the RecA‑independent intracellular homology‑dependent DNA assembly (InHDA) pathway in Escherichia coli. Together with ExoIII, ExoX performs non‑processive digestion of linear dsDNA ends to generate short 5′ single‑strand overhangs. Deletion of exoX (especially in combination with xthA) markedly reduces InHDA efficiency, and expression of exoX restores the activity, confirming its essential role in creating the 5′ overhangs required for this recombination process. {PubMed:33372330}. While a single exoX mutation shows little phenotype, loss of ExoX together with other ssDNA exonucleases reveals its biological roles: it contributes to recombination (especially in recD mutants), suppresses deletions between tandem repeats when combined with RecJ and ExoI, participates in mismatch‑repair pathways by providing 3′‑directional exonucleolysis, and its absence in combination with RecJ, ExoI and ExoVII leads to UV sensitivity, cold‑sensitive growth, a modest mutator phenotype, and markedly increased RecA‑independent recombination at short homologies. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in Fe(2+) ion uptake (PubMed:8407793). Does not stimulate the GTPase activity of the N-terminus of FeoB (residues 1-276). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23104801, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8407793}.

Together with the larger membrane protein FeoB, FeoA contributes to the transport of Fe²⁺ into the cell, especially under anaerobic conditions.  Disruption of feoA (feoA::Tn5) leads to a partial reduction (to about 60 % of wild‑type levels) in ferrous iron uptake, indicating that FeoA is required for full activity of the Feo transporter.  While the precise biochemical role of FeoA is not fully resolved in the article, it appears to act as an accessory or regulatory component that supports the FeoB‑driven, ATP‑dependent Fe²⁺ import. {PubMed:8407793}. FeoA is a small, cytosolic β‑barrel protein encoded in the feo operon.  It is described as an integral regulatory element that functions alongside the membrane component FeoB and the accessory protein FeoC to facilitate ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) uptake under acidic and/or anaerobic conditions.  Genetic studies cited in the article show that knockouts of feoA (and feoB) lead to decreased or abolished growth of several pathogenic bacteria, highlighting its role in bacterial iron acquisition and virulence. {PubMed:31713418}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex FepBDGC involved in ferric enterobactin uptake (PubMed:3011753). Binds ferric enterobactin (PubMed:10986237, PubMed:25173704, PubMed:7551033). Can also bind ferric enantioenterobactin, the left-handed stereoisomer of the natural E.coli siderophore, and the apo-siderophore, enterobactin, but does not bind ferric agrobactin (PubMed:10986237). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10986237, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25173704, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3011753, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7551033}.
Merged_Functions: FepB encodes a periplasmic substrate‑binding protein that is essential for the high‑affinity uptake of ferrienterobactin (FeEnt), the iron‑enterobactin complex, in Escherichia coli. After FeEnt is released from the outer‑membrane receptor FepA into the periplasm, FepB binds the FeEnt complex and delivers it to the inner‑membrane ABC‑type permease composed of FepC (ATP‑binding subunit) and the membrane proteins FepD and FepG, which together translocate FeEnt into the cytoplasm using ATP. Loss of FepB (or any of the other fep genes) blocks FeEnt uptake, demonstrating its role as the periplasmic carrier that specifically recognizes and transports ferrienterobactin. {PubMed:7551033}. Encodes a periplasmic binding protein that is essential for the uptake of ferric enterobactin in Escherichia coli. Its transcription is repressed by the Fur regulator under high‑iron conditions, and its translation is enhanced by an AU‑rich translational enhancer located in the 5' leader RNA, which increases ribosome binding, translational efficiency, and steady‑state mRNA levels. {PubMed:17400738}. The fepB gene encodes a periplasmic binding protein that is a component of the Escherichia coli ferric enterobactin (FeEnt) transport system. Mature FepB (≈31.6 kDa) resides in the periplasm where it avidly binds ferric enterobactin, its enantiomeric form, and the apo‑siderophore enterobactin with nanomolar dissociation constants (K_d ≈ 15–60 nM). By forming a high‑affinity complex with FeEnt, FepB facilitates the hand‑off of the siderophore to the inner‑membrane permease complex FepCDG for ATP‑dependent translocation into the cytoplasm. Localization experiments showed that mature FepB resides in the periplasm, whereas its precursor can be detected in membrane fractions. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Responsible for the coupling of flagellin expression to flagellar assembly by preventing expression of the flagellin genes when a component of the middle class of proteins is defective. It negatively regulates flagellar genes by inhibiting the activity of FliA by directly binding to FliA.
Merged_Functions: FlgM is an anti‑σ^28 (FliA) factor that blocks the activity of the alternative sigma factor σ^28 by binding directly to it and to the σ^28‑containing RNA polymerase holoenzyme, thereby preventing transcription from class 3 (late) flagellar promoters. By regulating σ^28 activity, FlgM influences the timing of late flagellar gene expression, the number and length of flagella, and overall efficiency of flagellar assembly. {PubMed:11104815}. Completion of the HBB triggers export of FlgM through the flagellar Type III secretion apparatus; removal of FlgM from the cytoplasm releases σ^28, allowing Class 3 gene expression and final flagellar assembly. This inhibition is relieved only after completion of the hook‑basal‑body (HBB) structure, when FlgM is secreted, allowing σ^28 to activate class III gene expression. In addition, FlgM binding protects σ^28 from degradation by the Lon protease. Deletion of flgM results in strong activation of class III promoters, confirming its role as a negative regulator of late flagellar gene expression. {PubMed:32133913}. FlgM is an anti‑sigma factor that regulates bacterial flagellar synthesis.  It binds to the transcription factor Sigma‑28 (σ^28), preventing σ^28 from activating transcription of late‑stage flagellar genes.  The interaction occurs primarily through transient α‑helices in the C‑terminal region of FlgM, which become stabilized upon binding, while the N‑terminal region remains intrinsically disordered even in the bound state.  This regulatory mechanism is conserved across diverse Gram‑positive and Gram‑negative bacteria, ensuring proper timing of flagellum assembly by inhibiting σ^28‑dependent gene expression until the appropriate stage of flagellar construction. {PubMed:23352839}. In Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, flgM encodes the anti‑σ28 factor FlgM. FlgM binds directly to the alternative sigma factor σ28 (FliA) via a C‑terminal binding domain (critical residues Ile85, Ala86 and Leu89), preventing σ28 from associating with RNA polymerase and thereby inhibiting transcription of σ28‑dependent (class III) flagellar genes such as fliC. This interaction is released when the hook‑basal body is completed, allowing secretion of FlgM and activation of σ28‑dependent transcription. Deletion of flgM abolishes swimming motility and results in loss of flagella, while complementation restores motility. flgM also influences the transcriptional hierarchy: its absence reduces fliA expression, increases flgM transcription in an fliA mutant (indicating σ28 represses flgM), and markedly up‑regulates fliC expression. Moreover, loss of FlgM alters expression of other σ‑dependent genes (cheW, flgD, csrA, fliZ), suggesting broader regulatory roles beyond σ28 inhibition. {PubMed:19383707}.
Curated_Functions: Inhibits σ^28 (FliA) activity by binding to σ^28 and the σ^28‑containing RNA polymerase holoenzyme, thereby preventing transcription of class 3 flagellar genes. {PubMed:11104815, PubMed:17537210, PubMed:9891799, PubMed:32133913, PubMed:23352839}. Modulates expression of additional σ‑dependent genes (e.g., cheW, flgD, csrA, fliZ), indicating broader regulatory roles. {PubMed:19383707}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Uptake of galactose across the boundary membrane with the concomitant transport of protons into the cell (symport system).

Higher galP expression improves glucose import, thereby supplying more phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) for L‑tryptophan biosynthesis and enhancing overall tryptophan production. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the binding-protein-dependent transport system for glutamine; probably responsible for the translocation of the substrate across the membrane.
Merged_Functions: The JW0795 gene encodes the glutamine transport protein GlnQ, a cytoplasmic ATP‑binding cassette (ABC) component that provides the energy for glutamine uptake in Group B Streptococcus.  Disruption of JW0795 abolishes radiolabeled glutamine transport and confers resistance to the toxic glutamine analog γ‑L‑glutamylhydrazide, confirming its role in glutamine import.  Loss of JW0795 also leads to a >90 % reduction in binding to immobilized fibronectin, decreased adherence to and invasion of respiratory epithelial cells, and a marked attenuation of virulence in a neonatal rat model (increased LD₅₀ by 1–3 log units).  JW0795 is co‑transcribed with the adjacent glnP gene in an operon; while it does not act as a surface adhesin itself, it appears to influence the expression or activity of fibronectin‑binding adhesins (such as ScpB) indirectly, likely through alterations in cytoplasmic glutamine levels and post‑transcriptional regulation. {PubMed:12010975}. Encodes a membrane‑bound component of the high‑affinity glutamine permease system in Escherichia coli. Together with the periplasmic glutamine‑binding protein (GlnH) and the third component GlnQ, GlnP is essential for active glutamine uptake. Mutations in glnP eliminate glutamine transport, prevent utilization of glutamine as a sole carbon source, and confer resistance to toxic glutamine analogues, indicating its critical role in the glutamine permease activity. {PubMed:3027504}. The article identifies glnP as the gene encoding the L‑glutamine transporter in Escherichia coli. Mutations in glnP dramatically reduce the rate of L‑glutamine uptake, confirming its role in importing glutamine into the cytoplasm. The intracellular glutamine pool, supplied via the GlnP transporter, serves as a feedback inhibitor of the ammonium (methylammonium) transport system (Amt). Consequently, glnP mutants, which lack functional glutamine transport, are refractory to glutamine‑mediated inhibition of ammonium transport, demonstrating that GlnP is essential for regulating Amt activity through glutamine‑dependent feedback inhibition. {PubMed:3542962}. The article describes glnP as the upstream gene in a glutamine transport operon that is cotranscribed with glnQ.  GlnP is predicted to encode a membrane protein with three distinct domains: the first two resemble the periplasmic glutamine‑binding protein GlnH, and the third resembles the glutamine permease GlnP found in E. coli.  Thus, GlnP is inferred to function as the permease component of a glutamine uptake system, working together with the cytoplasmic ATP‑binding cassette protein encoded by glnQ to transport glutamine into the cell.  The authors note that glnP transcription is not altered in glnQ mutants and that, although it was identified in a phage‑display screen as a possible fibronectin‑binding protein, no direct role in fibronectin adherence was demonstrated. {PubMed:12010975}. The article reports that the protein product of orf1 shows considerable sequence similarity (39‑36% identity) to the C‑terminal region of GlnP, a component of the glutamine permease operon in Escherichia coli, as well as to other amino‑acid permease proteins (HisM and ArtQ). Based on this similarity, the authors suggest that Orf1 (the B. subtilis homolog of GlnP) is likely a member of the permease family, implying a role in the transport of glutamine (and possibly other amino acids) across the cell membrane. {PubMed:7704255}.
Curated_Functions: Provides energy for glutamine uptake as the cytoplasmic ATP‑binding cassette component of the high‑affinity glutamine permease system; disruption abolishes transport and confers resistance to toxic glutamine analogs. {PubMed:12010975}. Influences expression or activity of fibronectin‑binding adhesins, thereby reducing fibronectin binding, epithelial cell adherence, invasion and virulence when absent. {PubMed:12010975}. Acts as the membrane permease component of the glutamine transporter, essential for active glutamine uptake and for utilization of glutamine as a sole carbon source; loss eliminates transport and confers resistance to toxic glutamine analogues. {PubMed:3027504}. Regulates the ammonium transporter Amt by supplying intracellular glutamine that functions as a feedback inhibitor, thereby mediating glutamine‑dependent inhibition of ammonium transport. {PubMed:3542962}. Does not directly mediate fibronectin binding despite identification in a phage‑display screen. {PubMed:12010975}. Likely functions as an amino‑acid permease involved in glutamine (and possibly other amino‑acid) transport, based on similarity to GlnP and related permeases. {PubMed:7704255}.

Is also part of the ABC transporter complex HisPMQ-ArgT involved in lysine/arginine/ornithine transport. Probably responsible for the translocation of the substrate across the membrane. {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P0A2I7}.
Merged_Functions: HisM encodes one of the two integral membrane proteins that together form the transmembrane core of the Salmonella typhimurium histidine permease (HisQ‑HisM).  It does not possess ATP‑hydrolyzing activity itself; instead it serves a structural and regulatory role.  HisM (with HisQ) is required to assemble the functional ABC transporter complex (HisQ‑HisM‑HisP₂), to relay the activation signal from the periplasmic histidine‑binding protein HisJ to the ATP‑binding subunit HisP, and to modulate (both stimulate and suppress) the ATPase activity of HisP during transport. {PubMed:9520394}. HisM encodes one of the two integral membrane (hydrophobic) subunits of the prokaryotic histidine permease ABC transporter. Together with the other hydrophobic subunit HisQ, HisM forms the membrane‑bound complex (HisQMP₂) that couples the periplasmic histidine‑binding protein HisJ to the ATP‑binding subunits HisP. HisM participates in transmitting the signal from the liganded HisJ across the membrane and in regulating/stimulating the ATPase activity of HisP, likely through physical interaction with the arm II region of HisP. {PubMed:10373434}. HisM encodes one of the two hydrophobic integral membrane proteins that constitute the membrane‑bound portion of the Salmonella typhimurium histidine periplasmic permease. Together with the other membrane protein HisQ and the nucleotide‑binding protein HisP, HisM forms a multicomponent complex that couples ATP hydrolysis to the active transport of histidine across the cytoplasmic membrane. The presence of HisM (along with HisQ and HisP) is absolutely required for ATP‑dependent histidine uptake in reconstituted proteoliposomes, indicating its essential role as a structural/transport component of the histidine permease. {PubMed:2674940}. The hisM gene encodes the M protein, one of the three membrane‑bound components of the Salmonella typhimurium histidine permease. Together with the Q and P proteins, the M protein forms part of the periplasmic histidine transport system that mediates uptake of histidine across the cytoplasmic membrane. {PubMed:3888290}.
Curated_Functions: Forms the membrane‑bound core of the histidine permease together with HisQ, acting as a structural component required for assembly of the functional ABC transporter complex and essential for ATP‑dependent histidine uptake. {PubMed:9520394, PubMed:10373434, PubMed:2674940, PubMed:3888290}. Relays the activation signal from the periplasmic histidine‑binding protein HisJ to the ATP‑binding subunit HisP across the membrane. {PubMed:9520394, PubMed:10373434}. Modulates the ATPase activity of HisP during histidine transport, both stimulating and suppressing it, likely via interaction with the arm II region. {PubMed:9520394, PubMed:10373434}.
